HighSEC-INT-001CCM CUSTOM_SQL runner executes arbitrary tenant-supplied SELECT as native SQL — cross-tenant data exfiltration
✎ AdjustedSecuritySQL Injection / Broken Access Control (A03 / A01)▾
Adversarial verification: adjusted (severity Critical→High) — Real but over-rated. CustomSqlRunner.execute (59-112) runs em.createNativeQuery(sql) with sql taken verbatim from the test definition's expectedConditionJson. The rejectionReason guard (118-138) is SELECT-only and blocks DML/DDL/EXEC/statement-chaining, but it does NOT tenant-scope the SELECT — a crafted SELECT against iam.users or another tenant's table returns cross-tenant rows, which surface in the run record (rowCount + echoed sql). So a cross-tenant READ exfiltration path is genuine. However the title implies broad "tenant-supplied" reachability; in fact authoring/updating a CUSTOM_SQL definition requires CcmController WRITE_GUARD = hasAnyRole('CISO','COMPLIANCE_OFFICER','PLATFORM_ADMIN') and running requires the same RUN_GUARD. It is not reachable by an ordinary authenticated user, and it is read-only (no DML/DDL injection — those are blocked). It remains a serious multi-tenant data-isolation breach abusable by a privileged-but-tenant-scoped role, so not refuted, but the Critical rating overstates exploitability; adjust to High.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ccm/runner/CustomSqlRunner.java:59-138 Effort L Risk CVSS 9.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:L) — authenticated operator reads any table in the shared DB, crossing the tenant boundary
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ccm/controller/CcmController.java:63-97
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ccm/service/CcmService.java:172-203
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ccm/dto/CcmDtos.java:22-36

Description

A CCM test definition of type CUSTOM_SQL stores a free-form SQL string in expected_condition_json.sql. The CustomSqlRunner reads that string and runs it verbatim through em.createNativeQuery(sql).getResultList(). The only gate is rejectionReason(): it requires the statement to begin with SELECT, rejects a fixed blacklist of DML/DDL tokens (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/...), and rejects ';'. None of this constrains WHICH tables or columns a SELECT may read, and there is no organisation_id predicate injected. The SQL runs against the single shared TSS_GRC database that holds every tenant's rows. Therefore any operator who can create/run a CUSTOM_SQL test (COMPLIANCE_OFFICER, CISO, PLATFORM_ADMIN per WRITE_GUARD/RUN_GUARD in CcmController) can read arbitrary data belonging to other tenants — e.g. SELECT username, password_hash FROM iam.users, or risk/incident/privacy rows for any organisation_id. The blacklist is irrelevant because exfiltration needs no forbidden keyword: a plain SELECT is sufficient. The blacklist itself is also weak (token must be surrounded by spaces, so 'DELETE(' or comment tricks can slip past), but the dominant impact is the unrestricted read.

Root cause

User-controlled SQL is executed as native SQL with no allow-list of tables/columns and no enforced organisation_id scoping. A deny-list of statement types is mistaken for an access-control boundary; SELECT-only does not prevent cross-tenant reads in a shared-schema multi-tenant DB.

Evidence / proof
Query q = em.createNativeQuery(sql);
List<?> result = q.getResultList();
// rejectionReason() only checks: starts-with SELECT, forbidden DML tokens, ';' — never which table/org

Real-world impact

Full cross-tenant confidentiality breach: a compliance officer in tenant A can dump credentials (password hashes), PDPL-protected PII, risk registers and incidents for tenants B and C from one shared DB. Because the runner is also reachable from the scheduler, a crafted definition runs repeatedly. This defeats the platform's #1 control (organisation_id scoping). Even within a single tenant it exposes columns the role would never be allowed to read through the normal API (e.g. auth secrets).

Reproduction

1. Authenticate as a COMPLIANCE_OFFICER (or CISO/PLATFORM_ADMIN).
2. POST /api/v1/ccm/tests with testType='CUSTOM_SQL', expectedConditionJson='{"sql":"SELECT username, password_hash FROM iam.users","maxRowCount":0}'.
3. POST /api/v1/ccm/tests/{externalId}/run-now.
4. GET /api/v1/ccm/tests/{externalId}/runs — the actualValueJson / failureReason and rowCount reveal data from every tenant (no organisation_id filter was applied). Swap the query to any other tenant's table to confirm cross-tenant read.

Resolution

Do not execute free-form tenant SQL. Replace CUSTOM_SQL with parameterised, pre-registered query templates whose table set is allow-listed, or run such queries only against a dedicated read-only schema that contains no other module/tenant data. If free SQL must stay, run it on a per-tenant least-privilege DB account that can only SELECT from that tenant's views, parse the statement with a real SQL grammar (not regex), reject any reference to tables outside an allow-list, and mandatorily append a WHERE organisation_id = :ctx predicate. Restrict the capability to PLATFORM_ADMIN at minimum and audit every definition.

List<?> result = q.getResultList();
▲ After (fixed)

// Resolve a pre-registered, parameterised template by id and bind the tenant:
QueryTemplate tmpl = templates.requireAllowListed(strOr(cond, "templateId", ""));
Query q = em.createNativeQuery(tmpl.sql());            // sql is developer-authored, table allow-listed
q.setParameter("orgId", TenantContext.getCurrentTenant());
List<?> result = q.getResultList();

It then mutates that link (lastKnownState/lastPulledAt) and publishes a DomainEvent under link.getOrganisationId() — i.e. under whatever tenant happens to own the first matching row, regardless of which tenant's service account called the webhook. The endpoint is guarded only by hasAnyRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN','SOC_AUTOMATION','INTEGRATION_SERVICE'); there is no check that the caller's TenantContext owns the matched link. ServiceNow incident numbers (INC0012345) are sequential and predictable, so a caller authenticated as one tenant's integration service account can drive state changes and emit automation-triggering events against another tenant's records by posting that tenant's INC number.

A by-natural-key lookup that omits organisation_id, combined with trusting the matched row's own org id instead of the authenticated caller's TenantContext. Multi-tenant scoping is the developer's per-query responsibility here and was skipped.

    .findFirstByIntegrationAndExternalNumber("SERVICENOW", number);
...
publisher.publishEvent(DomainEvent.of(link.getOrganisationId(), "SNOW_INCIDENT_UPDATED", ...));

A holder of one tenant's INTEGRATION_SERVICE/SOC_AUTOMATION account can flip the tracked state of another tenant's incident/finding/CAPA and fire that tenant's automation rules (e.g. auto-close a GRC item) by guessing/enumerating INC numbers. 1. As tenant-A's service account (one of the three allowed roles), POST /api/v1/integrations/servicenow/webhook/incident-updated with {"number":"INC0010001","state":"7"} where INC0010001 belongs to tenant B.
2. Response returns matched=true with tenant B's grcModule/grcRecordId, the tenant-B link row is updated, and a SNOW_INCIDENT_UPDATED event fires under tenant B's org id. No tenant-ownership check occurred.

Resolution

Scope the lookup by the caller's tenant: read orgId from TenantContext (the JWT filter populates it for an authenticated service account) and use a findByOrganisationIdAndIntegrationAndExternalNumber finder; treat a miss as 'not matched' (return 200 with matched=false). Never act on or attribute events to a row whose organisation_id differs from the authenticated context.

Description

Every @RestController in the ndi package guards 100% of its endpoints with @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") only. There is no use of the platform's ModulePermissionEvaluator (hasPermission('NDI','READ'/'WRITE') or hasRole(...)) anywhere in the module. As a result, the only access requirement is a valid JWT — any user of any role (AUDITOR, a basic RISK_MANAGER, or any seeded/self-registered role) can perform privileged write operations: create/update/delete assessment cycles, compliance assessments, gaps/CAPAs, evidence items, settings, report definitions, and submission packages. Read and write/delete are not separated, and operations that should be DPO/CISO/admin-restricted (approve, submit, archive, delete, settings mutation) are wide open to every authenticated principal. This contrasts sharply with sibling modules in this audit set: DataclassController (READ/WRITE/APPROVE role constants) and DataOfficerController (hasPermission('PRIVACY',...)) both implement proper granular authorization, confirming this is a defect in NDI rather than a platform convention.

Root cause

Authorization was stubbed with the placeholder isAuthenticated() during NDI development and never replaced with module-permission expressions. No class-level @PreAuthorize either, so there is no coarse fallback.

Evidence / proof
NdiAssessmentCycleController.java:62-66
    @PostMapping
    @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
    public ResponseEntity<NdiAssessmentCycle> create(@RequestBody NdiAssessmentCycle req) {
        return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(service.create(req));
    }
... and DELETE /{id}, PUT /{id}, /{id}/transition, /{id}/archive all also only @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()").

Real-world impact

A read-only/low-privilege tenant user can corrupt or destroy the organisation's entire SDAIA NDI assessment: delete cycles, falsify compliance statuses, soft-delete gaps and their CAPAs, mutate NDI settings, and tamper with submission packages destined for the regulator. This breaks segregation of duties and the integrity of regulatory submissions.

Reproduction

1. Log in as a low-privilege user (e.g. the seeded `auditor` / Audit@12345) to obtain a JWT.
2. curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8084/api/ndi/cycles/1 -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"  → 204, cycle soft-deleted.
3. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/ndi/settings -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"settingKey":"x","nameEn":"x"}'  → 200, setting created despite no NDI:WRITE permission.

Resolution

Replace isAuthenticated() with granular method security consistent with the rest of the platform: read endpoints -> hasPermission('NDI','READ'); create/update/state-change -> hasPermission('NDI','WRITE'); delete/approve/submit/settings -> a stricter permission or role (e.g. hasPermission('NDI','APPROVE') or hasAnyRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN','CISO','DPO')). Add an NDI module to the permission catalogue and consider a class-level default-deny.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@DeleteMapping("/{id}")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ResponseEntity<Void> delete(@PathVariable Long id) {
    service.softDelete(id);
    return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
}
▲ After (fixed)
@DeleteMapping("/{id}")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('NDI','WRITE') or hasRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN')")
public ResponseEntity<Void> delete(@PathVariable Long id) {
    service.softDelete(id);
    return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
}
// + read endpoints: @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('NDI','READ')")
// + write endpoints: @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('NDI','WRITE')")

✓ VerifiedSecuritySecurity Logging & Monitoring Failures (A09)▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Verified in source. NdiAuditController.java:37-41 exposes POST /api/ndi/audit gated only by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") and binds a raw NdiAuditEvent from the request body. NdiAuditService.record() only nulls id, stamps organisationId, requires action/entityType, and defaults severity, then repo.save(body) — occurredAt, actor identity, message and before/after values are all attacker-controlled. Any authenticated tenant user can forge or backdate entries in the same append-only ledger that NdiAuditPublisher writes, and the search/aggregate endpoints surface it to the Audit tab and AUDIT_TRAIL report. Genuine audit-log integrity (A09) flaw; High is correct.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/audit/controller/NdiAuditController.java:37-41 Effort S Risk CVSS 7.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — integrity loss on the regulatory audit trail
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/audit/service/NdiAuditService.java:57-64

Description

POST /api/ndi/audit is exposed with @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") and binds a raw NdiAuditEvent entity straight from the request body. The service comment describes the table as an "append-only ndi.audit_event table", but the only controls applied in record() are: id nulled, organisationId stamped from the tenant, and a default severity. Every other field — entityType, action, entityCode, cycleId, occurredAt, actor identity fields, before/after values, severity, message — is taken verbatim from the attacker. Any authenticated tenant user can therefore inject fabricated audit entries (e.g. forge an APPROVED transition by another user, or backdate occurredAt) into the same ledger that legitimate state-change code writes via NdiAuditPublisher. Because the search/aggregate endpoints surface this ledger to the Audit tab and to the AUDIT_TRAIL report, forged entries are indistinguishable from genuine ones.

Root cause

A write endpoint was provided on an audit ledger that is supposed to be system-generated only, with no authorization gate and no server-side control over the recorded fields (actor, timestamp, action).

Evidence / proof
NdiAuditService.record():
    public NdiAuditEvent record(NdiAuditEvent body) {
        body.setId(null);
        body.setOrganisationId(org());
        if (body.getAction() == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("action is required");
        if (body.getEntityType() == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("entityType is required");
        if (body.getSeverity() == null) body.setSeverity("INFO");
        return repo.save(body);   // occurredAt, actor, message all attacker-controlled
    }

Real-world impact

An insider can pollute or frame the NDI audit trail — fabricate evidence that an approval/submission happened, attribute actions to other users, or flood the ledger to bury real events. This undermines the evidentiary value of the audit trail used for SDAIA NDI compliance and incident investigation.

Reproduction

1. Obtain any tenant JWT.
2. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/ndi/audit -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"entityType":"COMPLIANCE","action":"APPROVE","severity":"INFO","message":"Approved by CISO","actorName":"ciso@victim","occurredAt":"2026-01-01T00:00:00"}'
3. GET /api/ndi/audit returns the forged, back-dated, mis-attributed event alongside genuine ones.

Resolution

Remove the public POST endpoint (audit events should only be produced internally by NdiAuditPublisher). If an external write must exist, restrict it to hasRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN'), and always stamp occurredAt and the actor from the SecurityContext server-side rather than trusting the body. Enforce table-level append-only (no UPDATE/DELETE grant) in the DB.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ResponseEntity<NdiAuditEvent> record(@RequestBody NdiAuditEvent body) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(service.record(body));
}
▲ After (fixed)
// Prefer removing this endpoint entirely; audit rows are produced by NdiAuditPublisher.
// If retained:
@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN')")
public ResponseEntity<NdiAuditEvent> record(@RequestBody NdiAuditEvent body) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(service.record(body));
}
// in service.record(): force server-controlled fields
//   body.setOccurredAt(LocalDateTime.now());
//   body.setActorUserId(currentUserId());  body.setActorName(currentUserName());

Description

POST /api/v1/licensing/modules (upsert) and POST /api/v1/licensing/modules/{code}/disable mutate the tenant's OrganisationLicense rows. The controller's own Javadoc labels these as '(admin)' operations, yet both are guarded only by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). LicensingService.upsert/disable perform no role check. Because enabled modules drive both the LicenseGuardAspect (RequireModule) gating and the JWT enabled_modules claim that hides/shows sidebar entries, any logged-in user — including a read-only AUDITOR — can grant their entire tenant access to paid modules (RISK, BCM, CYBER, PDPL, TPRM, REPORTING, etc.) they were never licensed for, or disable a module to deny the whole tenant access (DoS). upsert even lets the caller set tier=ENTERPRISE and validTo far in the future.

Root cause

Write endpoints that change commercial entitlements use the broadest possible guard (isAuthenticated()) instead of a platform-admin / PLATFORM:WRITE permission. The intended RBAC pattern — hasPermission('MODULE','ACTION') via ModulePermissionEvaluator — is used elsewhere (reporting, dashboard, help) but not enforced here.

Evidence / proof
@PostMapping("/modules")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ResponseEntity<OrganisationLicense> upsert(@RequestBody OrganisationLicense body) {
    body.setOrganisationId(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant());
    return ResponseEntity.ok(service.upsert(body));
}

@PostMapping("/modules/{code}/disable")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ResponseEntity<Void> disable(@PathVariable String code) { ... }

Real-world impact

License/entitlement bypass (revenue impact — any user self-grants paid modules) and tenant-wide denial of service (any user disables a module everyone depends on). The change is tenant-global, not per-user, so a single low-privilege account compromises the whole organisation's licensing state.

Reproduction

1. Log in as a low-privilege user (e.g. auditor / Audit@12345).
2. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/v1/licensing/modules -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"moduleCode":"CYBER","tier":"ENTERPRISE","enabled":true}'
3. Observe HTTP 200 and the CYBER module now enabled for the whole tenant.
4. POST /api/v1/licensing/modules/RISK/disable to disable RISK tenant-wide.

Resolution

Restrict licensing mutations to platform admins. Replace isAuthenticated() with @PreAuthorize("hasRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN')") (or a dedicated PLATFORM:WRITE / LICENSING:ADMIN permission). Keep the read endpoints (list, me/enabled, catalog) at isAuthenticated().

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping("/modules")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ResponseEntity<OrganisationLicense> upsert(@RequestBody OrganisationLicense body) {
    body.setOrganisationId(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant());
    return ResponseEntity.ok(service.upsert(body));
}

@PostMapping("/modules/{code}/disable")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ResponseEntity<Void> disable(@PathVariable String code) {
    service.disable(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(), code);
    return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
}
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping("/modules")
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN')")
public ResponseEntity<OrganisationLicense> upsert(@RequestBody OrganisationLicense body) {
    body.setOrganisationId(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant());
    return ResponseEntity.ok(service.upsert(body));
}

@PostMapping("/modules/{code}/disable")
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN')")
public ResponseEntity<Void> disable(@PathVariable String code) {
    service.disable(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(), code);
    return ResponseEntity.noContent().build();
}

Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/platform/automation/controller/AutomationRuleController.java:65-122 Effort S Risk CVSS 7.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:L) — tamper with org-wide automation/notification logic

Description

PATCH /api/v1/automation/rules/{id} lets any authenticated user rewrite an AutomationRule's conditionJson and actionJson, toggle enabled, and change priority; DELETE /api/v1/automation/rules/{id} soft-deletes a rule. Both are guarded only by isAuthenticated(). The F8 engine executes actionJson at rule-fire time: NOTIFY/ESCALATE fan a message out to every active holder of an arbitrary role (capped at 50), and CREATE_RECORD/FLAG drive cross-module side effects. A low-privilege user can therefore (a) disable safety/compliance escalation rules so breaches go unnotified, (b) re-point an ESCALATE rule at a different role to spam or socially-engineer recipients, or (c) silently neuter the SAMA/NCA/PDPL deadline-escalation automation the platform relies on.

Root cause

Administrative configuration endpoints (editing the automation engine's rules) are gated by authentication only, not by a platform-admin / AUTOMATION:WRITE permission, diverging from the hasPermission pattern used by the rest of the platform.

Evidence / proof
@PatchMapping("/rules/{id}")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
@Transactional
public AutomationRule patch(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody PatchBody body) {
    AutomationRule r = rules.findByIdAndOrganisationId(id, org()) ... ;
    if (body.conditionJson() != null) r.setConditionJson(body.conditionJson());
    if (body.actionJson()    != null) r.setActionJson(body.actionJson());
    ...
}

Real-world impact

Tampering with org-wide automation: suppression of compliance/breach escalations (integrity of the GRC control fabric), notification spam/abuse to arbitrary role holders, and disabling of the F8 engine's regulatory deadline chasers. Org scoping is correct (findByIdAndOrganisationId), so impact is confined within the tenant.

Reproduction

1. Log in as any low-privilege user.
2. GET /api/v1/automation/rules to enumerate rule ids (also isAuthenticated()).
3. curl -X PATCH http://localhost:8084/api/v1/automation/rules/1 -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"enabled":false}' to disable a compliance-escalation rule.
4. Or set actionJson to {"type":"NOTIFY","role":"PLATFORM_ADMIN","message":"..."} to re-target notifications.

Resolution

Gate PATCH and DELETE (and arguably the read endpoints) on a platform-admin or AUTOMATION:WRITE permission: @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('AUTOMATION','WRITE')") for patch/delete. Reads can stay on hasPermission('AUTOMATION','READ').

Description

The core PrivacyController, DpiaController and privacy_lc DsrCaseController correctly gate every endpoint with @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PRIVACY','READ'|'WRITE'|'DELETE')"). However an entire cluster of privacy sub-modules added in later sprints gate every endpoint with only @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"): Consent Records (PDPL Art.5 ledger), Data Sharing Agreements, Processor Assessments (PDPL Art.28), Cross-border Transfers (Art.29), Disposal Certificates, Privacy Notices, ROPA-workflows facade, and the PDPL Data-Flow graph. ModulePermissionEvaluator resolves hasPermission('PRIVACY','READ') to the granted authority PRIVACY_READ (or ROLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN); isAuthenticated() requires none of these. Consequently a user holding only, e.g., RISK_READ or AUDITOR authorities — who is deliberately NOT granted any PRIVACY authority — can list/read AND create/transition/withdraw these PDPL records. ConsentRecordController even exposes GET /consents/by-subject/{subjectRef}, letting any authenticated user enumerate a data subject's full consent history (dataSubjectRef is a PII reference). The records are returned as raw JPA entities, so all columns (data-subject references, destination orgs, data categories) are disclosed.

Root cause

These controllers were written with a coarse 'logged-in is enough' guard rather than the platform's MODULE:ACTION permission convention. The privacy module owns the PRIVACY permission namespace but only the original PrivacyController/DpiaController enforce it; the later sub-module controllers never adopted hasPermission('PRIVACY',…), so module-level access control is missing for them.

Evidence / proof
ConsentRecordController.java:38-42  @GetMapping("/by-subject/{subjectRef}") @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") public List<ConsentRecord> history(@PathVariable String subjectRef){ return service.historyFor(subjectRef); }  — compare PrivacyController.java:30-31 @GetMapping("/breaches") @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PRIVACY','READ')"). ModulePermissionEvaluator.java:41-43 returns true only for ROLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN or the MODULE_ACTION authority; isAuthenticated() bypasses it entirely.

Real-world impact

Confidentiality and integrity breach of PDPL-regulated data: any account on the tenant (e.g. a risk analyst, an auditor, a low-privilege operator) can read consent ledgers, processor due-diligence, cross-border transfer approvals and privacy notices, and can mutate them (grant/withdraw consent, approve/reject cross-border transfers, publish/supersede privacy notices, complete disposal certificates). For a Saudi bank this is a regulatory disclosure risk under SDAIA PDPL and undermines the segregation-of-duties the DPO role is supposed to enforce.

Reproduction

1) Log in as a user whose role grants e.g. RISK_READ but no PRIVACY_* authority (a non-DPO). 2) curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:8084/api/v1/privacy/consents → 200 with the full consent ledger. 3) curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" "http://localhost:8084/api/v1/privacy/consents/by-subject/NID-1234567890" → that subject's consent history. 4) POST /api/privacy/cross-border-transfers/{id}/approve with the same token → approves an Art.29 transfer. All succeed; the same calls with hasPermission('PRIVACY','READ') would 403 for this user.

Resolution

Replace isAuthenticated() with hasPermission('PRIVACY','READ') on every GET and hasPermission('PRIVACY','WRITE') (and 'DELETE' where applicable) on every mutating endpoint across these controllers, matching PrivacyController/DpiaController. Where a narrower role is warranted (e.g. expire/approve restricted to DPO), use hasAnyRole/hasPermission accordingly. Add an integration test that asserts a token without PRIVACY_* authority receives 403 on each privacy endpoint.

@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public Page<ConsentRecord> list(...) { return service.list(page, size); }

@PostMapping("/{id}/withdraw")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ConsentRecord withdraw(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody WithdrawBody body) { ... }
▲ After (fixed)
@GetMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PRIVACY','READ')")
public Page<ConsentRecord> list(...) { return service.list(page, size); }

@PostMapping("/{id}/withdraw")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PRIVACY','WRITE')")
public ConsentRecord withdraw(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody WithdrawBody body) { ... }

Forging breach/regulatory records and mutating incident state under no role check is a genuine High BFLA; severity unchanged.

Description

POST /api/privacy/cyber-bridge/trigger is guarded by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). The handler calls CyberPdplBridgeService.triggerForIncident, which (a) UPDATEs cyber.incidents to set affects_personal_data + PII classification fields, (b) INSERTs a row into privacy.data_breaches, and (c) cross-links the two. This is a privileged classification action that should require PRIVACY:WRITE (and arguably CYBER:WRITE since it mutates a cyber incident), yet any authenticated user can invoke it. The read endpoints on the same controller (GET /log, /log/by-incident/{id}) are likewise only isAuthenticated().

Root cause

The bridge controller was wired with a generic isAuthenticated() guard rather than the PRIVACY module permission. Because the underlying write spans two modules via native SQL, no method-level @PreAuthorize on the cyber side is consulted either.

Evidence / proof
CyberPdplBridgeController.java:42-44  @PostMapping("/trigger") @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") public ResponseEntity<Response> trigger(@Valid @RequestBody ManualTriggerRequest req, Authentication auth){...}. Service writes: CyberPdplBridgeService.java:95-109 UPDATE cyber.incidents SET affects_personal_data=1,...; :124-146 INSERT INTO privacy.data_breaches (...).

Real-world impact

Any authenticated user can fabricate a personal-data breach record (which may auto-flag a 72-hour SDAIA notification SLA via pdpc_notification_required) and reclassify an arbitrary cyber incident as PII-affecting within their tenant. This is a data-integrity and compliance-noise attack: false regulatory clocks, polluted breach register, and unauthorized mutation of incident records owned by the cyber module.

Reproduction

1) Log in as any non-DPO authenticated user. 2) POST /api/privacy/cyber-bridge/trigger {"cyberIncidentId":<an incident id in your tenant>,"dataSubjectsAffectedEst":600,"dataCategoriesAffected":"NATIONAL_ID","piiAssessment":"x"} with their Bearer token. 3) A privacy.data_breaches row is created with pdpc_notification_required=1 and the cyber incident is reclassified — returns 201.

Resolution

Gate /trigger with @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PRIVACY','WRITE')") (and consider also requiring CYBER:WRITE / restricting to DPO,CISO). Gate the read endpoints with hasPermission('PRIVACY','READ'). The native queries themselves are correctly parameterized — only the authorization guard needs tightening.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping("/trigger")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ResponseEntity<Response> trigger(@Valid @RequestBody ManualTriggerRequest req, Authentication auth) { ... }
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping("/trigger")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PRIVACY','WRITE') and hasPermission('CYBER','WRITE')")
public ResponseEntity<Response> trigger(@Valid @RequestBody ManualTriggerRequest req, Authentication auth) { ... }

Description

RiskTreatmentService.get(Long id) loads a RiskTreatment with a bare JpaRepository.findById(id) and performs NO organisation scoping before returning it. It is exposed directly by RiskAdvancedController.getTreatment (GET /api/v1/risk/treatments/{id}, guarded only by hasPermission('RISK','READ')). Because RiskTreatment surrogate ids are sequential Long PKs and every tenant's user holds RISK:READ, a user in organisation A can enumerate ids and read treatment plans (descriptionEn/Ar, ownerId, dueDate, status, treatmentType, parent riskId) belonging to organisation B. The platform's stated #1 invariant is that every repository read be org-scoped; the sibling write paths (update/transition/delete) are saved by their downstream ensureRiskInTenant(t.getRiskId()) check, and the list path is guarded by ensureRiskInTenant(riskId), but the single-entity read get() has neither guard and the repository has no findByIdAndOrganisationId finder to enforce it.

Root cause

Single-entity read uses an unscoped findById(id) and the controller relies on it without any TenantContext check; RiskTreatmentRepository exposes no org-scoped finder. The 'belongs to another organisation' guard exists only inside ensureRiskInTenant(riskId), which get() never calls.

Evidence / proof
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public RiskTreatment get(Long id) {
        return treatments.findById(id)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("Risk treatment not found: " + id));
    }
// exposed by RiskAdvancedController: 
//   @GetMapping("/treatments/{id}") @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('RISK','READ')")
//   public RiskTreatment getTreatment(@PathVariable Long id) { return treatmentService.get(id); }

Real-world impact

Confidentiality breach across tenants: any authenticated user with RISK:READ in one tenant can read risk-treatment records (mitigation strategy, owner, due dates, linked risk) of every other tenant by walking the integer id space. In a multi-tenant SaaS for banks/energy/telco this is a serious cross-customer data leak and a regulatory (SAMA/NCA/PDPL) reportable exposure.

Reproduction

1. Authenticate as a user in org A (e.g. riskmanager). 2. As org B, note a treatment id (or simply enumerate). 3. From org A's session call GET /api/v1/risk/treatments/{idOfOrgB} with the org A Bearer token. 4. Observe org B's treatment record returned with HTTP 200 (no org check) instead of 404.

Resolution

Scope the read to the current tenant. Add findByIdAndOrganisationId(id, orgId) to RiskTreatmentRepository (the entity has no organisationId column itself — it inherits org via its parent Risk) and in get(id) resolve the treatment then call ensureRiskInTenant(t.getRiskId()) exactly as update()/transition()/delete() already do. Throw EntityNotFoundException (404) on mismatch so ids cannot be probed.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public RiskTreatment get(Long id) {
        return treatments.findById(id)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("Risk treatment not found: " + id));
    }
▲ After (fixed)
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public RiskTreatment get(Long id) {
        RiskTreatment t = treatments.findById(id)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("Risk treatment not found: " + id));
        // Tenant guard: a treatment whose parent risk is not in this org is invisible.
        ensureRiskInTenant(t.getRiskId());
        return t;
    }

Description

TprmService.updateAssessment(id, req) and deleteAssessment(id) load the VendorAssessment with the bare JpaRepository method assessmentRepo.findById(id), with no organisation/tenant check. The Vendor-side methods in the same service (getVendor/updateVendor/deleteVendor) correctly filter on TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(), but the assessment methods do not. VendorAssessment carries only a vendor_id column and NO organisation_id (entity has no org field — see lines 16-24), so org ownership can only be enforced by resolving the parent vendor; neither method does this. The @Where(clause = "is_deleted = 0") on the entity does not constrain tenant. The controller endpoints PUT /api/v1/tprm/assessments/{id} and DELETE /api/v1/tprm/assessments/{id} are guarded by hasPermission('TPRM','WRITE'/'DELETE'), which any TPRM user in any tenant holds, so the permission check does not stop cross-tenant access.

Root cause

Assessment lookups use the unscoped JpaRepository.findById instead of resolving and validating the parent Vendor's organisationId (as getVendor does). VendorAssessment has no organisation_id column, so tenant isolation must be derived via the vendor and was omitted.

Evidence / proof
public VendorAssessment updateAssessment(Long id, VendorAssessment req) {
    VendorAssessment existing = assessmentRepo.findById(id)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("Assessment not found: " + id));
    ... // no org / vendor-ownership check
}
public void deleteAssessment(Long id) {
    VendorAssessment a = assessmentRepo.findById(id)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("Assessment not found: " + id));
    a.setIsDeleted(true); ...
}

Real-world impact

A user authenticated in tenant A with TPRM:WRITE/DELETE can enumerate sequential assessment ids and overwrite findings/risk scores/status or soft-delete vendor risk assessments belonging to any other tenant (e.g. another bank). This is cross-tenant data tampering and destruction of regulated third-party risk records.

Reproduction

1. Log in as a TPRM user in tenant A (e.g. riskmanager). 2. Identify an assessment id belonging to tenant B (ids are sequential IDENTITY values). 3. curl -X PUT http://localhost:8084/api/v1/tprm/assessments/{idFromTenantB} -H 'Authorization: Bearer <tenantA token>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"assessmentDate":"2026-01-01","riskScore":1,"riskRating":"LOW","status":"REVIEWED","findings":"tampered"}' . The response returns tenant B's mutated assessment. 4. DELETE the same id soft-deletes tenant B's record.

Resolution

Resolve the parent vendor and assert org ownership before mutating, exactly as getVendor does. Add an org-scoped finder (e.g. findByIdAndVendor_OrganisationId or join on vendor) or fetch the existing assessment, then call getVendor(existing.getVendorId()) to enforce the tenant guard before applying changes.

@Transactional
public VendorAssessment updateAssessment(Long id, VendorAssessment req) {

    getVendor(existing.getVendorId()); // tenant guard: throws if vendor not in current org
    existing.setAssessmentDate(req.getAssessmentDate());
    // ...
    return assessmentRepo.save(existing);
}

@Transactional
public void deleteAssessment(Long id) {
    VendorAssessment a = assessmentRepo.findById(id)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("Assessment not found: " + id));
    getVendor(a.getVendorId()); // tenant guard
    a.setIsDeleted(true);
    assessmentRepo.save(a);
}

Description

In QuestionnaireService, every assessment-workflow method loads the parent VendorAssessment with the unscoped assessments.findById(assessmentId): assignTemplate (line 214), upsertResponse (line 241), markComplete (line 299) and markReviewed (line 320). Unlike templates/questions/responses (which are loaded with findByIdAndOrganisationId / findByOrganisationId... finders), VendorAssessment is fetched without a tenant guard and VendorAssessment has no organisation_id column to let Hibernate filter it. The corresponding endpoints (POST /api/v1/tprm/assessments/{id}/assign-template, /responses, /complete, /review) only require hasPermission('TPRM','WRITE'), held by every TPRM writer in every tenant. A user in tenant A can therefore reference an assessment id owned by tenant B and: flip its workflow_status to IN_PROGRESS/COMPLETED/REVIEWED, overwrite its templateId/totalQuestions/answeredCount, and (when the foreign assessment has no template, so the template-mismatch guard at line 246 is skipped) write a response row and trigger recomputeAssessment, which saves a recomputed computedScorePct/riskScore/riskRating onto tenant B's assessment.

Root cause

VendorAssessment is loaded by id alone with no derivation of the owning organisation (it has no organisation_id and no parent-vendor org check), so tenant isolation is not enforced on the assessment object even though the questionnaire child entities are correctly org-scoped.

Evidence / proof
@Transactional
public VendorAssessment markComplete(Long assessmentId) {
    Long o = org();
    VendorAssessment va = assessments.findById(assessmentId)   // <-- not org-scoped
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("VendorAssessment not found: " + assessmentId));
    ...
    va.setWorkflowStatus("COMPLETED");
    return assessments.save(va);
}

Real-world impact

Cross-tenant integrity violation: an attacker in one tenant can corrupt the workflow state and computed risk scores of another tenant's third-party risk assessments, and prematurely mark them COMPLETED/REVIEWED — undermining the integrity of regulated vendor-risk records and audit trails.

Reproduction

1. Authenticate as a TPRM writer in tenant A. 2. Pick an assessment id belonging to tenant B. 3. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/v1/tprm/assessments/{idFromTenantB}/review -H 'Authorization: Bearer <tenantA token>' . If tenant B's assessment is COMPLETED, its workflow_status flips to REVIEWED under tenant A's action. The /complete and /assign-template endpoints similarly mutate it.

Resolution

Resolve the assessment through a tenant-aware path. Either add organisation_id to vendor_assessments and load via findByIdAndOrganisationId, or add a private helper that loads the assessment, then validates the owning vendor's org (vendorRepo.findById(va.getVendorId()).filter org == current). Apply it in assignTemplate, upsertResponse, markComplete, markReviewed and recomputeAssessment.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
VendorAssessment va = assessments.findById(assessmentId)
    .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("VendorAssessment not found: " + assessmentId));
▲ After (fixed)
VendorAssessment va = loadAssessmentInTenant(assessmentId); // new helper

private VendorAssessment loadAssessmentInTenant(Long id) {
    VendorAssessment va = assessments.findById(id)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("VendorAssessment not found: " + id));
    vendorRepo.findById(va.getVendorId())
        .filter(v -> v.getOrganisationId().equals(org()))
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("VendorAssessment not found: " + id));
    return va;
}

Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/iam/dto/UserRequest.java:6-21 Effort M Risk CVSS ~5.3 — weak passwords accepted, amplifies the lack of lockout in SEC-AUTH-001

Description

Passwords are validated only by Jakarta `@Size(min = 8, max = 100)` on UserRequest.password. There is no complexity requirement (no required mix of upper/lower/digit/symbol), no check against common/breached passwords, no maximum-repeat / dictionary check, and no dedicated change-password endpoint with re-validation (password is simply re-encoded in UserService.create/update). The field is also nullable (not @NotBlank), so passwords are set wherever provided with no policy beyond length. For a regulated GRC platform targeting SAMA/NCA controls, an 8-char minimum with no complexity is below typical baselines. (Note: PasswordPolicyRunner referencing minLength 14 is a STUB control-test for external AD systems, not enforcement of this application's own user passwords.)

Root cause

Password strength is enforced only by a bean-validation length annotation; no PasswordPolicy/validator component exists for the application's own user store.

Evidence / proof
public record UserRequest( @NotBlank @Size(min = 3, max = 100) String username, ..., @Size(min = 8, max = 100) String password, ...)  // only length, password not even @NotBlank

Real-world impact

Users (and admins creating users) can set trivially guessable passwords such as 'password' or 'aaaaaaaa'. Combined with the absence of lockout/throttling (SEC-AUTH-001), this materially increases the success probability of online guessing and credential stuffing.

Reproduction

1. As an admin, POST /api/v1/iam/users with password "password" (8 chars, all lowercase). 2. The request passes validation and the account is created with that password. 3. No complexity or breach-list rejection occurs.

Resolution

Introduce a password-policy validator (custom @StrongPassword constraint or a service-layer check) enforcing length >= 12, at least three of four character classes, rejection of the username/email substrings, and ideally a breached-password (k-anonymity HaveIBeenPwned) or local common-password blocklist. Apply it on create, update, and a dedicated self-service change-password endpoint that also requires the current password.

▲ After (fixed)

// where @StrongPassword enforces >=3 of {upper,lower,digit,symbol},
// rejects username/email substrings, and checks a breached-password list

Description

Across the bcm/cycle and bcm/drp subtrees, roughly 30 write and read endpoints are annotated `@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")` instead of the platform's documented `hasPermission('BCM','READ|WRITE|DELETE')` model (per CLAUDE.md and as correctly used by BcmController and bcm_lc/InvocationController). Because method security is enabled (SecurityConfig: @EnableMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled = true)), these annotations ARE enforced — but only to the level of 'has a valid JWT'. Any authenticated principal — including a read-only AUDITOR, or a user whose role grants no BCM module permission at all — can therefore create/update/transition/delete crisis events, BCP/DRP plans, BCM risks, gaps/CAPAs, assessment cycles, BIA assessments, and management reviews, and can fire the SIEM webhook that auto-escalates to a CrisisEvent (BcmAuditCompletionController.ingestSiem, severity>=3). Tenant isolation still holds (services scope by TenantContext), so this is intra-tenant privilege escalation / BFLA, not cross-tenant exposure.

Root cause

These controllers were built ahead of the BCM permission wiring and used isAuthenticated() as a placeholder; the TODO is even acknowledged inline on the SIEM webhook ('accepts any authenticated caller for now'). The module's own correct pattern (hasPermission) was never back-filled here.

Evidence / proof
CrisisEventController create: `@PostMapping  @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")  public ResponseEntity<CrisisEvent> create(@Valid @RequestBody CrisisEvent body)`. CrisisEventController delete-equivalent transition and activate-bcp/drp all `@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")`. BcmAuditCompletionController.ingestSiem (line 91-95) `@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")` with comment 'Webhook ingest — accepts any authenticated caller for now.' grep over the package found 30+ isAuthenticated() occurrences on mapped methods.

Real-world impact

A low-privilege or read-only user (e.g. AUDITOR, or any tenant employee with a JWT) can tamper with live crisis management: open or close crisis events, activate/deactivate BCP/DRP plans, alter risk scores, delete remediation gaps/CAPAs, or inject a fake high-severity SIEM alert that spins up a real crisis event — undermining segregation of duties required by ISO 22301 / SAMA BCF governance.

Reproduction

1. Log in as an AUDITOR (read-only seeded role) or any user lacking BCM:WRITE. 2. POST /api/v1/bcm/crisis-events with a minimal valid body → 200 Created. 3. POST /api/v1/bcm/crisis-events/{id}/transition {to:'CANCELLED'} → succeeds. 4. POST /api/v1/bcm/siem-events {severity:5,title:'x'} → auto-creates a CrisisEvent. None of these should be permitted for a read-only role.

Resolution

Replace `isAuthenticated()` with the module permission expressions: `hasPermission('BCM','READ')` on GET endpoints, `hasPermission('BCM','WRITE')` on POST/PUT/PATCH/transition, `hasPermission('BCM','DELETE')` on delete/archive. For the SIEM webhook, require a dedicated permission (e.g. BCM:INGEST) or a shared-secret integration credential rather than a user JWT.

Description

BiaQuantitativeController applies a single CLASS-level `@PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('BCM_MANAGER','CISO','PLATFORM_ADMIN','RISK_MANAGER','AUDITOR','CFO')")` to ALL nine endpoints, including create, update, submit, cfo-approve, board-approve and DELETE/archive. The same broad role set therefore lets an AUDITOR (a read-only assurance role) and a RISK_MANAGER create and mutate quantitative BIAs and even archive them — there is no per-method narrowing that restricts write/approval verbs to the appropriate roles. The same pattern (read roles permitted to mutate) appears on the crisis-comms template controller. This breaks segregation of duties: an auditor signing off on a control they themselves can edit is a governance integrity failure even though tenant isolation is intact (the service scopes by TenantContext.requireOrganisationId via loadOrThrow).

Root cause

Authorization expressed once at class level with the union of every role that needs ANY access, instead of per-method role sets that separate read from write/approve. The class-level grant is the lowest common denominator and over-grants the write verbs.

Evidence / proof
Class annotation: `@PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('BCM_MANAGER','CISO','PLATFORM_ADMIN','RISK_MANAGER','AUDITOR','CFO')")`. Methods create()/update()/cfoApprove()/boardApprove()/archive() carry NO method-level @PreAuthorize, so all inherit the class grant — AUDITOR can POST/PUT/DELETE.

Real-world impact

An auditor can fabricate or alter the financial avoidable-loss inputs that feed StrategyRoiService board recommendations, or archive a quantitative BIA, defeating the four-eyes / SoD controls expected by SAMA and an external ISO 22301 auditor.

Reproduction

1. Log in as AUDITOR. 2. POST /api/v1/bcm/bia/quantitative with a valid body → 201 Created (should be 403). 3. DELETE /api/v1/bcm/bia/quantitative/{externalId} → 200 archived.

Resolution

Keep the broad read grant at class level but add method-level `@PreAuthorize` that restricts writes/approvals: create/update to BCM_MANAGER/CISO/PLATFORM_ADMIN; cfo-approve to CFO/PLATFORM_ADMIN; board-approve to BOARD_MEMBER/PLATFORM_ADMIN; archive to BCM_MANAGER/PLATFORM_ADMIN. Remove AUDITOR/RISK_MANAGER from any mutating verb.

Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/common/exception/GlobalExceptionHandler.java:371-384 Effort S Risk CVSS ~5.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N) — information disclosure of internal exception types, SQL object names, and stack-trace-derived messages to any caller
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/common/exception/GlobalExceptionHandler.java:240-252
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/common/exception/GlobalExceptionHandler.java:225-235
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application-prod.yml:106-115

Description

The catch-all @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) builds the client-facing ProblemDetail 'detail' from the exception's simple class name plus its root-cause message, and additionally serialises the fully-qualified exception class name into an 'exception' property and the raw root message into a 'rootCause' property. This is returned to the HTTP client for ANY unhandled server error. The same root-message exposure occurs in missingObjectResponse() (line 249, 'rootCause' carries SQL Server's 'Invalid object name schema.table' verbatim). There is no profile gate — application-prod.yml contains no server.error override and no branch on the active profile, so production responses disclose the same internal detail as dev. For a multi-tenant GRC platform handling SAMA/NCA-regulated data, exposing internal class names (revealing framework versions and package structure), SQL object/schema names, and exception messages aids reconnaissance and can leak data-layer structure.

Root cause

The handler was intentionally designed to surface developer-friendly diagnostics in the toast/response body ('Real bugs surface clearly instead of hiding behind "An unexpected error occurred."' — comment at lines 368-369). This design was never gated to dev-only, so it ships in prod.

Evidence / proof
@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
public ProblemDetail handleGeneral(Exception ex) {
    log.error("Unhandled exception [{}]: {}", ex.getClass().getName(), ex.getMessage(), ex);
    String root = rootMessage(ex);
    String detail = ex.getClass().getSimpleName()
        + (root != null && !root.isBlank() ? ": " + root : "");
    ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, detail);
    ...
    pd.setProperty("exception", ex.getClass().getName());
    pd.setProperty("rootCause", root);

Real-world impact

An unauthenticated or low-privilege attacker who triggers any unhandled exception (malformed input down an unguarded path, a NullPointerException, a constraint failure) receives the internal exception type, package path, and root-cause text. SQL-layer messages disclose schema and table names (e.g. 'platform.users', 'admin.committee_*'). This accelerates targeted attacks (SQLi probing, dependency-CVE matching) and violates least-disclosure expectations for a regulated platform.

Reproduction

1. Authenticate (or hit any endpoint that can throw before auth). 2. Send input that triggers an unhandled RuntimeException, e.g. a payload that causes a downstream NPE or an uncategorised DataAccessException. 3. Observe the JSON ProblemDetail response contains 'detail' = '<ExceptionSimpleName>: <root message>', plus 'exception' = fully-qualified class name and 'rootCause' = raw message. Confirm identical behaviour with --spring.profiles.active=prod.

Resolution

Gate verbose diagnostics to non-prod only. In prod, return a generic detail ('An unexpected error occurred. Reference: <correlationId>') and omit the 'exception' and 'rootCause' properties; log full details server-side keyed by a correlation id returned to the client. Inject the active Environment/profile (or a @Value flag) into the handler and branch on it. Apply the same treatment to missingObjectResponse() so SQL object names are not echoed in prod.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
public ProblemDetail handleGeneral(Exception ex) {
    log.error("Unhandled exception [{}]: {}", ex.getClass().getName(), ex.getMessage(), ex);
    String root = rootMessage(ex);
    String detail = ex.getClass().getSimpleName()
        + (root != null && !root.isBlank() ? ": " + root : "");
    ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, detail);
    pd.setProperty("exception", ex.getClass().getName());
    pd.setProperty("rootCause", root);
    ...
    return pd;
}
▲ After (fixed)
@Value("${grc.errors.verbose:false}") private boolean verboseErrors; // true only in dev

@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
public ProblemDetail handleGeneral(Exception ex) {
    String ref = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
    log.error("Unhandled exception ref={} [{}]: {}", ref, ex.getClass().getName(), ex.getMessage(), ex);
    String detail = verboseErrors
        ? ex.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + rootMessage(ex)
        : "An unexpected error occurred. Reference: " + ref;
    ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, detail);
    pd.setProperty("reference", ref);
    if (verboseErrors) { pd.setProperty("exception", ex.getClass().getName()); pd.setProperty("rootCause", rootMessage(ex)); }
    pd.setProperty("timestamp", Instant.now());
    return pd;
}

SecurityBroken Access Control / Identification & Authentication Failures (A01/A07:2021 / CWE-307)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/SecurityConfig.java:91-117 Effort M Risk CVSS ~5.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — unauthenticated, token-guessing / enumeration risk on public token endpoints without rate limiting
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/SecurityConfig.java:96-98
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/SecurityConfig.java:102-117

Description

A set of public, unauthenticated endpoints are permitAll where a per-record token IS the only credential: TPRM vendor BCP attestation (/api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/** GET+POST), whistleblower portal (status/reply by token), customer-complaints tracking (/api/v1/complaints/public/track/**), case-intake tracking (/api/v1/intake/track/**), and PDPL public sub-processor list. The code comment at lines 95-96 explicitly acknowledges the control gap: 'Full vendor portal hardening (rate-limit, MFA bind, full audit) is a follow-up.' With no rate limiting, IP throttling, or lockout at this layer (and dev sets max-failed-login-attempts=99 which governs only login, not these token lookups), the token space is exposed to online brute-force / enumeration. If any token is short, sequential, timestamp-derived, or otherwise low-entropy (must be verified in the service/token-generator code), an attacker can enumerate other vendors'/reporters'/customers' confidential records — a serious confidentiality breach for whistleblower (SAMA CG Art.28 / CMA CG Art.87) and complaint PII data. The HTTP layer correctly permits these by design; the finding is the absence of compensating brute-force controls behind that permit, by the authors' own admission.

Root cause

Public token-keyed endpoints were shipped before the compensating controls (rate limiting, audit, token-entropy guarantees) that a credential-bearing public surface requires. Authorization is delegated entirely to token possession with no throttle.

Evidence / proof
// Slice 10-D: vendor BCP attestation submission portal — token IS
// the credential, so these two endpoints are auth-free. Full vendor
// portal hardening (rate-limit, MFA bind, full audit) is a follow-up.
.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET,  "/api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/**").permitAll()
.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/**").permitAll()

Real-world impact

An unauthenticated attacker can attempt to guess/enumerate per-record tokens at full request speed to read or submit against other tenants' vendor attestations, whistleblower cases, and customer complaints (which include PII per the comments). For a regulated GRC platform this risks exposure of confidential whistleblower identities and complaint PII, with regulatory consequences under PDPL and SAMA/CMA conduct rules.

Reproduction

1. Without authenticating, GET /api/v1/complaints/public/track/<guess> or /api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/<guess> in a loop. 2. Observe no rate limiting / lockout from the HTTP/security layer. 3. If tokens are sequential/low-entropy, valid records are discoverable; confirm token entropy by reviewing the token generator in the corresponding service.

Resolution

Add per-IP and per-token-prefix rate limiting / exponential backoff on all public token endpoints (e.g. bucket4j filter or gateway throttle). Enforce cryptographically-random, sufficiently-long tokens (>=128-bit). Audit-log access attempts (without logging reporter IP where policy forbids). Consider short token TTLs and single-use submission tokens. Track and close the acknowledged 'follow-up' hardening items before production exposure.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET,  "/api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/**").permitAll()
.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/**").permitAll()
// no throttling filter registered for these paths
▲ After (fixed)
// Register a rate-limit filter (e.g. bucket4j) before the JWT filter for /api/v1/**/public/** and /by-token/**
http.addFilterBefore(publicEndpointRateLimitFilter, JwtAuthenticationFilter.class);
// Ensure tokens are 128-bit+ random (SecureRandom), single-use where applicable, short TTL
.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET,  "/api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/**").permitAll()
.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/**").permitAll()

Description

TenantWriteGuardInterceptor is the platform-wide Hibernate-level backstop that throws SecurityException on cross-tenant writes performed without TenantContext.allowCrossTenantWrite(). It is gated by grc.security.tenant-write-guard.enabled which defaults to false (line 52-53) and is NOT set to true in any committed profile (neither application.yml, application-dev.yml, nor application-prod.yml define grc.security.tenant-write-guard). The code itself documents that with the guard off, 'Per-service setId(null) defense is the only mass-assignment guard active' (lines 92-93). Given the platform's stated #1 risk is org-scoping/tenant isolation, shipping the only centralized, defense-in-depth control for cross-tenant writes in a default-disabled state means a single missed per-service guard (a forgotten setId(null) or an unscoped repository save) results in an unguarded cross-tenant write with no backstop. The feature-flag rationale (soak in staging first) is reasonable for rollout but the committed prod profile never flips it on, so production likely runs without the backstop.

Root cause

New defensive interceptor was intentionally shipped default-off to allow staged activation (lines 26-45), but no profile (notably application-prod.yml) ever enables it, leaving the centralized cross-tenant write guard inactive in production by default.

Evidence / proof
@Value("${grc.security.tenant-write-guard.enabled:false}")
private boolean enabled;
...
} else {
    log.info("[TenantWriteGuard] interceptor NOT wired "
           + "(grc.security.tenant-write-guard.enabled=false). Per-service "
           + "setId(null) defense is the only mass-assignment guard active.");
}

Real-world impact

If any one of the many module services omits or mis-implements its per-call tenant/id scoping (mass-assignment of organisation_id, or a save that crosses tenants), the write proceeds and corrupts or injects data into another tenant's records, with no platform-level interceptor to block it. For a multi-tenant SAMA/NCA GRC platform this is a high-integrity, cross-tenant data-isolation breach.

Reproduction

1. Inspect committed profiles: grep grc.security.tenant-write-guard across application*.yml -> no enabled:true. 2. Start with profile prod -> log shows '[TenantWriteGuard] interceptor NOT wired'. 3. Exercise any service path that saves an entity with an attacker-supplied organisation_id where that service lacks the setId(null)/scope check -> write succeeds cross-tenant (no SecurityException).

Resolution

Enable grc.security.tenant-write-guard.enabled=true in application-prod.yml (after the documented staging soak) so the platform-wide backstop is active in production. Keep the per-service defenses as primary; treat the interceptor as defense-in-depth that should be ON by default in any real deployment. Add a startup assertion/health indicator that fails or warns loudly if the guard is disabled in prod.

▲ After (fixed)

    session-timeout-minutes: 30
    max-login-attempts: 5
    lockout-duration-minutes: 30
    tenant-write-guard:
      enabled: true   # platform-wide cross-tenant write backstop ON in prod

✎ AdjustedSecurityBroken Function Level Authorization (A01)▾
Adversarial verification: adjusted (severity High→Medium) — CONFIRMED that ControlMapController (tss-grc-backend/.../controlmap/controller/ControlMapController.java) carries NO @PreAuthorize on any of its three endpoints (GET list, GET evidence, PUT replace-set). With SecurityConfig's default rule .anyRequest().authenticated() and @EnableMethodSecurity NOT denying by default, any authenticated user — including read-only roles like AUDITOR — can replace an entity's control links via PUT /api/v1/control-links/{type}/{id}. This is a genuine BFLA, and the surrounding compliance/risk controllers all use the hasPermission('MODULE','ACTION') pattern, so this is a real deviation. However, the audit title also claims 'in-tenant IDOR': I REFUTE that aspect — ControlMapService is fully org-scoped (every method calls TenantContext.getCurrentTenant() and queries findByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityId / deleteForEntity(orgId,...)), so there is NO cross-tenant exposure and the data altered is the caller's own tenant. The exposed data is internal control-to-evidence mapping metadata (not PII/credentials), and the actor on writes is correctly taken from @AuthenticationPrincipal. Real authorization gap but the impact (in-tenant integrity of non-sensitive mapping data, no cross-tenant reach) is below the other High BFLA findings here; adjusting to Medium.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/controlmap/controller/ControlMapController.java:31-52 Effort S Risk CVSS 7.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N) — no function-level authz on a write endpoint
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/SecurityConfig.java:118
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/controlmap/service/ControlMapService.java:56-77

Description

None of the three ControlMapController endpoints (GET /{entityType}/{entityId}, GET .../evidence, and PUT /{entityType}/{entityId}) declare any @PreAuthorize. With @EnableMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled=true) and SecurityConfig's terminal rule anyRequest().authenticated(), the only gate is that a valid JWT is present. Every other controller in the compliance/regulatory domain enforces a module permission (hasPermission('COMPLIANCE',...)) or a role list. The PUT performs a destructive replace-set: it deletes ALL existing control links for the (org, entityType, entityId) tuple and re-inserts the supplied set. Any authenticated user of any role (e.g. a read-only AUDITOR, or a low-privilege operator) can wipe and rewrite the control-to-evidence mapping for any risk/control/policy in their own tenant.

Root cause

The controller relies solely on the global authenticated() floor and omits the method-level @PreAuthorize the rest of the platform uses, so authorization collapses from 'right module+action' down to 'any logged-in user'.

Evidence / proof
@PutMapping("/{entityType}/{entityId}")
@Operation(summary = "Replace the entity's control mappings with the supplied set")
public List<ControlLinkResponse> set(@PathVariable String entityType, @PathVariable Long entityId,
        @RequestBody ControlLinkSetRequest request, @AuthenticationPrincipal GrcUserDetails me) {
    return service.setMappings(...);   // <-- no @PreAuthorize anywhere on this controller
}

Real-world impact

Within a tenant, an under-privileged user can silently destroy and forge the manual control-mapping layer that feeds evidence-readiness and framework-coverage rollups, degrading the integrity of compliance reporting. There is no cross-tenant exposure (service is org-scoped via TenantContext), but the missing function-level check is a clear privilege gap relative to the platform's own conventions.

Reproduction

1. Log in as any low-privilege user (e.g. AUDITOR). 2. PUT /api/v1/control-links/RISK/123 with body {"subControlIds": []}. 3. The response is 200 and all control links for RISK 123 in the tenant are deleted — no COMPLIANCE:WRITE or admin role was required.

Resolution

Add method-level authorization to all three endpoints: COMPLIANCE:READ (or CONTROLMAP:READ) on the GETs and COMPLIANCE:WRITE on the PUT, matching the convention used by ControlController and FrameworkAnchorController.

        me != null ? me.getUserId() : null);

@PutMapping("/{entityType}/{entityId}")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('COMPLIANCE','WRITE')")
public List<ControlLinkResponse> set(@PathVariable String entityType, @PathVariable Long entityId,

Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/policy/service/PolicyService.java:447-480 Effort S Risk CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — integrity of attestation-of-record

Description

PolicyService.attest(id, evidenceRef) and decline(id, reason) load the attestation by (id, org) and flip its status to ATTESTED/DECLINED, but they never verify that the authenticated caller is the user named in PolicyAttestation.userUsername (the assignee). Combined with the controller's isAuthenticated()-only gate, any logged-in user in the tenant can complete or decline an attestation that was assigned to a different employee. The attested record (who confirmed they read and accepted the policy, with attestedAt timestamp and evidence) is then attributed to the original assignee, not the actor who actually pressed the button.

Root cause

No identity binding between the authenticated principal and the attestation's assignee (userUsername); authorization is reduced to 'authenticated + same tenant'.

Evidence / proof
public PolicyAttestation attest(Long id, String evidenceRef) {
    PolicyAttestation a = attestations.findByIdAndOrganisationId(id, org())
        .orElseThrow(...);
    if (!"PENDING".equals(a.getStatus())) throw ...;
    a.setStatus("ATTESTED");
    a.setAttestedAt(LocalDateTime.now());
    // <-- no check that current principal == a.getUserUsername()
    ...
}

Real-world impact

Attestation-of-record is a compliance artefact (proof an employee read/accepted a policy). A user can falsely complete attestations on behalf of colleagues, producing fraudulent acceptance records and false coverage in the policy aggregate KPIs — a repudiation and audit-integrity problem for SAMA/NCA policy governance.

Reproduction

1. Admin assigns attestation A to user 'alice' (PENDING). 2. User 'bob' (any role) calls POST /api/policy/attestations/{A}/attest. 3. Response 200; the record shows ATTESTED with userUsername='alice' and attestedAt=now, even though bob acted.

Resolution

Bind the action to the assignee: compare the authenticated principal's username/id to a.getUserUsername() and reject (403) when they differ, unless the caller holds an explicit compliance-admin override. Record the actual actor separately (updatedBy) for forensics.

▼ Before (vulnerable)

    a.setStatus("ATTESTED");
    a.setAttestedAt(LocalDateTime.now());
    ...
}

MediumSEC-CVE-002Spring Security Web 6.5.5 — HTTP response headers may not be written (security policy bypass & information disclosure)
✎ AdjustedSecurityVulnerable & Outdated Components (A06)▾
Adversarial verification: adjusted (severity Critical→Medium) — Version confirmed: built jar bundles spring-security-web-6.5.5.jar (and spring-security-config-6.5.5.jar), managed by Spring Boot parent 3.5.6. The cited advisory class — 'HTTP response (security) headers may not be written' — is a real documented Spring Security issue. But VMware/Broadcom rate this class Moderate, and the practical impact is weakened security headers (e.g. CSP/HSTS occasionally not emitted) leading to defence-in-depth degradation / minor information disclosure, not a direct 'security policy bypass' enabling compromise. Marking Critical is unjustified. 6.5.5 is also a recent release. Real but Medium.
Location tss-grc-backend/pom.xml:8-15 Effort M Risk 9.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N) — CVE-2026-22732
{'file': 'tss-grc-backend/pom.xml', 'lines': '8-15', 'note': 'spring-boot-starter-parent BOM manages the Spring Security version'}
{'file': 'tss-grc-backend/pom.xml', 'lines': '58-61', 'note': 'spring-boot-starter-security pulls in spring-security-web transitively'}

Description

spring-security-web 6.5.5 is affected by CVE-2026-22732 (CWE-425, CVSS 9.1): when servlet applications specify HTTP response headers via Spring Security and rely on the default lazy header-writing, there is a possibility that security-relevant HTTP headers are never written to the response, leading to a security policy bypass and information disclosure.

Root cause

Spring Security version is managed by the spring-boot-starter-parent BOM (pom.xml lines 8-15, Boot 3.5.6 pins Spring Security 6.5.5), which predates the 6.5.9 fix.

Evidence / proof
Trivy: {"VulnerabilityID": "CVE-2026-22732", "PkgName": "org.springframework.security:spring-security-web", "InstalledVersion": "6.5.5", "FixedVersion": "6.5.9, 7.0.4", "Severity": "CRITICAL"}.

Real-world impact

Security headers (e.g. cache-control, frame options, CSP) configured through Spring Security may silently fail to be written, bypassing the application's intended security policy and disclosing protected information — high risk for a security platform whose own headers harden the bilingual GRC UI and API.

Reproduction

Run `trivy fs --scanners vuln tss-grc-backend/pom.xml`; CVE-2026-22732 reports CRITICAL against spring-security-web 6.5.5. `mvn dependency:tree` confirms spring-security-web:6.5.5 is pulled by spring-boot-starter-security.

Resolution

Upgrade spring-boot-starter-parent to 3.5.14 (which pins Spring Security >= 6.5.9/6.5.10) or override <spring-security.version>6.5.10</spring-security.version> in <properties>. Re-scan to confirm spring-security-web and spring-security-core resolve to >= 6.5.10.

▲ After (fixed)

MediumSEC-CVE-003Microsoft SQL Server JDBC Driver 12.8.1.jre11 — improper input validation enables spoofing (CVE-2025-59250)
✎ AdjustedSecurityVulnerable & Outdated Components (A06)▾
Adversarial verification: adjusted (severity High→Medium) — PARTIALLY CONFIRMED. pom.xml line 32 declares mssql.version = 12.8.1.jre11 and lines 112-116 use it, so the vulnerable version claim is accurate; CVE-2025-59250 is a real Microsoft mssql-jdbc improper-input-validation/spoofing issue affecting this version (fixed in 12.10.1/13.2.1). It is a legitimate Vulnerable-&-Outdated-Components (A06) hygiene finding and the dependency should be bumped. However, the exploit precondition is a malicious or MITM SQL Server endpoint: the JDBC URL, host and credentials are server-side and operator-controlled (application-dev.yml/prod externalised secrets), not attacker-influenceable, so there is no direct user-facing attack surface. The CVSS for this class of spoofing CVE sits in the medium band and real-world exploitability in this single-trusted-DB deployment is low. Downgrading from High to Medium — valid patch obligation, limited practical risk.

Run `trivy fs --scanners vuln tss-grc-backend/pom.xml`; CVE-2026-22751 and CVE-2026-22746 report against spring-security-core 6.5.5.

Resolution

Upgrade spring-boot-starter-parent to 3.5.14 or override <spring-security.version>6.5.10</spring-security.version> in <properties> (covers SEC-CVE-002 and this finding). Re-scan to confirm spring-security-core resolves to >= 6.5.10.

Location tss-grc-ui-v2/package-lock.json:2048-2062 Effort S Risk 6.6 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N/E:U) — CVE-2026-40181
{'file': 'tss-grc-ui-v2/package-lock.json', 'lines': '2048-2062', 'note': 'react-router 6.30.3 locked entry'}
{'file': 'tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json', 'lines': '21', 'note': 'react-router-dom ^6.28.0 direct dependency pulls react-router 6.30.3 transitively'}

Description

react-router 6.30.3 is affected by CVE-2026-40181 (CWE-601, CVSS 6.6): URLs passed to the redirect function whose path starts with // are reinterpreted as protocol-relative URLs, triggering an open redirect to an external domain. Affects versions 6.7.0-6.30.3 and 7.0.0-7.14.0 (Framework/Data modes; not Declarative <BrowserRouter>).

Root cause

react-router is locked at 6.30.3 in tss-grc-ui-v2/package-lock.json (lines 2048-2062), pulled transitively by the direct dependency react-router-dom ^6.28.0 declared in tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json line 21. 6.30.3 is below the 6.30.4 fix.

Evidence / proof
Trivy: {"VulnerabilityID": "CVE-2026-40181", "PkgName": "react-router", "InstalledVersion": "6.30.3", "FixedVersion": "7.14.1, 6.30.4", "Severity": "MEDIUM"}. package-lock.json line 2049: "version": "6.30.3".

Real-world impact

If the React UI returns a redirect built from user-controlled input, an attacker can craft a // path to redirect victims to an external malicious domain (phishing / token theft), since impact depends on the app's pre-redirect validation. Note the same CVE also affects react-router 6.30.3 in TSS-Theme/package-lock.json (line 1611-1625).

Reproduction

Run `trivy fs --scanners vuln tss-grc-ui-v2/package-lock.json`; CVE-2026-40181 reports MEDIUM against react-router 6.30.3.

Resolution

Bump react-router-dom to ^6.30.4 in tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json (pulls react-router 6.30.4) and run `npm install` to refresh the lockfile. Re-scan to confirm react-router resolves to >= 6.30.4. Apply the same bump to TSS-Theme if it ships to production.

▲ After (fixed)

MediumSEC-ESG-002Separation-of-duties controls (CAPA verifier ≠ owner, evidence approver) are enforced against client-supplied name strings, not the authenticated principal
SecurityBroken Access Control / Business Logic (A01) — CWE-639 / CWE-602▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/sust/capa/service/CorrectiveActionService.java:151-161 Effort M Risk CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — bypass of segregation-of-duties / self-approval
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/sust/capa/controller/CorrectiveActionController.java:95-100
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/sust/evidence/service/SustainabilityEvidenceService.java:105-116
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/sust/evidence/controller/SustainabilityEvidenceController.java:62-66

Description

The corrective-action 'Rule A' separation-of-duties control rejects verification only when the supplied verifier name equals the stored ownerName. Both the verifier identity and the owner identity are free-text strings supplied by the client (the verify endpoint reads body.get("verifiedBy"); ownerName came from an earlier client-supplied create/update body). The check is a case-insensitive string compare, never tied to the authenticated user (GrcUserDetails). The same pattern applies to evidence approval, which records approvedBy from body.get("approvedBy") rather than the principal. An actor can therefore self-verify their own corrective action simply by passing any verifier string that differs from ownerName (e.g. add a space, change case differently, or supply an arbitrary colleague's name), and can attribute an approval to anyone. Combined with SEC-ESG-001 (no role enforcement), the 'four-eyes' guarantee these endpoints advertise is cosmetic.

Root cause

Actor identity for SoD-sensitive actions is taken from the request body instead of the authenticated SecurityContext / GrcUserDetails. The control compares two attacker-controllable values.

Evidence / proof
CorrectiveActionService.transition(...):
  case "VERIFIED" -> {
      if (verifierName == null || verifierName.isBlank())
          throw new IllegalArgumentException("Verification requires a verifier name.");
      // Rule A — separation of duties.
      if (cur.getOwnerName() != null
          && verifierName.trim().equalsIgnoreCase(cur.getOwnerName().trim()))
          throw new IllegalArgumentException("Verifier must differ from owner (Rule A ...).");
      cur.setVerifiedBy(verifierName);   // <-- client-supplied string, not the principal
  }

Real-world impact

Self-approval / self-verification of sustainability corrective actions and evidence, defeating the segregation-of-duties control that regulators (CMA, SAMA) expect on remediation sign-off. Approval/verification audit attribution is forgeable, breaking non-repudiation.

Reproduction

1. As any authenticated user, create a CAPA with ownerName="Alice" and attach evidenceRef. 2. POST /{id}/start, /{id}/complete. 3. POST /{id}/verify with body {"verifiedBy":"Alice "} (trailing space) or {"verifiedBy":"Bob"} — the same person verifies their own action; the row records VERIFIED by the supplied name with no link to the real caller.

Resolution

Derive the actor from the authenticated principal: inject @AuthenticationPrincipal GrcUserDetails and set verifiedBy/approvedBy from its user id/name. Enforce Rule A against the principal's user id versus the stored owner user id (store owner as a user id, not a display string). Reject the action if the principal equals the owner. Remove verifiedBy/approvedBy from the request body so attribution cannot be forged.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
public CorrectiveAction verify(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody(required=false) Map<String,String> body) {
    String verifier = body == null ? null : body.get("verifiedBy");
    return service.transition(id, "VERIFIED", verifier);
}
▲ After (fixed)
public CorrectiveAction verify(@PathVariable Long id, @AuthenticationPrincipal GrcUserDetails me) {
    return service.transition(id, "VERIFIED", me); // service compares me.getUserId() to owner userId
}

Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/sust/evidence/controller/SustainabilityEvidenceController.java:49-53 Effort L Risk CVSS 5.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — caller can set server-controlled lifecycle/attribution fields at create
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/sust/evidence/service/SustainabilityEvidenceService.java:62-72
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/sust/ghg/controller/GhgEmissionRecordController.java:69-79
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/sust/cma/controller/CmaDisclosureController.java:66-76
