Description

Every create/update endpoint in the Sustainability slices binds the persistent JPA @Entity directly as the @RequestBody (e.g. SustainabilityEvidence, GhgEmissionRecord, CmaDisclosure, MaterialTopic, SgiCommitment, CorrectiveAction) with no DTO and no @Valid. The services reset id and organisationId server-side (good — so tenant/identity cannot be forged), but they do NOT scrub the remaining server-controlled lifecycle and attribution columns. On create, the caller can pre-set approvalStatus/status (e.g. submit an evidence row directly as APPROVED, or a GHG record as APPROVED), approvedBy/approvedAt/reviewerName/verified/verificationDate, createdBy/createdAt, supersedesId, etc., bypassing the intended state machine and approval gates. Unlike the AI governance and climate sub-packages, which use dedicated request DTOs (MlModelRequest, FinancedEmissionsRequest) with @Valid + @NotBlank/@Size constraints and an explicit applyFields() whitelist, the Sustainability slices have no such boundary.

Root cause

Controllers expose the JPA entity as the API contract and rely on the service to selectively copy fields on UPDATE only; CREATE persists the inbound entity almost verbatim (after id/org reset), so any column the entity exposes is mass-assignable on creation.

Evidence / proof
SustainabilityEvidenceController.java:
  @PostMapping
  @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
  public ResponseEntity<SustainabilityEvidence> create(@RequestBody SustainabilityEvidence req) { ... }

SustainabilityEvidenceService.create():
  req.setId(null); req.setOrganisationId(org());
  if (req.getApprovalStatus()==null||blank) req.setApprovalStatus("PENDING_REVIEW");
  // approvedBy / approvedAt / reviewerName / supersedesId from the body are persisted as-is

Real-world impact

A caller can create records that skip the review/approval workflow (e.g. evidence born APPROVED with an arbitrary approvedBy, or a GHG/CMA record born APPROVED), forging approval attribution and defeating the lifecycle gates the module enforces on transitions. Audit columns (createdBy) are also client-settable. This compounds SEC-ESG-001 and SEC-ESG-002.

Reproduction

POST /api/sustainability/evidence with body {"titleEn":"x","approvalStatus":"APPROVED","approvedBy":"CFO","confidentiality":"PUBLIC"} → 201, row persisted APPROVED/approvedBy=CFO without ever passing through the approve() workflow or any approver check.

Resolution

Introduce request DTOs for each create/update (as the climate and AI sub-packages already do) carrying only client-settable fields, annotate the controller params with @Valid and the DTO fields with Jakarta constraints (@NotBlank/@Size/@Min). In the service, force initial lifecycle status and null out approval/attribution/audit fields on create regardless of input; set approvedBy/createdBy from the authenticated principal. Never accept the entity as the wire contract.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<SustainabilityEvidence> create(@RequestBody SustainabilityEvidence req) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(service.create(req));
}
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping
public ResponseEntity<SustainabilityEvidence> create(@Valid @RequestBody EvidenceCreateRequest req) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(service.create(req)); // service maps only safe fields,
}                                                                // forces approvalStatus=PENDING_REVIEW

MediumSEC-EVD-002Evidence item create accepts arbitrary client-supplied status — four-eyes Segregation-of-Duties and review workflow can be fully bypassed
✎ AdjustedSecurityBusiness Logic / Broken Access Control (A04/A01)▾
Adversarial verification: adjusted (severity High→Medium) — Real but severity overstated. EvidenceItemCreateRequest has a status field and create()→applyRequest() does `if (req.status() != null) item.setStatus(req.status())` with no validation that the value is a legal starting state, so an EVIDENCE:WRITE user can mint an item directly in APPROVED, bypassing the DRAFT→PENDING_REVIEW→APPROVED state machine and the EvidenceReviewController review record. However the 'four-eyes Segregation-of-Duties' framing is weak: the legitimate approve path (EvidenceItemController /approve) is itself only @PreAuthorize(hasPermission('EVIDENCE','WRITE')) — the same permission as create — so a single WRITE user can already approve their own evidence through the normal flow. The status-injection therefore adds an integrity/validation gap (skips the review row and transition guards) but not a fundamentally new privilege, and it still requires EVIDENCE:WRITE and is org-scoped. Net incremental impact is Medium, not High.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceItemService.java:369-384 Effort S Risk CVSS 7.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — a single user with EVIDENCE:WRITE self-approves compliance evidence, defeating the SoD control
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceItemService.java:383
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceItemService.java:156-168
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceItemService.java:186-201
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/controller/EvidenceItemController.java:68-74

Description

`EvidenceItemService.create()` calls `applyRequest()`, which blindly copies the client-supplied `status` onto a new entity: `if (req.status() != null) item.setStatus(req.status());` (line 383). There is no validation against `ITEM_STATUSES` and no transition-guard. The system deliberately enforces Segregation of Duties only on the `approve()` transition (lines 194-199: the creator may not approve their own evidence). Because `create` lets the caller set `status` directly, a user can `POST /api/v1/evidence/items` with `{"status":"APPROVED"}` and obtain an APPROVED evidence item without ever passing through submit -> review -> approve, never triggering the SoD check or producing an `EVIDENCE_APPROVED` review trail. The same hole lets the create path also seed EXPIRED/REJECTED or any free-text status. `update()` shares the same `applyRequest` and can re-set status on an existing item, again skipping `validateTransition`.

Root cause

Mass-assignment of a workflow-controlling field (`status`) on create/update, with the state-machine guard (`validateTransition`) and the SoD guard living only on the dedicated transition methods (`submitForReview`/`approve`/`reject`). The DTO exposes `status` as a freely settable input field.

Evidence / proof
private void applyRequest(EvidenceItem item, EvidenceItemCreateRequest req) {
    ...
    item.setFileName(req.fileName());
    if (req.status() != null) item.setStatus(req.status());   // <-- no validation, no SoD
}

// approve() — the SoD guard that create() sidesteps entirely:
if (currentUser != null && currentUser.equals(item.getCreatedBy())) {
    throw new BusinessRuleException("Segregation of duties: you cannot approve evidence you submitted...");
}

Real-world impact

Defeats the regulatory four-eyes / SoD control (ECC 2-3, ISO 27001 A.5.3, SAMA) the platform advertises for evidence approval. A single insider with EVIDENCE:WRITE can manufacture self-approved compliance evidence, which fulfils linked evidence-requests (`fulfilRequest`) and feeds coverage rollups, audit packs and attestations — directly enabling compliance fraud and undermining the integrity of every downstream assurance artefact.

Reproduction

1. Authenticate as a user with EVIDENCE:WRITE (e.g. `riskmanager`).
2. `curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
   -d '{"titleEn":"Self-approved control evidence","evidenceType":"DOCUMENT","status":"APPROVED"}' \
   http://localhost:8084/api/v1/evidence/items`
3. Response shows the item created directly in status APPROVED; no EvidenceReview row, no SoD check, no EVIDENCE_APPROVED transition event — yet the item now counts as approved evidence in the matrix and stats.

Resolution

On create, ignore any client `status` and force the canonical initial state (`DRAFT`); only allow an explicit non-DRAFT seed for trusted system/import flows behind a separate permission. On update, never mutate `status` via `applyRequest` — route all status changes exclusively through `transitionStatus`/`approve`/`reject` so `validateTransition` and the SoD guard always run. Validate any accepted status against `ITEM_STATUSES`.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
private void applyRequest(EvidenceItem item, EvidenceItemCreateRequest req) {
    item.setTitleEn(req.titleEn());
    ...
    item.setFileName(req.fileName());
    if (req.status() != null) item.setStatus(req.status());
}
▲ After (fixed)
private void applyRequest(EvidenceItem item, EvidenceItemCreateRequest req) {
    item.setTitleEn(req.titleEn());
    ...
    item.setFileName(req.fileName());
    // status is workflow-controlled: new items start DRAFT; existing items keep
    // their current status. All changes go through transitionStatus()/approve().
    if (item.getStatus() == null) item.setStatus("DRAFT");
}

SecurityBroken Access Control (A01)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/chain/controller/EvidenceChainController.java:24-40 Effort S Risk CVSS 5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — any authenticated user reads chain reports and triggers chain-status writes without EVIDENCE permission
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/chain/controller/EvidenceChainController.java:36-40
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/chain/service/EvidenceChainService.java:71-173

Description

Every endpoint of the evidence chain-of-custody controller uses `@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")` rather than the module guard `hasPermission('EVIDENCE','READ')`/`'WRITE'` used by the rest of the evidence module. The sibling `EvidenceItemController`/`EvidenceMatrixController` correctly gate reads on EVIDENCE:READ. More importantly, `POST /api/evidence/chain/{evidenceId}/verify` is a state-mutating operation: `verifyChain` runs `UPDATE evidence.evidence_versions ... SET chain_status, chain_verified_by, chain_break_reason` and `UPDATE evidence.evidence_items SET chain_status, chain_last_verified_by ...` (service lines 138-168). So any authenticated principal — including users with zero evidence permissions — can trigger verification writes and stamp themselves as `chain_verified_by`/`chain_last_verified_by` on tamper-evidence integrity records. The head queries ARE org-scoped (`WHERE id=:id AND organisation_id=:org`), so this is in-tenant BFLA, not cross-tenant; native queries are fully parameterised (no SQLi).

Root cause

Authorization for this sub-package was written to a weaker standard (presence of authentication) than the module convention (permission on EVIDENCE), and a write endpoint was placed behind the same weak guard as reads.

Evidence / proof
@PostMapping("/{evidenceId}/verify")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ChainReport verify(@PathVariable Long evidenceId, Authentication auth) {
    return service.verifyChain(evidenceId, userIdOf(auth));
}
// service.verifyChain executes UPDATE ... SET chain_status / chain_verified_by ...

Real-world impact

A user with no evidence rights can read chain-of-custody reports (which version content hashes are valid/broken) for any evidence in their tenant and can write to the integrity ledger (chain_status, verified_by). This pollutes the tamper-evidence audit trail and lets a low-privileged actor overwrite the recorded verifier identity on regulated WORM records.

Reproduction

1. Authenticate as a user with NO evidence permission.
2. Read: `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:8084/api/evidence/chain/15` — returns the full chain report.
3. Mutate: `curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:8084/api/evidence/chain/15/verify` — the chain_status/chain_verified_by columns are updated and the caller is stamped as verifier.

Resolution

Replace `isAuthenticated()` with `hasPermission('EVIDENCE','READ')` on the two GET endpoints and `hasPermission('EVIDENCE','WRITE')` (or a dedicated EVIDENCE:VERIFY) on the verify endpoint, matching the rest of the evidence module.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@GetMapping
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public List<ItemSummary> list(...) { ... }

@PostMapping("/{evidenceId}/verify")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ChainReport verify(@PathVariable Long evidenceId, Authentication auth) { ... }
▲ After (fixed)
@GetMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('EVIDENCE','READ')")
public List<ItemSummary> list(...) { ... }

@PostMapping("/{evidenceId}/verify")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('EVIDENCE','WRITE')")
public ChainReport verify(@PathVariable Long evidenceId, Authentication auth) { ... }

Description

`GET /api/board-pack/packs` (list) and `GET /api/board-pack/packs/{id}` (get) are annotated only `@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")`, while the write endpoints correctly require `PLATFORM_ADMIN`/`CRO`/`REPORTING_WRITE`. A BoardPack aggregates the most sensitive material in the platform — `riskSummaryJson`, `appetiteBreachesJson`, `auditEngagementsJson`, `incidentsJson`, `pdplSummaryJson`, `ccmSummaryJson`, `slaSummaryJson`, plus board audience and review comments (see `BoardPackService.create`, lines 67-75). The service is correctly tenant-scoped (`findByOrganisationId...`), so this is in-tenant over-exposure: any authenticated user — including roles with no reporting/governance rights — can enumerate and read every board pack in their organisation.

Root cause

Read authorization was set to bare authentication instead of a reporting/governance role or REPORTING:READ permission, inconsistent with the write-side guards on the same controller and with the read guards used by the audit-committee and pivot controllers.

Evidence / proof
@GetMapping
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public List<BoardPackDto> list() { return service.listForOrg(); }

@GetMapping("/{id}")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public BoardPackDto get(@PathVariable String id) { return service.get(id); }

Real-world impact

Confidential board-level governance reporting (consolidated risk posture, appetite breaches, open audit engagements, incidents, privacy and SLA summaries) leaks to any logged-in user, breaching need-to-know and the confidentiality expectations of SAMA/CMA corporate-governance reporting.

Reproduction

1. Authenticate as a low-privilege user (e.g. `auditor`).
2. `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:8084/api/board-pack/packs` — returns the list of board packs for the tenant.
3. `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:8084/api/board-pack/packs/BP-2026-XYZ` — returns the full board pack including all sensitive *_Json sections.

Resolution

Gate the read endpoints with a board/governance-appropriate guard mirroring the write side and the audit-committee controller, e.g. `@PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN','CRO','BOARD_MEMBER','AUDIT_COMMITTEE_CHAIR','AUDIT_COMMITTEE_MEMBER','COMPANY_SECRETARY') or hasAuthority('REPORTING_READ')")`.

private static final String READ_GUARD = "hasAnyRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN','CRO','BOARD_MEMBER'," +
    "'AUDIT_COMMITTEE_CHAIR','AUDIT_COMMITTEE_MEMBER','COMPANY_SECRETARY') or hasAuthority('REPORTING_READ')";

tss-grc-ui/assets/js/auth.js:9-27
tss-grc-ui/login.html:287-288

Description

Both frontends persist the bearer access token in Web Storage (`sessionStorage`), which is fully readable by any JavaScript running on the origin. v2: auth.ts stores under key `grc.accessToken` (getAccessToken reads `sessionStorage.getItem(TOKEN_KEY)`); api.ts:53 also writes the refreshed token straight to sessionStorage. v1: auth.js stores under `grc_jwt`; login.html:287 does the same. The refresh token is correctly kept in an HttpOnly cookie (good), but the access token is not. Any successful XSS (e.g. SEC-FE-001) can read the access token with a single `sessionStorage.getItem(...)` call and replay it against the API as a full bearer credential (1h lifetime in dev / 15m prod). This is the standard sessionStorage-vs-memory trade-off; it is acceptable only when XSS is otherwise fully controlled, which is not the case for the legacy UI.

Root cause

Design choice to persist the access token in Web Storage for convenience across reloads, rather than holding it only in a JS closure / in-memory variable and relying on the HttpOnly refresh cookie to re-mint it on reload.

Evidence / proof
auth.ts:15 `return sessionStorage.getItem(TOKEN_KEY);` ; auth.ts:25 `sessionStorage.setItem(TOKEN_KEY, accessToken);` ; api.ts:53 `sessionStorage.setItem('grc.accessToken', newToken);` ; auth.js:13 `return sessionStorage.getItem(this._TOKEN_KEY);`

Real-world impact

Turns any XSS from a nuisance into a full session/account takeover and (because the JWT carries the `org` tenant claim) a cross-tenant compromise vector. The token can be exfiltrated and replayed from anywhere until it expires.

Reproduction

With any XSS foothold (see SEC-FE-001), execute `sessionStorage.getItem('grc.accessToken')` (v2) or `sessionStorage.getItem('grc_jwt')` (v1) and POST it to an attacker endpoint; then call any `/api/v1/...` endpoint with `Authorization: Bearer <stolen>`.

Resolution

Hold the access token only in a module-scoped in-memory variable (JS closure), and rely on the existing HttpOnly refresh cookie + `/api/auth/refresh` to silently re-mint it on page reload (the v2 api.ts already has the refresh plumbing). This removes the token from any persistent JS-readable store, dramatically shrinking the XSS blast radius. If reload-survival is required, prefer a non-extractable approach (e.g. short-lived token in memory, refresh-on-load). Pair with strict CSP and the SEC-FE-001 fix.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
const TOKEN_KEY = 'grc.accessToken';
export function getAccessToken(): string | null {
  return sessionStorage.getItem(TOKEN_KEY);
}
export function setSession(accessToken: string, user: UserInfo): void {
  sessionStorage.setItem(TOKEN_KEY, accessToken);
  sessionStorage.setItem(USER_KEY, JSON.stringify(user));
}
▲ After (fixed)
let accessTokenInMemory: string | null = null;
export function getAccessToken(): string | null {
  return accessTokenInMemory;
}
export function setSession(accessToken: string, user: UserInfo): void {
  accessTokenInMemory = accessToken;            // not persisted to Web Storage
  sessionStorage.setItem(USER_KEY, JSON.stringify(user)); // non-secret display data only
}
// On boot, call /api/auth/refresh (HttpOnly cookie) to repopulate accessTokenInMemory.
References: CWE-922: Insecure Storage of Sensitive Information · OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures · OWASP JWT / Token Storage guidance (avoid localStorage/sessionStorage for tokens)
MediumSEC-FE-003Open redirect via unvalidated `redirect` parameter on legacy login page
SecurityURL Redirection to Untrusted Site / Open Redirect (A01:2021)▾
Location tss-grc-ui/login.html:181-184 Effort S Risk CVSS 4.7 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — phishing / token-relay aid; not direct code execution
tss-grc-ui/login.html:181-184
tss-grc-ui/login.html:290-291

Description

The legacy login page reads the `redirect` query parameter and passes it directly to `window.location.replace(redirect)` with no validation that it is a same-origin relative path. This happens in two places: the already-logged-in fast path (line 183-184) and the post-login success path (line 290-291). An attacker can craft `https://app/login.html?redirect=https://evil.example/login` (or the scheme-relative `redirect=//evil.example`) so that after a victim authenticates they are silently bounced to an attacker-controlled look-alike page. The v2 React login (tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/LoginPage.tsx:22-24) does this correctly — it only honours `next` if it `startsWith('/')` and not `'//'` — which confirms the team knows the mitigation but did not apply it to the legacy page. `javascript:` payloads are generally neutralised by `location.replace`, so this is an open-redirect (phishing) issue rather than direct XSS.

Root cause

User-controlled redirect target used in a navigation sink without an allowlist / same-origin check.

Evidence / proof
login.html:183-184 `const redirect = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('redirect') || '/dashboard.html'; window.location.replace(redirect);` (identical at 290-291).

Real-world impact

Enables convincing credential-phishing: a link to the legitimate, trusted login origin redirects the user to an attacker page immediately after they log in, where session/credentials can be harvested. Also useful in OAuth/token-relay chains.

Reproduction

1. Send victim `https://<app-host>/login.html?redirect=https://evil.example/`. 2. Victim logs in on the genuine site. 3. login.html:291 runs `window.location.replace('https://evil.example/')` and the victim lands on the attacker site still trusting the flow.

Resolution

Validate the redirect target is a same-origin relative path before navigating — exactly as the v2 LoginPage already does. Reject anything not starting with a single `/` (and not `//`).

▼ Before (vulnerable)
const redirect = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('redirect') || '/dashboard.html';
window.location.replace(redirect);
▲ After (fixed)
const raw = new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('redirect');
const redirect = (raw && raw.startsWith('/') && !raw.startsWith('//')) ? raw : '/dashboard.html';
window.location.replace(redirect);
References: CWE-601: URL Redirection to Untrusted Site (Open Redirect) · OWASP A01:2021 Broken Access Control · OWASP Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards Cheat Sheet
MediumSEC-FIN-003Tenant AML officer can inject/poison platform-global sanctions lists (OFAC/UN/EU) consumed by every tenant
SecurityBroken Access Control / Improper Authorization (A01, CWE-639)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/aml/sanctions/service/SanctionsListService.java:156-194 Effort S Risk CVSS ~6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:N/I:H/A:N) — cross-tenant data-integrity poisoning of shared screening lists
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/aml/sanctions/service/SanctionsListService.java:103-121
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/aml/sanctions/service/SanctionsListService.java:129-154
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/aml/sanctions/repository/SanctionsListRepository.java:35-49
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/aml/sanctions/controller/SanctionsScreeningController.java:115-125

Description

Platform-global sanctions lists are stored with organisation_id IS NULL and are visible to (and screened by) every tenant via findVisibleTo / findActiveVisibleTo. SanctionsListService.update() deliberately blocks edits to global lists from a tenant context ('Cannot edit platform-global list ... from tenant context'). However bulkImportEntries() and refresh() use the same loadOrThrow()->findByIdVisibleTo() lookup, which returns global lists to any tenant, and neither method applies the same org-NULL guard. A tenant AML_OFFICER (the role required by POST /lists/{id}/entries/bulk-import) can therefore append arbitrary entries to a global OFAC/UN/EU list. Imported rows take row.setOrganisationId(l.getOrganisationId()) = NULL, so they become globally visible. This lets one tenant inject false sanctions entries (causing false-positive hits and operational blocking for all other tenants) — or, if combined with future delete/refresh-overwrite logic, suppress entries.

Root cause

Inconsistent authorization across write paths: the org-NULL global-list guard exists only in update(), not in bulkImportEntries() or refresh(). findByIdVisibleTo intentionally returns shared global lists, so 'visible' is wrongly treated as 'writable'.

Evidence / proof
update(): `if (l.getOrganisationId() == null) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("Cannot edit platform-global list ..."); }`. bulkImportEntries(): `SanctionsList l = loadOrThrow(req.listId()); ... row.setOrganisationId(l.getOrganisationId()); entryRepo.save(row);` with NO org-NULL check. loadOrThrow -> `listRepo.findByIdVisibleTo(id, org())` which matches `l.organisationId IS NULL OR l.organisationId = :orgId`.

Real-world impact

Cross-tenant integrity compromise of a financial-crime control: a single tenant can degrade sanctions-screening accuracy for all tenants (mass false positives blocking onboarding, or noise masking true hits), violating SAMA AML/CFT obligations.

Reproduction

1) As AML_OFFICER in tenant 2, GET /api/v1/aml/sanctions/lists, note a global list id (organisationId null, e.g. OFAC). 2) POST /api/v1/aml/sanctions/lists/{id}/entries/bulk-import with listId={id} and fabricated entries. 3) The entries persist with organisation_id NULL. 4) As any user in tenant 3, POST /checks against that list — fabricated entries now produce hits.

Resolution

Apply the same org-NULL guard in bulkImportEntries() and refresh(): only the platform admin (cross-tenant scope) may write to organisation_id IS NULL lists; tenant officers may write only to lists they own (l.getOrganisationId() != null && equals(org())).

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@Transactional
public EntryBulkImportResponse bulkImportEntries(EntryBulkImportRequest req) {
    SanctionsList l = loadOrThrow(req.listId());
    // ... saves entries with row.setOrganisationId(l.getOrganisationId());
}
▲ After (fixed)
@Transactional
public EntryBulkImportResponse bulkImportEntries(EntryBulkImportRequest req) {
    SanctionsList l = loadOrThrow(req.listId());
    if (l.getOrganisationId() == null) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException(
            "Cannot import into platform-global list " + l.getListCode() + " from tenant context");
    }
    // ... rest unchanged
}
References: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key · OWASP A01:2021 Broken Access Control · OWASP API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization

Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/scm/fourthparty/service/FourthPartyExposureService.java:58-67 Effort M Risk CVSS ~5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:L) — workflow/state-field tampering and soft-delete via unfiltered create
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/scm/fourthparty/controller/FourthPartyExposureController.java:45-55

tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/common/tenant/TenantContext.java:74-112

Description

Several endpoints bind the JPA @Entity directly as the @RequestBody and persist it. FourthPartyExposureController.create(@RequestBody FourthPartyExposure req) and SupplierResilienceTestController.create(@RequestBody SupplierResilienceTest req) pass the client-supplied entity to repo.save() after only overriding organisationId and nulling id. The FourthPartyExposure entity exposes writable setters for workflow/state and audit columns — status, concentrationRisk, isDeleted, isActive, lastValidatedBy, validatorName, createdBy, updatedBy, rowVersion. A caller can therefore POST a record pre-set to status=VALIDATED with an arbitrary validatorName (bypassing the validate() workflow step), or set isDeleted=1 / isActive=0 at creation. The validate() invariant check only constrains dependencyType/downstreamCriticality/status enum membership — it does not stop status=VALIDATED or audit-field spoofing. organisationId itself is overridden so cross-tenant create is not possible, and update() copies a field whitelist so update is safe; the exposure is on create. Note also that the documented platform backstop (TenantWriteGuardInterceptor / TenantContext.allowCrossTenantWrite) is explicitly NOT wired in yet (see TenantContext lines 74-81), so there is no persistence-layer net catching entity mass-assignment.

Root cause

Controllers accept and persist mutable persistence entities instead of constrained request DTOs; no @Valid; the create path does repo.save(req) on the attacker-controlled object graph.

Evidence / proof
FourthPartyExposureService.create: `validate(req); req.setOrganisationId(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant()); req.setId(null); FourthPartyExposure saved = repo.save(req);`. Entity has `private String status = "DISCOVERED"; private String validatorName; private Short isDeleted = 0;` all with Lombok @Setter. Controller: `public ResponseEntity<FourthPartyExposure> create(@RequestBody FourthPartyExposure req)`.

Real-world impact

Integrity tampering of third-party-risk records: fabricated validation status/validator attribution, immediate soft-deletion or deactivation at create, and forged created_by/row_version audit metadata — eroding the auditability the GRC platform exists to provide.

Reproduction

1) POST /api/scm/fourth-party with body {"primaryVendorName":"x","fourthPartyName":"y","dependencyType":"SOFTWARE","downstreamCriticality":"HIGH","serviceDescriptionEn":"z","status":"VALIDATED","validatorName":"CISO","isDeleted":0,"createdBy":999}. 2) The persisted row reflects the attacker-chosen status/validatorName/createdBy.

Resolution

Bind a constrained request DTO (only client-settable fields) for create/update and map server-side; never expose status/concentrationRisk/isDeleted/isActive/createdBy/validatorName as inbound fields. Add @Valid. Wire the documented Hibernate TenantWriteGuardInterceptor as defence-in-depth.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ResponseEntity<FourthPartyExposure> create(@RequestBody FourthPartyExposure req) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(service.create(req));
}
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('SCM','WRITE')")
public ResponseEntity<FourthPartyExposureResponse> create(@Valid @RequestBody FourthPartyExposureCreateRequest req) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(FourthPartyExposureResponse.from(service.create(req)));
}
// service builds a fresh entity from the DTO and sets status=DISCOVERED, isDeleted=0 itself.

Description

POST /api/v1/workflow-submissions/{id}/review transitions a submission to APPROVED/REJECTED/CLOSED/UNDER_REVIEW but is guarded only by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). There is no role gate (e.g. reviewer/approver) and no check the caller is distinct from the submitter, so a user can approve their own submission. Reads/writes ARE org-scoped (repo.findByOrganisationIdAndId), so this is a same-tenant segregation-of-duties / BFLA issue rather than cross-tenant. Separately, the create endpoint (line 36-38) binds @RequestBody CreateBody with no @Valid; only manual null/blank checks in the service exist and payloadJson is stored unbounded/unparsed.

Root cause

Authorization for a state-changing review action is only 'authenticated'; no segregation-of-duties or approver role is enforced.

Evidence / proof
@PostMapping("/{id}/review") @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") public WorkflowSubmission review(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody ReviewBody body) { return service.review(id, body); }

Any authenticated tenant user can approve, reject or close any workflow submission in their organisation — including ones they themselves submitted — bypassing the reviewer/maker-checker control these submissions are meant to enforce (V127 seed rules route PDPL breaches, NCA incidents, above-appetite risk acceptances through this flow).

1. As any user, POST /api/v1/workflow-submissions to create a submission. 2. POST /api/v1/workflow-submissions/{id}/review with {"decision":"APPROVE"}. 3. Submission is APPROVED by its own author with no reviewer role required.

Resolution

Restrict /review to an approver/reviewer permission (e.g. hasPermission('WORKFLOW','APPROVE') or per-module reviewer roles), and reject self-review by comparing the submitter to the caller. Add @Valid + Jakarta constraints to CreateBody (size caps on titleEn/payloadJson, required fields) instead of relying on manual checks.

@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public WorkflowSubmission review(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody ReviewBody body) {

}
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping("/{id}/review")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('WORKFLOW','APPROVE') or hasRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN')")

                                 @RequestBody @Valid ReviewBody body,
                                 Authentication auth) {

}

Every endpoint in CommitteeController (the primary committee + meeting CRUD, including createCommittee, updateCommittee, dissolveCommittee, createMeeting, completeMeeting, approveMinutes, cancelMeeting) is guarded only by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). This is markedly weaker than — and inconsistent with — the sibling committee controllers (CommitteeResolutionController, CommitteeMeetingPapersController, CommitteeMemberRegistryController, CommitteeActionItemController, CommitteeCalendarController) which all require hasPermission('ADMIN','READ'|'WRITE'). The controller was not brought in line with the module's ADMIN:WRITE authorization convention; 'isAuthenticated()' grants every logged-in user (auditors, risk analysts, viewers) full write access to board/committee governance records.

MediumSEC-INT-003Outbound EDR/VM actions accept arbitrary host/asset IDs with no tenant-ownership check (cross-tenant containment / risk-acceptance)
SecurityBroken Object Level Authorization (A01)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/crowdstrike/service/CrowdStrikeOutboundService.java:70-134 Effort M Risk CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H) — applicable when one platform instance serves multiple tenants against one shared Falcon/Tenable
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/crowdstrike/controller/CrowdStrikeController.java:150-167

Description

containHost(hostId)/liftContainment(hostId)/hideHost(hostId) and Tenable recastSeverity/acceptRisk/removeRecast(pluginId, assetUuid) take the target identifier straight from the URL path/body and forward it to the single, globally-configured Falcon/Tenable instance. The services require a non-null TenantContext but never verify that the supplied hostId/assetUuid actually belongs to the calling tenant (there is no lookup against this tenant's known assets/detections). The integration credentials are platform-global config (one baseUrl + one credential pair), so when a single deployment serves more than one tenant they all share one upstream EDR/VM tenant. A SOC operator in tenant A can therefore isolate (network-quarantine) or un-isolate a host, or recast/accept-risk a finding, that belongs to tenant B simply by supplying B's host/asset id. Containment is a destructive, availability-impacting action.

Root cause

No binding between the tenant scope and the external object identifier. Authorization is purely functional (role can contain) with no object-level check that the host/asset is in the caller's tenant inventory; the upstream integration is shared across tenants.

Evidence / proof
public ContainmentResponse containHost(String falconHostId, String reasonText) {
    return runAction("CONTAIN_HOST", falconHostId, reasonText, () -> client.containHost(falconHostId, reasonText));
}
// runAction requires TenantContext != null but never checks falconHostId belongs to that tenant

Real-world impact

In a multi-tenant deployment sharing one Falcon/Tenable backend, a user can quarantine another tenant's production hosts (denial of service) or downgrade/accept-risk another tenant's vulnerabilities (integrity / compliance evasion). If each tenant maps 1:1 to its own integration instance the exposure is limited to intra-tenant BFLA; the audit trail records userId, which mitigates non-repudiation but not the action itself.

Reproduction

1. In a deployment where tenants A and B share one configured CrowdStrike instance, authenticate as tenant A SOC_TIER_2.
2. POST /api/v1/integrations/crowdstrike/contain/{hostId} with hostId = a Falcon device id owned by tenant B and any reason >0 chars.
3. The action is dispatched to the shared Falcon tenant and host B is isolated; no check confirmed host B belongs to tenant A.

Resolution

Before dispatching, resolve the target id against the calling tenant's own inventory (e.g. crowdstrike_detection_log / tenable_finding_log scoped by organisation_id, or an asset registry) and reject ids not owned by TenantContext. For genuinely multi-tenant deployments, also segregate upstream credentials per tenant so one tenant cannot act on another's upstream objects.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
public ContainmentResponse containHost(String falconHostId, String reasonText) {
    return runAction("CONTAIN_HOST", falconHostId, reasonText, () -> client.containHost(falconHostId, reasonText));
}
▲ After (fixed)
public ContainmentResponse containHost(String falconHostId, String reasonText) {
    Long orgId = TenantContext.getCurrentTenant();
    if (detectionLogRepo.findFirstByOrganisationIdAndFalconHostId(orgId, falconHostId).isEmpty())
        throw new AccessDeniedException("host not in this tenant's inventory");
    return runAction("CONTAIN_HOST", falconHostId, reasonText, () -> client.containHost(falconHostId, reasonText));
}

Description

recastSeverity/acceptRisk/removeRecast build the request path with IO_RECAST_PATH_FMT.formatted(assetUuid, pluginId) and pass the resulting string to RestClient .uri(url(path)). pluginId comes from the @PathVariable with no @Pattern (validatePluginId only checks non-blank), and assetUuid from the body has only @Size(max=80) with no character constraint (the /remove-recast RemoveRecastBody.assetUuid has no constraint at all). Because the values are concatenated raw into the URL path, a value such as a/../../session or one containing %2f / query-delimiter characters can traverse to a different Tenable API path or alter query semantics on the configured Tenable host. The base host is fixed by config so this is host-bounded path manipulation, not full SSRF, but it lets an authorized user reach Tenable endpoints other than the intended recast/accept-risk routes (e.g. read or mutate other workbench resources the API key can reach).

Root cause

Untrusted identifiers are placed into a URL path via String.format and a raw .uri(String) template instead of being validated against a strict format and passed as encoded URI variables.

Evidence / proof
return runOutbound("RECAST_SEVERITY", pluginId, assetUuid,
    assetUuid == null ? IO_RECAST_PATH_FMT.formatted("*", pluginId)
                      : IO_RECAST_PATH_FMT.formatted(assetUuid, pluginId), body);
// url(path): base + path  -> http.post().uri(url(path))   // pluginId/assetUuid unvalidated

Real-world impact

An authorized CISO/RISK_MANAGER can craft pluginId/assetUuid to redirect the outbound call to unintended Tenable API paths under the same host, using the platform's privileged API key — expanding the effective surface of the integration credential beyond recast/accept-risk and bypassing the justification/audit semantics those routes assume.

Reproduction

1. Authenticate as RISK_MANAGER.
2. POST /api/v1/integrations/tenable/recast/{pluginId} where pluginId = '1/../../scans' (URL-encoded as needed) with a valid body and a 30+ char justification.
3. Observe the outbound request path resolves to a non-recast Tenable endpoint (visible in stub recorded-calls or via the audit log/ruleId mismatch). Constrain pluginId to digits to confirm the fix blocks it.

Resolution

Validate pluginId (Tenable plugin ids are numeric) with @Pattern("\\d+") and assetUuid with a UUID @Pattern on both RecastRequest, AcceptRiskRequest and RemoveRecastBody; re-validate in the service. Pass identifiers as RestClient URI variables (uri(template, vars)) so they are percent-encoded, rather than pre-formatting them into the path string.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// controller
@PathVariable("pluginId") String pluginId
// client
IO_RECAST_PATH_FMT.formatted(assetUuid, pluginId)
▲ After (fixed)
// DTO / path var
@Pattern(regexp = "\\d{1,12}") String pluginId;
@Pattern(regexp = "[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}") String assetUuid;
// client — let RestClient encode the variables
http.post().uri("/workbenches/assets/{a}/vulnerabilities/{p}/recast", assetUuid, pluginId)

MediumSEC-INT-005Splunk webhook HMAC verification has a body-mismatch fallback that allows signature bypass
SecurityImproper Verification of Cryptographic Signature (A02/A08)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/splunk/webhook/SplunkWebhookController.java:286-315 Effort M Risk CVSS 5.3 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — forged alert ingestion when raw body is not cached
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/splunk/webhook/SplunkWebhookController.java:114-139

Description

The HMAC check computes the digest over the request body, but when the raw body was not cached as the 'RAW_BODY' request attribute it falls back to req.getReader().lines().reduce("", (a,b) -> a+b). By the time the handler runs, Spring's @RequestBody Map binder has already consumed the servlet input stream, so getReader() typically yields an empty string. The HMAC is then computed over "" — a value the attacker can also compute — while the actual JSON payload that gets ingested is the already-parsed Map. This decouples the signed bytes from the processed content: an attacker who knows the shared secret-over-empty-string (or who can force the empty-body path) can present a valid-looking signature for an arbitrary alert body. There is no servlet filter in this package that sets RAW_BODY, so the fragile fallback path is the default. Additionally the comparison uses a non-constant-time length check before the constant-time loop, and the whole verification is silently skipped when no shared secret is configured (role guard only).

Root cause

Signature is verified against a best-effort re-read of an already-consumed request stream rather than against the exact bytes that produced the parsed payload. No ContentCachingRequestWrapper / filter guarantees the signed bytes equal the processed bytes.

Evidence / proof
if (req.getAttribute("RAW_BODY") instanceof String cached) { body = cached; }
else { body = req.getReader().lines().reduce("", (a, b) -> a + b); }  // stream already consumed by @RequestBody
byte[] digest = mac.doFinal(body.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));

Real-world impact

The HMAC control intended to authenticate Splunk's outbound webhook can be defeated when the raw body is not cached (the default), letting a party that reaches the endpoint inject forged SIEM alerts into socops.security_event with attacker-chosen severity/host, polluting the SOC triage queue and SLA timers and triggering downstream automation. Combined with SEC-INT-002's missing tenant scoping, forged events are written under the caller's tenant.

Reproduction

1. Configure grc.integrations.splunk.webhook-shared-secret.
2. POST a JSON alert to /api/v1/integrations/splunk/webhook with X-Splunk-Signature = HMAC-SHA256('', secret).
3. Because @RequestBody already drained the stream, verifySignature computes HMAC over "" and matches the header, so the forged alert with attacker-controlled severity is accepted and stored.

Resolution

Register a ContentCachingRequestWrapper (or a filter that stores the exact raw bytes in RAW_BODY) for this route and verify the HMAC over those bytes; fail closed if the raw body is unavailable instead of hashing an empty string. Keep the constant-time compare but drop the early length-based exit only after confirming both inputs are fixed-length hex. Consider making the shared secret mandatory in non-dev profiles so verification is never silently skipped.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
if (req.getAttribute("RAW_BODY") instanceof String cached) { body = cached; }
else { body = req.getReader().lines().reduce("", (a, b) -> a + b); }
▲ After (fixed)
Object cached = req.getAttribute("RAW_BODY");
if (!(cached instanceof String raw) || raw.isEmpty()) {
    log.warn("[Splunk-Webhook] raw body unavailable — failing signature check closed");
    return false;   // fail closed; do not hash an empty/partial body
}
byte[] digest = mac.doFinal(raw.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));

MediumSEC-NDI-003Workflow approval / submission state changes have no segregation-of-duties control
SecurityBroken Access Control (A01)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/submission/controller/NdiSubmissionPackageController.java:74-90 Effort M Risk CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — any user can self-approve and submit regulatory packages
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/compliance/controller/NdiComplianceAssessmentController.java:116-124
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/compliance/service/NdiComplianceAssessmentService.java:247-266
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/evidence/controller/NdiEvidenceItemController.java:61-71

Description

The compliance, evidence, and submission-package workflows implement a maker/checker lifecycle (DRAFT -> SUBMITTED -> UNDER_REVIEW -> APPROVED; submission DRAFT -> READY -> SUBMITTED -> ACKNOWLEDGED). The state machine is enforced (illegal transitions throw), but the *authorization* on the privileged steps (approve, submit, acknowledge, reject) is only isAuthenticated(). The approver/submitter identity is also taken from a free-text body field (approverName, submitterName) rather than the authenticated principal. Consequently a single low-privilege user can drive an item all the way to APPROVED and submit the package to the regulator, and can name any person as the approver. There is no enforced separation between the user who prepares/submits and the user who approves.

Root cause

Same isAuthenticated() gap as SEC-NDI-001, compounded by attribution (approverName/submitterName) coming from the request body instead of the SecurityContext, so the recorded approver cannot be trusted.

Evidence / proof
NdiSubmissionPackageController.approve(): @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") ... service.approve(id, body.get("approverName"));
NdiComplianceAssessmentService.approve(): cur.setApproverName(approverName);  // free-text, from body

Real-world impact

Defeats the maker/checker control intended for NDI submissions. A single account compromise or a malicious insider can fabricate an approved, attested submission package and mark it SUBMITTED/ACKNOWLEDGED with an arbitrary named approver, producing a false regulatory record.

Reproduction

1. As any tenant user, create a compliance assessment, set status COMPLIANT with evidence, submit, mark-under-review, then approve — all with the same token.
2. POST /api/ndi/submission-package/{id}/approve with body {"approverName":"Some CISO"} succeeds; the package shows an approver who never acted.

Resolution

Gate approve/submit/acknowledge with a distinct permission (e.g. hasPermission('NDI','APPROVE') / hasRole) separate from WRITE, and derive approverName/submitterName from the authenticated principal, not the body. Optionally enforce that the approver != the last editor/submitter.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping("/{id}/approve")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public NdiComplianceAssessment approve(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody(required=false) Map<String,String> body) {
    return service.approve(id, body == null ? null : body.get("approverName"));
}
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping("/{id}/approve")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('NDI','APPROVE') or hasAnyRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN','CISO','DPO')")
public NdiComplianceAssessment approve(@PathVariable Long id) {
    // approverName resolved server-side from SecurityContext inside the service
    return service.approve(id);
}

MediumSEC-NDI-004Cross-tenant soft-FK references stored without ownership validation (dataclass / data_officer)
SecurityBroken Access Control (A01)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/data_officer/service/DataOfficerService.java:625-639 Effort M Risk CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — bounded cross-tenant linkage / referential integrity violation
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/data_officer/service/DataOfficerService.java:490-505
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/data_officer/service/DataOfficerService.java:643-686
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/dataclass/service/DataclassService.java:233-256

Description

Several create paths persist caller-supplied foreign-key ids onto new rows without verifying those ids belong to the caller's organisation. In DataOfficerService: createLineage() stores sourceEntryId/targetEntryId, scheduleDisposal() stores retentionRuleId, createQualityRule() stores catalogEntryId, and recordQualityRun() stores qualityRuleId — none re-load the referenced row with a findByOrganisationIdAndId check. In DataclassService.createException() the request's dataAssetId/dataFlowId are written directly to the exception (unlike createFlow(), which loads the asset via the org-scoped loadAsset()). Because the dependent listing endpoints (e.g. listLineage(sourceId), listQualityRuns(ruleId)) are themselves org-scoped, these do not directly leak another tenant's data, but they let one tenant create rows that point at another tenant's entity ids, corrupting referential integrity and producing misleading lineage/quality/exception linkages. The NDI module, by contrast, validates cross-module risk_id ownership via NdiCrossLinkService.validateRiskExists() — the data modules lack the equivalent.

Root cause

FK ids are trusted from the request DTO and set directly on the entity; no companion findByOrganisationIdAndId existence/ownership check is performed before persisting the link.

Evidence / proof
DataOfficerService.createLineage():
    CatalogLineage l = new CatalogLineage();
    l.setOrganisationId(org());
    l.setSourceEntryId(req.sourceEntryId());   // not validated against org
    l.setTargetEntryId(req.targetEntryId());   // not validated against org
    lineageRepo.save(l);
DataclassService.createException():
    e.setDataAssetId(req.dataAssetId());        // not validated
    e.setDataFlowId(req.dataFlowId());          // not validated

Real-world impact

A tenant can plant lineage edges, quality runs, disposal jobs, or data-classification exceptions that reference identifiers belonging to other tenants or to non-existent rows, polluting NDMO/PDPL records and dashboards and undermining data trustworthiness. Direct cross-tenant data disclosure is not achieved because read paths are org-filtered, hence Medium rather than High.

Reproduction

1. As tenant A user, POST /api/v1/data-officer/lineage with {"sourceEntryId": <a catalog id owned by tenant B>, "targetEntryId": <another tenant B id>}.
2. The lineage row is created under tenant A pointing at tenant B's ids; integrity of both tenants' catalogs is now questionable.

Resolution

For every caller-supplied FK, load the referenced row with the org-scoped finder (findByOrganisationIdAndId) and reject if absent, exactly as createFlow() already does with loadAsset() and as NdiCrossLinkService.validateRiskExists() does for NDI.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
public LineageResponse createLineage(CreateLineageRequest req) {
    CatalogLineage l = new CatalogLineage();
    l.setOrganisationId(org());
    l.setSourceEntryId(req.sourceEntryId());
    l.setTargetEntryId(req.targetEntryId());
    ...
}
▲ After (fixed)
public LineageResponse createLineage(CreateLineageRequest req) {
    Long o = org();
    catalogRepo.findByOrganisationIdAndId(o, req.sourceEntryId())
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("source catalog entry not in org"));
    catalogRepo.findByOrganisationIdAndId(o, req.targetEntryId())
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("target catalog entry not in org"));
    CatalogLineage l = new CatalogLineage();
    l.setOrganisationId(o);
    l.setSourceEntryId(req.sourceEntryId());
    l.setTargetEntryId(req.targetEntryId());
    ...
}

Adversarial verification: adjusted (severity High→Medium) — All cited facts verified: package-lock.json:2359 resolves vite 5.4.21 (in the vulnerable <=6.4.2 range for the three GHSA advisories) and vite.config.ts:20-27 sets host:true + allowedHosts:true, exposing the dev server on 0.0.0.0/LAN on a Windows host. However every one of these advisories targets the Vite DEV SERVER only; production ships a static `vite build` output with no dev server running, so the exposure exists solely on developer machines on a trusted LAN. Real but dev-only attack surface — High overstates production impact; Medium.
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json:32-32 Effort M Risk CVSS 7.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N) — GHSA-fx2h-pf6j-xcff rated High by npm; arbitrary file read off the dev host. Network-exploitable here because vite.config.ts sets host:true + allowedHosts:true (binds 0.0.0.0/LAN). Rated High (not Critical): read-only, dev/build-time tooling, not the production artifact.
tss-grc-ui-v2/package-lock.json:2358-2367
tss-grc-ui-v2/vite.config.ts:20-42

Description

tss-grc-ui-v2 pins vite ^5.4.10 and resolves to vite 5.4.21 (package-lock.json line 2359). npm audit flags three vite advisories against the installed version: (1) GHSA-fx2h-pf6j-xcff (HIGH) — server.fs.deny bypass on Windows alternate paths lets a request read files the deny-list was meant to protect; (2) GHSA-4w7w-66w2-5vf9 (moderate) — path traversal in optimized-deps `.map` handling (CWE-22/200); (3) GHSA-v6wh-96g9-6wx3 (moderate) — launch-editor NTLMv2 hash disclosure via UNC path handling on Windows (CWE-73/522). All three apply because 5.4.21 falls in the vulnerable range <=6.4.2. Crucially, vite.config.ts (lines 20-42) configures the dev server with `host: true` and `allowedHosts: true`, binding to 0.0.0.0 and accepting arbitrary Host headers, so the dev server is reachable from any machine on the LAN rather than localhost-only. This converts a localhost-only weakness into a LAN-reachable one. The platform runs on Windows (env: Windows 11), where the server.fs.deny bypass and the launch-editor NTLM disclosure are specifically Windows-path issues.

Root cause

Outdated vite (5.4.21) carrying multiple unpatched dev-server file-serving flaws, combined with a hardened-down dev-server config (host:true / allowedHosts:true) that exposes the server beyond localhost on a Windows host where the Windows-specific bypasses apply.

Evidence / proof
package.json:32  "vite": "^5.4.10"  -> resolved 5.4.21 (package-lock.json:2359 "version": "5.4.21"). vite.config.ts:20-27
  server: {
    port: 5173,
    strictPort: false,
    host: true,
    allowedHosts: true,

Real-world impact

An attacker on the same LAN (or anyone who can lure a developer's browser to a malicious page while the dev server is up) can read files outside the project root from the developer's workstation (source, .env.local with VITE_API_BASE and any secrets, SSH keys) and, via the launch-editor UNC path issue on Windows, trigger an SMB authentication that leaks the developer's NTLMv2 hash to an attacker-controlled host for offline cracking. Dev/build-time only — this tooling is not part of the shipped production bundle — but the LAN binding makes it a realistic internal-network exposure.

Reproduction

1. Start the dev server: cd tss-grc-ui-v2 && npm run dev (listens on 0.0.0.0:5173 due to host:true). 2. From another host on the LAN, request a file via the optimized-deps `.map` traversal (GHSA-4w7w-66w2-5vf9) or a server.fs.deny alternate-path bypass (GHSA-fx2h-pf6j-xcff) using a Windows alternate path form to read a file the deny list should block. 3. For the NTLM leak, induce a UNC path (\\attacker-host\share) through the launch-editor flow and capture the SMB auth with responder. npm audit --json confirms: vite range <=6.4.2, fixAvailable vite@8.0.16 (isSemVerMajor).

Resolution

Upgrade vite to a patched release. npm audit reports the fix as vite@8.0.16 (major). Validate the build/plugin compatibility (vite 8 requires @vitejs/plugin-react bump and Node version check), or as an interim mitigation set the dev server back to localhost-only (host: 'localhost' or host: false, drop allowedHosts:true) so the flaws are not LAN-reachable. Re-run `npm audit` after the bump.

    allowedHosts: true,
▲ After (fixed)

    port: 5173,
    strictPort: false,
    host: 'localhost',
    // allowedHosts removed / restricted to known dev hostnames

Transitive esbuild 0.21.5 (via vite 5.4.21) ships a dev server with wildcard CORS and no origin validation; vite 5.x has not bumped to a patched esbuild.

MediumSEC-NPM-003react-router open redirect via protocol-relative (//) URL reinterpretation (moderate)
SecurityOpen Redirect / Unvalidated Redirect (A01)▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json:21-21 Effort S Risk CVSS 6.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N) — GHSA-2j2x-hqr9-3h42, npm-rated moderate. Open redirect; ships in the production bundle (runtime dependency).
tss-grc-ui-v2/package-lock.json:2048-2071

Description

react-router-dom is a DIRECT runtime dependency (package.json line 21, ^6.28.0) and resolves to 6.30.3, which transitively pins react-router 6.30.3 (package-lock.json lines 2048-2071). GHSA-2j2x-hqr9-3h42 (CWE-601) describes that react-router's same-origin redirect handling treats a path beginning with `//` as same-origin, but the browser reinterprets `//evil.com` as a protocol-relative URL pointing to an external host — yielding an open redirect. The installed 6.30.3 is the top of the vulnerable range (>=6.7.0 <6.30.4); the fix landed in 6.30.4. Unlike the vite/esbuild/babel findings, react-router ships in the deployed production bundle, so this is a genuine runtime exposure, not a dev-tooling-only one.

Root cause

react-router 6.30.3 (and react-router-dom 6.30.3) classifies redirect targets starting with `//` as same-origin, ignoring that protocol-relative URLs resolve to an external authority in the browser.

Evidence / proof
package.json:21  "react-router-dom": "^6.28.0"
package-lock.json:2048-2051
    "node_modules/react-router": {
      "version": "6.30.3",
...
package-lock.json:2069-2070 (react-router-dom deps) "react-router": "6.30.3"

Real-world impact

If any redirect target in the app is derived from user-controllable input (e.g. a ?redirect= / ?next= / returnUrl query param after login), an attacker can craft a link to the trusted GRC app that bounces the authenticated user to //evil.com — enabling phishing and OAuth/token-forwarding attacks against high-value users (PLATFORM_ADMIN, AUDITOR). Impact is conditional on whether the app actually feeds external input into a router redirect; rated Medium accordingly.

Reproduction

1. Identify any redirect that passes a value to navigate()/redirect() from a query param. 2. Visit https://<grc-app>/login?redirect=//evil.com and authenticate. 3. Observe the browser navigate to https://evil.com (protocol-relative). If no user-controlled redirect path exists in the codebase, exploitability drops to theoretical.

Resolution

Upgrade react-router-dom (and the transitive react-router) to >=6.30.4, which fixes the same-origin check to reject protocol-relative `//` targets. npm audit reports fixAvailable:true (non-major) for both. Additionally, allowlist redirect targets to known internal paths rather than trusting incoming values.

tss-grc-ui-v2/package-lock.json:2063-2071

Description

react-router-dom is the DIRECT dependency the app declares (package.json line 21). npm audit lists it as a separate vulnerable package (isDirect:true, range 6.6.3-pre.0 - 6.30.3) whose vulnerability is `via: [react-router]` — i.e. it re-exports the vulnerable react-router 6.30.3 open redirect (GHSA-2j2x-hqr9-3h42, CWE-601). The installed react-router-dom is 6.30.3 (package-lock.json line 2064), which depends on react-router 6.30.3 (line 2070). This entry is the developer-facing handle for the fix: bumping react-router-dom is what actually pulls in the patched react-router. Reported as its own finding because npm audit tracks it as a distinct advisory entry, but it is the same underlying CWE-601 defect as SEC-NPM-003.

Root cause

Direct dependency react-router-dom 6.30.3 pins the vulnerable react-router 6.30.3, propagating the protocol-relative `//` open-redirect flaw into the application.

Evidence / proof
package.json:21  "react-router-dom": "^6.28.0"
package-lock.json:2063-2070
    "node_modules/react-router-dom": {
      "version": "6.30.3",
...      "react-router": "6.30.3"

Real-world impact

Same as SEC-NPM-003 — open redirect reachable in the shipped production bundle if user input drives a router redirect. Because react-router-dom is the declared direct dependency, this is the single line to change to remediate both audit entries.

Reproduction

Same as SEC-NPM-003: authenticate to the app with a crafted ?redirect=//evil.com and observe external navigation, provided a user-controlled redirect path exists.

Resolution

Bump the direct dependency react-router-dom to >=6.30.4 (npm audit fixAvailable:true, non-major). This transitively upgrades react-router to the patched version, closing both SEC-NPM-003 and SEC-NPM-004. Combine with a server/client-side redirect-target allowlist.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json
"react-router-dom": "^6.28.0"   // -> 6.30.3 (depends on react-router 6.30.3)
▲ After (fixed)
// tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json
"react-router-dom": "^6.30.4"   // -> react-router 6.30.4+ patched

Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/platform/controls/controller/ControlLibraryController.java:71-208 Effort M Risk CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N) — unauthorized creation/modification/deletion of GRC control & regulatory data
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/platform/regulatory/controller/AuthorityDocumentController.java:58-112

Description

Every mutating endpoint of the unified Control Library (POST/PUT/DELETE /controls, /control-objectives, /control-mappings, /risk-control-links, /control-assessments and their /transition actions) and of the Authority Documents catalog (POST/PUT/DELETE /authority-documents, /citations, /transition) is annotated @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). These are the system-of-record for the GRC spine (NCA ECC / SAMA / PDPL controls, citations, control-to-citation mappings, risk-control matrix, effectiveness assessments). Any authenticated user — regardless of role — can create, edit, retire, supersede or soft-delete this regulated content, and walk workflow state machines (e.g. transition a control DRAFT->ACTIVE or an authority document to SUPERSEDED). Data is correctly tenant-scoped, so this is BFLA within the tenant, not cross-tenant.

Root cause

Controllers in the platform F1/F2 slices were written with a uniform isAuthenticated() guard instead of the hasPermission('CONTROL_LIB'/'REGULATORY','WRITE'|'DELETE') checks the project's RBAC model (ModulePermissionEvaluator + the CONTROL_LIB/REGULATORY/POSTURE module codes in LicensingService.KNOWN_MODULES) clearly intends.

Evidence / proof
@PostMapping("/controls")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ResponseEntity<Control> createControl(@RequestBody Control body) { ... }

@DeleteMapping("/controls/{id}")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ResponseEntity<Void> deleteControl(@PathVariable Long id) { ... }

Real-world impact

Integrity loss of the control library and regulatory catalog: a non-privileged user can fabricate or retire controls, alter control-to-citation coverage (which directly feeds the F5/F6 compliance-posture heatmaps shown to examiners), or delete mappings — undermining the audit-defensibility the platform sells. No confidentiality/cross-tenant break.

Reproduction

1. Log in as a read-only role (auditor).
2. curl -X DELETE http://localhost:8084/api/v1/control-mappings/5 -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" — observe 204 and the mapping disappears from the posture heatmap.
3. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/v1/controls -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"controlCode":"X-1","titleEn":"fake","domain":"CYBER"}'.

Resolution

Apply module-scoped permissions: reads -> hasPermission('CONTROL_LIB','READ') / hasPermission('REGULATORY','READ'); writes -> ...'WRITE'; deletes -> ...'DELETE'. The transition endpoints should require WRITE.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping("/controls")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ResponseEntity<Control> createControl(@RequestBody Control body) { ... }
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping("/controls")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('CONTROL_LIB','WRITE')")
public ResponseEntity<Control> createControl(@RequestBody Control body) { ... }

Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/platform/auditlog/controller/AuditLogController.java:32-58 Effort S Risk CVSS 5.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N) — disclosure of the tenant security/audit trail to all users

Description

All four read endpoints of the F7 audit log (GET /api/v1/audit-log, /stats, /history, /trace/{correlationId}) are guarded only by isAuthenticated(). The audit log is the tenant's security ledger: it records who did what (usernames, roles, IP addresses, source endpoints, old/new value JSON diffs, workflow transitions, license changes, rule fires). Exposing it to every authenticated user — including the lowest-privilege role — lets any user reconstruct other users' and admins' activity, harvest internal entity ids, and read change diffs that may contain sensitive field values. Queries are tenant-scoped (findByOrganisationId...), so this is intra-tenant over-exposure, not cross-tenant.

Root cause

An inherently administrative/forensic data set is exposed at the authentication tier rather than behind an AUDIT_LOG:READ or platform-admin permission (the AUDIT_LOG module code already exists in LicensingService.KNOWN_MODULES).

Evidence / proof
@GetMapping
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public Page<AuditLogEntry> list(@RequestParam(required=false) String actionType, ...) {
    return service.list(actionType, sourceModule, severity, page, size);
}

Real-world impact

Information disclosure: any user can read the full tenant audit trail, including admin actions, value diffs, and source IPs — useful for reconnaissance and for an insider to monitor whether their own activity is being investigated. No data is mutated.

Reproduction

1. Log in as a low-privilege user.
2. curl http://localhost:8084/api/v1/audit-log -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" — returns the tenant-wide audit ledger including other users' actions and value diffs.

Gate all audit-log reads on a dedicated permission: @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('AUDIT_LOG','READ')") (or hasRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN')). ▲ After (fixed)

@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('AUDIT_LOG','READ')")
public Page<AuditLogEntry> list(...) { ... }

MediumSEC-PLAT-005Generic persistence append endpoint has no authorization guard
SecurityBroken Function Level Authorization (A01)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/platform/persistence/controller/PersistenceController.java:86-101 Effort S Risk CVSS 5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:L) — unauthorized writes to arbitrary tenant key/value stores

Description

PersistenceController is a generic key/value store backing the frontend's persistence adapter. PUT and DELETE correctly require hasPermission('PLATFORM','WRITE'), but POST /api/v1/persistence/{key} (append) carries NO @PreAuthorize at all. It is therefore covered only by the global SecurityConfig rule .anyRequest().authenticated(), meaning any authenticated user can append arbitrary JSON rows to any store key in their tenant. The body is @RequestBody Object serialized verbatim with no schema, size, or row-count validation, so a user can also write unbounded volumes. This is inconsistent with the bulk-write endpoints on the same controller, which are PLATFORM:WRITE.

Root cause

Missing method-level authorization annotation on the append handler; the author relied on the global authenticated() default while protecting the sibling PUT/DELETE with PLATFORM:WRITE, creating an inconsistent privilege boundary.

Evidence / proof
@PostMapping("/{key}")
@Transactional
public ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> append(
        @PathVariable String key,
        @RequestBody Object row) {
    Long orgId = TenantContext.requireOrganisationId();
    ...
    PersistenceRow saved = repo.save(new PersistenceRow(orgId, key, seq, json, "API_APPEND"));
    ...
}

Real-world impact

Any authenticated user (including read-only roles) can write/pollute arbitrary tenant persistence stores and inflate storage. Org scoping is enforced, so the write stays within the tenant; integrity/availability of frontend-persisted data is the concern.

Reproduction

1. Log in as an auditor.
2. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/v1/persistence/anyKey -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"injected":true}' — returns 200 with a new rowSeq even though the role has no PLATFORM:WRITE.

Resolution

Add @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PLATFORM','WRITE')") to the append handler to match PUT/DELETE, and add a payload-size / row-count bound.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping("/{key}")
@Transactional
public ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> append(
        @PathVariable String key,
        @RequestBody Object row) { ... }
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping("/{key}")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PLATFORM','WRITE')")
@Transactional
public ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> append(
        @PathVariable String key,
        @RequestBody Object row) { ... }

Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/platform/files/controller/FileUploadController.java:50-135 Effort M Risk CVSS 5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L) — unauthorized upload + enumeration of tenant file metadata

Description

FileUploadController.list (GET), upload (POST) and get (GET /{id}) have no @PreAuthorize (only the global authenticated() applies); only delete requires PLATFORM:WRITE. Consequences: (1) any authenticated user can upload files and can list metadata for any attachedTo key in their tenant (e.g. attachedTo='dsr/DSR-2026-013' or 'evidence/EV-1078'), enumerating which sensitive records have attachments and reading filename/uploadedBy/crNumber/residency — there is no per-record ownership or owning-module READ check, so a user with no privilege on the privacy/evidence module can still browse those files' metadata. (2) The upload performs only a stub virus scan (EICAR string + extension blocklist) and enforces no max file size, MIME allowlist, or filename sanitisation in code (file.getOriginalFilename() is stored and used to build the storage key verbatim).

Root cause

Missing method-level authorization on read/upload handlers, and reliance on a documented-but-unimplemented storage/scan backend. Access is scoped only by tenant + a free-text attachedTo string the caller supplies, with no link back to the owning record's module permission.

Evidence / proof
@GetMapping
public ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> list(@RequestParam String attachedTo) {
    Long orgId = TenantContext.requireOrganisationId();
    List<FileMetadata> rows = repo.findByOrganisationIdAndAttachedToOrderByUploadedAtDesc(orgId, attachedTo);
    ...
}

@PostMapping(consumes = MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE)
@Transactional
public ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> upload(@RequestParam("file") MultipartFile file, ...) { ... }

Real-world impact

Intra-tenant: enumeration/disclosure of file metadata attached to sensitive records (DSR/evidence/incident) by users lacking those modules' permissions, plus unauthorized uploads. The virus-scan/size gaps are latent risks until the real storage backend is wired, but the stored unsanitised originalFilename flows into the S3 key and into responses.

Reproduction

1. Log in as a low-privilege user.
2. curl 'http://localhost:8084/api/v1/files?attachedTo=dsr/DSR-2026-013' -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" — returns the file list/metadata for that DSR without any privacy-module permission.
3. curl -F file=@x.bin -F attachedTo=evidence/EV-1 http://localhost:8084/api/v1/files -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" — uploads successfully.

Resolution

Add @PreAuthorize to list/upload/get (at minimum hasPermission('PLATFORM','READ')/('PLATFORM','WRITE')); ideally derive the owning module from attachedTo and check that module's permission. Enforce a configured max-file-size (spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size + an in-code check), a MIME allowlist, and sanitise originalFilename before using it in the storage key.

▲ After (fixed)
@GetMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PLATFORM','READ')")
public ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> list(@RequestParam String attachedTo) { ... }

@PostMapping(consumes = MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE)
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PLATFORM','WRITE')")
@Transactional
public ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> upload(@RequestParam("file") MultipartFile file, ...) {
    // enforce max size + MIME allowlist + sanitise filename
}

Description

Several platform/cross-module write surfaces are guarded only by isAuthenticated(): BuyerGapController exposes POST risk-control links, POST risk attestations, and POST sweeps that mutate privacy DSR/breach state and emit domain events under /api/v1/risk/** and /api/v1/privacy/** without RISK:WRITE / PRIVACY:WRITE; DepartmentController create/update/archive; IssueController create/update/transition; CalendarController create/update/delete. None of these enforce a module permission, so any authenticated user can create or change this data. Tenant scoping is correctly enforced in every backing service (BuyerGapService explicitly validates risk.organisationId == current tenant), so there is no cross-tenant break — the issue is missing function-level RBAC, plus inconsistency with the well-guarded reporting/dashboard controllers.

These controllers (and the buyer-gap bundle that spans risk/privacy/evidence) were shipped with a blanket isAuthenticated() guard rather than the module-action permissions the platform's RBAC model defines.

Evidence / proof
@PostMapping("/api/v1/risk/risks/{id}/controls")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public RiskControl linkRiskControl(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody LinkControlBody body) { ... }

@PostMapping("/api/v1/privacy/dsr/sla/sweep")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public DsrSlaSweepResult dsrSlaSweep() { ... }

Real-world impact

Within a tenant, any role can mutate risk-control linkage, file risk attestations in another user's name, trigger PDPL/DSR breach sweeps (which flip DsrCase/CrisisEvent state and fire events), and create/edit departments, issues, and calendar events — eroding data integrity and segregation of duties that SAMA/NCA expect. MediumSEC-PRIV-003Unauthenticated public sub-processor list allows cross-tenant enumeration via attacker-controlled org parameter
SecurityBroken Access Control / IDOR (A01) / CWE-639▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/privacy/subprocessor/controller/SubprocessorController.java:157-162 Effort M Risk CVSS ~5.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N) — unauthenticated cross-tenant read of (intentionally public) vendor list for arbitrary orgs
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/privacy/subprocessor/service/SubprocessorPublicListService.java:36-40
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/SecurityConfig.java:101

Description

GET /api/v1/privacy/subprocessors/public is permitAll in SecurityConfig and takes a caller-supplied ?org=<id> query parameter that is passed straight into SubprocessorPublicListService.publicList(orgId) → repo.findByOrganisationIdAndLifecycleStageAndIsDeletedFalse(orgId,"APPROVED"). Because there is no JWT and thus no TenantContext, the org id is whatever the caller sends (defaulting to 1). An unauthenticated attacker can iterate org=1,2,3,… and harvest the APPROVED sub-processor list (legal name EN/AR, country, region, processing purpose, cross-border safeguard) for every tenant, not just the one whose public privacy notice references the endpoint. While PDPL Art.12 intends this list to be public, exposing every tenant's vendor map through one un-scoped, enumerable parameter is a tenant-isolation weakness and a competitive-intelligence leak.

Root cause

The endpoint is org-agnostic by design (no tenant context for anonymous callers) but trusts a client-supplied org id with no host-to-tenant binding, rate limiting, or allow-list of organisations that have opted into public disclosure.

Evidence / proof
SubprocessorController.java:157-162  @GetMapping("/public") public List<PublicSubprocessorResponse> publicList(@RequestParam(name="org",required=false) Long orgId){ return publicListService.publicList(orgId == null ? 1L : orgId); }  ;  SecurityConfig.java:101 .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/v1/privacy/subprocessors/public").permitAll().

Real-world impact

Anonymous enumeration of every tenant's approved sub-processor / vendor relationships and cross-border destinations. For multi-tenant SaaS this leaks one customer's supply chain to anyone, including competitors, and lets an attacker map which banks use which processors and in which countries.

Reproduction

1) Without any auth: for i in 1..50; curl "http://localhost:8084/api/v1/privacy/subprocessors/public?org=$i". 2) Each call returns the APPROVED sub-processors for tenant i, regardless of whether tenant i intended a public list.

Resolution

Bind the public list to a host-based tenant resolver (the planned ethics.<bank>.sa style) instead of a client-supplied org id, OR gate disclosure behind a per-org 'public_transparency_enabled' flag and return 404 for orgs that have not opted in. Add rate limiting to the permitAll path to blunt enumeration. At minimum, do not default to org 1 and reject requests where org cannot be resolved from the request context.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@GetMapping("/public")
public List<PublicSubprocessorResponse> publicList(@RequestParam(name = "org", required = false) Long orgId) {
    return publicListService.publicList(orgId == null ? 1L : orgId);
}
▲ After (fixed)
@GetMapping("/public")
public List<PublicSubprocessorResponse> publicList(HttpServletRequest request) {
    Long orgId = tenantResolver.resolveFromHost(request.getServerName()); // host -> org
    if (orgId == null || !orgSettings.isPublicTransparencyEnabled(orgId)) {
        throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND);
    }
    return publicListService.publicList(orgId);
}
