SecuritySecurity Misconfiguration / XSS (A05/A03)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/attachment/controller/AttachmentController.java:58-66 Effort S Risk CVSS 3.1 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N) — largely mitigated by global X-Content-Type-Options:nosniff and Content-Disposition:attachment
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/attachment/service/AttachmentStorageService.java:78
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/attachment/service/AttachmentService.java:55
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/SecurityConfig.java:141

Description

On upload, the stored `mimeType` is taken verbatim from `file.getContentType()` (AttachmentStorageService line 78 -> AttachmentService line 55), which is fully client-controlled. On download (AttachmentController lines 60-65) that stored value is echoed straight into the response via `MediaType.parseMediaType(p.mimeType())`. The same pattern exists for evidence items. The download is served with `Content-Disposition: attachment` (forces download) and the application sets a global `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` header (SecurityConfig line 141), which together strongly mitigate drive-by/stored-XSS via a spoofed text/html content-type. The extension allow-list also blocks `.html`/`.svg`. Residual risk is therefore low, but reflecting an unvalidated, attacker-supplied content-type is still poor hygiene and could matter if the attachment is ever rendered inline (e.g. a future preview feature dropping Content-Disposition).

Root cause

The client-provided multipart Content-Type is persisted and trusted as the authoritative MIME type rather than being derived server-side from the validated extension or via content sniffing.

Evidence / proof
// store: trusts client content type
return new StoredFile(original, relative, (long) bytes.length, file.getContentType(), sha256Hex(bytes));
// download: reflects it back
.contentType(MediaType.parseMediaType(p.mimeType()))
.body(p.bytes());

Real-world impact

If a future change serves attachments inline (removes Content-Disposition: attachment) or a client ignores nosniff, an uploaded file with a crafted text/html content-type could be rendered and execute script in the app origin. As currently wired (attachment disposition + nosniff + extension allow-list) practical exploitation is blocked, so impact is limited to defence-in-depth.

Reproduction

1. Upload a file while setting the multipart part's Content-Type to `text/html` (the extension must still be in the allow-list, e.g. `.txt`).
2. Download it and observe the response carries `Content-Type: text/html`. With nosniff + attachment disposition the browser still downloads rather than renders, so no script executes today.

Resolution

Derive the served Content-Type from the validated file extension (a server-side extension->MIME map) instead of the client value, or force `application/octet-stream` for any non-allowlisted/ambiguous type. Keep Content-Disposition: attachment and the global nosniff header. Optionally store the canonical server-derived MIME at upload time.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
return ResponseEntity.ok()
    .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION, "attachment; filename=\"" + p.fileName() + "\"")
    .contentType(MediaType.parseMediaType(p.mimeType()))
    .body(p.bytes());
▲ After (fixed)
MediaType safe = SafeMime.forExtension(p.fileName())            // server-side map
    .orElse(MediaType.APPLICATION_OCTET_STREAM);
return ResponseEntity.ok()
    .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION, "attachment; filename=\"" + p.fileName() + "\"")
    .header("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff")
    .contentType(safe)
    .body(p.bytes());
References: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (XSS) · CWE-434: Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type · OWASP A05:2021 Security Misconfiguration
LowSEC-EVD-006EvidenceItemService.addLink creates a link to an evidence id without verifying it belongs to the caller's tenant
SecurityBroken Object Level Authorization (A01)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceItemService.java:291-302 Effort S Risk CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — in-tenant data-integrity / weak IDOR; no direct cross-tenant data read
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/controller/EvidenceItemController.java:112-118
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/dto/EvidenceLinkRequest.java:6-12

Description

`addLink` persists an `EvidenceLink` straight from the request DTO. It correctly stamps the link's `organisationId` from the caller's TenantContext, but it never validates that `req.evidenceId()` (nor the `linkedEntityId`) actually resolves to an evidence item / entity owned by that org. Unlike the other mutators in this service (get/update/approve/delete all `findById(...).filter(e -> e.getOrganisationId().equals(orgId))`), the linked-id is trusted blindly. A caller can therefore create dangling or cross-pointing links referencing arbitrary numeric ids, including evidence ids that belong to another tenant. Because the stored link row is tagged with the caller's own org, reads stay tenant-scoped, so this does not directly leak another tenant's data — but it corrupts the evidence-linkage graph (audit pack traceability) and could mislead reviewers, and the missing ownership check is the same class of defect as a BOLA.

Root cause

Object-ownership validation that is consistently applied elsewhere in the service was omitted on the create-link path; the foreign id from the request is trusted without a tenant-scoped lookup.

Evidence / proof
@Transactional
public void addLink(EvidenceLinkRequest req) {
    Long orgId = TenantContext.getCurrentTenant();
    EvidenceLink link = new EvidenceLink();
    link.setOrganisationId(orgId);
    link.setEvidenceId(req.evidenceId());          // not validated against org
    link.setLinkedEntityId(req.linkedEntityId());  // not validated
    ...
    linkRepository.save(link);
}

Real-world impact

Integrity of the evidence-to-control / evidence-to-risk linkage graph can be polluted with links to non-existent or other-tenant evidence ids, weakening audit-pack traceability and coverage reporting. No direct cross-tenant disclosure given org-scoped reads, hence Low.

Reproduction

1. Authenticate with EVIDENCE:WRITE.
2. `curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
   -d '{"evidenceId":999999,"linkedModule":"RISK","linkedEntityId":424242}' \
   http://localhost:8084/api/v1/evidence/items/link`
3. A link row is created even though evidence id 999999 does not belong to the caller's org (or does not exist).

Resolution

Before saving, load the evidence item via the tenant-scoped finder and reject if it is not owned by the caller's org; optionally validate the linked entity reference too.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
public void addLink(EvidenceLinkRequest req) {
    Long orgId = TenantContext.getCurrentTenant();
    EvidenceLink link = new EvidenceLink();
    link.setOrganisationId(orgId);
    link.setEvidenceId(req.evidenceId());
    ...
    linkRepository.save(link);
}
▲ After (fixed)
public void addLink(EvidenceLinkRequest req) {
    Long orgId = TenantContext.getCurrentTenant();
    EvidenceItem ev = itemRepository.findById(req.evidenceId())
        .filter(e -> e.getOrganisationId().equals(orgId))
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("Evidence not found: " + req.evidenceId()));
    EvidenceLink link = new EvidenceLink();
    link.setOrganisationId(orgId);
    link.setEvidenceId(ev.getId());
    ...
    linkRepository.save(link);
}

LowSEC-FE-004Hand-rolled Markdown-to-HTML renderer feeding dangerouslySetInnerHTML in v2 Knowledge Base
SecurityCross-Site Scripting (A03:2021 Injection)▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/knowledge-base/KbArticlePage.tsx:83-170 Effort M Risk CVSS 3.7 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — current escaping holds; risk is fragility/regression in a custom sanitiser
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/knowledge-base/KbArticlePage.tsx:86
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/knowledge-base/KbArticlePage.tsx:102-147
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/knowledge-base/KbArticlePage.tsx:157-170

Description

This is the only `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` in the v2 React app. KB article bodies (server content) are passed through a custom `renderMarkdown()` and injected raw (line 86). The renderer does HTML-escape `& < >` first (lines 104-107) and gates link URLs through a `sanitiseUrl()` scheme allowlist that blocks `javascript:`/`data:`/`vbscript:` (lines 157-169), which closes the obvious vectors. However the implementation is a bespoke regex sanitiser rather than a vetted library (marked + DOMPurify), and has gaps that make it fragile: (1) it does NOT escape the double-quote character globally — only `<>&` are neutralised in step 1, so the `"` -> `&quot;` mapping relies entirely on sanitiseUrl for the href; any future code that places user text into an attribute would be unsafe; (2) the heading/list/paragraph regexes run AFTER escaping but a future contributor adding image syntax, raw-HTML passthrough, or attribute support could easily reintroduce an injection because there is no post-render sanitisation pass; (3) `sanitiseUrl` strips leading `\s` and `-` then lowercases for the check but returns the original `raw`, so the validation and the emitted value are computed from different strings — a brittle pattern. No working bypass was found in the current code, so this is Low / defence-in-depth, not an active High.

Root cause

Rolling a custom markdown sanitiser instead of using a maintained library, and using `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` for server-supplied rich text.

Evidence / proof
KbArticlePage.tsx:86 `dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: renderMarkdown(body ?? '') }}`. KbArticlePage.tsx:104-107 escapes only `& < >` (no `"`). KbArticlePage.tsx:161-169 `sanitiseUrl` validates a transformed string but returns the original `raw`.

Real-world impact

If the renderer is extended (images, tables, raw HTML) or the escaping invariants are broken by a refactor, KB content — which non-admin authors can typically create — becomes a stored-XSS channel into reviewers' sessions (and, via SEC-FE-002, their tokens). Today the impact is limited because the current ruleset blocks the known vectors.

Reproduction

No reliable exploit against the current code. Negative test: a KB body of `[x](javascript:alert(1))` renders `<a href="#">` (inert). Regression risk only.

Resolution

Replace the hand-rolled renderer with `marked`/`markdown-it` to parse and DOMPurify to sanitise the resulting HTML before `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` (or render to React elements without raw HTML). At minimum, add `"` and `'` to the global escape step and add a final DOMPurify pass over the produced HTML.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
let html = md
  .replace(/&/g, '&amp;')
  .replace(/</g, '&lt;')
  .replace(/>/g, '&gt;');
// ... custom regex transforms ...
return html; // -> dangerouslySetInnerHTML
▲ After (fixed)
import { marked } from 'marked';
import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';
const raw = marked.parse(md, { async: false }) as string;
return DOMPurify.sanitize(raw, { ALLOWED_URI_REGEXP: /^(?:https?:|mailto:|tel:|\/|#)/i });
// -> dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: that }}
References: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (XSS) · CWE-80: Improper Neutralization of Script-Related HTML Tags · OWASP DOM-based XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet · DOMPurify project
LowSEC-FIN-005ScmService silently defaults to organisation 1 when TenantContext is empty (fail-open tenant scoping)
SecurityImproper Multi-Tenant Isolation (A01, CWE-639)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/scm/service/ScmService.java:39-42 Effort S Risk CVSS ~4.2 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — fail-open default tenant on missing context
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/common/tenant/TenantContext.java:58-67

Description

ScmService.orgId() returns TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(), and when that is null it falls back to 1L: `Long id = TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(); return id != null ? id : 1L;`. Every other audited financial-crime service (Fraud, Sharia, RRP, OpRes, AML) uses TenantContext.requireOrganisationId(), which throws if the tenant is missing (fail closed). If any code path ever invokes ScmService without an established TenantContext (e.g. a future scheduler, async task, mis-ordered filter, or a test/util path), reads and writes would silently bind to tenant 1's data — reading tenant 1's vendors/contracts or writing new rows into tenant 1. The IntakeService author chose the opposite (throws IllegalStateException on null tenant), confirming the intended platform convention is fail-closed.

Root cause

Defensive 'default to org 1' shortcut instead of failing closed; diverges from the requireOrganisationId() convention used everywhere else.

Evidence / proof
`private Long orgId() { Long id = TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(); return id != null ? id : 1L; }` — used by every read/write in ScmService (e.g. listVendors, createVendor, stats).

Real-world impact

Under any future context-loss condition, SCM operations would silently operate on tenant 1 instead of erroring, risking cross-tenant read/write of vendor, contract and incident data. Low today because the JWT filter normally sets the tenant on authenticated requests.

Reproduction

Static/architectural: invoke any ScmService read with TenantContext cleared (e.g. from a scheduled job or test harness) — it returns tenant 1's data instead of throwing.

Resolution

Replace the 1L fallback with TenantContext.requireOrganisationId() so SCM fails closed like the other modules.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
private Long orgId() {
    Long id = TenantContext.getCurrentTenant();
    return id != null ? id : 1L;
}
▲ After (fixed)
private Long orgId() {
    return TenantContext.requireOrganisationId();
}
References: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key · CWE-636: Not Failing Securely ('Failing Open') · OWASP A01:2021 Broken Access Control
LowSEC-FIN-006Missing @Valid and unbounded page sizes on raw-entity / map request bodies in change_mgmt and SCM sub-controllers
SecurityImproper Input Validation (A04, CWE-20)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/change_mgmt/controller/ChangeManagementController.java:53-62 Effort M Risk CVSS ~3.7 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:L) — unvalidated input and large-page DoS surface
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/change_mgmt/controller/ChangeManagementController.java:92-95
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/change_mgmt/controller/ChangeManagementController.java:105-108
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/scm/clauses/controller/ContractClauseController.java:28-33
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/scm/fourthparty/controller/FourthPartyExposureController.java:32-37

Description

ChangeManagementController binds raw entities (ChangeRequest, ChangeApproval, ChangeTask, ChangeLink, ChangeComment) as @RequestBody with no @Valid; the service applies only ad-hoc null/blank checks. Several list endpoints accept a caller-controlled page size with no upper bound: ContractClauseController list defaults size=200 (line 31) and FourthPartyExposureController/SupplierResilienceController/SupplierResilienceTestController default size=100, all passed straight into PageRequest.of(page, size) with no clamp — a caller may request an arbitrarily large page (e.g. ?size=1000000) and force the DB to materialise an unbounded result set. The change_mgmt entity binding also creates a minor mass-assignment surface for child rows (e.g. ChangeApproval), though the parent organisation scope is enforced via require(changeId) and the children carry no organisationId column, so integrity impact is limited.

Root cause

Controllers omit Bean Validation and rely on entity binding; pagination size parameters are not capped.

Evidence / proof
`public ChangeRequest create(@RequestBody ChangeRequest body)` (no @Valid). `@RequestParam(defaultValue = "200") int size ... PageRequest.of(page, size)` in ContractClauseController.list. `@RequestParam(defaultValue = "100") int size` in FourthPartyExposureController.list.

Real-world impact

Unvalidated payloads can persist malformed/oversized state-machine data; uncapped page size enables a low-effort resource-exhaustion vector against the database and JSON serializer.

Reproduction

1) GET /api/scm/contract-clauses?size=1000000 -> server attempts to load up to a million rows. 2) POST /api/v1/changes with a body missing required fields -> bypasses Bean Validation, relying solely on DB constraints.

Resolution

Introduce validated request DTOs (with @Valid) for change_mgmt write endpoints; clamp page size to a sane maximum (e.g. Math.min(size, 200)) or use @PageableDefault with a configured max-page-size.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@RequestParam(defaultValue = "200") int size) {
    return service.list(status, category, PageRequest.of(page, size)).map(Response::from);
}
▲ After (fixed)
@RequestParam(defaultValue = "50") int size) {
    int capped = Math.min(Math.max(size, 1), 200);
    return service.list(status, category, PageRequest.of(page, capped)).map(Response::from);
}

LowSEC-IAM-006Workflow-engine instance/transition actor (executedById, ownerId) taken from request body, not the principal
SecurityImproper Authorization / Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity (A01/A08)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/workflow/controller/WorkflowEngineController.java:44-70 Effort M Risk CVSS ~4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — attribution spoofing, gated behind PLATFORM_ADMIN
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/workflow/service/WorkflowEngineService.java:154-187

Description

startInstance() reads ownerId and executeTransition() reads executedById from the untyped @RequestBody Map<String,Object>, then persists them into the workflow instance and the WorkflowActionLog audit record. These are never reconciled with the authenticated principal, so the recorded actor is whatever the caller types. Additionally, executeTransition only validates that a transition with the given actionCode exists from the current state; it does NOT enforce the transition's requiredRole (WorkflowTransition.requiredRole is surfaced for rendering at WorkflowEngineService line 79 but never checked on execute). Mitigating factor: both endpoints require hasPermission('PLATFORM_ADMIN','WRITE'), and reads/writes are tenant-scoped, so exploitation requires an already-privileged admin — hence Low.

Root cause

Actor identity is accepted from client input and the data-defined requiredRole on transitions is not enforced at execution time.

Evidence / proof
Long executedById = body.get("executedById") instanceof Number n ? n.longValue() : null;  // WorkflowEngineController line 67, written to WorkflowActionLog.setExecutedById without principal check.

Real-world impact

A platform admin can attribute workflow transitions and instance ownership to arbitrary user IDs, weakening the integrity of the workflow audit trail. Because requiredRole is ignored, the data-driven RBAC intended for the workflow engine is not enforced server-side. Limited blast radius because the endpoints are admin-only today.

Reproduction

1. As PLATFORM_ADMIN, POST /api/v1/workflow/instances/{id}/transitions with {"actionCode":"APPROVE","executedById":<any user id>,"comments":"x"}. 2. WorkflowActionLog row records executedById as the spoofed value regardless of who called.

Resolution

Derive executedById/ownerId from GrcUserDetails.getUserId() instead of the body. Replace the untyped Map bodies with validated DTOs. Enforce WorkflowTransition.requiredRole against the caller's authorities inside executeTransition before applying the transition.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
Long executedById = body.get("executedById") instanceof Number n ? n.longValue() : null;
String comments   = (String) body.get("comments");
return engine.executeTransition(id, actionCode, executedById, comments);
▲ After (fixed)
@AuthenticationPrincipal GrcUserDetails me;
return engine.executeTransition(id, req.actionCode(), me.getUserId(), req.comments());
// engine.executeTransition additionally: if (tr.getRequiredRole()!=null && !callerHasRole(tr.getRequiredRole())) throw new AccessDeniedException(...);

LowSEC-IAM-007Committee controllers bind raw JPA @Entity objects as request bodies (mass-assignment surface)
SecurityMass Assignment / Improper Input Handling (A08)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/admin/committee/controller/CommitteeResolutionController.java:46-50 Effort M Risk CVSS ~3.7 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — largely mitigated by service-layer id/org reset
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/admin/committee/controller/CommitteeMeetingPapersController.java:37-41
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/admin/committee/controller/CommitteeMemberRegistryController.java:41-45
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/admin/committee/controller/CommitteeActionItemController.java:63-67

Description

Several committee write endpoints accept the persistence entity directly as @RequestBody (create(@RequestBody CommitteeResolution in), circulate(@RequestBody CommitteeMeetingPaper in), appoint(@RequestBody CommitteeMemberTerm in), addSkill(@RequestBody CommitteeMemberSkill in), create(@RequestBody CommitteeActionItem in)). Clients can therefore submit server-managed fields (id, organisationId, isDeleted, createdAt, audit columns) and cross-tenant foreign keys (committeeId/meetingId). The corresponding services largely neutralise this: each create-style method calls in.setId(null) and in.setOrganisationId(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant()) (see CommitteeResolutionService:89-92, CommitteeMeetingPapersService:63-66, CommitteeMemberRegistryService:76-79,209-212) and the comments explicitly cite mass-assignment defence. Residual gap: the foreign-key fields (committeeId, meetingId) are NOT validated to belong to the caller's tenant on these create paths, so a row can be linked to a committee/meeting id from another tenant; because the row itself is org-stamped it does not leak data, but it can corrupt referential integrity and pollute another tenant's by-committee/by-meeting aggregates only if that id collides within the same org (cross-tenant linkage is invisible to reads, which are all org-scoped).

Root cause

Entities are used as the API binding type instead of purpose-built request DTOs, exposing server-owned columns; foreign-key ownership is not verified.

Evidence / proof
@PostMapping @PreAuthorize("hasPermission('ADMIN','WRITE')") public CommitteeResolution create(@RequestBody CommitteeResolution in) { return service.create(in); }

Real-world impact

Primary mass-assignment vectors (id/organisationId override) are already blocked in the service layer, so cross-tenant takeover is not achievable on these paths. Remaining risk is referential-integrity pollution via unvalidated committeeId/meetingId and reliance on every future service method remembering to reset id/org — a fragile invariant. No validation annotations are applied to the entity bodies either.

Reproduction

1. As an ADMIN:WRITE user, POST /api/v1/committees/resolutions with a body that includes {"id":999,"organisationId":2,...}. 2. Confirm the saved row keeps the caller's org and a new id (service resets them) — i.e. the defence holds today, demonstrating the dependency on it.

Resolution

Introduce explicit create/update DTOs for these endpoints (mirroring CommitteeDtos) that expose only client-settable fields, with Jakarta validation. Validate that committeeId/meetingId resolve to a row in the caller's tenant before persisting. Keep the service-layer id/org reset as defence in depth.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('ADMIN','WRITE')")
public CommitteeResolution create(@RequestBody CommitteeResolution in) {
    return service.create(in);
}
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('ADMIN','WRITE')")
public CommitteeResolution create(@RequestBody @Valid ResolutionCreateRequest req) {
    return service.create(req); // service validates req.committeeId()/meetingId() belong to TenantContext org
}

LowSEC-INT-006Inbound webhooks rely on user-JWT roles for machine-to-machine auth (no dedicated webhook authentication)
SecurityIdentification & Authentication Failures (A07)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/servicenow/webhook/ServiceNowWebhookController.java:68-69 Effort M Risk CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — broad standing credential for inbound integration traffic
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/splunk/webhook/SplunkWebhookController.java:114-115

Description

Both inbound webhooks authenticate the external system as a normal platform user holding one of PLATFORM_ADMIN / SOC_AUTOMATION / INTEGRATION_SERVICE roles (a long-lived bearer JWT). The ServiceNow webhook has no payload signature at all; the Splunk webhook's HMAC is optional and skipped when no shared secret is configured (and is itself bypassable — see SEC-INT-005). The design comment acknowledges 'The platform does not yet have a dedicated machine-to-machine auth scheme'. A leaked service-account token grants full webhook access and (per the code) the SOC_AUTOMATION/INTEGRATION_SERVICE roles are reused across multiple sensitive endpoints (poll triggers, etc.).

Root cause

No purpose-scoped credential or mandatory request signing for inbound integration callbacks; reuse of broad human-style roles for system-to-system calls.

Evidence / proof
@PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN','SOC_AUTOMATION','INTEGRATION_SERVICE')")  // ServiceNow: no signature
// SplunkWebhookController: same role guard; HMAC only when a shared secret is configured

Real-world impact

A single compromised/over-shared service-account JWT lets an attacker post forged incident-update and alert events for whatever the lookup matches (amplified by SEC-INT-002). No per-message authenticity for ServiceNow. Standing broad roles increase blast radius of token leakage.

Reproduction

1. Obtain a JWT for an account with INTEGRATION_SERVICE (e.g. via token reuse/leak).
2. POST to either webhook with a crafted payload; it is accepted with only the role check (ServiceNow) or with an optional/bypassable HMAC (Splunk).

Resolution

Introduce a dedicated webhook authentication mechanism: mandatory per-integration HMAC signing (correctly implemented over raw bytes), short-lived/narrowly-scoped credentials, and a least-privilege role used only for the specific webhook route. Make the Splunk shared secret mandatory outside dev and add an equivalent signature for ServiceNow.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('PLATFORM_ADMIN','SOC_AUTOMATION','INTEGRATION_SERVICE')")
public ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> incidentUpdated(@RequestBody Map<String, Object> payload) {
▲ After (fixed)
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('INTEGRATION_SERVICE')")  // narrow, webhook-only role
public ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> incidentUpdated(
        @RequestBody Map<String, Object> payload,
        @RequestHeader("X-Snow-Signature") String sig, HttpServletRequest req) {
    if (!verifyMandatorySignature(req, sig)) return ResponseEntity.status(401).build();

LowSEC-INT-007CCM run-listing endpoints accept an unbounded limit parameter
SecurityImproper Input Validation / Resource Exhaustion (A04)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ccm/controller/CcmController.java:101-114 Effort S Risk CVSS 3.7 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L) — authenticated resource-consumption via large page size
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ccm/service/CcmService.java:298-321

Description

GET /tests/{externalId}/runs and GET /runs/recent take @RequestParam(defaultValue="50") int limit with no upper bound (no @Max / clamp). The service passes it straight into PageRequest.of(0, Math.max(1, limit)), so limit=2000000000 requests an enormous page. An authenticated reader can repeatedly request very large pages to pressure the DB and heap.

Root cause

Page size is taken from the client without a maximum bound.

Evidence / proof
public List<TestRunResponse> recent(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "50") int limit) {
    return service.listLatestRuns(limit);
}
// service: runRepo.findRecent(orgId, PageRequest.of(0, Math.max(1, limit)))

Real-world impact

Low-severity denial-of-service / memory pressure from oversized result sets; bounded to the caller's own tenant data and requires a valid read role, so impact is limited.

Reproduction

1. Authenticate with any READ_GUARD role.
2. GET /api/v1/ccm/runs/recent?limit=100000000 and observe the server attempt to materialise a very large page.

Resolution

Clamp the page size to a sane maximum (e.g. 200) in the controller or service, or annotate the param with @Max.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
public List<TestRunResponse> recent(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "50") int limit) {
    return service.listLatestRuns(limit);
}
▲ After (fixed)
public List<TestRunResponse> recent(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "50") @Max(200) @Min(1) int limit) {
    return service.listLatestRuns(Math.min(Math.max(1, limit), 200));
}

LowSEC-LEAK-004Hardcoded vendor-portal access codes shipped in the frontend bundle
SecurityIdentification and Authentication Failures (A07) / CWE-798 Use of Hard-coded Credentials▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/lib/vendorPortal.ts:228-330 Effort M Risk CVSS 3.7 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N) — demo-only vendor data, client-side plaintext auth; no real tenant data behind it
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/lib/vendorPortal.ts:231
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/lib/vendorPortal.ts:267
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/lib/vendorPortal.ts:300
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/lib/vendorPortal.ts:328-330

Description

The vendor self-service portal authenticates vendors by an `accessCode` field. The full set of valid access codes is hard-coded as plaintext string literals in the `DEMO_VENDORS` array (e.g. 'NEOM-2026-A4Z9' line 231, 'TABUK-LOG-2026-X7M2' line 267, 'JEDDAH-CON-2026-B2K8' line 300) and matched at runtime by `findVendorByAccessCode()`, which performs a simple case-insensitive plaintext equality check (`v.accessCode.toLowerCase() === code.toLowerCase()`, line 329). Because this is a static frontend, these codes ship in the served JS bundle and the entire authentication decision happens client-side. Gitleaks flagged 'NEOM-2026-A4Z9' as a generic API key; on inspection it is a hard-coded vendor login credential rather than an API key. The data set is explicitly demo data ('Demo vendor accounts' comment, line 222) — the named orgs (NEOM/Tabuk/Jeddah) are illustrative, not live customers — which is why this is Low and not High.

Root cause

Demo/seed authentication data was embedded directly in the shipped frontend source as plaintext literals, and the vendor-portal login is implemented as a pure client-side string comparison with no backend verification.

Evidence / proof
vendorPortal.ts:231  `vendorCode: 'V-204', accessCode: 'NEOM-2026-A4Z9',`
vendorPortal.ts:328-330  `export function findVendorByAccessCode(code: string): VendorProfile | undefined {
  return DEMO_VENDORS.find(v => v.accessCode.toLowerCase() === code.toLowerCase());
}`

Real-world impact

Anyone who reads the (publicly served) frontend bundle can recover every demo vendor's login code and impersonate that vendor in the portal. In the current state the blast radius is limited to demo data, but the pattern is a trap: if real vendors are onboarded by adding rows to this array, their credentials would be exposed the same way, and the client-side-only auth would let any client bypass it entirely (DevTools / call `findVendorByAccessCode` directly).

Reproduction

1. Build/serve tss-grc-ui-v2. 2. Open the served bundle (or vendorPortal.ts in source) and read the `accessCode` literals. 3. Navigate to the vendor portal login and submit 'NEOM-2026-A4Z9' — you are logged in as NEOM Tech Services LLC (V-204) without any server check.

Resolution

Move vendor authentication server-side: verify the access code against a hashed value stored per-vendor on the backend (org-scoped, behind the existing JWT/TenantContext model) and return a real session token. Keep the frontend free of any credential material; the DEMO_VENDORS array should hold display fields only, with access codes provisioned out-of-band. Treat access codes as secrets (random, single-tenant, rotatable, hashed at rest).

▼ Before (vulnerable)
export const DEMO_VENDORS: VendorProfile[] = [
  {
    vendorCode: 'V-204', accessCode: 'NEOM-2026-A4Z9',
    ...
  },
];

export function findVendorByAccessCode(code: string): VendorProfile | undefined {
  return DEMO_VENDORS.find(v => v.accessCode.toLowerCase() === code.toLowerCase());
}
▲ After (fixed)
// No access codes in the bundle. Auth is delegated to the backend.
export const DEMO_VENDORS: VendorProfile[] = [
  { vendorCode: 'V-204', /* accessCode removed */ ... },
];

export async function authenticateVendor(code: string): Promise<VendorSession> {
  // backend hashes + compares, org-scoped, returns a JWT
  return Api.post('/api/v1/tprm/vendor-portal/login', { accessCode: code });
}

LowSEC-NDI-005Unbounded page size and unpaged in-memory aggregation enable resource exhaustion
SecurityResource Exhaustion / Uncontrolled Resource Consumption (A05)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/compliance/controller/NdiComplianceAssessmentController.java:43-55 Effort S Risk CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L) — authenticated DoS / memory pressure
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/gap/controller/NdiGapController.java:44-52
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/audit/controller/NdiAuditController.java:22-31
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/evidence/controller/NdiEvidenceItemController.java:25-33
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/audit/service/NdiAuditService.java:42-55

Description

Paged list endpoints accept a client-controlled `size` parameter (defaults 50-200) with no upper bound, so a caller may request size=1000000 and force the DB and JSON serializer to materialise an arbitrarily large result set. Separately, NdiAuditService.aggregate() calls repo.findByOrganisationIdOrderByOccurredAtDesc(o, Pageable.unpaged()), loading the tenant's entire audit_event table into memory on every dashboard/aggregate request. For a tenant with a large audit history (or after the audit-injection issue SEC-NDI-002 is abused to flood the table) this is a cheap way to drive memory/CPU pressure.

Root cause

No server-side clamp on the requested page size, and an unpaged full-table scan used to compute aggregates instead of a DB-side GROUP BY/COUNT.

Evidence / proof
NdiComplianceAssessmentController.list(... @RequestParam(defaultValue = "200") int size) -> PageRequest.of(page, size);  // size never clamped
NdiAuditService.aggregate(): Page<NdiAuditEvent> page = repo.findByOrganisationIdOrderByOccurredAtDesc(o, Pageable.unpaged());

Real-world impact

An authenticated user can degrade availability for the tenant (and potentially the JVM) by requesting huge pages or repeatedly hitting the audit aggregate endpoint; risk grows with data volume.

Reproduction

1. GET /api/ndi/compliance?cycleId=1&size=10000000 with a valid token — server attempts to load and serialize up to 10M rows.
2. Repeatedly GET /api/ndi/audit/aggregate on a tenant with a large audit table — each call loads the full table.

Resolution

Clamp size to a sane maximum (e.g. Math.min(size, 200)) in each controller or via a shared Pageable resolver, and compute audit aggregates with DB-side count/group-by queries instead of Pageable.unpaged().

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@RequestParam(defaultValue = "200") int size) {
    var p = PageRequest.of(page, size);
▲ After (fixed)
@RequestParam(defaultValue = "200") int size) {
    var p = PageRequest.of(page, Math.min(Math.max(size, 1), 200));
References: CWE-770: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling · CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption · OWASP API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption
LowSEC-NDI-006Raw JPA entities bound from request bodies (mass assignment exposure)
SecurityMass Assignment / Improper Input Handling (A08)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/reports/controller/NdiReportController.java:37-47 Effort L Risk CVSS 3.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — limited; server overrides the security-sensitive fields
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/cycle/controller/NdiAssessmentCycleController.java:62-71
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/gap/controller/NdiGapController.java:69-79
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/evidence/controller/NdiEvidenceItemController.java:49-59
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/settings/controller/NdiSettingController.java:46-50
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/audit/controller/NdiAuditController.java:37-41

Description

Across the NDI module the controllers accept the persistence entities themselves as @RequestBody (NdiReportDefinition, NdiAssessmentCycle, NdiGap, NdiComplianceAssessment, NdiEvidenceItem, NdiSetting, NdiAuditEvent) with no @Valid and no DTO boundary. The client can therefore set any settable field on the entity, including id, organisationId, isDeleted, createdAt/createdBy, and last_run_* audit columns. In the create()/update() service methods reviewed, the sensitive fields are defended (id forced to null, organisationId stamped from TenantContext, update() whitelists fields), which prevents cross-tenant writes — so the practical impact today is low. However the pattern is fragile: any future entity field added becomes silently client-writable, and the lack of bean validation means malformed/oversized values reach the DB layer. NdiAuditEvent is the worst case (see SEC-NDI-002) because record() does not whitelist fields.

Root cause

No DTO/validation layer for NDI write endpoints; JPA entities are used directly as the API contract.

Evidence / proof
NdiReportController.create(@RequestBody NdiReportDefinition body) ...; NdiAssessmentCycleController.create(@RequestBody NdiAssessmentCycle req) ...; NdiAuditController.record(@RequestBody NdiAuditEvent body) — no @Valid, entity bound directly.

Real-world impact

Defence-in-depth weakness: relies entirely on each service method remembering to null id and stamp organisationId. A missed override (as in NdiAuditService.record for non-id/org fields) becomes an injection of attacker-chosen state. No structural protection against over-posting or invalid input.

Reproduction

1. POST /api/ndi/reports with extra fields {"nameEn":"x","reportType":"GAP_REGISTER","organisationId":999,"isDeleted":true,"lastRunStatus":"SUCCESS"}.
2. organisationId/id are overridden by the service (good), but lastRunStatus and other non-whitelisted-on-create fields are persisted as supplied.

Resolution

Introduce request DTOs with Jakarta @Valid constraints (as dataclass and data_officer already do) and map explicitly to entities, never binding @Entity types at the controller. Continue to stamp organisationId/id server-side.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public ResponseEntity<NdiReportDefinition> create(@RequestBody NdiReportDefinition body) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(service.create(body));
}
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('NDI','WRITE')")
public ResponseEntity<NdiReportDefinition> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateReportDefinitionRequest req) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(service.create(req));   // service maps DTO -> entity, sets org & id
}

LowSEC-NPM-005@babel/core arbitrary file read via sourceMappingURL comment (build-time, low)
SecurityPath Traversal / Information Exposure (A05)▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/package-lock.json:57-62 Effort S Risk CVSS 3.2 (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:L/I:N/A:N) — GHSA-4x5r-pxfx-6jf8. Local, high attack complexity, low confidentiality; transitive build-time-only dependency.
tss-grc-ui-v2/package-lock.json:1440-1447

Description

@babel/core 7.29.0 (package-lock.json lines 57-62, marked dev:true) is a transitive dependency of @vitejs/plugin-react 4.7.0 (which declares @babel/core ^7.28.0 at package-lock.json line 1447). GHSA-4x5r-pxfx-6jf8 (CWE-22, CWE-200) reports that @babel/core can perform an arbitrary file read when processing a crafted `//# sourceMappingURL=` comment that points at a local file path, causing Babel to read and embed that file's contents into the source map. Installed 7.29.0 is at the top of the vulnerable range <=7.29.0; the fix is the next patch. This is a build-time tool only (dev dependency, never shipped to the browser bundle), so exploitation requires the build to process attacker-controlled source — a low-likelihood scenario for an internal app.

Root cause

Transitive dev dependency @babel/core 7.29.0 (via @vitejs/plugin-react 4.7.0) honours sourceMappingURL comments pointing at local files without restricting the path, allowing file content to be read into the generated source map.

Evidence / proof
package-lock.json:57-61
    "node_modules/@babel/core": {
      "version": "7.29.0",
...
      "dev": true,
package-lock.json:1447  "@babel/core": "^7.28.0"   (under @vitejs/plugin-react)

Real-world impact

If the build pipeline ever compiles source files supplied by an untrusted party (e.g. a malicious dependency or contributed module), a crafted sourceMappingURL comment can cause Babel to read an arbitrary local file from the build host and leak it into the emitted source map (which the project ships, since vite.config.ts sets build.sourcemap:true). Low real-world risk for a first-party internal UI; included for completeness.

Reproduction

1. Place a source file containing //# sourceMappingURL=../../../../etc/passwd (or a Windows path) in the build input. 2. Run npm run build (tsc -b && vite build). 3. Inspect the generated .map output for the leaked file content. npm audit --json: @babel/core range <=7.29.0, fixAvailable:true.

Resolution

Upgrade @babel/core past 7.29.0. It is transitive, so either bump @vitejs/plugin-react to a release pinning the patched @babel/core, or add an npm `overrides` entry forcing @babel/core to the fixed version. npm audit reports fixAvailable:true (non-major). Re-run `npm audit` to confirm.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// transitive dev dep via @vitejs/plugin-react 4.7.0
node_modules/@babel/core -> 7.29.0  (dev:true)
▲ After (fixed)
// tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json — pin the fix via overrides
"overrides": {
  "@babel/core": ">=7.29.1"
}

LowSEC-PLAT-008Unbounded page size on Issue and AutomationRule list endpoints (resource exhaustion)
SecurityResource Exhaustion / Uncontrolled Resource Consumption (A04)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/platform/controller/IssueController.java:31-36 Effort S Risk CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L) — memory/DB pressure via oversized page requests
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/platform/service/IssueService.java:78-82

Description

GET /api/v1/issues accepts a caller-controlled `size` query parameter (default 50) and passes it straight to PageRequest.of(page, size) in IssueService.list with no upper bound. A caller can request size=100000000 and force the server to materialise a very large result page in one query/heap allocation. Other list endpoints in this audit scope correctly cap the page size (AuditLogService caps at 200, AutomationRuleController.listRuns uses Math.min(size,200)), making the Issue endpoint an outlier. Note the AutomationRuleController.list() rule list is also unbounded but reads a typically-small table.

Root cause

The page-size parameter is trusted without a maximum clamp, unlike the capped list endpoints elsewhere in the module.

Evidence / proof
@GetMapping
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public Page<Issue> list(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
                        @RequestParam(defaultValue = "50") int size) {
    return service.list(page, size);
}
// IssueService.list:
return repo.findByOrganisationIdOrderByIdDesc(
    TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(), PageRequest.of(page, size));

Real-world impact

A single authenticated user can degrade availability by requesting huge pages, causing large DB reads and heap pressure (potential OutOfMemoryError on tenants with many issues). Low severity because it requires authentication and only affects the caller's tenant data volume.

Reproduction

1. Log in as any user.
2. curl 'http://localhost:8084/api/v1/issues?page=0&size=100000000' -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" and observe the server attempting to load an unbounded page.

Resolution

Clamp the page size, e.g. PageRequest.of(page, Math.min(Math.max(size,1), 200)) in IssueService.list (mirroring AuditLogService). Prefer @PageableDefault/Pageable with a configured max page size for consistency.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public Page<Issue> list(int page, int size) {
    return repo.findByOrganisationIdOrderByIdDesc(
        TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(), PageRequest.of(page, size));
}
▲ After (fixed)
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public Page<Issue> list(int page, int size) {
    int safeSize = Math.min(Math.max(size, 1), 200);
    return repo.findByOrganisationIdOrderByIdDesc(
        TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(), PageRequest.of(page, safeSize));
}

LowSEC-PLAT-009Audit-log source IP taken from unvalidated X-Forwarded-For (audit-trail spoofing)
SecurityInsufficient Logging Integrity (A09)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/platform/auditlog/service/AuditLogService.java:159-166 Effort S Risk CVSS 3.7 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — forgeable source IP in the security audit trail

Description

AuditLogService.extractIp reads the X-Forwarded-For request header and stores the first value as the audit row's ip_address whenever the header is present, with no allowlist of trusted proxies. Any authenticated user can set an arbitrary X-Forwarded-For on their requests, so every audited action they perform can be attributed to a forged source IP in the F7 audit ledger. This weakens the evidentiary value of the audit trail that SAMA/NCA examinations rely on.

Root cause

The forwarded-header is trusted unconditionally instead of only when the request arrives from a known/trusted reverse proxy (or via Spring's ForwardedHeaderFilter configured for the deployment topology).

Evidence / proof
private static String extractIp(HttpServletRequest req) {
    String xff = req.getHeader("X-Forwarded-For");
    if (xff != null && !xff.isBlank()) {
        int comma = xff.indexOf(',');
        return truncate((comma < 0 ? xff : xff.substring(0, comma)).trim(), 60);
    }
    return truncate(req.getRemoteAddr(), 60);
}

Real-world impact

Forensic/repudiation risk: audit entries can be made to point at an attacker-chosen IP, frustrating incident investigation and undermining non-repudiation. Low severity — it does not grant access, only degrades log integrity, and the username/role fields remain trustworthy (derived from the JWT).

Reproduction

1. Log in as any user.
2. Perform any audited action with header: -H 'X-Forwarded-For: 8.8.8.8'.
3. GET /api/v1/audit-log and observe the new entry's ip_address recorded as 8.8.8.8 rather than the real client address.

Resolution

Only honour X-Forwarded-For when the immediate peer (req.getRemoteAddr()) is a configured trusted proxy; otherwise use req.getRemoteAddr(). Better, configure Spring's ForwardedHeaderFilter / server.forward-headers-strategy per deployment and read the resolved remote address.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
private static String extractIp(HttpServletRequest req) {
    String xff = req.getHeader("X-Forwarded-For");
    if (xff != null && !xff.isBlank()) {
        int comma = xff.indexOf(',');
        return truncate((comma < 0 ? xff : xff.substring(0, comma)).trim(), 60);
    }
    return truncate(req.getRemoteAddr(), 60);
}
▲ After (fixed)
private static String extractIp(HttpServletRequest req) {
    // Only trust XFF when the direct peer is a known proxy; otherwise use the socket address.
    String peer = req.getRemoteAddr();
    if (isTrustedProxy(peer)) {
        String xff = req.getHeader("X-Forwarded-For");
        if (xff != null && !xff.isBlank()) {
            int comma = xff.indexOf(',');
            return truncate((comma < 0 ? xff : xff.substring(0, comma)).trim(), 60);
        }
    }
    return truncate(peer, 60);
}

LowSEC-PRIV-004SDAIA breach-submission and DSR-extend endpoints accept unbounded/untyped Map<String,Object> bodies (no DTO validation)
SecurityInsufficient Input Validation (A04/A08) / CWE-20▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/privacy/controller/PrivacyController.java:200-211 Effort M Risk CVSS ~3.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) — weak input typing/validation on privileged workflow mutations
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/privacy/controller/PrivacyController.java:74-83
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/privacy/controller/DpiaController.java:69-79
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ethics/controller/AmlAlertController.java:58-70
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ethics/controller/EthicsCaseController.java:77-81

Description

Several privileged mutation endpoints accept raw @RequestBody Map<String,Object> or unvalidated entity bodies instead of @Valid DTOs with Jakarta constraints. Examples: PrivacyController.extendDsr reads body.get("days") as a Number with no bounds (a caller can pass days=2_000_000 to push the PDPL SLA arbitrarily far out); recordSdaiaSubmission takes a record with no @Valid/@NotBlank; DpiaController.approve/reject and the Ethics AML/EthicsCase transition handlers accept untyped maps. The CRUD create/update endpoints on PrivacyController (createBreach/createDsr/createRopa) and the ethics controllers bind the JPA entity directly via @RequestBody with no @Valid, so client-supplied audit/server-managed fields are accepted from the wire (mass-assignment surface), though the services re-stamp organisationId and (for DPIA) null the id.

Root cause

Workflow endpoints were implemented with ad-hoc Map parsing rather than typed, validated request DTOs. No @Valid is applied and no @Min/@Max/@NotBlank constraints bound the values.

Evidence / proof
PrivacyController.java:200-205  @PostMapping("/dsrs/{id}/extend") public DataSubjectRequest extendDsr(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Map<String,Object> body){ Integer days = body.get("days") instanceof Number n ? n.intValue() : null; return privacyService.extendDsr(id, days);} — PrivacyService.extendDsr only floors at 30 when null/<=0; no upper bound. createBreach(@RequestBody DataBreach req) at lines 45-47 has no @Valid.

Real-world impact

Weak typing allows out-of-range or unexpected values to drive regulated SLA clocks (DSR due date, breach states) and produces inconsistent validation behaviour. Direct entity binding without @Valid widens the mass-assignment surface and bypasses the bean-validation messages the platform ships. No direct confidentiality breach, hence Low.

Reproduction

1) As a PRIVACY_WRITE user: POST /api/v1/privacy/dsrs/{id}/extend {"days":3650}. 2) The DSR due date is pushed out 10 years with no rejection, defeating the PDPL 30/60-day SLA model.

Resolution

Introduce typed request records with Jakarta constraints (e.g. ExtendDsrRequest(@Min(1) @Max(60) int days)), annotate every mutating handler body with @Valid, and replace Map<String,Object> transition bodies with explicit DTOs. For create/update, bind a request DTO (not the JPA entity) and map server-managed fields server-side.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping("/dsrs/{id}/extend")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PRIVACY', 'WRITE')")
public DataSubjectRequest extendDsr(@PathVariable Long id, @RequestBody Map<String, Object> body) {
    Integer days = body.get("days") instanceof Number n ? n.intValue() : null;
    return privacyService.extendDsr(id, days);
}
▲ After (fixed)
public record ExtendDsrRequest(@NotNull @Min(1) @Max(60) Integer days) {}

@PostMapping("/dsrs/{id}/extend")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('PRIVACY', 'WRITE')")
public DataSubjectRequest extendDsr(@PathVariable Long id, @Valid @RequestBody ExtendDsrRequest body) {
    return privacyService.extendDsr(id, body.days());
}

LowSEC-PRIV-005Sensitive PII written into audit-log/business-event messages (consent subject refs, KYC names/IDs, whistleblower actors)
SecuritySensitive Data Exposure (A09/A02) / CWE-532 Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/privacy/service/ConsentRecordService.java:124-127 Effort M Risk CVSS ~3.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N) — PII persisted into audit ledger / event payloads readable by lower-privileged log/automation consumers
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/privacy/service/ConsentRecordService.java:64-77
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ethics/service/WhistleblowerRetaliationService.java:99-101
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ethics/coi/service/CoiService.java:260-263
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ethics/coi/service/CoiService.java:343-345

Description

Multiple services embed personal data directly into audit-log free-text messages and DomainEvent payloads. ConsentRecordService logs 'Consent granted: subject=<dataSubjectRef> purpose=… basis=…' and emits the dataSubjectRef in every CONSENT_* event payload and as the event correlation id ('consent:'+dataSubjectRef+':'+purposeCode). CoiService logs the declarant's full name and employee number into COI_DECLARATION_* audit rows and event payloads. WhistleblowerRetaliationService logs the named claimed actor. These audit rows and F8 event payloads are consumed by separate audit/automation subsystems whose access control is broader than the privacy/ethics module permission — so PII leaks to viewers who should not see the underlying record.

Root cause

Audit/event messages were built by string-concatenating the human-readable record including PII identifiers, instead of referencing the entity by surrogate id and keeping PII in the tenant-scoped entity tables only.

Evidence / proof
ConsentRecordService.java:124-127 audit.log("CREATE","ConsentRecord", saved.getId(), "Consent granted: subject=" + saved.getDataSubjectRef() + " purpose=" + saved.getPurposeCode() + " basis=" + saved.getLegalBasis()); and emit(...) payload includes m.put("dataSubjectRef", nullSafeStr(c.getDataSubjectRef())) (lines 66-67, 86-87). CoiService.java:260-263 logs finalDecl.getFullNameEn() + employeeNo.

Real-world impact

Personal data (PDPL-regulated subject references, employee names/IDs, named subjects of whistleblower retaliation claims) is duplicated into the audit ledger and the automation event bus. Anyone with audit-log read or rule-engine visibility — a broader population than the data owner — can recover PII, contradicting data-minimisation (PDPL Art.4) and the module's own access scoping.

Reproduction

1) Grant a consent via POST /api/v1/privacy/consents. 2) Read the audit log (audit-log module) as a user with audit read but no PRIVACY permission → the row text contains the data subject reference. 3) Inspect the CONSENT_GRANTED DomainEvent payload in the automation subsystem → dataSubjectRef present.

Resolution

Reference records in audit/event text by surrogate id only (e.g. 'ConsentRecord#<id>') and keep PII identifiers out of free-text messages and event payloads, or hash/tokenise the subject reference for correlation. If a subject correlation key is genuinely required for rule matching, use a non-reversible token rather than the raw reference, and ensure audit/event consumers enforce the same data-classification controls as the source module.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
audit.log("CREATE", "ConsentRecord", saved.getId(),
    "Consent granted: subject=" + saved.getDataSubjectRef()
        + " purpose=" + saved.getPurposeCode()
        + " basis=" + saved.getLegalBasis());
// payload: m.put("dataSubjectRef", nullSafeStr(c.getDataSubjectRef()));
▲ After (fixed)
audit.log("CREATE", "ConsentRecord", saved.getId(),
    "Consent granted for ConsentRecord#" + saved.getId()
        + " purpose=" + saved.getPurposeCode()
        + " basis=" + saved.getLegalBasis());
// payload: m.put("dataSubjectToken", hash(c.getDataSubjectRef())); // no raw PII
References: CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File · OWASP Top 10 2021 — A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures · SDAIA PDPL Art.4 (data minimisation)
LowSEC-PY-001SQL built by Python string/f-string interpolation in DB bootstrap & seed scripts (B608 x56)
SecuritySQL Injection (A03)▾
Location seed_real_data.py:305-319 Effort M Risk Risk rationale: Bandit rates B608 MEDIUM, but exploitability here is LOW. The interpolated tokens are trusted internal constants (integers such as days_ago/hours_ago, or schema/index names read from the live dev DB) while all external/business data is passed via parameterised '?' placeholders. No untrusted-input path reaches the string-built portion, and the scripts are dev-only DB bootstrap utilities run by an operator with the sa account. Reported as a pattern-hygiene/defence-in-depth issue per scope.
seed_real_data.py:369-382
seed_socops_data.py:432-450
.tools/introspect_schema.py:208-209
.tools/introspect_schema.py:240-241
setup_data_officer_seed.py (2 hits)
setup_cyber_db.py (1 hit)
fix_arabic_mojibake.py (2 hits)
.tools/fix_arabic_mojibake.py (3 hits)
.tmp/reset_pw.py:16-23

Description

Bandit flagged 56 B608 'Possible SQL injection via string-based query construction' occurrences across the repo-root Python DB scripts. The two largest concentrations are seed_real_data.py (19) and seed_socops_data.py (12); the rest are spread across ~19 other setup_*/seed_*/.tools scripts. Verified two representative cases. In seed_real_data.py the SQL is an f-string, but business data (email, name, status, org_id) is bound through '?' placeholders; the only interpolated value is the integer day-offset {days_ago} taken from a hardcoded Python constant list, used inside DATEADD(day, -{days_ago}, ...). Same shape in seed_socops_data.py (interpolated {-hours_ago}/{sla_offset} integers). The genuinely string-built case is .tools/introspect_schema.py, a DDL generator that interpolates schema/table/index names (e.g. CREATE {unique_kw}INDEX [{ix['name']}] ON {schema}.{table}) — but those identifiers come from the live dev DB's own sys.schemas/sys.indexes catalog, not from any external input. Confidence breakdown from the scan: 36 LOW / 20 MEDIUM, 0 HIGH.

Root cause

Convenience pattern of assembling SQL with Python f-strings/concatenation instead of fully parameterising every value. Integers and schema identifiers cannot be bound the same way as values, so authors inlined them. None of the inlined tokens originate from untrusted input, but the pattern is brittle: a future edit that interpolates an attacker-influenced field would silently become injectable.

Evidence / proof
seed_real_data.py:305-319
for rtype, rname, remail, status, days_ago in DSRS:
    run(
        f"""
        IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM privacy.data_subject_requests
                       WHERE requester_email = ? AND organisation_id = ? AND request_type = ?)
        INSERT INTO privacy.data_subject_requests (...)
        VALUES (NEWID(), ?, ?, ?, ?, DATEADD(day, -{days_ago}, GETDATE()),
            DATEADD(day, -{days_ago} + 30, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)), ?, 0, ...)
        """,
        remail, ORG_TSS, rtype, ORG_TSS, rtype, rname, remail, status, ...)

.tools/introspect_schema.py:208
out.append(f"IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sys.indexes WHERE name = '{ix['name']}' AND object_id = OBJECT_ID('{schema}.{table}'))")

Real-world impact

In the current code there is no exploitable injection: the inlined tokens are trusted constants/catalog names and these scripts never accept network/user input. The real impact is maintenance risk and a poor pattern that scanners (and auditors) will keep flagging, plus the chance of a regression if someone later inlines a user/business field. If any of these scripts were ever repurposed to accept caller-supplied parameters, the string-built portions would become first-order SQL injection against the dev/prod database under the sa login.

Reproduction

1. bandit -r . -f json | jq '.results[] | select(.test_id=="B608")' — yields 56 hits.
2. Open seed_real_data.py:307 and confirm DATEADD(day, -{days_ago}, ...) is f-string-interpolated while data uses '?'.
3. Trace DSRS (line ~289) — days_ago is a hardcoded int literal, not input. No injection reachable as written.
4. Open .tools/introspect_schema.py:208 — confirm identifiers come from sys.indexes/sys.schemas, not external input.

Resolution

For integer day/hour offsets, bind them as parameters too (pyodbc supports binding the DATEADD operand: DATEADD(day, -?, GETDATE()) with the int passed in the args tuple) rather than f-string interpolation. For the DDL generator, validate identifiers against an allowlist regex (^[A-Za-z0-9_]+$) before interpolation and/or use QUOTENAME() in the emitted T-SQL. Add a repo lint gate (bandit B608) so new string-built SQL is caught in review. Because these are dev-only, the priority is low — but standardising on a single parameterised run() helper across all setup_*/seed_* scripts removes the whole class.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
run(
    f"""
    ... VALUES (NEWID(), ?, ?, ?, ?, DATEADD(day, -{days_ago}, GETDATE()),
        DATEADD(day, -{days_ago} + 30, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)), ?, 0, ...)
    """,
    remail, ORG_TSS, rtype, ORG_TSS, rtype, rname, remail, status)
▲ After (fixed)
run(
    """
    ... VALUES (NEWID(), ?, ?, ?, ?, DATEADD(day, -?, GETDATE()),
        DATEADD(day, -? + 30, CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)), ?, 0, ...)
    """,
    remail, ORG_TSS, rtype, ORG_TSS, rtype, rname, remail,
    days_ago, days_ago, status)

# introspect_schema.py — validate identifiers before interpolation
import re
assert re.fullmatch(r'[A-Za-z0-9_]+', ix['name']), f"unsafe index name {ix['name']!r}"
References: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command · OWASP A03:2021 Injection · Bandit B608: hardcoded_sql_expressions
LowSEC-PY-004Silent exception suppression: try/except/pass and try/except/continue (B110 x8, B112 x6)
SecurityImproper Error Handling (A09)▾
Location .tools/forensic_final.py:22-25 Effort S Risk Risk rationale: dev-tooling robustness/observability issue, not a vulnerability. Broad except: pass / except: continue blocks swallow all errors (including KeyboardInterrupt-adjacent and unexpected failures), which can mask data-corruption or partial-failure bugs in the bootstrap/seed scripts but has no direct exploit path.
.tools/fix_arabic_mojibake.py:145
.tools/fix_ccm_mojibake.py:28
.tools/verify_ccm_fix.py:7
.tmp/dump_edit.py:14
.tmp/dump_full_edit.py:18
.tmp/dump_translations_edits.py:17
.tmp/extract_evidence.py:74

Description

Bandit raised 8 B110 (try/except/pass, CWE-703) and 6 B112 (try/except/continue) hits across dev tooling under .tools/ and .tmp/. Verified .tools/forensic_final.py:22-25 (try: sys.stdout.reconfigure(...) except Exception: pass) and .tmp/dump_edit.py:13-14 (try: rec = json.loads(line) except: continue). These suppress errors during stdout reconfiguration and per-line JSON parsing.

Root cause

Quick scripts that intentionally skip malformed lines / optional setup steps, using a catch-all that discards the exception instead of catching the specific expected type and logging it.

Evidence / proof
.tools/forensic_final.py:22-25
try:
    sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")
except Exception:
    pass

.tmp/dump_edit.py:13-14
        try: rec = json.loads(line)
        except: continue

Real-world impact

Operational, not security. Swallowed exceptions can hide partial seed/bootstrap failures (a script reports success while having skipped rows), complicating audit reproducibility. A bare 'except:' (dump_edit.py:14) also catches SystemExit/KeyboardInterrupt, which is poor practice.

Reproduction

1. bandit -r . | grep -E 'B110|B112' -> 14 hits.
2. Open .tmp/dump_edit.py:14 -> bare 'except: continue'.

Resolution

Catch the specific expected exception (json.JSONDecodeError, AttributeError) and at minimum log/count the skipped item. Replace bare 'except:' with 'except Exception:' (or the precise type) so control-flow signals propagate. Low priority given dev-only scope.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
        try: rec = json.loads(line)
        except: continue
▲ After (fixed)
        try:
            rec = json.loads(line)
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            skipped += 1
            continue
References: CWE-703: Improper Check or Handling of Exceptional Conditions · Bandit B110: try_except_pass · Bandit B112: try_except_continue
LowSEC-RISK-005Unchecked casts on free-form Map body in correctAssessment / KRI reading / appetite exposure
SecurityImproper Input Validation (A03/A04)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/controller/RiskAdvancedController.java:56-65 Effort M Risk CVSS 3.1 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L) — malformed JSON triggers 500/ClassCastException
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/controller/KriAppetiteController.java:74-83
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/controller/KriAppetiteController.java:164-173
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/controller/KriAppetiteController.java:97-108

Description

Several endpoints accept an untyped Map<String,Object> body and perform unchecked casts: correctAssessment casts ((Number) body.get("likelihood")) and (String) body.get("assessmentNotesEn"); recordReading/updateExposure dereference body.get("value").toString() (NPE if 'value' absent) and parse it with new BigDecimal(...) (NumberFormatException on non-numeric); acknowledgeBreach reads userId from the body. A client sending the wrong JSON type or omitting a required key triggers an uncaught ClassCastException / NullPointerException / NumberFormatException surfacing as a 500. These are not typed, validated DTOs, so no Jakarta constraints apply and error handling is inconsistent. There is no injection or privilege impact (values are numeric/notes only), but it is poor input hygiene and a minor availability/robustness issue, and acknowledgeBreach trusts a body-supplied userId for attribution rather than the principal.

Root cause

Use of weakly-typed Map<String,Object> request bodies with manual casting/parsing instead of validated request DTOs; missing null/type checks.

Evidence / proof
        Integer likelihood = body.get("likelihood") == null ? null : ((Number) body.get("likelihood")).intValue();
        ...
        BigDecimal value = body.get("value") instanceof Number n
            ? new BigDecimal(n.toString())
            : new BigDecimal(body.get("value").toString()); // NPE if 'value' missing

Real-world impact

Authenticated clients can trigger 500 responses (and noisy stack traces in non-prod) with malformed payloads; breach acknowledgement is attributed to a caller-supplied userId rather than the authenticated user, weakening the acknowledgement audit trail.

Reproduction

1. As a RISK:WRITE user, PUT /api/v1/risk/assessments/{id} with body {"likelihood":"abc"} -> ClassCastException 500. 2. POST /api/v1/risk/kris/{id}/readings with body {} -> NPE on body.get("value") 500.

Resolution

Replace the Map bodies with typed DTOs (e.g. AssessmentCorrectionRequest, KriReadingRequest, ExposureUpdateRequest) carrying @NotNull/@DecimalMin constraints validated with @Valid; derive acknowledger userId from the authenticated principal instead of the body.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
    public KriBreachEvent acknowledgeBreach(@PathVariable Long breachId, @RequestBody Map<String, Object> body) {
        Long userId = body.get("userId") instanceof Number n ? n.longValue() : null;
        return kriService.acknowledgeBreach(breachId, userId);
    }
▲ After (fixed)
    public KriBreachEvent acknowledgeBreach(@PathVariable Long breachId,
                                            @AuthenticationPrincipal GrcUserDetails principal) {
        return kriService.acknowledgeBreach(breachId, principal == null ? null : principal.getUserId());
    }
References: CWE-20 Improper Input Validation · CWE-704 Incorrect Type Conversion or Cast · OWASP A04:2021 Insecure Design
LowSEC-SEC-002TLS certificate validation disabled in DB connections (TrustServerCertificate / Encrypt=No)
SecurityImproper Certificate Validation (CWE-295)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application.yml:15-15 Effort S Risk CVSS 3.7 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — MITM exposure on the DB channel; localhost-only in practice for the dev scripts, but the prod JDBC default also trusts any cert
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application-dev.yml:24
.tools/introspect_schema.py:19-20
.tools/apply_v21.py:4-5
fix_arabic_mojibake.py:29-30
setup_attachments_table.py:10-11

Description

The base/dev JDBC URL uses `encrypt=true;trustServerCertificate=true`, which encrypts the channel but disables certificate validation, defeating MITM protection. The ~14 Python scripts that connect via ODBC use `TrustServerCertificate=yes` or `Encrypt=No`, which similarly disable validation (or encryption entirely). For the localhost dev scripts the practical exposure is negligible, but the same `trustServerCertificate=true` pattern is carried in the base `application.yml` datasource URL that the prod profile's documented `DB_URL` comment also references — meaning an operator copying the example connects to the production database over a channel that trusts any presented certificate.

Root cause

Certificate trust was disabled to avoid configuring a CA/trust store during local development, and the insecure setting was left in the base configuration and the prod URL example rather than scoped strictly to dev.

Evidence / proof
application.yml:15 — "url: ${DB_URL:jdbc:sqlserver://localhost:1433;databaseName=TSS_GRC;encrypt=true;trustServerCertificate=true;sendStringParametersAsUnicode=true}"

Real-world impact

An attacker positioned between the application (or a script) and the SQL Server can present a forged certificate and transparently intercept/modify all database traffic, including the `sa` login and every tenant's data. Risk is high only on untrusted networks; on localhost it is informational.

Reproduction

1. Inspect application.yml:15 and the prod DB_URL example comment (application-prod.yml:9). 2. Note `trustServerCertificate=true` (Java) and `TrustServerCertificate=yes`/`Encrypt=No` (Python). 3. On a non-localhost link, an ARP/DNS-spoof MITM with a self-signed cert is accepted without error.

Resolution

For non-dev environments set `encrypt=true;trustServerCertificate=false;hostNameInCertificate=<cn>` and provision the SQL Server CA into the JVM trust store (the prod example URL already hints at this — make it the enforced default, not a comment). For the dev scripts, gate trust-disabling behind an explicit env flag so it cannot leak into shared instances.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
url: ${DB_URL:jdbc:sqlserver://localhost:1433;databaseName=TSS_GRC;encrypt=true;trustServerCertificate=true;sendStringParametersAsUnicode=true}
▲ After (fixed)
url: ${DB_URL:jdbc:sqlserver://localhost:1433;databaseName=TSS_GRC;encrypt=true;trustServerCertificate=true;sendStringParametersAsUnicode=true}
# NOTE: trustServerCertificate=true is the LOCAL-DEV default only. Non-dev DB_URL
# MUST use trustServerCertificate=false;hostNameInCertificate=<cn> with the SQL
# Server CA in the JVM trust store. application-prod.yml has no default for DB_URL,
# so prod is forced to supply a validated URL.
References: CWE-295: Improper Certificate Validation · OWASP A02:2021 Cryptographic Failures · Microsoft JDBC: Connecting with SSL encryption
LowSEC-SEC-003Production CORS allow-list not overridden; falls back to permissive credentialed pattern matching
SecurityCross-Origin Resource Sharing Misconfiguration (CWE-942)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application-prod.yml:106-115 Effort S Risk CVSS 4.2 (AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — contingent on CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS being mis-set in prod; default fallback is localhost-only so direct exploitability is limited
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application.yml:142-145
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/CorsConfig.java:34-44
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application-dev.yml:65-71

Description

The base config comment states "In production, set to empty list (same-origin via Nginx reverse proxy)" and CorsConfig.java repeats that the prod profile sets `grc.cors.allowed-origins` empty. In reality `application-prod.yml` contains NO `grc.cors` block (verified — grep for cors/allowed-origins in application-prod.yml returns no matches), so prod inherits the base default `${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS:http://localhost:3000}`. Combined with `CorsConfig` using `setAllowedOriginPatterns(...)` + `setAllowCredentials(true)`, this is a documentation-vs-reality gap: the security relies entirely on the operator remembering to export `CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` correctly. Because `setAllowedOriginPatterns` treats entries as wildcard patterns (the dev profile uses `http://192.168.*:[*]`, `http://10.*:[*]`, `http://172.*:[*]` together with credentials), any over-broad value supplied via the env var in prod would allow credentialed cross-origin reads from a wide range of origins.

Root cause

Prod relies on an env var the YAML never asserts, and the comment claiming an explicit empty prod list was never implemented. The pattern-matching CORS source plus allowCredentials=true makes any wildcard origin value dangerous.

Evidence / proof
application-prod.yml has no `grc.cors:` key (grep returns 'No matches found'); base default at application.yml:145 — "allowed-origins: ${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS:http://localhost:3000}"; CorsConfig.java:39,43 — "config.setAllowedOriginPatterns(allowedOrigins); ... config.setAllowCredentials(true);"

Real-world impact

If CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS is left unset or set to a broad pattern in production, browsers will attach the HttpOnly refresh cookie / Authorization responses for cross-origin requests from attacker-controlled origins matching the pattern, enabling session-riding data theft. With the documented intent (empty list) unimplemented, this depends on operator discipline rather than a safe default.

Reproduction

1. Deploy with `--spring.profiles.active=prod` and no CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS exported. 2. Observe Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:3000 with Allow-Credentials: true on /api/** preflights. 3. Set CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS to a wildcard pattern and any matching origin can make credentialed cross-origin calls.

Resolution

Make prod fail-closed: add an explicit `grc.cors.allowed-origins: ${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS:}` (empty) to application-prod.yml so an unset value yields no allowed origins, and document that wildcard patterns must never be used in prod. Consider rejecting wildcard patterns when allowCredentials is true.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
# application-prod.yml — (no grc.cors block; inherits base default http://localhost:3000)
▲ After (fixed)
grc:
  cors:
    # Same-origin behind Nginx in prod -> no cross-origin allowed by default.
    # Wildcard patterns are forbidden here (allowCredentials=true is on).
    allowed-origins: ${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS:}
References: CWE-942: Permissive Cross-domain Policy with Untrusted Domains · OWASP A05:2021 Security Misconfiguration · MDN: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials with wildcard origins
LowSEC-SEC-004Dev profile ships broad LAN CORS wildcards with credentials enabled and lockout effectively disabled
SecuritySecurity Misconfiguration (A05)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application-dev.yml:65-74 Effort S Risk Risk rationale: dev-only profile, but the allowed-origin set (entire 192.168/10/172 RFC1918 space, any port) plus allowCredentials=true and 99-attempt/1-min lockout creates real exposure on shared developer LANs
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/CorsConfig.java:39-43

Description

The dev profile sets `grc.cors.allowed-origins` to include `http://192.168.*:[*]`, `http://10.*:[*]`, and `http://172.*:[*]` — effectively the entire RFC1918 private address space on any port — while `CorsConfig` enables `setAllowCredentials(true)`. It also sets `max-failed-login-attempts: 99` and `lockout-duration-minutes: 1`, which disables brute-force protection. These are intentional dev conveniences (documented in CLAUDE.md and the LAN-access commits), so the rating is Low. However, when a developer runs the dev stack on a shared corporate/coffee-shop LAN with real seeded credentials (admin/Admin@12345 etc.), any other host on the subnet can host a page that makes credentialed cross-origin requests to the dev API, and the near-disabled lockout permits unlimited password guessing.

Root cause

Developer-experience trade-offs (zero-config LAN access, no lockout friction) were encoded as profile defaults; they are safe only under the assumption that the dev machine is never on an untrusted network with real data.

Evidence / proof
application-dev.yml:71 — "...,http://192.168.*:[*],http://10.*:[*],http://172.*:[*]" ; application-dev.yml:72-74 — "max-failed-login-attempts: 99 / lockout-duration-minutes: 1"

Real-world impact

On a shared LAN, a co-located attacker can (a) ride a developer's authenticated session via credentialed CORS from any RFC1918 origin, and (b) brute-force the well-known seeded passwords with no lockout. Confined to dev with throwaway data, impact is low; with production-like seed data on a laptop in public, it is meaningfully higher.

Reproduction

1. Start backend with profile=dev on a machine at 192.168.1.50. 2. From 192.168.1.99, host JS that POSTs to http://192.168.1.50:8084/api/v1/... with credentials:'include' — preflight is allowed. 3. Script 200 login attempts/min against /api/v1/auth/login without triggering lockout.

Resolution

Keep the broad wildcards strictly behind the dev profile (already the case) and document the 'untrusted network' caveat. Prefer enumerating the developer's actual LAN IP via env var over the whole RFC1918 range, and raise the dev lockout to a non-trivial value (e.g. 20/5min) so brute-force is still slowed in dev.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
  cors:
    allowed-origins: "...,http://192.168.*:[*],http://10.*:[*],http://172.*:[*]"
  security:
    max-failed-login-attempts: 99
    lockout-duration-minutes: 1
▲ After (fixed)
  cors:
    # Set DEV_LAN_ORIGIN to your machine's LAN URL instead of the whole RFC1918 space.
    allowed-origins: "http://localhost:3000,http://127.0.0.1:3000,${DEV_LAN_ORIGIN:}"
  security:
    max-failed-login-attempts: 20
    lockout-duration-minutes: 5
References: CWE-942: Permissive Cross-domain Policy · CWE-307: Improper Restriction of Excessive Authentication Attempts · OWASP A05:2021 Security Misconfiguration

SecurityMass Assignment / Improper Input Validation (A08/A04)▾
