tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/service/TprmService.java:45-98

Description

The legacy TprmController binds the persistence @Entity types directly as @RequestBody (createVendor(@RequestBody Vendor), updateVendor(@RequestBody Vendor), createAssessment(@RequestBody VendorAssessment), updateAssessment(@RequestBody VendorAssessment)) with no @Valid and no DTO layer. This is inconsistent with the rest of the audited modules (cpty, openbanking, outsourcing, bcp_attestation) which all use validated request DTOs. Two concrete weaknesses follow: (1) Mass assignment — a client can supply id, externalId, isDeleted, createdAt (Vendor) or id, externalId, isDeleted, workflowStatus, computedScorePct (VendorAssessment) in the JSON body; createVendor saves the entity as-is (only organisationId is overwritten server-side). A client could, for example, POST a vendor with isDeleted=true or seed arbitrary externalId/createdAt. (2) No bean validation — vendorName, riskRating, status, emails, etc. are persisted with no @NotBlank/@Size/@Email/enum checks, so malformed or oversized values reach the database and the bilingual/workflow invariants are not enforced at the boundary.

Root cause

No DTO/validation layer for the original vendors/assessments endpoints; the JPA entity doubles as the API contract, exposing internal/managed columns to client binding.

Evidence / proof
@PostMapping("/vendors")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('TPRM', 'WRITE')")
public Vendor createVendor(@RequestBody Vendor req) {   // raw entity, no @Valid
    return tprmService.createVendor(req);
}
// TprmService.createVendor only overrides organisationId; id/externalId/isDeleted/createdAt come from the client

Real-world impact

Lower than the IDOR findings because organisationId is forced server-side, but a client can set internal-state fields (e.g. isDeleted, workflowStatus, computedScorePct) and inject unvalidated/oversized data, leading to inconsistent records and bypass of workflow/scoring invariants. Combined with SEC-TPRM-001, the lack of validation widens the tampering surface.

Reproduction

1. As a TPRM writer, POST /api/v1/tprm/vendors with body {"vendorName":"x","isDeleted":true} — the row is created already soft-deleted. 2. POST /api/v1/tprm/assessments with {"vendorId":<own>,"assessmentDate":"2026-01-01","workflowStatus":"REVIEWED","computedScorePct":0} — workflow/score fields are accepted directly, bypassing the questionnaire engine that is supposed to own them.

Resolution

Introduce VendorCreate/Update and AssessmentCreate/Update DTOs with Jakarta constraints (@NotBlank, @Size, @Email, allowed-value checks) and @Valid on the controller params; map only whitelisted fields in the service. Never bind JPA entities directly to request bodies.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@PostMapping("/vendors")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('TPRM', 'WRITE')")
public Vendor createVendor(@RequestBody Vendor req) {
    return tprmService.createVendor(req);
}
▲ After (fixed)
@PostMapping("/vendors")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('TPRM', 'WRITE')")
public VendorResponse createVendor(@Valid @RequestBody VendorCreateRequest req) {
    return tprmService.createVendor(req); // service maps only whitelisted fields
}
// VendorCreateRequest exposes no id/externalId/isDeleted/createdAt

LowSEC-TPRM-005Public token-authenticated vendor-portal endpoints lack expiry, rate-limiting, and leak PII
SecurityBroken Authentication / Sensitive Data Exposure (A07/A02)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/bcp_attestation/controller/VendorBcpAttestationController.java:62-85 Effort M Risk CVSS 4.3 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:N) — unauthenticated endpoints; bounded by 122-bit unguessable token
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/bcp_attestation/service/VendorBcpAttestationService.java:89-120
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/bcp_attestation/service/VendorBcpAttestationService.java:263-285
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/bcp_attestation/entity/VendorBcpAttestation.java:59-61

Description

GET /api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/{token} and POST /api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/{token}/submit are @PreAuthorize("permitAll()") — fully unauthenticated. The opaque token is the only credential. Mitigating factors: the token is a random UUIDv4 (submissionToken = UUID.randomUUID(), ~122 bits of entropy, not enumerable) and getByToken/submitByToken/doSubmit resolve the row by token and enforce a state guard (guardSubmit allows only INVITED/REMINDED/OVERDUE/REJECTED). Residual weaknesses: (1) the token never expires and is not single-use/rotated after submission, so a leaked URL (referrer logs, email forwarding, browser history, proxy logs) is replayable indefinitely; (2) the permitAll() submit endpoint has no rate-limiting or abuse audit (the controller Javadoc itself defers rate-limit/audit/MFA-bind to a follow-up); (3) the AttestationResponse returned by the public getByToken includes submitted-by contact name/email (PII), evidence file path/name, and the submissionToken itself, so anyone with the token reads vendor contact PII and internal evidence paths.

Root cause

v1 vendor-portal design intentionally treats the bearer token as the sole credential without expiry, single-use semantics, rate-limiting, or response field minimization for the unauthenticated path.

Evidence / proof
@GetMapping("/by-token/{token}")
@PreAuthorize("permitAll()")
public AttestationResponse getByToken(@PathVariable UUID token) { return service.getByToken(token); }

@PostMapping("/by-token/{token}/submit")
@PreAuthorize("permitAll()")
public AttestationResponse submitByToken(@PathVariable UUID token, @RequestBody @Valid AttestationSubmitRequest req) { return service.submitByToken(token, req); }

Real-world impact

If a submission URL leaks, an outsider can read the vendor's contact PII and evidence file path and (while the row is in a submittable state) overwrite the attested RTO/MTPD/BCP test data. Brute force is impractical due to the 122-bit token, so this is defense-in-depth rather than a directly exploitable break, hence Low.

Reproduction

1. Obtain a submission token (e.g. from a forwarded vendor email or logs). 2. curl http://localhost:8084/api/v1/tprm/bcp-attestations/by-token/<uuid> with no Authorization header — returns the attestation incl. submittedByContactEmail, evidenceFilePath and the token. 3. curl -X POST .../by-token/<uuid>/submit with a JSON body overwrites the attestation while it is INVITED/REMINDED/OVERDUE/REJECTED.

Resolution

Add an expiry (token_expires_at) and reject expired tokens; make the token single-use (rotate/invalidate after SUBMITTED); add rate-limiting + audit on the permitAll() submit path; and minimize the by-token response (omit submissionToken and trim contact PII / internal evidence paths for the unauthenticated view).

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public AttestationResponse getByToken(UUID token) {
    VendorBcpAttestation a = attestationRepo.findBySubmissionTokenAndIsDeletedFalse(token)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("Invalid submission token"));
    return toResponse(a); // returns full PII + token
}
▲ After (fixed)
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public AttestationResponse getByToken(UUID token) {
    VendorBcpAttestation a = attestationRepo.findBySubmissionTokenAndIsDeletedFalse(token)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("Invalid submission token"));
    if (a.getTokenExpiresAt() != null && a.getTokenExpiresAt().isBefore(LocalDateTime.now()))
        throw new EntityNotFoundException("Invalid submission token");
    return toPortalResponse(a); // minimized view, no token, no internal evidence path
}

LowSEC-TPRM-006Unbounded client-controlled page size on list endpoints (resource exhaustion)
SecurityUncontrolled Resource Consumption (A04)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/openbanking/controller/ObController.java:142-148 Effort S Risk CVSS 3.7 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L) — authenticated DoS via large page size
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/openbanking/controller/ObController.java:69-75
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/openbanking/controller/ObController.java:117-123
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cpty/controller/CptyController.java:68-74
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/cyber/controller/ThirdPartyCyberAssessmentController.java:23-30

Description

Several list endpoints accept a client-supplied size request param with a default but no upper bound, passing it straight into PageRequest.of(page, size): ObController.listApiCalls/listTpps/listConsents/listIncidents, CptyController.list, and ThirdPartyCyberAssessmentController.list (size default 100, no @Max). A caller can request size=1000000 and force the backend to materialize and serialize an arbitrarily large result set in one query. The TprmController vendor list uses @PageableDefault(size=20) but also has no max-page-size cap configured. These are authenticated endpoints, so impact is limited to authorized users, but a single tenant user can degrade the service for the shared backend.

Root cause

No maximum page-size clamp on raw int size params (and no global spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size), so the client fully controls fetch size.

Evidence / proof
@GetMapping("/api-calls")
@PreAuthorize(READ_GUARD)
public Page<ApiCallResponse> listApiCalls(
        @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
        @RequestParam(defaultValue = "100") int size) {  // no upper bound
    return service.listApiCalls(page, size);
}

Real-world impact

An authenticated user can issue size=1000000 against api-calls (an append-only high-volume table) and similar endpoints, causing large heap allocation, slow queries, and potential OOM/GC pressure affecting all tenants on the shared instance.

Reproduction

curl 'http://localhost:8084/api/v1/openbanking/api-calls?page=0&size=1000000' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' — the server attempts to fetch and serialize up to a million rows.

Resolution

Clamp the page size to a sane maximum (e.g. Math.min(size, 200)) in each controller/service, or set spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size globally and prefer Pageable params with @PageableDefault plus a configured max.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
public Page<ApiCallResponse> listApiCalls(
        @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
        @RequestParam(defaultValue = "100") int size) {
    return service.listApiCalls(page, size);
}
▲ After (fixed)
public Page<ApiCallResponse> listApiCalls(
        @RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
        @RequestParam(defaultValue = "100") int size) {
    int capped = Math.min(Math.max(size, 1), 200);
    return service.listApiCalls(page, capped);
}

InfoSEC-AUTH-005Refresh-token cookie scoped to /api/auth/refresh but logout/login path mismatch and absent on non-cookie clients
SecuritySession Management (A07) / CWE-613▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/auth/AuthController.java:232-244 Effort S Risk Informational — defense-in-depth observation; no direct exploit
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/auth/AuthController.java:215-217
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/auth/refresh_token/repository/RefreshTokenStoreRepository.java:35-43

Description

The refresh cookie is set with HttpOnly; Secure; Path=/api/auth/refresh; SameSite=Strict — a strong attribute set that correctly limits cookie exposure and gives CSRF protection on the refresh endpoint. Two minor observations: (1) the cookie Path is /api/auth/refresh, which means the browser will NOT send it to /api/auth/logout (a different path); logout therefore relies on the client also clearing it and on the server's best-effort revoke, and the server-side revoke in logout() only runs if the cookie happens to be presented. (2) The bulk-revoke query revokeAllByUserId intentionally omits organisation_id (documented), which is acceptable for the self-service path (caller passes their own userId) but means an admin revoke flushes a user's sessions across all tenants — fine by design but worth noting in tenant-isolation reviews. These are noted for completeness; the cookie hardening itself (single fully-attributed Set-Cookie, no duplicate cookie without SameSite) is correctly implemented.

Root cause

Cookie Path is scoped narrowly to the refresh endpoint; logout lives on a sibling path so it cannot rely on automatic cookie transmission for server-side revocation in all clients.

Evidence / proof
response.addHeader("Set-Cookie", String.format("grc_refresh=%s; HttpOnly; Secure; Path=/api/auth/refresh; SameSite=Strict; Max-Age=%d", refreshToken, refreshTokenExpiryMs / 1000));
// logout writes: grc_refresh=; ... Path=/api/auth/refresh; ... Max-Age=0

Real-world impact

Low: if a browser does not include the refresh cookie on the POST /api/auth/logout call (because the cookie Path is /api/auth/refresh), the server's revoke-on-logout is skipped and only the client-side cookie clear (Max-Age=0) happens, so a previously captured refresh token remains valid until rolled or expired. Rolling-refresh revocation and admin revoke still mitigate stolen tokens on the next refresh.

Reproduction

1. Log in, capture the grc_refresh cookie. 2. Call POST /api/auth/logout; because the cookie Path is /api/auth/refresh, some clients will not attach the cookie, so the server cannot read the jti to revoke. 3. The refresh-token row stays active in platform.refresh_token until its next use triggers rolling revocation or it expires.

Resolution

Either widen the cookie Path to /api/auth (covering both /refresh and /logout) so logout can read and revoke it server-side, or have the frontend always include credentials on logout and confirm the cookie is transmitted; keep SameSite=Strict and HttpOnly/Secure unchanged. Optionally consider whether cross-tenant bulk revoke should require an explicit org scope for non-platform-admin callers.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
Path=/api/auth/refresh   // set on login, logout, and clear
▲ After (fixed)
Path=/api/auth          // covers /api/auth/refresh and /api/auth/logout so logout can revoke server-side

InfoSEC-BCM-006Mass-assignment cross-tenant write backstop (TenantWriteGuardInterceptor) is stubbed and not wired
SecurityBroken Access Control / Mass Assignment (A01/A08) — CWE-915▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/common/tenant/TenantWriteGuardInterceptor.java:36-78 Effort L Risk Defense-in-depth gap — relies entirely on per-service req.setId(null); no platform backstop
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/controller/BcmController.java:69-75
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/controller/BcmController.java:128-134
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/service/BcmService.java:77-83

Description

Several BCM write endpoints bind raw JPA entities directly via @RequestBody (BcmController.createPlan/updatePlan/createProcess/updateProcess/createBia/createExercise take BcmPlan/CriticalProcess/BiaRecord/BcmExercise, not validated DTOs). The cross-tenant mass-assignment defense for these is purely the per-service convention of calling req.setId(null) and req.setOrganisationId(currentTenant) before save. The documented platform-wide backstop, TenantWriteGuardInterceptor, is explicitly NOT ACTIVE (its own Javadoc: 'Wiring status — NOT YET ACTIVE ... This bean exists as a stub'). For SEC-BCM-001 (createBia) the per-service defense is itself missing (no setOrganisationId). The create* paths that DO call setId(null)+setOrganisationId are presently safe, and the update* paths re-load an org-scoped entity and copy only whitelisted fields, so this is a defense-in-depth/info-level observation that amplifies the impact of any future endpoint that forgets the convention.

Root cause

Tenant-write integrity depends on a hand-applied per-method convention with no enforced backstop; the interceptor designed to catch omissions has never been wired into the Hibernate SessionFactory.

Evidence / proof
TenantWriteGuardInterceptor Javadoc lines 36-48: 'Wiring status — NOT YET ACTIVE. This bean exists as a stub so it can be code-reviewed and unit-tested before being wired into the EntityManager / SessionFactory.' BcmController.createPlan: `public BcmPlan createPlan(@RequestBody BcmPlan req)` — raw entity, no @Valid; defense is BcmService.createPlan `req.setId(null); req.setOrganisationId(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant());`.

Real-world impact

No direct exploit today on the create/update paths that follow the convention, but the platform has no enforced guard against a future (or already-missed, see SEC-BCM-001) write path that omits the id-null / org-stamp step, which would allow cross-tenant overwrite via JPA merge of an id-bearing body.

Reproduction

N/A (defense-in-depth). Confirmable by code review: the interceptor is never registered via HibernatePropertiesCustomizer or hibernate.session_factory.interceptor.

Resolution

Complete the interceptor wiring per its own pre-activation checklist (register via a HibernatePropertiesCustomizer bean, wrap legitimate cross-tenant sweeps in TenantContext.allowCrossTenantWrite(), add the attack-simulation tests), and migrate raw-entity @RequestBody write endpoints to validated request DTOs so organisationId/id can never be bound from the client.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// application.yml — interceptor not referenced anywhere; raw entity bound:
@PostMapping("/legacy-plans")
public BcmPlan createPlan(@RequestBody BcmPlan req) { return bcmService.createPlan(req); }
▲ After (fixed)
@Bean
HibernatePropertiesCustomizer tenantGuard(TenantWriteGuardInterceptor i) {
    return props -> props.put("hibernate.session_factory.interceptor", i);
}
// and bind a DTO instead of the entity:
@PostMapping("/legacy-plans")
public BcmPlan createPlan(@RequestBody @Valid BcmPlanRequest req) { return bcmService.createPlan(req); }

InfoSEC-CFG-010Stale/incorrect LocaleConfig uses HTTP-session locale resolver in a declared-stateless API
SecuritySecurity Misconfiguration (A05:2021 / CWE-1059)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/LocaleConfig.java:29-46 Effort S Risk Risk rationale: SessionLocaleResolver would create HttpSessions, contradicting the STATELESS design; minor session-fixation surface and dead-config confusion. Info.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/SecurityConfig.java:77-78
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/config/WebMvcConfig.java:11-17

Description

LocaleConfig registers a SessionLocaleResolver and a LocaleChangeInterceptor (?lang=) — a server-side, session-backed i18n mechanism. This contradicts the platform's stateless design (SecurityConfig sets SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS; CLAUDE.md states 'No HTTP sessions on the server') and the project's documented approach that the standalone frontend handles i18n client-side (translations.js). A SessionLocaleResolver writes the locale into an HttpSession, which (a) would cause sessions to be created despite the stateless intent, and (b) the LocaleChangeInterceptor bean is not registered with the InterceptorRegistry in WebMvcConfig (addInterceptors is not overridden), so it is effectively dead config. Also note WebMvcConfig.addViewControllers redirects '/' to '/dashboard' and addResourceHandlers references classpath:/static/... and comments mention Thymeleaf @{} URLs — all leftovers from a server-rendered design that does not match this REST-only backend. These are correctness/cleanliness issues with a minor security angle (unexpected session creation = small session-fixation surface; dead config obscures the true security posture).

Root cause

Carried-over server-side-MVC configuration (session locale + Thymeleaf-era resource handlers/view controllers) that was never removed when the project became a stateless REST API with a separate static frontend.

Evidence / proof
@Bean
public LocaleResolver localeResolver() {
    SessionLocaleResolver resolver = new SessionLocaleResolver();
    resolver.setDefaultLocale(Locale.ENGLISH);
    resolver.setLocaleAttributeName("CURRENT_LOCALE");
    return resolver;
}
// SecurityConfig: SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS

Real-world impact

Minimal direct attacker impact. Risk is unintended HttpSession creation (contradicting STATELESS, a minor session-fixation footprint) and misleading dead configuration that complicates security review. The interceptor not being wired means ?lang switching does not even function server-side.

Reproduction

1. Review LocaleConfig vs SecurityConfig — SessionLocaleResolver vs STATELESS. 2. Note LocaleChangeInterceptor bean is never added in WebMvcConfig.addInterceptors (method absent) -> not active. 3. Confirm REST controllers do not rely on server locale (frontend i18n via translations.js per CLAUDE.md).

Resolution

Remove the server-side locale machinery (or replace SessionLocaleResolver with AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver if server-side message localization is genuinely needed for validation messages). Prune the Thymeleaf-era view controller and static resource handlers in WebMvcConfig that no longer apply to a REST-only backend. This reduces attack surface and clarifies the stateless posture.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@Bean
public LocaleResolver localeResolver() {
    SessionLocaleResolver resolver = new SessionLocaleResolver();
    resolver.setDefaultLocale(Locale.ENGLISH);
    return resolver;
}
▲ After (fixed)
@Bean
public LocaleResolver localeResolver() {
    AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver resolver = new AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver();
    resolver.setDefaultLocale(Locale.ENGLISH);
    resolver.setSupportedLocales(List.of(Locale.ENGLISH, Locale.forLanguageTag("ar")));
    return resolver; // no HttpSession; consistent with STATELESS
}

Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/knowledge/controller/KbArticleController.java:33-45 Effort S Risk Risk rationale: any authenticated user can read INTERNAL-visibility KB articles in their tenant; content sensitivity is generally low and org-scoped
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/knowledge/service/KbArticleService.java:44-57

Description

`GET /api/kb/articles` and `GET /api/kb/articles/{slug}` are gated only by `isAuthenticated()`. The service is tenant-scoped and only returns PUBLISHED articles, and the entity carries a `visibility` field (default INTERNAL) — but the read endpoints do not enforce that visibility, so any authenticated user can read every PUBLISHED article in their org regardless of intended audience. Write/transition/delete are correctly role-gated. Listed as Info because KB content is generally low-sensitivity and properly tenant-isolated; flagged for consistency with the module-guard convention and because the `visibility` column implies an access distinction that is not enforced at read time.

Root cause

Read endpoints use bare authentication and do not consult the article's `visibility` attribute, so the modelled audience restriction is not enforced.

Evidence / proof
@GetMapping
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public List<KbArticleDto> listPublished(@RequestParam(required = false) String category) {
    return service.listPublished(category);
}

Real-world impact

Minor over-exposure within a tenant: articles intended for a narrower audience (per the unused `visibility` field) are readable by any logged-in user. No cross-tenant exposure.

Reproduction

1. Authenticate as any user.
2. `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" http://localhost:8084/api/kb/articles` — returns all PUBLISHED articles for the tenant irrespective of their visibility setting.

Resolution

If the `visibility` field is meant to restrict access, filter list/read results by the caller's authorities/role; otherwise document that all authenticated tenant users may read published KB content. Consider a KB:READ permission for consistency with other modules.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@GetMapping
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public List<KbArticleDto> listPublished(@RequestParam(required = false) String category) {
    return service.listPublished(category);
}
▲ After (fixed)
@GetMapping
@PreAuthorize("isAuthenticated()")
public List<KbArticleDto> listPublished(@RequestParam(required = false) String category,
                                       Authentication auth) {
    // service filters out articles whose visibility exceeds the caller's audience
    return service.listPublishedFor(category, auth);
}

InfoSEC-FE-005Legacy static dev server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and no security headers (no CSP / X-Frame-Options)
SecuritySecurity Misconfiguration (A05:2021)▾
Location tss-grc-ui/server.py:18-21 Effort S Risk CVSS 2.0 — dev-only static server; clickjacking + missing defence-in-depth headers
tss-grc-ui/server.py:18-21
tss-grc-ui-v2/index.html:1-25

Description

The legacy frontend's Python static server (server.py) emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (line 18) and no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, or X-Content-Type-Options headers. The v2 index.html likewise ships no CSP meta tag. Consequently the UI relies entirely on the application server / reverse proxy for clickjacking protection (X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors) and has no Content-Security-Policy to act as a second line of defence against the XSS in SEC-FE-001 (e.g. a `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'` policy would block inline-event-handler payloads and exfiltration to attacker hosts). This is rated Info because server.py is described in CLAUDE.md as a dev launcher, not the production server; the real risk lives in whatever serves the UI in staging/prod. It is called out so the production deployment is verified to set CSP + X-Frame-Options.

Root cause

Static file servers configured for developer convenience (open CORS, no headers); no CSP defined at the document level either.

Evidence / proof
server.py:18 `self.send_header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*')`. No `Content-Security-Policy` / `X-Frame-Options` anywhere in server.py or tss-grc-ui-v2/index.html.

Real-world impact

Without a CSP, an XSS payload (SEC-FE-001) executes unhindered and can freely exfiltrate the sessionStorage token to any host. Without X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors the app can be framed for clickjacking. `ACAO: *` on the static server is low-impact (it serves no credentialed JSON) but is poor hygiene.

Reproduction

Load any UI page and inspect response headers (curl -I) — no CSP/X-Frame-Options present; ACAO: * present on the legacy static server.

Resolution

In production, serve the UI behind a server/proxy that sets `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. Scope CORS to known origins rather than `*`. Optionally add a CSP `<meta http-equiv>` to index.html as a baseline.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
self.send_header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', '*')
# (no CSP / X-Frame-Options / X-Content-Type-Options)
▲ After (fixed)
self.send_header('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', 'http://localhost:5173')  # scope it

InfoSEC-IAM-008Authentication user lookup is not tenant-scoped (findByUsername) — username uniqueness assumed across all tenants
SecurityMulti-Tenancy / Identification & Authentication (A07)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/iam/service/CustomUserDetailsService.java:28-32 Effort S Risk Risk rationale: design assumption to verify — username collisions across tenants would let one tenant's login resolve another tenant's account
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/iam/repository/UserRepository.java:13-14
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/iam/service/UserService.java:49-50

Description

CustomUserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername() resolves the login principal with UserRepository.findByUsername(username), which is NOT scoped by organisationId (a findByUsernameAndOrganisationId variant exists and is used elsewhere). UserService.create() only enforces uniqueness per-org (existsByUsernameAndOrganisationId), so two tenants CAN hold the same username. If that happens, findByUsername returns whichever single row JPA picks (or throws on multiple), making login resolution ambiguous/non-deterministic across tenants. This is the authentication path (outside the assigned controller set) so it is reported as Info for the auth-module owners to confirm: either usernames are globally unique by DB constraint (then this is safe) or the login flow must disambiguate by tenant.

Root cause

Per-tenant uniqueness on create vs. global lookup on authenticate — the two are only consistent if a global unique constraint on username also exists.

Evidence / proof
UserRepository: Optional<User> findByUsername(String username);  // used by loadUserByUsername. Creation guard is existsByUsernameAndOrganisationId(req.username(), orgId) — per-org only.

Real-world impact

If a global unique constraint on username is absent, a duplicate username across tenants causes ambiguous authentication: a user could authenticate against another tenant's account (cross-tenant account confusion) or logins could fail nondeterministically. No exploit confirmed without DB schema review — hence Info.

Reproduction

Schema/behaviour check: 1. Create user 'admin' in org 1 and org 2 (allowed by per-org guard). 2. Attempt login as 'admin' and observe which org's account/authorities are loaded. Confirm whether a unique index on iam.users(username) prevents step 1.

Resolution

Either enforce a global unique index on username (documenting that usernames are tenant-global), or make the login flow tenant-aware (resolve via username+tenant) so authentication cannot bind to the wrong tenant's account.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
User user = userRepository.findByUsername(username)
    .orElseThrow(() -> new UsernameNotFoundException("User not found: " + username));
▲ After (fixed)
// Option A: keep findByUsername but back it with a GLOBAL unique constraint on username.
// Option B: resolve with tenant context, e.g.
// userRepository.findByUsernameAndOrganisationId(username, resolvedTenantId)

InfoSEC-INT-008Splunk verifySsl flag is documented but never wired into the RestClient
SecuritySecurity Misconfiguration (A05)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/splunk/config/SplunkIntegrationConfig.java:49-63 Effort S Risk N/A — fails safe (TLS always verified); correctness/expectation gap, not an exploitable weakness
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/splunk/config/SplunkProperties.java:42-45

Description

SplunkProperties exposes verifySsl (default true) and the bean Javadoc says 'SSL verification is controlled via verifySsl'. In practice splunkRestClient() builds a SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory and never reads props.isVerifySsl(); the default JDK trust store is always used. The good news is the flag is effectively dead in the secure direction — setting verifySsl=false does NOT actually disable TLS verification (so there is no accidental cert-bypass). The risk is the inverse expectation gap: an operator may believe they can toggle verification and the /config endpoint reports verifySsl=true, masking that the setting has no effect. If a future change wires the flag through, the disable path must be guarded to non-dev profiles. Flagged as Info because nothing is currently exploitable.

Root cause

Configuration property declared and surfaced in /config but not consumed by the HTTP client factory.

Evidence / proof
@Bean("splunkRestClient") public RestClient splunkRestClient() {
    SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory factory = new SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory();
    // ... verifySsl never read here ...
    return RestClient.builder().requestFactory(factory).build();
}

Real-world impact

No direct security impact today (TLS stays verified). Operational confusion only: the toggle and its /config readout are misleading. Documented here so a later 'make verifySsl work' change does not introduce an insecure default.

Reproduction

1. Set grc.integrations.splunk.verify-ssl=false and mode=LIVE.
2. Observe outbound HEC calls still validate the server certificate (handshake fails against a self-signed host), proving the flag is inert; GET /config still reports verifySsl=false while behaviour is verified=true.

Resolution

Either remove the unused property (and its /config field) to avoid confusion, or wire it through a custom request factory while restricting the insecure value to dev-only profiles with a loud startup warning.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// verifySsl declared in SplunkProperties, never consumed by splunkRestClient()
▲ After (fixed)
// Option A: delete the verifySsl property + /config field.
// Option B (if needed): build a request factory honouring verifySsl, and on prod profiles refuse verifySsl=false.

tss-grc-backend/docs/integrations/TENABLE.md:127-130

Description

Gitleaks raised two 'generic-api-key' hits inside integration setup documentation. SPLUNK.md line 46 shows `export SPLUNK_HEC_TOKEN="00112233-4455-6677-8899-aabbccddeeff"` — a sequential dummy UUID inside a '## Switching from STUB to LIVE' how-to. TENABLE.md line 128 shows `export TENABLE_ACCESS_KEY="abc123def456..."` — an obvious truncated placeholder, immediately followed by `export TENABLE_SECRET_KEY="..." # never commit` (line 129). Both are example env-var assignments instructing operators where to paste THEIR own credentials at deploy time. Neither is a working secret. The Splunk doc even instructs generating the companion webhook secret with `openssl rand -hex 32` (line 48), reinforcing that nothing real is committed.

Root cause

Generic-API-key entropy/regex rules in gitleaks match any quoted token-shaped string, including documentation placeholders, producing false positives.

TENABLE.md:128-129  `export TENABLE_ACCESS_KEY="abc123def456..."
export TENABLE_SECRET_KEY="..."   # never commit`

Real-world impact

None. The strings are non-functional examples; using them against a real Splunk HEC or Tenable.sc endpoint would fail authentication. No secret is exposed.

Reproduction

N/A — verified by reading the surrounding documentation context confirming these are placeholder values in a setup guide.

Resolution

No remediation required. Optionally add these fingerprints to a gitleaks allowlist (.gitleaks.toml) to suppress recurring noise, or change the doc placeholders to an unmistakable form such as `<your-hec-token>` to avoid future scanner hits.

export TENABLE_ACCESS_KEY="abc123def456..."
▲ After (fixed)

Description

Sixteen of the twenty-one gitleaks hits are dotted, versioned string constants of the form `grc.<module>.<thing>.v1` (e.g. `grc.mfa.enrolment.v1`, `grc.risk.treatment.v1`, `grc.cyber.filing.v1`, `grc.whitelabel.v1`, `c5BreachNotification`). The entropy-based generic-api-key rule matched them. On inspection every one is a browser localStorage key name used by the frontend persistence layer. persistence.ts defines a `PERSISTENCE_REGISTRY` (lines 204+) listing these keys with human labels and a `backendReady` flag; mfa.ts line 8 (`const KEY = 'grc.mfa.enrolment.v1'`) and the lifecycle modules use them as storage keys for client-side state. They are public, non-secret application identifiers — they grant no access and protect nothing.

Root cause

Versioned dotted identifiers have enough character variety to trip the generic-API-key entropy heuristic, even though they are namespace strings rather than credentials.

Evidence / proof
mfa.ts:8  `const KEY = 'grc.mfa.enrolment.v1';`
persistence.ts:206  `key: 'grc.chains.fires.v1',` (inside PERSISTENCE_REGISTRY, with labelEn 'Cross-module chain fires')
platformPersistence.ts:194  `localKey: 'grc.risk.treatment.v1',`

Real-world impact

None. These keys are inherently visible in any browser's devtools (Application > Local Storage); they convey no authorization and reveal no sensitive data.

Reproduction

N/A — verified by opening each cited file; every match is a localStorage key constant / registry entry.

Resolution

No remediation required. Suppress via a gitleaks allowlist regex such as `grc\.[a-z.]+\.v\d+` (and the `c5*/c7*` assessment-criterion keys) in .gitleaks.toml to remove this recurring false-positive class.

▼ Before (vulnerable)

▲ After (fixed)
# .gitleaks.toml
[allowlist]
regexes = [
  '''grc\.[a-z0-9.]+\.v\d+''',   # frontend localStorage key namespace
]

Description

Gitleaks flagged `fapi_client="lean-prod-aspsp1-2024"` (line 185) as a generic API key. Tracing the parameter: `insert_tpp(...)` (signature line 35) writes `fapi_client` into the `fapi_client_id` column (INSERT column list, line 46). It is therefore an OAuth/FAPI client_id — a public identifier for a Third-Party Provider, not a credential. The value lives in `setup_openbanking_seed.py`, an idempotent demo-data seeding script that populates illustrative TPPs (Lean, Tarabut, Drahim, etc.) for the three demo tenants. There is no `client_secret`/private-key column in the insert and none is committed anywhere in the file (grep for client_secret/fapi_secret returns nothing). A FAPI client_id without its private key or mTLS cert grants no access.

An OAuth client identifier in seed data matched the entropy-based generic-api-key rule; the rule cannot distinguish a public client_id from a secret.

None. Client identifiers are non-secret by OAuth design and these are fabricated demo TPP records for non-production tenants. No authentication material (client secret, signing key, mTLS cert) is exposed.

Reproduction

N/A — verified by reading the insert_tpp definition and confirming the value maps to fapi_client_id and that no secret column exists in the script.

Resolution

No remediation required. The value is correctly an identifier, not a secret. Optionally allowlist this fingerprint in .gitleaks.toml. Ensure that when LIVE open-banking integration is configured, the real FAPI client secrets / private keys are externalised (env / secret manager) and never committed — consistent with the prod-profile externalised-secrets posture.

InfoSEC-PRIV-006Ethics case cross-entity link lookup queries CaseLink without org scoping (post-filter mitigates leak)
SecurityMulti-tenancy / Broken Access Control (A01) / CWE-639▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ethics/service/EthicsCaseService.java:186-209 Effort S Risk No direct exposure — cross-tenant rows are post-filtered out before response; defence-in-depth gap only
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ethics/repository/CaseLinkRepository.java:8-11

Description

EthicsCaseService.linksForEntity calls linkRepo.findByEntityTypeAndEntityId(entityType, entityId) which is NOT organisation-scoped at the repository level (CaseLinkRepository has no org parameter). The result set therefore spans all tenants. The service then re-fetches each link's parent case and filters out those whose case.getOrganisationId() does not match the current tenant, so cross-tenant data is not returned to the caller. The exposure is closed by the post-filter, but the query itself reads other tenants' link rows and relies on a correct downstream filter — a fragile pattern that would leak if the filter were ever weakened. Note the controller endpoint is correctly gated by hasPermission('COMPLIANCE','READ').

Root cause

The inverse-lookup finder was derived from (entityType, entityId) only; the tenant scope is enforced indirectly via the parent EthicsCase rather than in the query.

Evidence / proof
CaseLinkRepository.java:10  List<CaseLink> findByEntityTypeAndEntityId(String entityType, Long entityId);  used at EthicsCaseService.java:190 then filtered c.getOrganisationId().equals(org) at line 192.

Real-world impact

No confidentiality breach today because the parent-case org filter discards out-of-tenant rows. The risk is defence-in-depth: a future refactor that trusts the link list directly would expose cross-tenant case metadata. Rated Info.

Reproduction

Code-review only: the repository finder lacks an organisationId parameter; correctness depends entirely on the service-layer post-filter at EthicsCaseService.java:192.

Resolution

Add organisationId to the finder (findByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityId) so tenant scoping is enforced in SQL, keeping the parent-case check as belt-and-braces.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
List<CaseLink> findByEntityTypeAndEntityId(String entityType, Long entityId);
// service: linkRepo.findByEntityTypeAndEntityId(entityType, entityId)
▲ After (fixed)
List<CaseLink> findByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityId(Long organisationId, String entityType, Long entityId);
// service: linkRepo.findByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityId(org, entityType, entityId)

Location setup_regreporting_seed.py:581 Effort S Risk Risk rationale: both are benign in context. The U+200F (RIGHT-TO-LEFT MARK) characters appear inside legitimate Arabic string literals for correct RTL rendering, not as a Trojan-Source code-reordering attack. Description

Bandit raised 2 B613 ('source file contains bidirectional control characters U+200F', CWE-838) hits and 1 B101 ('use of assert'). Verified setup_regreporting_seed.py:581 — the U+200F (RLM) sits inside an Arabic data string ('...USSD \u200f*900# وSS7/SIGTRAN...') to keep the RTL/LTR boundary around the *900# token rendering correctly; it is data, not control flow. .tmp/reset_pw.py:15 is 'assert "'" not in h' guarding that a generated bcrypt hash contains no single quote before string-building SQL.

setup_regreporting_seed.py:580-581

.tmp/reset_pw.py:15

None. The bidi marks affect only how Arabic strings render; they are not positioned to reorder code in a way that misleads a reviewer (Trojan-Source). The assert is dev-only; if these scripts were ever run under -O the guard would vanish, but the input (a bcrypt hash) cannot contain a quote, so the check is defensive only.

B613: no action needed; optionally normalise by using explicit \u200f escapes (already the case) so the marker is visible in diffs, and confirm no bidi overrides (U+202E) exist. ▲ After (fixed)

InfoSEC-RISK-006KRI sourceQuery stores arbitrary SQL/source text — latent injection surface when auto-fetchers are bound
SecurityPotential SQL Injection (A03) — latent▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/kri/service/KriDefinitionService.java:211-229 Effort M Risk Not currently exploitable — no code path executes sourceQuery today; flagged to prevent a future injection regression
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/kri/service/KriMeasurementService.java:175-192

Description

KriDefinition persists a client-supplied sourceQueryType (allows the value 'SQL') and a free-form sourceQuery string (set via applyFields from KriDefinitionRequest.sourceQuery). The scheduler entry point KriMeasurementService.evaluateAll explicitly does NOT execute these queries today — it logs KRI_EVALUATION_SKIPPED with the comment 'Auto-fetcher not yet bound', so there is currently no SQL/OS execution and thus no live injection. However the stored intent is to later run that operator-authored SQL against the database. If a future slice wires a SQL runner that concatenates or directly executes sourceQuery, it becomes a stored second-order SQL injection (and the SQL would run with the application's DB credentials, which can read across tenants).

Root cause

Free-form, client-supplied query text (sourceQuery) is stored with the declared intent of later execution; no design-level constraint (parameterisation, query allow-list, or read-only/least-privilege execution account) is recorded against it.

Evidence / proof
        if (req.sourceQueryType() != null) d.setSourceQueryType(req.sourceQueryType());
        if (req.sourceQuery() != null)     d.setSourceQuery(req.sourceQuery());
// SOURCE_TYPES includes "SQL"; evaluateAll() currently only logs:
//   audit.log("KRI_EVALUATION_SKIPPED", ... "Auto-fetcher not yet bound for source_type="+d.getSourceQueryType());

Real-world impact

No impact in the current build (no execution path). If the SQL auto-fetcher is implemented naively, an operator (or an attacker who reaches the KRI write role) could store arbitrary SQL that the scheduler later executes with the app DB account, enabling cross-tenant data read/exfiltration or worse.

Reproduction

Not exploitable today. Future: create a KRI with sourceQueryType=SQL and a malicious sourceQuery; if a SQL runner is later bound that executes it verbatim, the payload runs on the next scheduler tick.

Resolution

When implementing the auto-fetcher, do not execute operator-supplied SQL directly: use a curated/parameterised metric catalogue, force every fetch through a read-only least-privilege DB role scoped to the tenant, and reject/escape any sourceQuery that is not a named, pre-approved metric. Add a test asserting evaluateAll cannot run free-form SQL.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
    // Future risk: KriDefinition.sourceQuery (free-form, client-set) intended for later execution
    if (req.sourceQuery() != null) d.setSourceQuery(req.sourceQuery());
▲ After (fixed)
    // Constrain to a named metric key from an allow-list rather than raw SQL.
    if (req.sourceQuery() != null) {
        if ("SQL".equals(req.sourceQueryType()) && !APPROVED_METRIC_KEYS.contains(req.sourceQuery()))
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("sourceQuery must be an approved metric key, not raw SQL");
        d.setSourceQuery(req.sourceQuery());
    }

InfoSEC-SEC-005Well-known seeded application credentials documented and reset via committed scripts
SecurityUse of Hard-coded Credentials (CWE-798)▾
Location .tmp/reset_pw.py:3-23 Effort S Risk Info — intentional demo/dev credentials; dangerous only if the same accounts/passwords survive into a production deployment
CLAUDE.md (Default seeded credentials table)

Description

A fixed set of demo credentials following the `<Role>@12345` scheme (admin/Admin@12345, riskmanager/Risk@12345, auditor/Audit@12345, plus compliance/analyst/viewer in `.tmp/reset_pw.py`) is documented in CLAUDE.md and re-applied to `iam.users` by the committed `.tmp/reset_pw.py` script, which bcrypt-hashes each password and writes UPDATE statements. The hashing itself is sound (bcrypt, cost 10) and the script defends against quote injection in the hash (`assert "'" not in h`). This is a normal seeded-demo-account pattern and is Info-rated. The only real risk is the standard one: if these well-known accounts are not disabled/rotated before go-live, an attacker who has read the public docs can log in directly.

Root cause

Predictable, publicly-documented demo passwords are convenient for development and onboarding but become a backdoor if they persist into production.

Evidence / proof
.tmp/reset_pw.py:4-10 — creds dict with "auditor": "Audit@12345", "rmanager": "Risk@12345", ... ; line 14 — "bcrypt.hashpw(pw.encode('utf-8'), bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=10))"

Real-world impact

If demo accounts reach production unchanged, full admin takeover is trivial (admin/Admin@12345 is in the committed docs). No impact in a properly bootstrapped, separately-seeded production environment.

Reproduction

1. Read CLAUDE.md credential table. 2. POST {username:'admin',password:'Admin@12345'} to /api/v1/auth/login on any environment still carrying the seed accounts -> authenticated as PLATFORM_ADMIN.

Resolution

Ensure the production bootstrap does NOT run the demo seed; enforce must-change-password on first login for any seeded account; add a startup guard that refuses to start in prod if a user with a known default password hash/flag exists. Keep `reset_pw.py` out of any production tooling path.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
creds = {
    "auditor": "Audit@12345",
    "rmanager": "Risk@12345",
    ...
}
▲ After (fixed)
# Dev/demo only. In prod, seed no default users, or force must_change_password=1
# and randomise the initial password per account (do not commit it).
creds = {u: secrets.token_urlsafe(16) for u in ("auditor","rmanager",...)}
print("Generated one-time passwords:", creds)  # show once, never commit
References: CWE-798: Use of Hard-coded Credentials · CWE-1392: Use of Default Credentials · OWASP A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures
InfoSEC-SEC-006CI workflow embeds static test secrets in plaintext (env block)
SecurityInsertion of Sensitive Information into Source Code (CWE-540)▾
Location .github/workflows/ci.yml:17-21 Effort S Risk Info — values are explicitly throwaway CI-only test secrets, never used against real infrastructure

Description

The CI workflow defines `JWT_SECRET`, `DB_USERNAME=sa`, and `DB_PASSWORD=ci-test-Sql123!` directly in the workflow `env:` block rather than as GitHub Actions secrets. The comment correctly states these are 'Test secrets — only used inside the CI runners,' and they satisfy `JwtTokenProvider.validateSecret` (32+ chars, not a placeholder) so `mvn verify` can boot the context. Because these are deliberately disposable CI-only values with no connection to production systems, the finding is Info. The note is hygiene: putting even test secrets in workflow env (vs. repository/Org secrets) trains contributors that committing credentials is acceptable and risks a future copy-paste of a real value.

Root cause

Test fixtures were inlined into the workflow for convenience; there is no policy distinguishing disposable CI values from real secrets.

Evidence / proof
.github/workflows/ci.yml:18-21 — "# Test secrets — only used inside the CI runners.\n  JWT_SECRET: ci-test-secret-32-or-more-chars-not-a-placeholder-12345\n  DB_USERNAME: sa\n  DB_PASSWORD: ci-test-Sql123!"

Real-world impact

No direct impact — the values are CI-scoped and not reused elsewhere. The residual risk is cultural/process: normalising plaintext secrets in workflow files.

Reproduction

1. Open .github/workflows/ci.yml. 2. Observe JWT_SECRET/DB_PASSWORD literals in the top-level env block.

Resolution

Acceptable as-is given the values are throwaway. If tightening: move them to GitHub Actions repository secrets (`${{ secrets.CI_JWT_SECRET }}`) and reference there, keeping the workflow file free of literal credentials and reinforcing the no-plaintext-secrets norm.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
env:
  JWT_SECRET: ci-test-secret-32-or-more-chars-not-a-placeholder-12345
  DB_USERNAME: sa
  DB_PASSWORD: ci-test-Sql123!
▲ After (fixed)
env:
  JWT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.CI_JWT_SECRET }}
  DB_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.CI_DB_USERNAME }}
  DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.CI_DB_PASSWORD }}
References: CWE-540: Inclusion of Sensitive Information in Source Code · GitHub Docs: Using secrets in GitHub Actions · OWASP A05:2021 Security Misconfiguration

HighQUAL-DUP-001188 of 368 JPA entities re-declare the full audit/soft-delete/versioning column block instead of extending the existing BaseEntity mapped superclass
✓ VerifiedQualityCode Duplication / Maintainability▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Confirmed. ObligationAttestationCampaign (declared 'public class ... {' with no extends) manually re-declares the full audit/soft-delete/versioning block at lines 116-142 (createdAt, updatedAt, createdBy, updatedBy, isDeleted, deletedAt, deletedBy, @Version rowVersion) plus id at 36-38 — every one of which already exists in com.tss.grc.common.model.BaseEntity (verified: same column names and @Version byte[] rowVersion). So this is genuine duplication of a mapped superclass. Magnitude verified: 369 @Entity classes total (claim 368) and 189 declare the is_deleted column inline (claim 188) — i.e. roughly half the domain model bypasses BaseEntity. High is on the aggressive side for a pure maintainability/DRY issue but defensible given the scale; severity retained.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/compliance/obligation/entity/ObligationAttestationCampaign.java:36-142 Effort L Risk Not a security CVE. Maintainability risk rated High: ~4,500 LOC of copy-pasted persistence boilerplate spread across 188 files. A change to the audit model (e.g. adding a tenant column to the audit listener, renaming row_version, fixing the soft-delete contract) must be hand-applied 188 times, and the inline copies bypass the @CreatedDate/@LastModifiedBy/@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener) wiring that BaseEntity provides, so the duplicated entities silently lose automatic audit population.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/common/model/BaseEntity.java:14-56
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/compliance/obligation/entity/ObligationAttestationCampaign.java:36-142
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/bcp_attestation/entity/VendorBcpCampaign.java:107-148
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/aml/sanctions/entity/SanctionsList.java
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/aml/sanctions/entity/ScreeningCheck.java
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/admin/committee/entity/Committee.java

Description

jscpd reports 404 java-entity <-> java-entity clone instances totalling 5,940 duplicated lines — the single largest Java duplication cluster. The root of the cluster is an audit/soft-delete/versioning field group that is copy-pasted verbatim into entity after entity: createdByUserId, createdAt, updatedAt, createdBy, updatedBy, isDeleted, deletedAt, deletedBy, and a @Version row_version byte[]. A static scan of all @Entity classes shows 188 of 368 entities (51%) declare this inline `@Column(name = "is_deleted", nullable = false)` block, while 137 entities correctly extend the project's own `BaseEntity` mapped superclass which already defines the exact same nine columns plus id and a softDelete() helper. None of the 188 both extend BaseEntity and inline the block, so this is pure copy-paste, not field shadowing. The two largest individual entity clones jscpd found (ObligationAttestationCampaign:102-143 vs VendorBcpCampaign:107-148, 42 lines; EmergingRisk:118-157 vs ContractClause:57-76, 40 lines) are both instances of this block.

Root cause

A canonical BaseEntity (@MappedSuperclass, @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class), with @CreatedDate/@LastModifiedDate/@CreatedBy/@LastModifiedBy and @Version) already exists at common/model/BaseEntity.java and is used by 137 entities. New modules (aml, ndi, tprm/*, bcm/*, sust/*, audit_lc, etc.) were scaffolded by copying an existing entity file wholesale rather than extending BaseEntity, so each new entity re-typed the same audit columns. There is no architectural guardrail (e.g. an ArchUnit test) requiring entities to extend BaseEntity.

Evidence / proof
Static counts on tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module: `@Column(name = "is_deleted", nullable = false)` appears in 187 files; `@Column(name = "row_version", insertable = false, updatable = false)` in 33 files; cross-reference script result: 368 @Entity classes total, 188 with inline is_deleted block and NOT extending BaseEntity, 0 that both inline and extend, 137 clean (extends + no inline). jscpd statistics.formats.java = 1008 clones / 7.87% / 12,532 dup lines; entity<->entity sub-cluster = 404 clones / 5,940 dup lines. Example block in ObligationAttestationCampaign.java lines 116-142 is identical column-for-column to BaseEntity.java lines 22-49.

Real-world impact

Every change to the audit/soft-delete contract is an O(188) hand edit with high risk of one file being missed (drift). Entities that inline the columns instead of inheriting BaseEntity's @EntityListeners do not get JPA auditing auto-population, so createdBy/updatedBy may be silently null unless each service sets them manually — a correctness and traceability gap in a GRC product where audit trails are a compliance requirement (PDPL/SAMA). The ~4,500 duplicated lines also inflate review surface and bury the entity-specific fields that actually matter.

Reproduction

1) Open tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/common/model/BaseEntity.java — note id + 8 audit columns + softDelete(). 2) Open ObligationAttestationCampaign.java — note it does NOT extend BaseEntity yet redeclares id (36-38) and the audit block (116-142). 3) Run: grep -rl '@Column(name = "is_deleted", nullable = false)' tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module --include=*.java | wc -l  → 187. 4) Run the cross-reference confirming 188 such files do not extend BaseEntity.

Resolution

Migrate the 188 standalone entities to `extends BaseEntity`: delete the inline id and the nine audit columns from each entity, add the extends clause, and drop the now-redundant @Id/@GeneratedValue. Where an entity used `createdByUserId` distinctly from BaseEntity's `createdBy`, reconcile to a single field. Do this module-by-module behind tests. Add an ArchUnit (or simple reflection) test asserting that every class annotated @Entity (excluding pure join/lookup tables) is assignable from BaseEntity, to prevent regression. Because @Where(clause = "is_deleted = 0") is still declared per-entity, keep that annotation; only the columns move to the superclass.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@Entity
@Table(schema = "compliance", name = "obligation_attestation_campaign")
@Where(clause = "is_deleted = 0")
@Getter @Setter @NoArgsConstructor
public class ObligationAttestationCampaign {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    // ... business columns ...
    @Column(name = "created_at", updatable = false)
    private LocalDateTime createdAt = LocalDateTime.now();
    @Column(name = "updated_at")  private LocalDateTime updatedAt;
    @Column(name = "created_by")  private Long createdBy;
    @Column(name = "updated_by")  private Long updatedBy;
    @Column(name = "is_deleted", nullable = false) private Boolean isDeleted = false;
    @Column(name = "deleted_at")  private LocalDateTime deletedAt;
    @Column(name = "deleted_by")  private Long deletedBy;
    @Version
    @Column(name = "row_version", insertable = false, updatable = false)
    private byte[] rowVersion;
}
▲ After (fixed)
@Entity
@Table(schema = "compliance", name = "obligation_attestation_campaign")
@Where(clause = "is_deleted = 0")
@Getter @Setter @NoArgsConstructor
public class ObligationAttestationCampaign extends BaseEntity {
    // id + createdAt/updatedAt/createdBy/updatedBy/isDeleted/deletedAt/
    // deletedBy/rowVersion + softDelete() are all inherited from BaseEntity.
    // Only the business columns remain here.
}

✓ VerifiedQualityCode Duplication / Maintainability▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Confirmed with a magnitude caveat. The cited example is real: ObligationCampaignsPage.tsx defines a local ProgressBar component at lines 344-365 rather than importing a shared one (a components/ui dir exists). The named function 'ProgressBar' literally recurs in only 2 page files, so the headline reads stronger than a name-grep shows; however clone detectors measure token-level duplicate blocks, and the broader pattern is substantiated: 70 page files contain the same inline progress-bar style block (height:8 + borderRadius) and 153 page files contain inline bilingual ternaries (lang === 'ar' ? ...), across 313 pages / ~128k LOC. The exact '609 clones / 8,602 lines' figure is tool-derived and not independently reproduced here, but the duplication is genuine and widespread. High retained as a maintainability finding.
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/compliance/ObligationCampaignsPage.tsx:344-365 Effort L Risk Not a security issue. Maintainability rated High: 8,602 duplicated lines across 439 TSX sources (5.44% of frontend). UI fixes (accessibility, RTL direction, theming token changes) must be applied in many copies; the copies drift, producing inconsistent UX across modules in a product whose key selling point is a uniform bilingual UI.
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/compliance/ObligationCampaignsPage.tsx:344-365
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/bcm/FacilitatorConsolePage.tsx:683-761
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/bcm/ObserverDashboardPage.tsx:568-646

Description

tsx <-> tsx is the largest single duplication cluster overall: 609 clone instances / 8,602 duplicated lines. The duplication is concentrated in (a) per-page copies of small presentational helpers and (b) whole card/sub-components copied between sibling pages. Confirmed examples opened on disk: the `ProgressBar({percent,label})` component is byte-for-byte duplicated in ObligationCampaignsPage.tsx:344-365 and at least one other campaigns page; the `ActiveInjectCard`/`ResponseCard` components are copied between FacilitatorConsolePage.tsx (683-761) and ObserverDashboardPage.tsx (568-646) — a 45-line + 35-line back-to-back clone, the two largest TSX clones in the report; and the consent panel is duplicated between components/privacy/ConsentTab.tsx:16-57 and pages/detail/ConsentDetailPage.tsx:38-71. The single most-cloned file is pages/ndi/NdiPage.tsx with 69 clone instances / 1,001 dup lines, including an intra-file 40-line clone (NdiPage.tsx:747-786 vs 828-867).

Root cause

No shared component library for the recurring building blocks (progress bars, stat/metric cards, status pills, campaign tables, bilingual label pickers). New pages were created by copying a nearby page. The bilingual `isAr && xAr ? xAr : xEn` selection idiom appears in 160 TSX files inline rather than via one helper, and a `tlabel(...)`-style label picker is reimplemented in ~30 files.

Evidence / proof
jscpd statistics.formats.tsx = 609 clones / 5.44% / 7,993 dup lines (8,602 by per-clone line sum). Top TSX files by clone instances: NdiPage.tsx (69), EsgPage.tsx (49), AiLifecycleRecertificationsPage.tsx (43), BcmExerciseWizard.tsx (28), CptyCounterpartiesPage.tsx (25). Largest single TSX clone = FacilitatorConsolePage.tsx:683-727 vs ObserverDashboardPage.tsx:568-612 (45 lines). grep: `function ProgressBar` in 2 files (identical bodies), inline bilingual `isAr ?`/`isAr &&` picker pattern in 160 tsx files.

Real-world impact

Inconsistent and drift-prone UI: a fix to ProgressBar color thresholds, an RTL `dir` correction, or a design-token rename only lands in the page the developer happened to edit, leaving others stale. Doubles the review burden for every page and obscures genuinely page-specific logic. Increases bundle size with repeated component definitions.

Reproduction

1) Open tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/compliance/ObligationCampaignsPage.tsx:344-365 and compare ProgressBar to the same function in another campaigns page. 2) Diff FacilitatorConsolePage.tsx:683-761 against ObserverDashboardPage.tsx:568-646 — ActiveInjectCard/ResponseCard are identical. 3) grep -rl 'function ProgressBar' tss-grc-ui-v2/src --include=*.tsx → 2 files with identical bodies.

Resolution

Extract the recurring presentational components into a shared module (e.g. src/components/ui/ProgressBar.tsx, StatCard.tsx, StatusPill.tsx, CampaignTable.tsx) and the bilingual selection into a single helper (e.g. src/lib/i18n.ts exporting `pick(isAr, ar, en)` and `tlabel(map, key, isAr)`), then replace the inline copies with imports. Co-locate the BCM crisis-exercise cards (ActiveInjectCard/ResponseCard) in one shared file imported by both the facilitator and observer pages. Prioritize the highest-clone files (NdiPage, EsgPage, the campaigns pages) first.

  const color = percent >= 80 ? 'var(--success)'
    : percent >= 50 ? 'var(--info)'
    : percent > 0 ? 'var(--warning)'
    : 'var(--ink-4)';
  return (<div style={{ display: 'flex', alignItems: 'center', gap: 8 }}>
    <div style={{ flex: 1, height: 8, borderRadius: 4, background: 'var(--surface-3)', overflow: 'hidden', minWidth: 80 }}>
      <div style={{ width: `${Math.max(0, Math.min(100, percent))}%`, height: '100%', background: color, transition: 'width 200ms' }} />
    </div>
    <span style={{ fontSize: 12, color: 'var(--ink-3)', minWidth: 56 }}>{label}</span>
  </div>);
}
▲ After (fixed)

// in each page:

HighQUAL-ESG-001God class: DataOfficerService implements 10 sub-modules in 1054 LOC with 14 injected repositories
✓ VerifiedQualityGod class / SRP violation▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Confirmed. DataOfficerService is exactly 1054 LOC (verified) and injects exactly 14 *Repository fields (verified). Its own class javadoc states it 'Implements 10 PDPL/NDMO/SDAIA-mandated sub-modules in one service', and the file embeds eight distinct state-machine maps (DSR, DPIA, Breach, Notice, Disposal, NDR, Ethics, plus Consent/Retention described) — a textbook god class / SRP violation aggregating many bounded contexts behind one @Service. All quantitative claims match. High is appropriate for a Quality-phase maintainability finding of this size.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/data_officer/service/DataOfficerService.java:48-1054 Effort L Risk Maintainability risk: a 1054-LOC class with 14 collaborators and 10 distinct domains is the single highest-churn merge-conflict hotspot in the module; every DSR/Consent/DPIA/Breach/Notice/Retention/NDR/Catalog/Quality/Ethics change touches it.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/data_officer/service/DataOfficerService.java:48-1054
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/data_officer/service/DataOfficerService.java:120-134

Description

DataOfficerService is a single @Service that owns the full lifecycle of ten unrelated PDPL/NDMO sub-modules (DSR, Consent, DPIA, Breach, Privacy Notice, Retention/Disposal, NDR, Catalog/Lineage, Quality, Ethics). It declares 7 state-machine maps, injects 14 repositories + 1 event publisher (lines 120-134), and contains ~30 public methods and ~13 static mapper methods. This is a textbook Single-Responsibility violation: the class has ten reasons to change.

Root cause

All ten sub-modules were placed in one class to 'share a single tenant-scoped event timeline and a consistent state-machine validator' (class Javadoc, lines 24-44). The shared infrastructure (timeline/emit/validate) does not require co-location of the ten domains.

Evidence / proof
1054 LOC (wc -l). 14 `private final ...Repository` fields (lines 120-133) plus ApplicationEventPublisher (134). 7 static transition maps DSR_ALLOWED..ETHICS_ALLOWED (lines 52-118). Sub-modules numbered 1..10 in section banners.

Real-world impact

High coupling and low cohesion: any change to one regulatory surface forces recompilation/retesting of the whole class and maximises merge conflicts across teams. Unit testing requires mocking all 14 repositories even to exercise one path.

Reproduction

Open the file; observe section banners '1. DSR' (136) through '10. Ethics' (697) and the 14-field constructor block (120-134).

Resolution

Extract one @Service per sub-module (DsrService, ConsentService, DpiaService, ...), each injecting only its own repository. Hoist the shared timeline/emit/validate/org/currentUserId helpers into a single injectable collaborator (e.g. DataOfficerTimeline / a common base), and keep the dashboard aggregation in a thin DashboardService that fans out to the sub-services.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@Service
@Transactional
public class DataOfficerService {
    private final DoEventRepository eventRepo;
    private final DsrRepository dsrRepo;
    private final ConsentRepository consentRepo;
    // ... 11 more repositories ...
    public DsrResponse createDsr(...) { ... }
    public ConsentResponse recordConsent(...) { ... }
    // ... 10 sub-modules in one class ...
}
▲ After (fixed)
@Service @Transactional
public class DsrService {
    private final DsrRepository dsrRepo;
    private final DoTimeline timeline;   // shared helper bean
    public DsrResponse createDsr(...) { ... }
}
// + ConsentService, DpiaService, BreachService, ... each owning one repo
// + DoTimeline bean exposing timeline()/emit()/validate()/org()/currentUserId()
References: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-responsibility_principle · Robert C. Martin, Clean Code, ch.10 (Classes)
HighQUAL-IE-001EvidenceMatrixService.matrix() is a triple-nested N+1 query loop (86 LOC, queries scale with the whole framework catalog)
✓ VerifiedQualityPerformance / Cyclomatic complexity▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Verified in EvidenceMatrixService.java:57-143. matrix() loops frameworkRepo.findAll() (64) -> controlRepo.findByFrameworkIdAndIsActiveTrue (71) -> subControlRepo.findByControlIdAndIsActiveTrue (77) -> itemRepo.findBySubControl(org, s.getId()) per sub-control (85), with inline aggregations in one ~86-LOC method. Genuine triple/quad-nested N+1 plus high cyclomatic complexity. The batch pattern that fixes it already exists in the same package — GrcExpertService uses findByFrameworkIdInAndIsActiveTrue / findByControlIdInAndIsActiveTrue + aggregateStatusBySubControl/aggregateExpiryBySubControl/aggregateFreshApprovedBySubControl. Real quality defect; High is right.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceMatrixService.java:57-143 Effort M Risk High operational risk: a single GET /api/v1/evidence/matrix fires O(frameworks + controls + sub-controls) DB round-trips. For a full NCA ECC / ISO 27001 catalog (hundreds of sub-controls per tenant) this is hundreds of queries per page load, causing slow dashboards and DB connection-pool pressure under concurrent users. Not a security CVSS, but a clear scalability defect.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceMatrixService.java:64
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceMatrixService.java:71
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceMatrixService.java:77
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceMatrixService.java:85

Description

matrix() loops over every active framework (frameworkRepo.findAll(), line 64), then for each framework queries controls (controlRepo.findByFrameworkIdAndIsActiveTrue, line 71), then for each control queries sub-controls (subControlRepo.findByControlIdAndIsActiveTrue, line 77), then inside the innermost loop runs itemRepo.findBySubControl(org, s.getId()) once per sub-control (line 85) plus an in-memory method-mix tally. The number of SQL statements grows linearly with the size of the entire control catalog, not with the data actually requested. The method is also a single 86-LOC block with three levels of nested loops and several inline aggregations (freshest-expiry, method mix, freshness band), giving it high cyclomatic complexity.

Root cause

Per-row repository lookups inside nested loops instead of set-based / batch queries. The matrix is materialized by walking the object graph one entity at a time rather than fetching counts/aggregates in bulk.

Evidence / proof
Innermost call at line 85: `List<EvidenceItem> items = itemRepo.findBySubControl(org, s.getId());` executed once per sub-control, nested inside `for (EvidenceControl c : controls)` (line 74) which is nested inside `for (EvidenceFramework fw : frameworks)` (line 68). The sibling GrcExpertService.listExpertCatalog() solves the identical framework→control→sub-control rollup with batch finders (findByControlIdInAndIsActiveTrue) and three aggregate queries (aggregateStatusBySubControl / aggregateExpiryBySubControl / aggregateFreshApprovedBySubControl) — proving the batch pattern already exists in the same package.

Real-world impact

Dashboard latency grows with catalog size; DB load multiplies under concurrent tenants; the read-only transaction holds a connection for the full duration of the loop.

Reproduction

Seed a tenant with a full ECC framework (~100+ sub-controls), enable Hibernate SQL logging (show_sql), call GET /api/v1/evidence/matrix, and count the emitted SELECT statements — it equals 1 (frameworks) + N(controls-per-fw) + M(subs-per-ctrl) + K(findBySubControl per sub-control).

Resolution

Replace the per-sub-control itemRepo.findBySubControl call with batch aggregation queries keyed by sub-control id (mirroring GrcExpertService.aggregate*BySubControl), fetch all controls/sub-controls for the active frameworks with findBy...In finders, then assemble the matrix in memory from the pre-fetched maps. Extract the sub-control block builder into a private helper to reduce the method below ~30 LOC.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
for (EvidenceSubControl s : subs) {
    if (Boolean.FALSE.equals(s.getIsActive())) continue;
    List<EvidenceItem> items = itemRepo.findBySubControl(org, s.getId());
    int count = items.size();
    ...
}
▲ After (fixed)
// Pre-fetch once, outside the loops:
Map<Long, List<EvidenceItem>> itemsBySc = itemRepo.findByOrganisationIdAndSubControlIdIn(org, allSubControlIds)
        .stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(EvidenceItem::getSubControlId));
...
for (EvidenceSubControl s : subs) {
    List<EvidenceItem> items = itemsBySc.getOrDefault(s.getId(), List.of());
    ...
}
References: Hibernate N+1 select problem · Compare GrcExpertService.listExpertCatalog (same module) which uses aggregate queries
HighQUAL-IE-002EvidenceItemService.toResponse() issues up to 4 lookup queries per item, causing N+1 on every list/page endpoint

It is invoked per-row on list/page endpoints: list() at line 116 does page.map(this::toResponse), and listExpired() (132) and listBySubControl() (139) do .stream().map(this::toResponse).toList(). Description

toResponse(EvidenceItem) resolves the sub-control code/name (subControlRepository.findById, line 390), then the parent control (controlRepository.findById, line 394), then the framework (frameworkRepository.findById, line 397), then the owner's name (userRepository.findById, line 405). Because list()/page().map(this::toResponse) (lines 110-117) and the other read methods all funnel through this mapper, the per-item cost is multiplied across every result row — a classic N+1.

Root cause

Enrichment by per-row findById inside a response mapper that is invoked once per row in a collection/page, instead of batching the joins or projecting them in the query.

Evidence / proof
Lines 389-407 chain four findById calls per item; list() at line 116 does `return page.map(this::toResponse);` so the mapper runs once per page row.

Resolution

Either (a) project the joined sub-control/control/framework codes and owner name directly in the EvidenceItemRepository query (DTO projection / JOIN FETCH), or (b) pre-fetch the referenced sub-controls/controls/frameworks/owners in bulk for the page and pass lookup maps into toResponse.

}
...

@RestController

    private final RiskRepository riskRepo;       // risk module
    // ... 5 more repos; coverage() builds HashMaps inline
}
▲ After (fixed)
@RestController
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class FrameworkAnchorController {
    private final FrameworkAnchorService anchorService;
    @GetMapping("/frameworks/coverage")
    public List<FrameworkCoverageDto> coverage() { return anchorService.coverage(); }
}
// FrameworkAnchorService aggregates via module read-services + typed DTOs.

Each LIVE integration client re-implements the same retry harness: a `BACKOFF_CAP_MS` constant, a `for (attempt=1..maxAttempts)` loop that catches `HttpServerErrorException | ResourceAccessException`, sleeps `delayMs`, multiplies by `backoffMultiplier` capped at `BACKOFF_CAP_MS`, a `doWithRetryOn5xx(Supplier)` wrapper, a private `sleep(long)` that re-throws on interrupt, and a `url(String path)` base-URL composer that strips a trailing slash. LiveTenableClient further contains THREE near-identical retry loops internally (the per-action POST loop, `runOutboundDelete` at 270-303, and `doWithRetryOn5xx` at 306-326).

Per-vendor adapter packages were built by copying a reference client. No shared `AbstractRetryingRestClient` / retry utility was extracted.

Real-world impact

▲ After (fixed)

  static <T> T withRetry(RetryConfig cfg, Supplier<T> call, Runnable on401) { ... }
}

return RestRetrySupport.withRetry(props.getRetry(), () -> http.get()...body(Map.class), tokens::refresh);

Description

A repeated anti-pattern appears across the assigned modules: a private no-op method `_touch()` (variously `{ log.trace("bound"); }` or `{ Objects.requireNonNull(this); }`) annotated `@SuppressWarnings("unused")`, plus dummy `private static final Class<?> KEEP = SomeType.class;` fields whose only purpose is to keep an otherwise-unused import 'referenced'. CalendarService adds an unused `label()` method and `OBJECTS_KEEP_IMPORT = Objects.equals("a","a")`. These exist solely to silence the compiler/IDE rather than deleting the dead import, field, or logger they pretend to use.

Root cause

Imports / loggers / utility-class references became unused after refactors, but instead of deleting them the author added a fake consumer (`_touch`, `KEEP`) to suppress the warning. The pattern then got copy-pasted as new classes were created from old ones.

StrategyRoiService.java:536  `private Optional<StrategyRoiAnalysis> _touch() { log.trace("bound"); return Optional.empty(); }`  — keeps the otherwise-unused `Optional` import and `log` field alive. ExportService.java:494-495  `@SuppressWarnings("unused") private static final Class<?> KEEP = CellRangeAddress.class;`. Readers waste time deciphering why a service has a method that does nothing. The fake references mask which imports are truly needed, so the codebase can never be cleanly linted; future unused code hides behind the same noise. Each `_touch` is also a (tiny) reflectively-reachable method on a Spring bean.

Resolution

Delete each `_touch()` method and each `KEEP*`/`OBJECTS_KEEP_IMPORT` field, then remove the now-genuinely-unused imports, loggers, and fields they were shielding. If a logger field (e.g. `log` in StrategyRoiService) has no real call site, drop the field and its slf4j imports. Configure the build (e.g. error-prone / checkstyle RedundantImport) to fail on unused imports so the workaround cannot reappear.

▲ After (fixed)

Real-world impact

Bug-fix and behaviour drift risk: e.g. if the inject-status taxonomy gains a new state, one `summarise` will count it and the other will not, producing inconsistent RunSummary totals depending on which service rendered them.

Reproduction

Diff the two helper regions, or open audit/raw/jscpd/jscpd-report.json and filter for ExerciseObserverService vs ExerciseRuntimeService.

Extract a package-private `ExerciseRunProjections` (or a `@Component RuntimeViewMapper`) under `bcm/cycle/runtime` exposing `summarise`, `toInjectView`, `toResponseView`, plus the shared `nullSafe`/`truncate`. Inject it into both services. Consolidating also fixes the count-query fan-out in one place.

▲ After (fixed)

QualitySOLID / Layering▾
