LowQUAL-DUP-004REST controllers replicate identical import + class-annotation boilerplate header across 200+ controllers (CommitteeController is the canonical donor)
QualityCode Duplication / Maintainability▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/admin/committee/controller/CommitteeController.java:5-39 Effort M Risk Not a security issue. Largely unavoidable Spring framework scaffolding; rated Low. 202 controller<->controller clones / 2,635 dup lines, but most is the import block + @RestController/@RequestMapping/@RequiredArgsConstructor/@Tag/@SecurityRequirement header that idiomatic Spring requires per class. Real but limited dedupe opportunity.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/admin/committee/controller/CommitteeController.java:5-39
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/openbanking/controller/ObController.java:18-40
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/opres/controller/OpResController.java:9-31
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/reginspect/controller/RegInspectController.java:12-34
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/rrp/controller/RrpController.java:18-40
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/sharia/controller/ShariaController.java:22-44

Description

java-controller <-> java-controller = 202 clones / 2,635 dup lines. CommitteeController.java:5-39 is the most frequent clone donor in the whole report — it forms a 31-to-35-line clone with at least 30 distinct module controllers (openbanking, opres, reginspect, rrp, sharia, fraud, evidence, incident, intake, ...). The duplicated span is the import list plus the class-level annotation header: @RestController, @RequestMapping("/api/..."), @RequiredArgsConstructor, @Tag(...), @SecurityRequirement(name = "bearerAuth"), and the `private final XService service;` field. Beyond the header, many endpoint methods follow an identical CRUD shape (@GetMapping list with status/page/size params, @GetMapping/{id}, @PostMapping create returning 201, @PutMapping/{id}). There is no abstract base controller in the codebase (grep for BaseController/abstract *Controller → 0).

Root cause

Spring's annotation-driven style requires the same import set and class-level annotations on every @RestController, and the team standardized on a fixed header (RequiredArgsConstructor + Tag + SecurityRequirement). New controllers are created by copying the header from an existing one. No shared @PageableDefault/constant or meta-annotation consolidates the repeated @PreAuthorize/@SecurityRequirement.

Evidence / proof
jscpd: controller<->controller = 202 clones / 2,635 dup lines. CommitteeController.java:5-39 partners with 30 distinct controllers in the duplicates array (count of unique partner files). 233 files contain @RestController. Confirmed header identity by reading CommitteeController.java:20-27 and ObController.java:43-48 (same @RestController/@RequestMapping/@RequiredArgsConstructor/@Tag/@SecurityRequirement stack).

Real-world impact

Low functional risk — this is mostly idiomatic framework boilerplate. The realistic cost is that cross-cutting controller conventions (e.g. standardizing the default page size, adding a common @SecurityRequirement, a shared pagination param) can't be changed in one place. The repeated CRUD method bodies (list/get/create/update) are a secondary, more valuable dedupe target than the import header.

Reproduction

1) Open CommitteeController.java:5-39 and ObController.java:18-48 — identical annotation header. 2) In jscpd-report.json, filter duplicates where firstFile/secondFile contains CommitteeController.java → 30 distinct partner controllers. 3) grep -rl 'abstract class.*Controller' tss-grc-backend → 0 (no base controller).

Resolution

Two targeted moves: (a) introduce a composed meta-annotation, e.g. `@GrcRestController` bundling @RestController + @RequiredArgsConstructor + @SecurityRequirement(name="bearerAuth") + @Tag, to collapse the annotation header; (b) for the genuinely repeated CRUD bodies, consider a thin generic `AbstractCrudController<TResp, TCreate, TUpdate>` or shared response helpers — but keep this optional, since over-abstracting controllers can hurt readability. The import-block portion of the clone is inherent to Java/Spring and is acceptable to leave; do not chase it. Prioritize this finding below DUP-001/002/003.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/admin/committees")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
@Tag(name = "Committee Workflows")
@SecurityRequirement(name = "bearerAuth")
public class CommitteeController {
    private final CommitteeService service;
    // ...
}
▲ After (fixed)
// common/web/GrcRestController.java
@Target(ElementType.TYPE) @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@RestController @RequiredArgsConstructor
@SecurityRequirement(name = "bearerAuth")
public @interface GrcRestController { }

// controller:
@GrcRestController
@RequestMapping("/api/admin/committees")
@Tag(name = "Committee Workflows")
public class CommitteeController {
    private final CommitteeService service;
}

QualityCode duplication / boilerplate▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/reports/service/NdiReportService.java:184-436 Effort M Risk Maintainability: 12 private synthesizer methods (184-436) each repeat the same LinkedHashMap-build + stream-map-row + ReportResult-wrap shape, so a change to the result envelope or row convention must be replicated 12 times.

Description

executiveSummary, maturityHeatmap, complianceStatus, opexDashboard, gapRegister, capaRegister, roadmap, evidenceInventory, domainRollup, cycleHistory, auditTrail, submissionExport all follow the same template: build a summary LinkedHashMap, map a row list with `Map<String,Object> row = new LinkedHashMap<>(); row.put(...); return row;`, and wrap in a ReportResult. The per-field row.put blocks (e.g. 215-222, 235-244, 257-267) are structurally identical and only differ in the entity getters.

Root cause

No generic row-projection helper; each report type was authored independently.

Evidence / proof
Pattern `Map<String, Object> row = new LinkedHashMap<>();` followed by N row.put(...) calls appears in 10 of the 12 synthesizers. dispatch switch at 165-179 routes to all of them.

Real-world impact

Adding a column convention (e.g. always include 'id') or changing ReportResult shape is a 12-site edit; high copy-paste surface invites inconsistency between report types.

Reproduction

Compare maturityHeatmap (207-225) and complianceStatus (227-247) — same skeleton, different getters.

Resolution

Extract a small generic helper `rows(List<T> src, Function<T, Map<String,Object>> projector)` and a `result(type, cycleId, summary, rows)` factory so each synthesizer reduces to a projector lambda; or drive projection from a column-definition map.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
List<Map<String,Object>> out = rows.stream().map(m -> {
    Map<String,Object> row = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    row.put("id", m.getId()); row.put("domain", m.getDomain()); ...
    return row;
}).toList();
return new ReportResult("MATURITY_HEATMAP", cycleId, LocalDateTime.now(), sum, out);
▲ After (fixed)
return result("MATURITY_HEATMAP", cycleId, sum, project(rows, m -> Map.of(
    "id", m.getId(), "domain", m.getDomain(), "currentLevel", m.getCurrentLevel(), ...)));

LowQUAL-ESG-008Per-instance new ObjectMapper() in AiSuggestionService instead of injecting the shared bean
QualityResource handling / consistency▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ai/service/AiSuggestionService.java:35 Effort S Risk Minor: constructing a fresh ObjectMapper as a field initialiser ignores the Spring-managed, configured ObjectMapper used elsewhere (NdiReportService/NdiSubmissionPackageService inject it), so any project-wide Jackson config (modules, date handling) does not apply here.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ai/service/AiSuggestionService.java:35

Root cause

Inconsistent dependency strategy — this service self-instantiates Jackson rather than injecting the application bean.

Line 35 `new ObjectMapper()`; compare NdiSubmissionPackageService line 60 / NdiReportService line 58 which take ObjectMapper via constructor injection.

Resolution

Inject ObjectMapper via the constructor (Lombok @RequiredArgsConstructor already in use) and drop the `new ObjectMapper()` initialiser.

LowQUAL-ESG-009Cross-tenant findAll() in NdiScheduler report loop and org-discovery shortcut
QualityLayering / multi-tenancy smell▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/scheduler/NdiScheduler.java:82-127 Effort M Risk Correctness/scalability: reportScheduleSweep iterates reportDefs.findAll() across every tenant each minute and distinctOrgIds() derives the tenant universe from the report-definition table, a self-admitted demo shortcut that loads all orgs' rows into memory.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/scheduler/NdiScheduler.java:84
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ndi/scheduler/NdiScheduler.java:119-127

Description

reportScheduleSweep (82) calls reportDefs.findAll() — a non-tenant-scoped query that pulls every organisation's report definitions every 60s. distinctOrgIds() (119-127) also calls findAll() and maps to distinct organisation ids to drive the evidence-expiry sweep. The class Javadoc (lines 34-41) explicitly notes this is a demo shortcut that 'in production a proper org-iteration service would replace'.

Root cause

No platform-level tenant registry; the scheduler improvises tenant discovery from a domain table and bypasses the org-scoped repository finders the rest of the module uses.

Evidence / proof
Line 84 `for (NdiReportDefinition def : reportDefs.findAll())`; lines 122-126 `reportDefs.findAll().stream().map(...).distinct().toList()`. Javadoc 34-41 documents the shortcut.

Reproduction

Add a tenant with NDI evidence but no report definitions; observe its evidence is never swept (distinctOrgIds omits it).

Resolution

Introduce a platform tenant-registry service and iterate that; or add a dedicated paged/streamed query keyed by 'has schedule cron' to avoid full-table scans. Decouple expiry-sweep org discovery from the report-definition table.

for (NdiReportDefinition def : reportDefs.findAll()) { ... }
...
return reportDefs.findAll().stream().map(NdiReportDefinition::getOrganisationId).distinct().toList();
▲ After (fixed)
for (Long orgId : tenantRegistry.activeOrgIds()) { ... reportDefs.findScheduledByOrg(orgId) ... }

LowQUAL-FA-002Per-entity DTO mappers and *_ALLOWED transition tables duplicated wholesale across sister services
QualityCode Duplication▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/rrp/service/RrpService.java:621-712 Effort L Risk Each new column on an entity requires touching both the entity, the request-apply block, AND the hand-written builder mapper; the builder-chain mappers are long, near-mechanical, and structurally identical between modules, so they are a steady source of 'forgot to map field X' defects.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/rrp/service/RrpService.java:621-712
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/sharia/service/ShariaService.java:701-819
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/fraud/service/FraudService.java:404-481
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/opres/service/OpResService.java:315-367

Description

Every service hand-rolls `private static XResponse toX(XEntity)` builder chains (RrpService has 5, ShariaService has 6, FraudService 3, OpResService 3) that mechanically copy 15-30 getters into a builder. The same pattern of static transition maps (`RESOLUTION_ALLOWED`, `FINDING_ALLOWED`, `NC_ALLOWED`, `PRODUCT_ALLOWED` in ShariaService; `ALLOWED` in Rrp/Fraud/OpRes/Finding/IaEngagement/SanctionsHit) plus an identical `guardTransition` body is repeated. jscpd flags the mapper region directly (RiskControlFindingPivotService:622 <-> :638; CptyService:528 <-> RrpService:592, 30 lines).

Root cause

Project convention is hand-written builder mappers (no MapStruct) and a private transition-map-per-service. Both are valid choices individually, but the verbatim repetition is unmanaged.

Evidence / proof
RrpService 5 mappers (lines 621-712, ~92 LOC of pure builder chains). ShariaService 6 mappers (701-819, ~119 LOC). ShariaService declares 4 separate `Map<String,Set<String>>` ALLOWED tables (78-105). The guardTransition body in FraudService:350-356 and OpResService:274-280 is identical apart from the message prefix.

Real-world impact

Field-mapping omissions are silent (a forgotten `.fieldX()` compiles fine and just returns null to the UI). High line-count with low information density inflates every service file.

Reproduction

Compare RrpService.toOption (652-666) with the entity setters in addOption (220-241): both enumerate the same 14 fields; adding a 15th requires editing both.

Resolution

Adopt MapStruct (or a shared reflective copy like the BeanUtils approach ScmService already uses) for response mapping, and factor the transition-guard into a tiny generic helper `StateMachine.guard(map, from, to, label)` reused by all services.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
private static OptionResponse toOption(RrpRecoveryOption o) {
    return OptionResponse.builder()
        .id(o.getId()).cycleId(o.getCycleId())
        .optionCode(o.getOptionCode()).category(o.getCategory())
        // ...14 more lines...
        .build();
}
▲ After (fixed)
@Mapper(componentModel = "spring")
interface RrpMapper { OptionResponse toOption(RrpRecoveryOption o); }
// or a shared StateMachine.guard(ALLOWED, from, to, "Resolution")
References: MapStruct · DRY principle
LowQUAL-FA-003Dead dashboard query: FraudService counts status="TRIAGE" which the state machine never assigns
QualityDead Code▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/fraud/service/FraudService.java:333 Effort S Risk Functional-correctness smell rather than crash: the `triageCount` tile on the Fraud dashboard is hard-wired to always read 0 because no case is ever persisted with status TRIAGE, yet the field is presented to users as a live count.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/fraud/service/FraudService.java:333
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/fraud/service/FraudService.java:71-84

Description

`dashboard()` populates `.triageCount(caseRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndStatus(orgId, "TRIAGE"))`. The class-level comment (lines 71-76) and the ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS map (77-84) explicitly state TRIAGE is NOT a held state — `triage()` (151-183) sets `triagedAt` and immediately advances to INVESTIGATING or FALSE_POSITIVE. No code path ever calls `setStatus("TRIAGE")`. Therefore this count is permanently 0 and is dead/misleading.

Root cause

Dashboard was written against an earlier design where TRIAGE was a held state; when the team collapsed TRIAGE into a transient decision step (documented in the NOTE comment) the dashboard query was not removed.

Reproduction

Create a fraud case, call triage(); query `dashboard().triageCount` — it returns 0 regardless of how many cases were triaged.

Either remove the triageCount tile, or repurpose it to count cases with `triagedAt != null && status == 'INVESTIGATING'` (i.e. currently-in-investigation-post-triage). Removing is cleaner given the documented design.

▲ After (fixed)
.detectedCount(caseRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndStatus(orgId, "DETECTED"))
.investigatingCount(caseRepo.countByOrganisationIdAndStatus(orgId, "INVESTIGATING"))

LowQUAL-FA-004Unreachable guard branch in RrpService.transitionCycle for SUBMITTED
QualityDead Code▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/rrp/service/RrpService.java:144-152 Effort S Risk Logic-correctness smell: the defensive `if (Set.of("SUBMITTED").contains(to))` block can never be entered because the ALLOWED map upstream already rejects any transition whose target is SUBMITTED, so the bespoke 'use the /submit endpoint' message is dead and an actual SUBMITTED attempt yields the generic 'Illegal transition' message instead.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/rrp/service/RrpService.java:71-78
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/rrp/service/RrpService.java:144-152

Description

`transitionCycle` first computes `allowed = ALLOWED.getOrDefault(from, Set.of())` and throws if `!allowed.contains(to)` (144-148). The ALLOWED map (71-78) never lists SUBMITTED as a reachable target from any state. So by the time control reaches line 149 `if (Set.of("SUBMITTED").contains(to))`, `to` cannot be SUBMITTED — the branch is unreachable and its informative message ('Use the dedicated /submit endpoint to lodge with SAMA') is never shown.

Root cause

The author added a friendly redirect for SUBMITTED but placed it after the generic allow-list check that already short-circuits the same case.

Evidence / proof
ALLOWED map values: DRAFT->{IN_PREPARATION}, IN_PREPARATION->{BOARD_REVIEW}, BOARD_REVIEW->{APPROVED,IN_PREPARATION}, APPROVED->{IN_PREPARATION}, SUBMITTED->{ACKNOWLEDGED}, ACKNOWLEDGED->{CLOSED}, CLOSED->{}. No value set contains SUBMITTED.

Real-world impact

Misleading dead code; an operator who POSTs a SUBMITTED transition gets the generic error instead of the intended hint to use /submit. Minor, but the branch will confuse future maintainers reasoning about reachability.

Reproduction

Call transitionCycle with toStatus=SUBMITTED on an APPROVED cycle: it throws 'Illegal transition APPROVED → SUBMITTED' from line 146, never reaching the friendlier message at 150.

Resolution

Move the SUBMITTED hint ahead of the allow-list check, or delete it and document /submit in the controller. Preferred: hoist the special-case before the generic guard.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
Set<String> allowed = ALLOWED.getOrDefault(from, Set.of());
if (!allowed.contains(to)) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("Illegal transition " + from + " → " + to + ...);
}
if (Set.of("SUBMITTED").contains(to)) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("Use the dedicated /submit endpoint to lodge with SAMA");
}
▲ After (fixed)
if ("SUBMITTED".equals(to)) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("Use the dedicated /submit endpoint to lodge with SAMA");
}
Set<String> allowed = ALLOWED.getOrDefault(from, Set.of());
if (!allowed.contains(to)) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("Illegal transition " + from + " → " + to + ...);
}
References: Unreachable code

Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/sharia/service/ShariaService.java:561-633 Effort M Risk Readability/testability risk: several single methods bundle querying, in-memory bucketing, builder assembly and side-effects, making them hard to unit-test in isolation and easy to break when a column is added.

tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/sharia/service/ShariaService.java:496-551

Description

Measured method spans over the ~40-LOC guideline: ShariaService.dashboard() = 73 LOC with ~20 repository calls plus three in-place LinkedHashMap bucketing loops (561-633); ShariaService.transitionProduct() = 56 LOC switch with 7 cases each mutating different fields (496-551); IncidentService.regulatoryTemplates() = 57 LOC building 5 near-identical template maps (282-338); ThreeLinesService.overview() = ~73 LOC mixing role resolution, 4 register pulls, in-memory bucketing and a hard-coded 8-arg band() builder (111-183). transitionResolution (235-282, 48 LOC) and transitionCycle in RrpService are similar.

Real-world impact

Each method is hard to read and test; the positional band(...) calls in ThreeLinesService (e.g. `band(LINE_1, roles, line1Risks, 0, line1Capa, 0, 0, line1Overdue, 0)`) are especially fragile — a transposed zero is a silent metric bug.

Reproduction

Open the cited ranges; count branches/statements. dashboard() has 3 loops + ~20 sequential repo calls in one method body.

Resolution

Extract per-section private helpers (e.g. resolutionStats(), findingStats(), productStats() for the dashboard; one renderTemplate-driven loop over a small template descriptor list for regulatoryTemplates) and replace the 8-positional-arg band() with a small builder/record to make the zeros self-documenting.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
public DashboardResponse dashboard() {
    Long o = org();
    long activeScholars = ...; // ~20 repo calls + 3 bucketing loops inline, 73 LOC
    ...
    return DashboardResponse.builder()....build();
}
▲ After (fixed)
public DashboardResponse dashboard() {
    Long o = org();
    return DashboardResponse.builder()
        .scholars(scholarStats(o))
        .resolutions(resolutionStats(o))
        .findings(findingStats(o))
        .products(productStats(o))
        .build();
}

LowQUAL-FA-009IllegalTransitionException constructed with an empty allowed-set, discarding the real allowed transitions from the error message
QualityError Handling▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/audit_lc/service/AuditLifecycleService.java:94-104 Effort S Risk Diagnostics-quality smell: the transition exception is designed to carry the set of legal next states, but several call sites pass Set.of(), so the resulting 400 error tells the caller nothing about what would have been valid — degrading API ergonomics and support triage.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/audit_lc/service/AuditLifecycleService.java:104
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/audit_lc/service/AuditLifecycleService.java:178
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/audit_lc/service/AuditLifecycleService.java:250

Description

AuditLifecycleService validates transitions with an inline `switch` returning a boolean and, on failure, throws `new IllegalTransitionException(from, to, Set.of())` (lines 104, 178, 250). The exception's third argument is meant to be the legal target set (cf. FindingService.java:115 and IaEngagementService.java:234 which pass the real `allowed` set). Because the allowed set was computed implicitly inside the switch and never materialised, an empty set is passed and the helpful 'allowed: [...]' detail is lost.

Root cause

AuditLifecycleService uses a boolean-returning switch for transition validation instead of the Map<String,Set<String>> approach the other services use, so there is no allowed-set object to hand to the exception.

Evidence / proof
AuditLifecycleService.java:104 `if (!ok) throw new IllegalTransitionException(from, to, Set.of());` (repeated at 178, 250). Compare FindingService.java:113-115 which builds `allowed` then throws `new IllegalTransitionException(f.getStatus(), req.getStatus(), allowed)`.

Real-world impact

Clients/operators receive 'illegal transition X -> Y' with no hint of valid targets; inconsistent error payloads between audit_lc artefacts (AnnualPlan/WorkingPaper/CapaTask) and the rest of the platform.

Reproduction

POST an invalid AnnualPlan transition (e.g. DRAFT -> CLOSED): the IllegalTransitionException is raised with an empty allowed set, so the message omits the legal {AC_REVIEW}.

Resolution

Replace the boolean switches with the same `Map<String,Set<String>>` pattern (AP_ALLOWED/WP_ALLOWED/CAPA_ALLOWED) used elsewhere and pass the resolved set to the exception, restoring the informative message.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
boolean ok = switch (from) {
    case "DRAFT" -> "AC_REVIEW".equals(to);
    ...
};
if (!ok) throw new IllegalTransitionException(from, to, Set.of());
▲ After (fixed)
Set<String> allowed = AP_ALLOWED.getOrDefault(from, Set.of());
if (!allowed.contains(to)) throw new IllegalTransitionException(from, to, allowed);
References: Meaningful error messages · Consistency of error contracts
LowQUAL-FA-010FraudService.closeCase reconstructs prior status from timestamps after overwriting it — fragile derivation with stale comment
QualityNaming / Maintainability▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/fraud/service/FraudService.java:295-301 Effort S Risk Correctness-fragility smell: the F8 event's priorStatus is guessed from outcome timestamps because the real prior status was already overwritten, producing values ('RESOLVED','OPEN') that are not even members of the case status vocabulary and can mislead downstream rules.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/fraud/service/FraudService.java:283-301

Description

closeCase() sets status to CLOSED at line 283, then at 295-301 emits FRAUD_CASE_CLOSED with `priorStatus` derived as `saved.getConfirmedLossSar() != null ? "CONFIRMED" : saved.getOutcomeSetAt() != null ? "RESOLVED" : "OPEN"`. The real prior status (CONFIRMED/CLEARED/FALSE_POSITIVE) was available before the overwrite but was not captured. The emitted strings 'RESOLVED' and 'OPEN' are not valid FraudCase statuses, so any rule matching on priorStatus equality will misfire.

Root cause

The prior status was not saved into a local before `c.setStatus("CLOSED")`, forcing a lossy timestamp-based reconstruction (the inline comment admits 'we already overwrote it').

Evidence / proof
Line 283 `c.setStatus("CLOSED")`; lines 297-300 reconstruct priorStatus from confirmedLossSar/outcomeSetAt yielding 'CONFIRMED'/'RESOLVED'/'OPEN'. ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS shows the only legal pre-CLOSED states are CONFIRMED, CLEARED, FALSE_POSITIVE — none of which is 'RESOLVED' or 'OPEN'.

Real-world impact

Automation rules conditioning on the FRAUD_CASE_CLOSED priorStatus receive fabricated/incorrect values (CLEARED and FALSE_POSITIVE both collapse to 'RESOLVED'); breaks the F8 contract subtly.

Reproduction

Close a CLEARED case: the emitted priorStatus is 'RESOLVED', not 'CLEARED'.

Resolution

Capture `String prior = c.getStatus();` before setting CLOSED and emit the real value, mirroring how transitionResolution/transitionProduct capture `from` first.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
c.setStatus("CLOSED");
...
emit("FRAUD_CASE_CLOSED", ..., Map.of("priorStatus",
    saved.getConfirmedLossSar() != null ? "CONFIRMED"
        : saved.getOutcomeSetAt() != null ? "RESOLVED" : "OPEN"));
▲ After (fixed)
String prior = c.getStatus();
c.setStatus("CLOSED");
...
emit("FRAUD_CASE_CLOSED", ..., Map.of("priorStatus", prior));
References: Avoid lossy state reconstruction · Stale comment smell

Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/iam/ldap/LdapRoleMapper.java:52-55 Effort S Risk Low: redundant/confusing stereotype. Both @Configuration and @Component are class-level stereotypes that register the bean; pairing them on a plain ConfigurationProperties POJO is contradictory and can mislead readers into thinking the class is a @Bean factory.

A bean should not be both @Component and @Configuration; @Configuration implies a CGLIB-proxied @Bean factory, which this class is not. Annotation scaffolding left over from an earlier shape; the @Configuration import was never removed when @Component was chosen.

Resolution

Remove the unused @Configuration import. Keep exactly one stereotype — @Component (with @ConfigurationProperties) is correct for this binder POJO.

...

LowQUAL-IE-007AttachmentService duplicates docType-validation logic across upload/replaceVersion/update; DOC_TYPES check copied 3x
QualityCode duplication / DRY▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/attachment/service/AttachmentService.java:37-132 Effort S Risk Low maintainability risk: the same 'normalize to upper-case, validate against DOC_TYPES, throw IllegalArgumentException' block is hand-copied into three methods. A change to the validation rule must be applied in all three.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/attachment/service/AttachmentService.java:41-44
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/attachment/service/AttachmentService.java:78-81
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/attachment/service/AttachmentService.java:122-127

Description

upload() (41-44), replaceVersion() (78-81) and update() (122-127) each repeat the pattern: derive `type` from docType (defaulting/upper-casing), then `if (!DOC_TYPES.contains(type)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown docType ...")`. Three copies of the same string-literal error message and the same allow-list check.

Root cause

No shared resolveDocType(...) helper; the validation was inlined where needed.

Evidence / proof
Identical `if (!DOC_TYPES.contains(type)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown docType '" + docType + "'. Valid: " + DOC_TYPES);` at lines 42-44, 79-81 and 124-126.

Real-world impact

Drift risk if the error wording or normalization changes; mild bloat.

Reproduction

Read the three methods; compare the validation blocks.

Resolution

Extract a private `String resolveDocType(String docType, String fallback)` helper that normalizes and validates once, and call it from all three methods.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
String type = (docType == null || docType.isBlank()) ? "OTHER" : docType.toUpperCase();
if (!DOC_TYPES.contains(type)) {
    throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown docType '" + docType + "'. Valid: " + DOC_TYPES);
}
▲ After (fixed)
String type = resolveDocType(docType, "OTHER");
...
private String resolveDocType(String docType, String fallback) {
    String t = (docType == null || docType.isBlank()) ? fallback : docType.toUpperCase();
    if (!DOC_TYPES.contains(t)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown docType '" + docType + "'. Valid: " + DOC_TYPES);
    return t;
}

LowQUAL-IE-010Status state machines hard-coded as string literals scattered per service (magic strings, no shared enum/constant)

Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/approvals/service/ApprovalRequestService.java:144-211 Effort L Risk Low risk: lifecycle states ('PENDING', 'APPROVED', 'REJECTED', 'DELEGATED', 'EXPIRED', 'IN_PROGRESS', etc.) are bare string literals compared with .equals across multiple services. A typo in any branch silently fails to match, and there is no compile-time guarantee transition tables and branches use the same vocabulary.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/approvals/service/ApprovalRequestService.java:157-176
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/workflow/approval_chains/service/ApprovalChainInstanceService.java:81
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/signature/service/DigitalSignatureService.java:147-153
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceItemService.java:48-58

Description

Each lifecycle service re-expresses its states as raw strings: ApprovalRequestService compares req.getStatus() against "APPROVED"/"REJECTED"/"DELEGATED"/"PENDING"/"EXPIRED" (157-176); DigitalSignatureService against "REQUESTED"/"SIGNED"/"REJECTED"/"EXPIRED" (138, 147-153); ApprovalChainInstanceService against "APPROVED"/"REJECTED"/"DELEGATED" plus a TERMINAL_STATUSES set (81); EvidenceItemService keeps a transition Map keyed by string states (48-58). Root cause

Statuses modeled as free-form String columns and compared with literal .equals rather than enums or named constants.

Evidence / proof
ApprovalRequestService:157 `if ("APPROVED".equals(req.getStatus()) || "REJECTED".equals(req.getStatus()))`; DigitalSignatureService:138 `if (!"REQUESTED".equals(d.getStatus())) return d;`. The literals recur across at least four services in scope.

Real-world impact

Typos in a state literal fail silently (no match) rather than at compile time; harder to enumerate valid states for docs/UI.

grep -rn '"APPROVED"\|"REJECTED"\|"PENDING"' across the in-scope services to see the literal spread.

Resolution

Introduce per-domain status enums (or at minimum a constants class per module) and convert at the persistence boundary; replace literal comparisons with enum/constant references.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
if ("APPROVED".equals(req.getStatus()) || "REJECTED".equals(req.getStatus())) { ... }
▲ After (fixed)
if (status == ApprovalStatus.APPROVED || status == ApprovalStatus.REJECTED) { ... }
References: Replace magic strings with enums
LowQUAL-IE-011noRollbackFor + missing-table swallowing pattern duplicated across committee services and lacks try/catch on get()
QualityError handling / Duplication▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/admin/committee/service/CommitteeActionItemService.java:43-106 Effort M Risk Low risk: the 'catch RuntimeException, sniff message for invalid object name, return empty page' workaround is repeated in CommitteeService and CommitteeActionItemService, and one method declares noRollbackFor without any try/catch, making the annotation misleading. Message-string sniffing for schema errors is brittle.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/admin/committee/service/CommitteeActionItemService.java:56-60
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/admin/committee/service/CommitteeService.java:51-86

Description

CommitteeService.listCommittees/listMeetings (72-86, 152-166) and CommitteeActionItemService.list/listByMeeting/listByCommittee/openActions* (43-106) all repeat: @Transactional(noRollbackFor=RuntimeException.class) + try { repo... } catch (RuntimeException e) { if (isMissingObjectError/CommitteeSqlGuards.isMissingObjectError) return empty; throw e; }. isMissingObjectError works by lower-casing the exception message and searching for 'invalid object name'/'does not exist'/'not found' — fragile message-sniffing. Dev-profile schema-not-bootstrapped tolerance bolted on per read method via copy-paste, with string-based error detection; the annotation was pasted onto get() without the matching handler.

Real-world impact

Message-sniffing breaks if the DB driver/locale changes the wording; the no-op noRollbackFor on get() is confusing; logic is duplicated across two services.

Resolution

Centralize the missing-table tolerance in a single helper (CommitteeSqlGuards already exists — use it everywhere instead of CommitteeService's private copy) and prefer detecting SQLServerException error code over message text. Remove noRollbackFor from get() since it has no handler.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@Transactional(readOnly = true, noRollbackFor = RuntimeException.class)
public CommitteeActionItem get(Long id) {
    return repo.findByIdAndOrganisationId(id, TenantContext.getCurrentTenant())
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("CommitteeActionItem " + id));
}
▲ After (fixed)
@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public CommitteeActionItem get(Long id) {
    return repo.findByIdAndOrganisationId(id, TenantContext.getCurrentTenant())
        .orElseThrow(() -> new EntityNotFoundException("CommitteeActionItem " + id));
}

evaluateAll(orgId) walks active non-MANUAL KRIs and, for each, writes an audit row 'KRI_EVALUATION_SKIPPED ... Auto-fetcher not yet bound' then does `dispatched++` and returns dispatched. The return value is named 'dispatched' but counts KRIs that were explicitly NOT dispatched (auto-fetchers are unimplemented per the Javadoc 'ships the orchestration shell'). The loop body has no effect other than logging, so the variable misreports work done and the scheduler emits one audit row per KRI per tick indefinitely.

Root cause

Placeholder/shell code (auto-fetchers deferred to a 'future slice') left in a state where the counter and audit semantics imply real evaluation occurred.

Evidence / proof
Lines 180-190: `if ("MANUAL".equals(d.getSourceQueryType())) continue; audit.log("KRI_EVALUATION_SKIPPED", ... "Auto-fetcher not yet bound"); dispatched++;` then `return dispatched;`.

Real-world impact

Scheduler monitoring sees a non-zero 'dispatched' that is meaningless; the audit_log accumulates a skipped-row per KRI on every run, inflating volume and obscuring real activity.

Reproduction

Invoke evaluateAll with N active non-MANUAL KRIs; observe return == N and N audit rows even though no measurement was taken.

Resolution

Either rename the counter to 'considered'/'skipped' and downgrade per-KRI logging to debug/aggregate one summary row, or guard the whole loop behind a feature flag until auto-fetchers land. Do not count skips as dispatches.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
for (KriDefinition d : active) {
    if ("MANUAL".equals(d.getSourceQueryType())) continue;
    audit.log("KRI_EVALUATION_SKIPPED", "KriDefinition", d.getId(),
        "Auto-fetcher not yet bound ...");
    dispatched++;
}
return dispatched;
▲ After (fixed)
int skipped = 0;
for (KriDefinition d : active) {
    if ("MANUAL".equals(d.getSourceQueryType())) continue;
    skipped++;   // auto-fetchers not yet implemented
}
if (skipped > 0) log.debug("KRI auto-evaluation skipped for {} KRIs (no fetcher bound)", skipped);
return 0;   // nothing actually dispatched yet
References: CWE-561: Dead Code
LowQUAL-RC-010Frequency cycle math (period start/end/reference) re-implemented across regreporting and obligation services with magic offsets
QualityDuplication / Magic numbers▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/regreporting/service/RegReportingService.java:564-627 Effort M Risk Maintainability risk: per-frequency calendar arithmetic (DAILY/WEEKLY/MONTHLY/QUARTERLY/SEMIANNUAL/ANNUAL) is implemented in at least three independent switch statements with embedded magic numbers; a calendar rule change must be made in multiple places.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/regreporting/service/RegReportingService.java:564-627
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/compliance/obligation/service/ObligationService.java:245-259
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/compliance/obligation/service/ObligationCampaignService.java:378-402

Description

RegReportingService has three frequency switches — periodStartFor() (564-582), nextPeriodEnd() (585-610) and buildReference() (612-627) — each repeating the DAILY/WEEKLY/MONTHLY/QUARTERLY/SEMIANNUAL/ANNUAL cases with inline quarter math `(periodEnd.getMonthValue()-1)/3` and half-year `<= 6 ? ... : ...` logic. ObligationService.computeNextDueDate() (245-259) and ObligationCampaignService.periodStart()/periodEnd() (378-402) independently re-encode the same frequency vocabulary (note ObligationService uses 'SEMI_ANNUAL'/'BIENNIAL' while RegReportingService uses 'SEMIANNUAL' — divergent enum spellings for the same concept). Magic numbers (3 for quarters, 6 for half-years, default offset 5 business days at RegReportingService:190) are scattered.

Root cause

No shared Frequency value-object/enum encapsulating period boundaries and rollover; each service hand-rolls the calendar arithmetic, and even the string vocabulary drifted (SEMIANNUAL vs SEMI_ANNUAL).

Evidence / proof
RegReportingService.java:570 `int q = ((periodEnd.getMonthValue() - 1) / 3);` (also at 597-599, 621); :575 `int h = periodEnd.getMonthValue() <= 6 ? 1 : 7;`. ObligationService.java:253 `case "SEMI_ANNUAL" -> base.plusMonths(6);` vs RegReportingService.java:602 `case "SEMIANNUAL"`. RegReportingService.java:189-190 default `5` business-day offset literal.

Real-world impact

A change to how a quarter/half-year boundary is computed (or adding a frequency) requires edits in 5+ switch blocks; the SEMIANNUAL vs SEMI_ANNUAL mismatch means data created by one module won't match the other's switch (falls to default).

Reproduction

Compare the frequency switch in RegReportingService.periodStartFor / nextPeriodEnd / buildReference with ObligationService.computeNextDueDate and ObligationCampaignService.periodStart/End.

Resolution

Introduce a single ReportingFrequency enum (canonical spelling) with methods periodStart(end), nextPeriodEnd(seed), referenceSuffix(end) and named constants for quarter/half-year. Replace the hand-rolled switches; reconcile SEMIANNUAL/SEMI_ANNUAL to one token.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
case "QUARTERLY" -> { int q = ((periodEnd.getMonthValue()-1)/3); yield periodEnd.withMonth(q*3+1)...; }
// repeated in 3 methods here + 2 in obligation services; SEMIANNUAL vs SEMI_ANNUAL diverge
▲ After (fixed)
enum ReportingFrequency {
    QUARTERLY { LocalDate periodStart(LocalDate end){ ... } LocalDate next(LocalDate seed){ ... } },
    SEMIANNUAL { ... }, ...;
}
// all services call ReportingFrequency.valueOf(code).periodStart(end) etc.
References: https://refactoring.guru/replace-type-code-with-class · Magic Number smell
LowQUAL-TI-009Pervasive cause-loss in catch blocks: only ex.getMessage() logged, exception/stacktrace dropped
QualityError handling (lost root cause / no stacktrace)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/automation/TprmAutomationService.java:60-62 Effort S Risk Diagnosability: best-effort catches across CCM and integrations log `{}` with `ex.getMessage()` but never pass the Throwable, so stacktraces and chained causes are lost from logs — making production incident triage on integration failures and auto-CAPA failures hard.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/automation/TprmAutomationService.java:60-62
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/automation/TprmAutomationService.java:83-85
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/automation/TprmAutomationService.java:107-109
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ccm/service/CcmService.java:197-199
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ccm/service/CcmService.java:286-293
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ccm/service/CcmSchedulerService.java:84-89
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/crowdstrike/service/CrowdStrikeInboundService.java:125-129
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/crowdstrike/client/LiveCrowdStrikeClient.java:143-146

Description

A consistent pattern of `catch (Exception ex) { log.warn("... {}", ..., ex.getMessage()); }` (and `catch (RuntimeException ex)` variants) where the Throwable itself is not passed to the logger. Examples: TprmAutomationService auto-CAPA hooks (60,83,107), CcmService runner-guard (197) and openConsecutiveFailureIssue (291), CcmSchedulerService dispatch (85), and most integration inbound/outbound/health catches. These are legitimately best-effort (the design intentionally continues), but dropping the cause makes failures opaque.

Root cause

Logging convention used `ex.getMessage()` as a format arg instead of passing `ex` as the last SLF4J argument (which would render the stacktrace).

Evidence / proof
TprmAutomationService.java:61 `log.warn("Auto-CAPA for 4P {} failed: {}", ex.getFourthPartyName(), e.getMessage());` (no Throwable). CrowdStrikeInboundService.java:128 `log.warn("[CrowdStrike] scheduled poll failed: {}", ex.getMessage());`. CcmService.java:197 `log.warn("CCM runner threw for test {}: {}", d.getTestCode(), ex.getMessage());`.

Real-world impact

When integration polls or auto-CAPA creation fail in production, logs show only the top-level message (often null for NPE) with no stacktrace or chained cause, slowing incident triage.

Reproduction

Trigger an exception with a null/uninformative message (e.g. NPE) in any of these paths; the warn line shows 'failed: null' with no stack.

Resolution

Pass the Throwable as the final SLF4J argument so the stacktrace is rendered: `log.warn("...failed for {}", id, ex);` (keep WARN level for best-effort paths). For the CcmSchedulerService cron-parse swallow (CcmSchedulerService.isDue catch at 108-110) add at least a debug log.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
catch (Exception ex) {
    log.warn("[CrowdStrike] scheduled poll failed: {}", ex.getMessage());
}
▲ After (fixed)
catch (Exception ex) {
    log.warn("[CrowdStrike] scheduled poll failed", ex);
}
References: SLF4J: pass Throwable as last arg to log the stacktrace · Do not lose exception cause

InfoQUAL-BCMP-014Dashboard KPI-trend builds native SQL by concatenating table names and filter clauses from a config map
QualityMaintainability / Layering▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/dashboard/service/DashboardService.java:133-205 Effort L Risk getKpiTrend() assembles native SQL by string-concatenating table names, open-filters, and date columns drawn from a static METRICS map spanning 7 modules' tables. Values are from a fixed allowlist (not user input) so this is not SQL injection, but raw cross-module SQL string-building in the dashboard service is brittle and couples the dashboard to other modules' physical schemas.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/dashboard/service/DashboardService.java:135-157
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/dashboard/service/DashboardService.java:168-185
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/dashboard/service/DashboardService.java:65-72

Description

The METRICS map hard-codes 12 metric keys to (table, openFilter, extra, dateColumn) tuples referencing risk.risks, cyber.incidents, compliance.findings, privacy.data_subject_requests, privacy.data_breaches, scm.vendors, and bcm.exercises. getKpiTrend() then builds the query as `" FROM " + src.table() + " WHERE organisation_id = :org AND is_deleted = 0" + src.openFilter() + src.extra()` and `"SELECT " + dateCol + base + ...`. getStats() similarly issues a hand-written native COUNT against compliance.findings. The metric key is lower-cased and defaulted to 'risks', and all interpolated fragments come from the constant map, so there is no injection vector — but the dashboard service now embeds knowledge of seven other modules' table names, columns, and status vocabularies.

Root cause

Trend logic implemented generically via SQL templating instead of per-module query methods, to avoid writing one finder per metric.

Evidence / proof
DashboardService.java:169-170 string-concatenates table/filter; :173 and :182 concatenate dateCol; the METRICS map (135-157) lists physical schema.table names for 7 modules; getStats() :65-72 hand-writes native SQL for overdue findings.

Real-world impact

If any of those modules rename a table, status value, or the is_deleted/created_at columns, the dashboard breaks at runtime with no compile-time signal. The dashboard becomes a hidden consumer of every module's schema, undermining module boundaries. The string-concat style is also a latent injection footgun if a future edit lets any fragment come from request input.

Reproduction

Rename e.g. scm.vendors or its status column; the 'vendors' KPI trend throws at runtime; nothing in dashboard compiles-against the change.

Resolution

Prefer per-module repository/query methods (or read-model views owned by each module) that the dashboard calls, returning the weekly buckets, rather than templating physical SQL in the dashboard layer. At minimum, centralise the table/column metadata behind module-provided constants and add an integration test per metric so schema drift is caught. Keep all interpolated fragments compile-time constants (never request-derived).

▼ Before (vulnerable)
String base = " FROM " + src.table() + " WHERE organisation_id = :org AND is_deleted = 0" + src.openFilter() + src.extra();
em.createNativeQuery("SELECT " + dateCol + base + " AND " + dateCol + " >= :start")
▲ After (fixed)
// Each module exposes a TrendSource bean returning its open-item timestamps:
//   interface TrendSource { String metricKey(); List<LocalDateTime> openSince(Long org, LocalDateTime from); }
// DashboardService injects List<TrendSource>, buckets in Java — no cross-module SQL strings.
References: https://docs.spring.io/spring-data/jpa/reference/jpa/query-methods.html

Phase 3 — Stress / Performance

28 findings — 11 High · 13 Medium · 3 Low · 1 Info
HighPERF-FE-001Heaviest module pages are statically (eagerly) imported into the entry bundle, so /login downloads 8 unrelated workspace pages (~7,000 LOC)
✓ VerifiedPerformanceBundle size / code splitting▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Confirmed at tss-grc-ui-v2/src/App.tsx lines 8-18: LoginPage, DashboardPage, SettingsPage, RiskRegisterPage, CyberPage, BcmWorkspacePage, PrivacyPage, CompliancePage, TprmPage, IncidentsPage, EvidencePage are all statically (eagerly) imported, while the rest of the ~300 module pages use React.lazy(). Because LoginPage shares the entry chunk with these 10 other heavy workspace pages, /login pulls them all on first paint. The comment 'Critical-path pages stay eager' acknowledges the intent, but login does not need risk/cyber/bcm/privacy/compliance/tprm/incidents/evidence workspaces. This is a real bundle-bloat / TTI regression on the unauthenticated entry route. High is appropriate for a perf finding; it is a performance issue, not a correctness/security bug, so not Critical.
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/App.tsx:8-18,167 Effort S Risk High user-facing impact: the public, unauthenticated /login route (Lighthouse Performance 38) is forced to parse/execute the four single largest page modules in the app (Compliance 337 KiB, Scm 289 KiB, Cyber 287 KiB, Tprm 258 KiB transferred) plus four more, none of which /login can navigate to. Affects every first visit and every logged-out user. Not a security issue; pure load-time cost.
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/App.tsx:8-18
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/App.tsx:167
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/compliance/CompliancePage.tsx:1-1302
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/scm/ScmPage.tsx:1-1241
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/cyber/CyberPage.tsx:1-1164
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/tprm/TprmPage.tsx:1-1110

Description

App.tsx does use route-level code splitting for the vast majority of routes: 295 pages are wrapped in React.lazy() and there are 323 <Route> elements, all under a single <Suspense>. The problem is the deliberate exception. Lines 8-18 statically import 11 pages, and line 167 statically imports ScmPage, with the comment '// Critical-path pages (sidebar landings + login + dashboard) stay eager.' These 12 static imports are NOT all critical-path: LoginPage (119 LOC) and DashboardPage are reasonable to keep eager, but the eager set also pulls in the eight single heaviest page modules in the codebase — CompliancePage (1,302 LOC), ScmPage (1,241), CyberPage (1,164), TprmPage (1,110), RiskRegisterPage (842), EvidencePage (721), IncidentsPage (645) and PrivacyPage (530). Because they are static `import { X } from './pages/...'` (not lazy()), Rollup/Vite places them in the same entry chunk as App.tsx. A user sitting on /login (who cannot reach any of those routes without authenticating) downloads, parses and executes all of them.

Root cause

A static ES import is a hard dependency edge: the bundler must include the module in whatever chunk reaches it. App.tsx is the entry, so every `import { CompliancePage } from './pages/compliance/CompliancePage'` (line 15) forces CompliancePage and its entire transitive import graph into the initial chunk. The 'sidebar landings stay eager' decision conflated 'frequently visited after login' with 'must be in the entry bundle', and applied it to the largest pages instead of the smallest.

Evidence / proof
App.tsx:8-18 + 167 — twelve `import { ... } from './pages/...'` statements (LoginPage, DashboardPage, SettingsPage, RiskRegisterPage, CyberPage, BcmWorkspacePage, PrivacyPage, CompliancePage, TprmPage, IncidentsPage, EvidencePage, ScmPage). `grep -c "lazy(()" App.tsx` = 295 lazy pages vs 12 eager. LOC of the eager module pages: CompliancePage 1302, ScmPage 1241, CyberPage 1164, TprmPage 1110, RiskRegisterPage 842, EvidencePage 721, IncidentsPage 645, PrivacyPage 530 = ~7,555 LOC forced onto /login. Lighthouse total-byte-weight items confirm these four arrive on the /login load: CompliancePage 337,307 B, ScmPage 289,426 B, CyberPage 286,941 B, TprmPage 258,133 B; App.tsx itself 463,783 B (dev-server unbundled figures).

Real-world impact

Inflated entry chunk → larger FCP/LCP/TTI and more main-thread parse/compile work on the most-hit route in the product. unused-javascript audit attributes large wasted bytes specifically to these eager pages on /login: CompliancePage 108,588 B wasted, TprmPage 95,159 B, ScmPage 93,529 B, CyberPage 82,234 B, EvidencePage 63,525 B, RiskRegisterPage 56,072 B — all of it dead weight for an unauthenticated visitor.

Reproduction

1) Build: `npm run build` in tss-grc-ui-v2. 2) Inspect dist/assets — the entry chunk includes Compliance/Scm/Cyber/Tprm page code (search the entry chunk for strings unique to those pages). 3) Or run Lighthouse against /login (audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json): Performance 38, and unused-javascript lists CompliancePage/TprmPage/ScmPage/CyberPage as top wasted-bytes items on a route that never renders them.

Resolution

Convert the heavy module pages to React.lazy() like the other 295 pages. Keep eager ONLY LoginPage (and optionally DashboardPage as the post-login landing). Everything reachable solely behind the authenticated shell — Compliance, Scm, Cyber, Tprm, Risk, Privacy, Incidents, Evidence, Bcm — should be lazy so its chunk loads on navigation, not on /login. Optionally add a route-prefetch on hover/idle for the sidebar links to hide the lazy latency.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// App.tsx lines 11-18, 167 (eager)
import { RiskRegisterPage } from './pages/risk/RiskRegisterPage';
import { CyberPage } from './pages/cyber/CyberPage';
import { BcmWorkspacePage } from './pages/bcm/BcmWorkspacePage';
import { PrivacyPage } from './pages/privacy/PrivacyPage';
import { CompliancePage } from './pages/compliance/CompliancePage';
import { TprmPage } from './pages/tprm/TprmPage';
import { IncidentsPage } from './pages/incidents/IncidentsPage';
import { EvidencePage } from './pages/evidence/EvidencePage';
// ...
import { ScmPage } from './pages/scm/ScmPage';
▲ After (fixed)
// Keep only LoginPage (+ DashboardPage) eager; lazy-load the module pages.
import { LoginPage } from './pages/LoginPage';
import { DashboardPage } from './pages/DashboardPage';
const RiskRegisterPage = lazy(() => import('./pages/risk/RiskRegisterPage').then(m => ({ default: m.RiskRegisterPage })));
const CyberPage       = lazy(() => import('./pages/cyber/CyberPage').then(m => ({ default: m.CyberPage })));
const CompliancePage  = lazy(() => import('./pages/compliance/CompliancePage').then(m => ({ default: m.CompliancePage })));
const TprmPage        = lazy(() => import('./pages/tprm/TprmPage').then(m => ({ default: m.TprmPage })));
const ScmPage         = lazy(() => import('./pages/scm/ScmPage').then(m => ({ default: m.ScmPage })));
const PrivacyPage     = lazy(() => import('./pages/privacy/PrivacyPage').then(m => ({ default: m.PrivacyPage })));
const IncidentsPage   = lazy(() => import('./pages/incidents/IncidentsPage').then(m => ({ default: m.IncidentsPage })));
const EvidencePage    = lazy(() => import('./pages/evidence/EvidencePage').then(m => ({ default: m.EvidencePage })));
const BcmWorkspacePage = lazy(() => import('./pages/bcm/BcmWorkspacePage').then(m => ({ default: m.BcmWorkspacePage })));
