HighPERF-FE-002Both full translation dictionaries (Arabic 418 KB + English 325 KB source) are statically imported on the critical path; only one language is ever active
✓ VerifiedPerformanceBundle size / i18n▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Confirmed at tss-grc-ui-v2/src/lib/i18n.tsx lines 2-3: both dictionaries are statically imported (import { en } from '../translations/en'; import { ar } from '../translations/ar';) and assembled eagerly into the dictionaries map at line 24 inside the always-mounted I18nProvider. Verified on disk: ar.ts = 417,903 bytes (6,061 lines), en.ts = 325,194 bytes (6,081 lines). Only one language is ever active (lang state, line 27), yet both ~408KB+318KB source dictionaries land on the critical path of the entry bundle. Real, avoidable bundle cost; correct as High.
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/lib/i18n.tsx:2-3 Effort M Risk High first-load cost on every route including /login: ~1.94 MiB of translation JS arrives on the dev-server /login load (ar.ts 1,076,314 B + en.ts 860,108 B transferred). i18n.tsx is imported by App.tsx and LoginPage, so this is unavoidable on the entry path. The user only ever uses one language at a time, so roughly half is pure waste. No security impact.
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/lib/i18n.tsx:2-3
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/lib/i18n.tsx:24
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/ar.ts:1-6061
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:1-6081

Description

lib/i18n.tsx statically imports both dictionaries at module top: `import { en } from '../translations/en'` and `import { ar } from '../translations/ar'` (lines 2-3), then builds a static map `const dictionaries: Record<Lang, Dictionary> = { en, ar }` (line 24). en.ts is 6,081 lines / 325,194 bytes of source and ar.ts is 6,061 lines / 417,903 bytes of source. Because i18n.tsx is imported by App.tsx (line 3) and by LoginPage (line 4), both dictionaries are pulled into the initial bundle regardless of which language the user has selected. The default language is Arabic (i18n.tsx selects 'ar' unless localStorage says 'en'), so an Arabic user still downloads the entire English dictionary, and vice-versa.

Root cause

Eager static import of both locale modules plus a synchronous lookup map. There is no dynamic import per locale and no split of the dictionary by feature/route. The dictionaries are flat key/value maps loaded whole.

Evidence / proof
i18n.tsx:2 `import { en } from '../translations/en';`, i18n.tsx:3 `import { ar } from '../translations/ar';`, i18n.tsx:24 `const dictionaries: Record<Lang, Dictionary> = { en: en as Dictionary, ar: ar as Dictionary };`. File sizes via wc: translations/en.ts = 6081 lines / 325,194 B; translations/ar.ts = 6061 lines / 417,903 B. Lighthouse total-byte-weight on /login lists src/translations/ar.ts = 1,076,314 B (transferred, dev) as the #2 heaviest resource and src/translations/en.ts = 860,108 B as #4.

Real-world impact

~1.9 MiB of JS on every page including the login screen, of which roughly half (the inactive language) is never used in a given session. Increases parse/compile time and entry-chunk size, directly worsening FCP/LCP on /login.

Reproduction

1) `wc -c tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/*.ts` → en 325 KB + ar 418 KB source. 2) Build and inspect the entry chunk — both en and ar key/value tables are present. 3) Lighthouse /login report total-byte-weight: ar.ts and en.ts are the #2 and #4 heaviest resources, both loaded before any language switch.

Resolution

Lazy-load the active dictionary with dynamic import keyed on the selected language, so only one locale ships initially and the other is fetched on language switch. Replace the static map with `await import(`../translations/${lang}.ts`)` inside an effect (or a loader that suspends), keeping the current dictionary in state. This roughly halves the i18n payload on first load and removes ~325-418 KB from the entry bundle.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
import { en } from '../translations/en';
import { ar } from '../translations/ar';
// ...
const dictionaries: Record<Lang, Dictionary> = { en: en as Dictionary, ar: ar as Dictionary };

export function I18nProvider({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const [lang, setLangState] = useState<Lang>(/* ... */);
  const t = useCallback((key, fallback) => dictionaries[lang][key] ?? fallback ?? key, [lang]);
▲ After (fixed)
const loaders: Record<Lang, () => Promise<Dictionary>> = {
  en: () => import('../translations/en').then(m => m.en as Dictionary),
  ar: () => import('../translations/ar').then(m => m.ar as Dictionary),
};

export function I18nProvider({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
  const [lang, setLangState] = useState<Lang>(/* ... */);
  const [dict, setDict] = useState<Dictionary>({});
  useEffect(() => { let live = true; loaders[lang]().then(d => { if (live) setDict(d); }); return () => { live = false; }; }, [lang]);
  const t = useCallback((key, fallback) => dict[key] ?? fallback ?? key, [dict]);
References: https://vitejs.dev/guide/features.html#dynamic-import · https://web.dev/articles/reduce-javascript-payloads-with-code-splitting
HighPERF-IO-001Outbound integration HTTP calls execute inside @Transactional methods, holding a Hikari DB connection across the remote round-trip
✓ VerifiedPerformanceConnection pool exhaustion / blocking I/O under transaction▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Confirmed at ServiceNowOutboundService.java: push() is annotated @Transactional (line 83) and calls client.createIncident(enriched) (line 109) — a remote ServiceNow HTTP round-trip — then recordExternalLink() persists, all inside the same transaction. The injected client is LiveServiceNowClient, which uses a blocking Spring RestClient (line 46) with an exponential-backoff RETRY loop on 5xx/connection errors (class javadoc lines 35-37). So the Hikari DB connection is held open across the remote call AND its retries. The pushCyberIncident/pushFinding/pushCapaTask/pushComplianceGap facades (lines 59-77) are also @Transactional and route through pushGeneric->createIncident, so the pattern is module-wide. Classic connection-pool-exhaustion-under-load anti-pattern. Caveat: only active when servicenow.mode=LIVE and enabled=true (in dev the stub/disabled path is a no-op), but the finding targets the production code path; High is correct.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/servicenow/service/ServiceNowOutboundService.java:83-114 Effort M Risk High — under a remote-system slowdown (ServiceNow/Splunk/CrowdStrike/Tenable degraded but not down), each in-flight push/poll pins one of only 20 (base) / 10 (dev) Hikari connections for the full remote latency. A burst of integration calls during a security incident (exactly when these adapters fire hardest) can drain the pool and stall ALL unrelated DB traffic platform-wide. Availability impact, not confidentiality/integrity.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/servicenow/service/ServiceNowOutboundService.java:83-114
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/splunk/service/SplunkOutboundService.java:164-204
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/crowdstrike/service/CrowdStrikeOutboundService.java:70-83
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/tenable/service/TenableOutboundService.java:89-134

Description

All four outbound integration services declare their public entry-point methods @Transactional and then invoke a synchronous, blocking remote HTTP client from inside that transaction. Spring opens (or borrows) a JDBC connection for the transaction at method entry and does not release it until the method returns. Because the remote HTTP call sits inside that boundary, the borrowed Hikari connection stays checked out for the ENTIRE network round-trip plus all in-thread retry sleeps. ServiceNowOutboundService.push() (line 83 @Transactional) calls client.createIncident() at line 109; SplunkOutboundService.push() (line 164 @Transactional) calls client.pushEvent() at line 176; CrowdStrikeOutboundService.containHost()/liftContainment()/hideHost() (lines 70/75/80 @Transactional) call client.* via runAction()->call.get() at line 111; TenableOutboundService.recastSeverity()/acceptRisk()/removeRecast() (lines 89/112/127 @Transactional) call client.* via runAction()->call.get() at line 162. The actual DB write (recordExternalLink / persistAuditRow / persistActionLog / persistRecastLog) is a sub-millisecond operation; the seconds-to-minutes are spent waiting on the remote socket while needlessly holding the connection.

Root cause

The @Transactional boundary is drawn around the whole 'call remote system then persist outcome' unit of work instead of only around the persistence. There is no architectural separation between the I/O-bound remote call and the DB-bound audit write, so the connection is borrowed before the remote call begins and returned only after it completes.

Evidence / proof
ServiceNowOutboundService.java:83-84 '@Transactional public ServiceNowIncidentResponse push(...)' then line 109 'ServiceNowIncidentResponse resp = client.createIncident(enriched);' (blocking) then line 110 'recordExternalLink(enriched, resp);' (the only DB work). Same shape in SplunkOutboundService.java:164 @Transactional / line 176 'resp = client.pushEvent(request);'. CrowdStrikeOutboundService.java:70 @Transactional / line 111 'resp = call.get();'. TenableOutboundService.java:89 @Transactional / line 162 'resp = call.get();'. Pool ceiling: application.yml:22 'maximum-pool-size: 20'; application-dev.yml:29 'maximum-pool-size: 10'.

Real-world impact

With base maximum-pool-size=20, twenty concurrent slow integration pushes saturate the entire pool. Any unrelated request needing the DB then waits up to connection-timeout=30000ms (application.yml:24) and fails with a connection-timeout exception — a platform-wide stall triggered by a single sluggish third party. The integrations most likely to fire in bursts (CrowdStrike containment, Splunk SOC event push, ServiceNow incident creation) are exactly the ones invoked during an active security incident, so the failure mode peaks when the platform is needed most.

Reproduction

1) Flip any adapter to LIVE (e.g. grc.integrations.servicenow.mode=LIVE) pointing at an endpoint that delays its response (e.g. a mock returning after 20s). 2) Fire 20 concurrent POST /api/v1/integrations/servicenow/test-push requests. 3) Observe all 20 Hikari connections checked out (GrcHikariPool active=20) for ~20s. 4) Concurrently issue any normal DB-backed request (e.g. GET /api/v1/risk/risks) — it blocks for up to 30s then throws a HikariPool connection-timeout. The leak-detection-threshold=60000 (application.yml:26) will also log 'Connection leak detection' warnings once a single retry chain exceeds 60s.

Resolution

Decouple the remote call from the transaction. Perform the blocking HTTP call OUTSIDE any @Transactional scope, then open a short, separate transaction only to persist the audit/external-link row. Concretely: remove @Transactional from the public push/poll methods; do the client.* call with no connection borrowed; then call a small @Transactional helper (e.g. an injected self-proxy method or a dedicated *PersistenceService.recordOutcome(...)) that writes the row and returns immediately. Better still, move the entire push off the request thread via @Async (the app already declares @EnableAsync on GrcApplication) or an outbox table drained by a worker, so request threads never block on third-party latency at all.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@Transactional
public ServiceNowIncidentResponse push(ServiceNowIncidentRequest request) {
    ...
    ServiceNowIncidentResponse resp = client.createIncident(enriched); // blocking HTTP under tx
    recordExternalLink(enriched, resp);                                 // the only DB work
    return resp;
}
▲ After (fixed)
// No @Transactional here — the remote call must not hold a DB connection.
public ServiceNowIncidentResponse push(ServiceNowIncidentRequest request) {
    ...
    ServiceNowIncidentResponse resp = client.createIncident(enriched); // blocking HTTP, NO connection borrowed
    persistence.recordExternalLink(enriched, resp);                    // short, separate tx
    return resp;
}

@Service
class ServiceNowPersistence {
    @Transactional
    public void recordExternalLink(ServiceNowIncidentRequest req, ServiceNowIncidentResponse resp) { /* DB only */ }
}
References: https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP/wiki/About-Pool-Sizing · https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/data-access/transaction/declarative/annotations.html · https://vladmihalcea.com/spring-transaction-best-practices/
HighPERF-IO-002Scheduled and manual integration polls hold one DB connection across the remote poll PLUS the entire per-finding ingest loop
✓ VerifiedPerformanceLong-lived transaction / connection hold across remote I/O + batch loop▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Confirmed at TenableInboundService.java: pollFindings() is @Transactional (line 144) and (a) makes the remote poll via client.pollFindings() (line 158) and then (b) iterates the entire returned batch (lines 168-183), running a dedupe lookup query per finding (findByOrganisationIdAndTenableAssetUuidAndTenablePluginId, lines 171-172) and calling ingestOne() which save()s a Vulnerability row per item (line 208) — all inside the one transaction. scheduledPoll() (line 120) invokes the same transactional method. So a single DB connection is held across the remote poll plus the full per-finding ingest loop, exactly as described. The remote client also follows the same retry harness as ServiceNow (per QUAL-TI-002). Connection-hold-across-remote-IO + batch loop is real; High is correct. Same LIVE/enabled caveat applies but does not change the verdict.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/tenable/service/TenableInboundService.java:144-185 Effort M Risk High — the @Transactional poll methods borrow a connection, make a multi-call blocking HTTP fetch (CrowdStrike does TWO sequential HTTP round-trips, with retries), then iterate the whole returned batch writing 3 rows per finding plus an audit row and a domain event, all inside the same transaction. One slow Tenable/Falcon endpoint or a large batch holds a scarce connection for the full duration and produces an oversized transaction that bloats the SQL Server Express log.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/tenable/service/TenableInboundService.java:144-185
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/crowdstrike/service/CrowdStrikeInboundService.java:142-181
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/crowdstrike/client/LiveCrowdStrikeClient.java:79-115

Description

TenableInboundService.pollFindings() (line 144 @Transactional) calls the blocking client.pollFindings() at line 158 BEFORE writing anything, then loops the returned batch calling ingestOne() (line 176) which performs three saves (vulnerabilities.save, findingLogRepo.save, linkRepo.save) plus audit.log and publisher.publishEvent per finding. The same shape is in CrowdStrikeInboundService.pollDetections() (line 142 @Transactional, blocking client.pollDetections() at line 156, ingestOne() per detection at line 172). CrowdStrike's poll is doubly expensive on I/O: LiveCrowdStrikeClient.pollDetections() (lines 79-115) makes TWO sequential remote calls — the ids query (line 82) then the bulk summaries fetch (line 98) — each wrapped in its own retry loop, all while the transaction's DB connection is held. The connection is checked out for: remote_latency + (retries x backoff) + N x (3 inserts + audit + event publish).

Root cause

The remote fetch and the entire ingest batch share a single transactional/connection scope. The poll method opens the transaction, the connection is borrowed immediately, and it is not returned until the last finding in the batch is persisted — including the time spent on the remote HTTP fetch that does not need a DB connection at all.

Evidence / proof
TenableInboundService.java:144 '@Transactional public int pollFindings()'; line 158 'batch = client.pollFindings();' (blocking, retries inside LiveTenableClient); lines 168-183 per-finding loop calling ingestOne() (lines 189-253: three .save() calls + audit.log + publishEvent). CrowdStrikeInboundService.java:142 '@Transactional public int pollDetections()'; line 156 'batch = client.pollDetections();'. LiveCrowdStrikeClient.java:81-106 two sequential doWithRetryOn5xx() HTTP calls. Both polls are also driven by @Scheduled (TenableInboundService.java:119 fixedDelay 900s; CrowdStrikeInboundService.java:117 fixedDelay 60s) under @EnableScheduling (GrcApplication.java:24).

Real-world impact

Each poll cycle consumes a pool connection for the full remote+ingest duration. With CrowdStrike polling every 60s and Tenable every 900s on a 10-connection dev pool (20 in base), a slow EDR/VM endpoint during heavy DB activity can tip the pool toward exhaustion. The long-running transaction also keeps locks and an open log section on SQL Server Express, contributing to the 10 GB Express size ceiling that the platform already monitors (application.yml:258-263 db-size health thresholds).

Reproduction

1) Enable Tenable/CrowdStrike LIVE + pollingEnabled=true against a mock returning a 500-finding batch after a 10s delay. 2) Watch GrcHikariPool active-connection metric (actuator /metrics) jump by one and stay elevated for remote_delay + ingest_time. 3) Manually trigger pollFindings() via the controller concurrently with the scheduled loop and N concurrent app requests; observe connection-acquisition latency on unrelated endpoints climb. 4) Inspect the SQL Server transaction log growth during a large ingest — a single transaction spans the whole batch.

Resolution

Fetch the remote batch with NO transaction open (move client.poll*() out of the @Transactional method), then persist findings in short, per-finding (or small-chunk) transactions so each borrows and returns a connection quickly. This caps connection-hold time at a single DB write, lets other work interleave, and keeps SQL Server transactions small. Pattern: pollOnce() (no @Transactional) -> List<Dto> = client.poll(); for (dto : batch) persistence.ingestOne(orgId, dto) where ingestOne is @Transactional(propagation=REQUIRES_NEW) on a separate bean.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
@Transactional
public int pollFindings() {
    ...
    batch = client.pollFindings();          // blocking HTTP while connection is held
    for (TenableFindingDto d : batch) {
        ingestOne(orgId, d);                 // 3 inserts + audit + event, same tx
    }
    return ingested;
}
▲ After (fixed)
// No @Transactional — remote fetch must not hold a connection.
public int pollFindings() {
    ...
    List<TenableFindingDto> batch = client.pollFindings();   // no connection borrowed
    int ingested = 0;
    for (TenableFindingDto d : batch) {
        ingested += persistence.ingestOne(orgId, d) ? 1 : 0;  // short, separate tx each
    }
    return ingested;
}

@Service
class TenableIngestPersistence {
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public boolean ingestOne(Long orgId, TenableFindingDto d) { /* DB only */ }
}
References: https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/data-access/transaction.html · https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP/wiki/About-Pool-Sizing · https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/logs/the-transaction-log-sql-server
HighPERF-IX-00174 multi-tenant tables carry organisation_id but have no supporting index — every org-scoped query is a full clustered-index scan
✓ VerifiedPerformanceDatabase Indexing / Multi-Tenancy▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Confirmed at V3__compliance_module.sql lines 15-108: tables compliance.controls, compliance.assessments and compliance.findings each declare organisation_id BIGINT NOT NULL (lines 17, 51, 83) but create only a CLUSTERED PRIMARY KEY on id and a single FK constraint (FK_findings_assessment) — no nonclustered index on organisation_id on any of the three. Since every repository query is org-scoped (findBy*OrganisationId per CLAUDE.md multi-tenancy rules), each becomes a full clustered-index scan filtered by organisation_id. Grep confirms organisation_id appears in 189 migration files (~2,467 occurrences) while CREATE INDEX appears in only ~126 files, and the early core tables (V3 here) have none — supporting the systemic 'many multi-tenant tables lack the supporting index' claim. The exact '74 tables' count is a quantitative assertion I could not fully enumerate, but the cited file/lines clearly demonstrate the pattern and the missing index. High is appropriate for a query-performance/scalability issue.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V3__compliance_module.sql:15-108 Effort L Risk High operational risk: the platform's universal access pattern (1,377 repository methods filter by organisation_id) hits 74 tables whose only index is the clustered PK on id. As soon as any tenant table grows past a few thousand rows, every list/search/dashboard read degrades to an O(N) scan with a residual organisation_id predicate, and degradation compounds under multi-tenant concurrency. Not a confidentiality issue, hence not CVSS-scored, but a direct throughput/latency and cost driver in production.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V3__compliance_module.sql:15-108
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V7__tprm_module.sql:18-46
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V4__incident_module.sql:1-60
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V1__core_schemas.sql:1178-1208
setup_cyber_db.py:79-320
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/asm/repository/AttackSurfaceAssetRepository.java:19-27

Description

The platform is multi-tenant by design: TenantContext puts organisation_id on every thread and CLAUDE.md mandates 'every repository query must filter by organisation_id'. Static analysis of the applied Flyway DDL (V1__core_schemas.sql .. V224__*, the set wired into prod via application-prod.yml `locations: classpath:db/migration/sqlserver`) shows 303 tables declare an org_id/organisation_id column, but only 230 have any index that references that column. That leaves 74 tenant tables (24%) with no organisation_id index at all; 46 of those 74 have no secondary index whatsoever (clustered PK on `id` only). The missing-index tables span every core module: bcm (14), cyber (11), privacy (6), risk (6), scm (6), workflow (4), compliance (3), platform (3), reporting (3), tprm (3), plus iam, ndi, kb, admin, aml and the *_lc lifecycle schemas. Concretely, canonical hot tables are affected: compliance.controls / compliance.assessments / compliance.findings, tprm.vendors, cyber.cyber_assets / cyber.vulnerabilities / cyber.cyber_incidents, privacy.processing_activities / privacy.data_subject_requests / privacy.consents, iam.users, platform.business_units, platform.notifications, and reporting.report_executions.

Root cause

Index creation was treated as optional and applied inconsistently per migration rather than as a schema-wide standard. The early Sprint-1/Sprint-2 module migrations (V3 compliance, V4 incident, V7 tprm) and the dev Python bootstrap (setup_cyber_db.py, setup_bcm_db.py) create tables with only a clustered PK and never add an organisation_id index. SQL Server does not auto-create any index for a NOT NULL FK/tenant column, so the omission is silent. There is no convention or lint that requires a leading-organisation_id index for every tenant table.

Evidence / proof
Parser over all V*.sql migrations: 344 distinct CREATE TABLE; 303 declare a tenant column; only 230 have an index referencing org_id/organisation_id => 74 tenant tables with NO org index, 46 with NO secondary index at all. Example DDL — compliance.assessments (V3 lines 49-73): `organisation_id BIGINT NOT NULL, ... status NVARCHAR(50) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PLANNED', ... CONSTRAINT PK_assessments PRIMARY KEY CLUSTERED (id ASC)` and the file contains ZERO CREATE INDEX statements (grep -c CREATE INDEX V3 = 0). Repository side: `grep findByOrganisationId` = 1,377 hits; the single most common method is findByIdAndOrganisationId (313 declarations), then findByOrganisationId (141) and findByOrganisationIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc (120).

Real-world impact

On the curated dev DB (~450 rows) the scans are invisible, but production tenants accumulate registers (risks, assessments, vulnerabilities, DSRs, audit findings) into the thousands-to-millions of rows. Every list view, dashboard widget, export, and pagination query on these 74 tables performs a clustered-index scan reading the entire table and discarding rows for other tenants. Under multi-tenant concurrency this multiplies buffer-pool pressure and lock/latch contention, producing slow dashboards, export timeouts, and a noisy-neighbour effect where one large tenant degrades all tenants on the shared SQL Server 2019 Express instance (which itself caps at 1 GB buffer pool / 10 GB per DB, amplifying scan cost).

Reproduction

1) Pick any affected table, e.g. compliance.assessments. 2) Seed e.g. 100k rows across 3 org_ids. 3) Run `SET STATISTICS IO ON; SELECT * FROM compliance.assessments WHERE organisation_id = 1 AND is_deleted = 0 ORDER BY created_at DESC;` and inspect the actual execution plan: it shows a Clustered Index Scan on PK_assessments with a residual predicate on organisation_id (logical reads ~= total pages of the table), not a seek. 4) Repeat for cyber.vulnerabilities, tprm.vendors, iam.users — same scan. 5) Confirm in the DB: `SELECT t.name FROM sys.tables t WHERE EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM sys.columns c WHERE c.object_id=t.object_id AND c.name IN ('organisation_id','org_id')) AND NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM sys.index_columns ic JOIN sys.columns c2 ON ic.object_id=c2.object_id AND ic.column_id=c2.column_id WHERE ic.object_id=t.object_id AND ic.key_ordinal=1 AND c2.name IN ('organisation_id','org_id'));`

Resolution

Adopt a schema-wide standard: every tenant table gets a nonclustered index with organisation_id as the leading key, extended with is_deleted (filtered `WHERE is_deleted = 0`) and the columns most queries sort/filter on (status, created_at). Backfill the 74 missing tables in a new Flyway migration so it applies in prod. For tables soft-deleted via @Where, use a filtered index to keep it small. Prioritise by row growth: risk.*, cyber.*, compliance.*, privacy.*, tprm.vendors, iam.users, platform.notifications.

    id              BIGINT IDENTITY(1,1) NOT NULL,
    organisation_id BIGINT               NOT NULL,
    framework       NVARCHAR(100)        NOT NULL,
    status          NVARCHAR(50)         NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PLANNED',
    ...
    CONSTRAINT PK_assessments PRIMARY KEY CLUSTERED (id ASC)
);
-- (no CREATE INDEX anywhere in this file)
▲ After (fixed)
-- New Flyway migration, e.g. V225__backfill_tenant_org_indexes.sql
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_assessments_org_status
    ON compliance.assessments (organisation_id, status)
    WHERE is_deleted = 0
    INCLUDE (framework, score, assessment_date);
GO
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_findings_org_status
    ON compliance.findings (organisation_id, status, severity)
    WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_tprm_vendors_org_status
    ON tprm.vendors (organisation_id, status)
    WHERE is_deleted = 0
    INCLUDE (vendor_name, risk_rating);
GO
-- ... repeat for the remaining 71 tenant tables, leading on organisation_id

HighPERF-IX-003iam.users has no index beyond the clustered PK — username/email login lookups and per-request principal resolution scan the user table; no unique constraint on username/email
✓ VerifiedPerformanceDatabase Indexing / Authentication Hot Path▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Verified V1__core_schemas.sql lines 1178-1209: iam.users CREATE TABLE declares only CONSTRAINT pk_users PRIMARY KEY ([id]) — no index on [username] or [email], and no UNIQUE constraint on either. A grep across the entire db/migration/sqlserver tree finds no CREATE INDEX / UNIQUE for iam.users in any migration. Username/email are the login lookup keys (V2 seed and auth path query by username), so every login and per-request principal resolution does a clustered-index scan, and there is no DB-level guard against duplicate usernames/emails. Real and on the authentication hot path. High is appropriate (performance/integrity, not a direct security exploit).
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V1__core_schemas.sql:1178-1209 Effort S Risk High: iam.users is on the critical path of every authentication and every JWT-authenticated request (principal lookup). With only PK_users on id, the canonical 'find user by username' login query scans the whole table. The missing UNIQUE on (organisation_id, username)/(email) is also a data-integrity gap (duplicate usernames are physically possible) layered on top of the performance problem.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V1__core_schemas.sql:1178-1209

Description

iam.users is created in V1__core_schemas.sql (lines 1178-1209) with username, email, password_hash and organisation_id columns and only `CONSTRAINT pk_users PRIMARY KEY (id)`. There is no index on username, no index on email, no unique constraint on either, and no organisation_id index — confirmed by grepping the entire migration set for any index referencing iam.users (zero matches). The authentication flow looks up users by username (and resolves the principal by id on every request via the JWT filter); the by-username lookup has no supporting index and degrades to a scan.

Root cause

The table was hand-written in the consolidated V1 core-schema file without the supporting indexes/unique constraints. A separate, never-applied file (db/sqlserver/indexes/01-shared-indexes.sql lines 40-55) defines IX_users_org and IX_users_active_login INCLUDE(username, email, password_hash, ...), showing the indexes were designed but never reached the applied schema (see PERF-IX-006).

Evidence / proof
V1 lines 1178-1208: only `CONSTRAINT [pk_users] PRIMARY KEY ([id])`; no UNIQUE/INDEX on username or email. `grep -rniE 'INDEX.*iam\.users|ON +iam\.users|UNIQUE.*username' db/migration/sqlserver/` returns no rows. The orphaned design file db/sqlserver/indexes/01-shared-indexes.sql:51-55 shows the intended `IX_users_active_login ON iam.users (is_active, is_locked) ... INCLUDE (username, email, password_hash, org_id, bu_id)`.

Real-world impact

Login throughput is bounded by a full scan of iam.users per attempt — and because dev disables lockout (99 attempts/min) and prod relies on this table, credential-stuffing or simple growth (thousands of users across tenants) turns auth into a hotspot. The absence of a UNIQUE on (organisation_id, username) and on email also permits duplicate accounts, which can corrupt login resolution.

Reproduction

1) `SELECT name, type_desc FROM sys.indexes WHERE object_id = OBJECT_ID('iam.users');` returns only the clustered PK. 2) `SELECT * FROM iam.users WHERE username = 'admin' AND is_deleted = 0;` shows a Clustered Index Scan in the actual plan. 3) `INSERT` two rows with the same username succeeds (no unique constraint).

Resolution

Add a unique index on (organisation_id, username) and a unique index on email (filtered on is_deleted=0), which simultaneously fixes the lookup performance and enforces uniqueness. Add a covering index for the login path including password_hash/is_active/is_locked.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
CREATE TABLE iam.users (
    [id] BIGINT IDENTITY(1,1) NOT NULL,
    [organisation_id] BIGINT NOT NULL,
    [username] NVARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    [email] NVARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    [password_hash] NVARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    [is_active] BIT NOT NULL DEFAULT ((1)),
    [is_locked] BIT NOT NULL DEFAULT ((0)),
    ...
    CONSTRAINT [pk_users] PRIMARY KEY ([id])
);
-- no index/unique on username, email, or organisation_id
▲ After (fixed)
-- backfill migration
CREATE UNIQUE NONCLUSTERED INDEX UX_users_org_username
    ON iam.users (organisation_id, username) WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO
CREATE UNIQUE NONCLUSTERED INDEX UX_users_email
    ON iam.users (email) WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_users_login
    ON iam.users (username, is_deleted)
    INCLUDE (password_hash, is_active, is_locked, organisation_id);
GO

HighPERF-NQ-001Risk register list endpoint issues 2N+1 queries (category + owner per row) and triggers the EAGER User graph per owner
✓ VerifiedPerformanceN+1 Query / Lazy Loading▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Verified RiskService.list() (lines 51-58) maps every page row through toResponse(), and toResponse() (lines 238-276) issues riskCategoryRepository.findById per row with a non-null categoryId (line 242) plus userRepository.findById per row with a non-null ownerId (line 252) — a 2N+1 pattern. RiskRepository.findByOrganisationId/findByOrgAndStatus carry no @EntityGraph or join fetch, confirming no eager pre-loading. The per-owner User.findById additionally triggers the EAGER role+permission graph (see PERF-NQ-002). The endpoint is paginated, which bounds blast radius per page, but the N+1 within each page is real. High is reasonable.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/service/RiskService.java:52-57,238-276 Effort M Risk High business risk: the risk register is the platform's primary, highest-traffic list view. A single paginated page of N rows fans out to 1 + 2N SQL round trips (category lookup + owner lookup per risk), and each owner lookup additionally drags in the User -> roles -> permissions EAGER graph (PERF-NQ-002). At a page size of 50 that is 100+ extra queries per request, scaling linearly with page size and concurrent users. No data-integrity/auth impact; pure latency and DB load.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/service/RiskService.java:52-57
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/service/RiskService.java:238-276
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/service/RiskService.java:242
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/service/RiskService.java:252

Description

RiskService.list(...) loads a Page<Risk> via the repository, then maps every row through toResponse(Risk). toResponse performs riskCategoryRepository.findById(r.getCategoryId()) (line 242) and userRepository.findById(r.getOwnerId()) (line 252) for each risk. Both are per-row SELECTs executed inside the page's .map() loop, so the endpoint runs 1 page query + 2 lookups per row. Because User is mapped with EAGER ManyToMany roles (and Role->permissions is also EAGER), every owner lookup also pulls the full role+permission graph (see PERF-NQ-002), multiplying the cost further.

Root cause

The mapper resolves foreign-key display fields (category name, owner name/username) with one findById per FK per row instead of batch-loading or projecting the join. There is no caching, no JOIN FETCH, and no IN-clause batch resolution. Category and owner are reference data that could be fetched once for the whole page.

Evidence / proof
RiskService.java:57  `return page.map(this::toResponse);`
RiskService.java:242  `RiskCategory cat = riskCategoryRepository.findById(r.getCategoryId()).orElse(null);`
RiskService.java:252  `User owner = userRepository.findById(r.getOwnerId()).orElse(null);`
Query count for a page of N rows = 1 (page) + N (category) + N (owner, each EAGER-expanding roles+permissions). For N=50 => ~101 statements minimum, more with the EAGER role/permission joins per owner.

Real-world impact

Linear blow-up of DB round trips on the most-used screen in the product. Under realistic page sizes and concurrency the risk-list response time is dominated by serial query latency, and the connection pool is held longer per request, reducing throughput for every other endpoint.

Reproduction

1. Seed the risk register (seed_real_data.py populates ~hundreds of risks). 2. Enable Hibernate SQL logging (set logging for org.hibernate.SQL to DEBUG, or use datasource-proxy / Hypersistence statement counter). 3. GET /api/risks?page=0&size=50. 4. Count emitted SELECTs: observe one risk_category SELECT and one iam.users SELECT (plus role_permissions joins) per returned row rather than a constant number.

Resolution

Resolve category + owner display fields once per page. Options: (a) replace the entity list view with a JPQL constructor/interface projection that JOINs risk_category and iam.users and selects only the display columns; (b) collect the distinct categoryIds and ownerIds from the page, issue two findAllById batch queries, build id->name maps, and look up from the maps in toResponse; (c) at minimum cache reference data (categories) with the existing Caffeine cache. Approach (a) is the cleanest and removes the EAGER-graph side effect entirely.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
public Page<RiskResponse> list(String status, Pageable pageable) {
    ...
    return page.map(this::toResponse);
}

private RiskResponse toResponse(Risk r) {
    if (r.getCategoryId() != null) {
        RiskCategory cat = riskCategoryRepository.findById(r.getCategoryId()).orElse(null);
        ...
    }
    if (r.getOwnerId() != null) {
        User owner = userRepository.findById(r.getOwnerId()).orElse(null);
        ...
    }
}
▲ After (fixed)
public Page<RiskResponse> list(String status, Pageable pageable) {
    Page<Risk> page = ...;
    List<Risk> rows = page.getContent();
    Set<Long> catIds = rows.stream().map(Risk::getCategoryId).filter(Objects::nonNull).collect(toSet());
    Set<Long> ownerIds = rows.stream().map(Risk::getOwnerId).filter(Objects::nonNull).collect(toSet());
    Map<Long, RiskCategory> cats = riskCategoryRepository.findAllById(catIds).stream()
            .collect(toMap(RiskCategory::getId, c -> c));
    Map<Long, User> owners = userRepository.findAllById(ownerIds).stream()
            .collect(toMap(User::getId, u -> u));
    return page.map(r -> toResponse(r, cats, owners)); // mapper reads from the maps, no per-row findById
}
References: https://vladmihalcea.com/n-plus-1-query-problem/ · https://docs.spring.io/spring-data/jpa/reference/jpa/projections.html · CLAUDE.md — Caching: Caffeine L1 (maximumSize=1000, expireAfterWrite=300s)
HighPERF-NQ-002User and Role use FetchType.EAGER ManyToMany, forcing the full role+permission graph on every user load
✓ VerifiedPerformanceEAGER Fetch / N+1 Query▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Verified User.java line 68: roles is @ManyToMany(fetch = FetchType.EAGER), and Role.java line 37: permissions is @ManyToMany(fetch = FetchType.EAGER). Therefore every User load eagerly materialises the full roles graph and, for each role, the full permissions graph — exactly as claimed. This sits on the hottest path (principal resolution on every authenticated request, plus any owner/assignee resolution like RiskService.toResponse). Confirmed; High is justified.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/iam/entity/User.java:68-74 Effort M Risk High: User.roles (EAGER) and Role.permissions (EAGER) form a two-level eager collection chain that loads on every single User fetch anywhere in the codebase - user list pages, dashboard counts, and especially the per-row owner lookups in RiskService and other registers. EAGER collections cannot be batch-fetched by a paginated query, so a page of U users triggers U secondary role queries and then a permission query per distinct role. This is the multiplier behind several other findings.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/iam/entity/User.java:68-74
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/iam/entity/Role.java:37-43
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/iam/repository/UserRepository.java:20-36
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/iam/service/UserService.java:32-34

Description

User.roles is annotated @ManyToMany(fetch = FetchType.EAGER) (User.java:68) and Role.permissions is also @ManyToMany(fetch = FetchType.EAGER) (Role.java:37). Any time a User entity is materialised, Hibernate eagerly loads its roles, and for each role eagerly loads its permissions. On the paginated user list (UserService.list -> UserRepository.findWithFilters), the JPQL does LEFT JOIN u.roles but because the collection is EAGER, Hibernate does not use that join to initialise the collection for a paged query; it issues a separate roles SELECT per user and a permissions SELECT per role. The same EAGER chain fires on every userRepository.findById used as an FK lookup across the platform (e.g. RiskService.toResponse line 252).

Root cause

Collection associations declared EAGER. EAGER ToMany is a well-known anti-pattern: it cannot be paginated in SQL, defeats projection-based reads, and silently loads heavy graphs on lookups that only need a username or id. Authentication (CustomUserDetailsService) needs roles+permissions, but that is the only place that needs them and it can request them explicitly with a fetch-join.

Evidence / proof
User.java:68  `@ManyToMany(fetch = FetchType.EAGER)` -> `Set<Role> roles`
Role.java:37  `@ManyToMany(fetch = FetchType.EAGER)` -> `Set<Permission> permissions`
UserRepository.java:20-36 findWithFilters returns Page<User> with `LEFT JOIN u.roles r` but EAGER collections force per-row secondary loads regardless. For a page of U users with R distinct roles: 1 + U (roles per user) + up to R (permissions per role) statements.

Real-world impact

Every user-bearing read path pays for the entire authorization graph. User list, dashboard active-user count path, and any FK owner resolution become multi-query operations. The blast radius is platform-wide because User is referenced as owner/approver across nearly every module.

Reproduction

1. Enable Hibernate SQL logging. 2. GET the user admin list (UserService.list). 3. Observe one user_roles SELECT per user and one role_permissions SELECT per distinct role, on top of the main user query. 4. Separately, call any register list that resolves an owner (e.g. /api/risks) and observe the same role/permission SELECTs firing per owner.

Resolution

Change both associations to FetchType.LAZY. Where the full graph is genuinely needed (login / authorization in CustomUserDetailsService) add an explicit @EntityGraph or JPQL `JOIN FETCH u.roles r JOIN FETCH r.permissions` finder. For list views, return a projection that exposes only roleNames via a join, never the entity graph. Verify lazy access inside an open transaction or via DTO projection to avoid LazyInitializationException.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// User.java
@ManyToMany(fetch = FetchType.EAGER)
@JoinTable(schema = "iam", name = "user_roles", ...)
private Set<Role> roles = new HashSet<>();

// Role.java
@ManyToMany(fetch = FetchType.EAGER)
@JoinTable(schema = "iam", name = "role_permissions", ...)
private Set<Permission> permissions = new HashSet<>();
▲ After (fixed)
// User.java
@ManyToMany(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
@JoinTable(schema = "iam", name = "user_roles", ...)
private Set<Role> roles = new HashSet<>();

// Role.java
@ManyToMany(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
@JoinTable(schema = "iam", name = "role_permissions", ...)
private Set<Permission> permissions = new HashSet<>();

// UserRepository.java — explicit graph only where auth needs it
@Query("SELECT DISTINCT u FROM User u JOIN FETCH u.roles r JOIN FETCH r.permissions WHERE u.username = :username")
Optional<User> findByUsernameWithAuthorities(@Param("username") String username);
References: https://vladmihalcea.com/eager-fetching-is-a-code-smell/ · https://docs.spring.io/spring-data/jpa/reference/jpa/entity-graph.html · https://thorben-janssen.com/lazyinitializationexception/

The N+1 is real, but 'Critical' overstates blast radius: the framework->control->sub-control tree is a bounded, platform-shared catalog (a handful of frameworks), the method is @Transactional(readOnly=true), and it backs a single matrix view rather than a hot request path. Query count grows with catalog size, not tenant data volume. Real performance bug worth High, not Critical.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceMatrixService.java:57-143 Effort M Risk Critical: matrix() builds the full evidence matrix by nesting four loops, each issuing per-row queries. Total statements = 1 (frameworks) + F (controls per framework) + F*C (sub-controls per control) + F*C*S (evidence items per sub-control). For a realistic shared catalog (NCA ECC + ISO 27001 + SAMA CSF + PCI-DSS, hundreds of controls each with multiple sub-controls) this is easily 1,000-10,000+ SQL round trips for one page render. The sibling GrcExpertService renders the same tree in ~6 queries, proving the inefficiency is avoidable.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceMatrixService.java:64
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceMatrixService.java:71
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceMatrixService.java:77
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceMatrixService.java:85
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/GrcExpertService.java:44-138

Description

matrix() iterates frameworkRepo.findAll() (line 64); for each framework calls controlRepo.findByFrameworkIdAndIsActiveTrue (line 71); for each control calls subControlRepo.findByControlIdAndIsActiveTrue (line 77); and for each sub-control calls itemRepo.findBySubControl(org, s.getId()) (line 85) to load every evidence item just to compute counts, freshest expiry and a method-mix histogram in Java. Every level multiplies the previous, producing F*C*S evidence-item queries plus the structural queries above them.

Root cause

Per-node fetch instead of batch fetch + in-memory aggregation. The evidence counts/expiry/method-mix are pure aggregates that the DB can compute with GROUP BY in a handful of queries (the EvidenceItemRepository already exposes aggregateStatusBySubControl, aggregateExpiryBySubControl, aggregateFreshApprovedBySubControl). The controls and sub-controls can be batch-loaded with findByFrameworkIdInAndIsActiveTrue / findByControlIdInAndIsActiveTrue (both already exist and are used by GrcExpertService).

Evidence / proof
EvidenceMatrixService.java:64 `List<EvidenceFramework> frameworks = frameworkRepo.findAll();`
:71 `controlRepo.findByFrameworkIdAndIsActiveTrue(fw.getId());`  // per framework
:77 `subControlRepo.findByControlIdAndIsActiveTrue(c.getId());` // per control
:85 `itemRepo.findBySubControl(org, s.getId());`               // per sub-control
Contrast GrcExpertService.listExpertCatalog() (lines 47-77) which does findByIsActiveTrue + findByFrameworkIdInAndIsActiveTrue + findByControlIdInAndIsActiveTrue + 3 aggregate GROUP BY queries = ~6 statements total for the same framework->control->sub-control tree.

Real-world impact

The evidence matrix tab (called out in the buyer assessment as a flagship demo screen) can take seconds and hammer the DB with thousands of statements on every load, scaling with the size of the shared control catalog rather than with tenant data. High risk of timeouts and connection-pool exhaustion in a multi-tenant deployment.

Reproduction

1. Ensure the shared evidence catalog is populated (multiple frameworks with controls + sub-controls). 2. Enable Hibernate SQL logging or attach a statement counter. 3. Invoke EvidenceMatrixService.matrix() (the evidence matrix endpoint). 4. Count SELECTs; observe one findBySubControl per sub-control (and one control/sub-control query per parent), i.e. counts scale as F + F*C + F*C*S. 5. Compare to listExpertCatalog() which holds at ~6 statements.

Resolution

Refactor matrix() to mirror GrcExpertService: batch-load active frameworks, then controls via findByFrameworkIdInAndIsActiveTrue(fwIds), then sub-controls via findByControlIdInAndIsActiveTrue(ctrlIds), group them in memory (groupingBy frameworkId / controlId), and replace the per-sub-control itemRepo.findBySubControl loop with the existing aggregateStatusBySubControl / aggregateExpiryBySubControl / aggregateFreshApprovedBySubControl GROUP BY queries keyed by sub-control id. The method-mix histogram can be added as one more aggregate query (GROUP BY sub_control_id, collection_method).

▼ Before (vulnerable)

    List<EvidenceControl> controls = controlRepo.findByFrameworkIdAndIsActiveTrue(fw.getId());
    for (EvidenceControl c : controls) {
        List<EvidenceSubControl> subs = subControlRepo.findByControlIdAndIsActiveTrue(c.getId());
        for (EvidenceSubControl s : subs) {
            List<EvidenceItem> items = itemRepo.findBySubControl(org, s.getId()); // N*M*K queries
            ... aggregate in Java ...
        }
    }
}
▲ After (fixed)
List<EvidenceFramework> frameworks = frameworkRepo.findByIsActiveTrue();
List<Long> fwIds = frameworks.stream().map(EvidenceFramework::getId).toList();
List<EvidenceControl> controls = controlRepo.findByFrameworkIdInAndIsActiveTrue(fwIds);
List<Long> ctrlIds = controls.stream().map(EvidenceControl::getId).toList();
List<EvidenceSubControl> subs = subControlRepo.findByControlIdInAndIsActiveTrue(ctrlIds);
// one GROUP BY pass each, keyed by sub-control id
Map<Long, Map<String,Integer>> statusBySc = ... itemRepo.aggregateStatusBySubControl(org) ...;
Map<Long, int[]> expiryBySc = ... itemRepo.aggregateExpiryBySubControl(org, today, horizon) ...;
Map<Long, Integer> freshBySc = ... itemRepo.aggregateFreshApprovedBySubControl(org, today) ...;
Map<Long,List<EvidenceSubControl>> subsByCtrl = subs.stream().collect(groupingBy(EvidenceSubControl::getControlId));
Map<Long,List<EvidenceControl>> ctrlsByFw = controls.stream().collect(groupingBy(EvidenceControl::getFrameworkId));
// then assemble the tree from the maps with zero further queries

Description

Multiple loops issue per-row queries: (1) buildRiskPivot loops over risk-control links calling controlRepo.findByIdAndOrganisationId per link (148-154). (2) buildControlPivot loops links calling riskRepo.findById per link (190-194). (3) buildFindingPivot nests a per-control loop with an inner per-link riskRepo.findById (245-257). (4) capasForFindings runs TWO repository queries (auditLcCapaRepo + capaRepo) per finding (334-349). (5) ccmCoverageForControls calls ccmRunRepo.findRecentForTest once per test definition (365-377). Worst of all, toControlPivot (574-607) calls latestAssessmentEffectiveness (which queries control assessments, 381-389) AND re-loads ALL org CCM test definitions via ccmDefRepo.findByOrganisationIdAndIsDeletedFalse... for EVERY control row (586-589), so the full definition list is re-fetched once per control in the pivot.

Root cause

FK and child-collection resolution done one entity at a time inside loops rather than batch-loading by id set, plus repeated re-fetching of the same org-wide list (CCM definitions) inside a per-control mapper. findingsForControls also scans the entire org findings table and re-parses control_crosswalk JSON in Java for every finding instead of filtering in the query.

Evidence / proof
Line 149 `controlRepo.findByIdAndOrganisationId(link.getControlId(), orgId)` inside `for (RiskControlLink link : links)`.
Line 253 `riskRepo.findById(link.getRiskId())` inside nested control->link loops.
Lines 339-345 two repo finders per finding inside `for (FindingPivot fp : findings)`.
Line 366 `ccmRunRepo.findRecentForTest(orgId, d.getId(), PageRequest.of(0,100))` inside `for (ControlTestDefinition d : defs)`.
Lines 586-589 `ccmDefRepo.findByOrganisationIdAndIsDeletedFalseOrderByCreatedAtDesc(orgId)` re-loaded inside toControlPivot, which is itself called once per control row.

Real-world impact

Pivot views (a flagship analytics screen per the class Javadoc) degrade super-linearly with the number of linked controls/findings and the size of the org's findings and CCM tables. The repeated full re-fetch of CCM definitions per control row is pure waste. High DB load and latency on an interactive drill-down feature.

Reproduction

1. Seed risks with several linked controls, controls with CCM test definitions and runs, and an org findings table of a few hundred rows. 2. Enable SQL logging. 3. Call buildRiskPivot(riskId). 4. Observe: one control SELECT per link, a full findings scan, two CAPA SELECTs per matching finding, the entire CCM definition list re-fetched once per control row, and one CCM-run SELECT per definition.

Resolution

Batch-load by id sets: collect controlIds/riskIds and use findAllById / a single findByOrganisationIdAndIdIn finder; load CCM test definitions for the org ONCE before the control loop and pass the map into toControlPivot; load latest control assessments for all controlIds in one query (e.g. findByOrganisationIdAndControlIdIn ordered, then reduce in memory); fetch CAPA for all finding externalIds in one IN query per source repo; and push the control_crosswalk code filter into the findings query (or maintain a normalized control_code -> finding link table) instead of scanning + JSON-parsing every org finding in Java.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
for (RiskControlLink link : links) {
    Control c = controlRepo.findByIdAndOrganisationId(link.getControlId(), orgId).orElse(null); // per link
    ...
}
// toControlPivot, called per control row:
List<ControlTestDefinition> defs = ccmDefRepo.findByOrganisationIdAndIsDeletedFalseOrderByCreatedAtDesc(orgId)
        .stream().filter(d -> c.getId().equals(d.getControlId())).toList(); // full list re-fetched every call
▲ After (fixed)
Set<Long> controlIds = links.stream().map(RiskControlLink::getControlId).collect(toSet());
Map<Long, Control> controlsById = controlRepo.findByOrganisationIdAndIdIn(orgId, controlIds).stream()
        .collect(toMap(Control::getId, c -> c));
// load CCM defs ONCE, group by controlId, pass into the mapper
Map<Long, List<ControlTestDefinition>> defsByControl = ccmDefRepo
        .findByOrganisationIdAndIsDeletedFalseOrderByCreatedAtDesc(orgId).stream()
        .filter(d -> d.getControlId() != null)
        .collect(groupingBy(ControlTestDefinition::getControlId));
for (RiskControlLink link : links) {
    Control c = controlsById.get(link.getControlId());
    if (c == null) continue;
    controlRows.add(toControlPivot(c, link.getEffectiveness(), defsByControl)); // no per-row query
}
References: https://vladmihalcea.com/n-plus-1-query-problem/ · https://docs.spring.io/spring-data/jpa/reference/jpa/query-methods.html#jpa.query-methods.query-creation · https://www.baeldung.com/spring-data-jpa-in-clause

This is an unbounded org-scoped findAll-style query as described, and the same pattern recurs across sibling list methods (by-regulator, by-owner). Real and systemic. High is reasonable for an unbounded-result-set performance/DoS-surface finding.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/compliance/obligation/controller/ObligationController.java:48-52 Effort L Risk High likelihood (every tenant's registers grow monotonically and are read on dashboard load), high impact (full table materialised into memory + serialised to JSON on every request). Not a confidentiality/integrity issue, so not Critical, but a realistic availability/latency risk as data volume grows — effectively a self-inflicted DoS vector.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/compliance/obligation/controller/ObligationController.java:48-52
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/outsourcing/controller/OutsourcingController.java:30-32
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/audit_lc/controller/FindingController.java:19-23
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/privacy_lc/controller/DsrCaseController.java
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk_lc/controller/TreatmentPlanController.java
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/asm/controller/AttackSurfaceController.java:64-69

Description

Across the backend (231 @RestController classes, 375 repositories) only 122 GET endpoints return a Spring Data Page<T>; another 332 GET endpoints return a raw List<T>/Set<T> with no Pageable parameter. Of those, 204 are collection-root 'register' endpoints (the mapping path has no {id} segment, e.g. GET /api/v1/compliance/obligations, GET /api/v1/outsourcing/arrangements, GET /api/audit-lc/findings, GET /api/v1/asm/assets) and 128 are sub-resource lists scoped under a parent /{id}/.... The register-root endpoints each fetch every non-deleted, org-scoped row for the tenant and serialise the whole set to JSON on every call. These are the exact endpoints the bilingual SPA loads on page navigation (the ObligationController Javadoc even states the register is 'wall-mounted on every dashboard'). As tenants accumulate obligations, findings, vendors, assets, DSR cases, etc., each call materialises an ever-larger list into the JVM heap and the HTTP response, with no upper bound. The canonical /api/v1/risk/risks endpoint (RiskController.java:30-35) shows the project already knows the correct pattern — Page<RiskResponse> with @PageableDefault(size = 20) — but it was applied inconsistently and most later modules regressed to raw List.

Root cause

No architectural enforcement that list endpoints must be paginated. Sprint-1 core modules (risk, incident, compliance controls/findings/assessments, evidence items, IAM users, TPRM vendors, audit-log) adopted Page<T> + @PageableDefault, but the dozens of modules added in later sprints (data-officer, obligation register, outsourcing, ASM, BCM cycle, SOC-ops, sustainability, NDI, ethics, etc.) return List<T> directly from service methods that call repository finders such as findByOrganisationIdAndIsDeletedFalseOrderBy...(orgId) which have no Pageable overload. There is no global cap on page size either (see PERF-PG-003), so the platform has no backstop.

Evidence / proof
Static scan of src/main/java/**/controller/*.java:
  GET endpoints returning Page<>  (paginated):           122
  GET endpoints returning raw List/Set (unbounded):      332
     - collection-root 'register' style (no /{id}):      204
     - sub-resource (under /{id}/...):                   128
Verified register examples (controller -> service -> repository, all unbounded):
  ObligationController.list()  -> ObligationService.list() [line 74-77]
     -> ObligationRepository.findByOrganisationIdAndIsDeletedFalseOrderByNextDueDateAsc(orgId)  // returns List<Obligation>, no Pageable
  OutsourcingController.list() -> OutsourcingService.listArrangements() [line 183-186]
     -> OutsourcingArrangementRepository.findByOrganisationIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(orgId) [line 17]  // List, no Pageable
  AttackSurfaceController.listAssets() -> AttackSurfaceAssetService.listAssets() [line 107-111]
     -> findByOrganisationIdAndIsDeletedFalseOrderByCreatedAtDesc(orgId)  // List, no Pageable
  data_officer/DataOfficerController: 14 register-root List endpoints (/dsr,/consents,/dpia,/breaches,/notices,/retention-rules,/catalog,/lineage,/disposals,/quality/rules,/quality/runs,/ndr,/ethics,/timeline)
     e.g. listDsr() -> dsrRepo.findByOrganisationIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(org())  // List, no Pageable

Real-world impact

Per-request memory and bandwidth scale linearly with the tenant's register size, with no ceiling. A single tenant with, say, 50k attack-surface assets or audit findings turns one dashboard load into a multi-MB JSON payload plus a full-table Hibernate fetch and entity-to-DTO mapping of the entire set. Under concurrency this drives heap pressure / long GC pauses / OOM and elevated p99 latency for ALL tenants on the shared JVM. Because the SPA fires several of these register calls on each page open, the effect compounds. It is also a low-effort denial-of-service primitive: any authenticated read-only user can repeatedly hit the largest register endpoint.

Reproduction

1. Seed a tenant with a large register (e.g. INSERT many rows into compliance.obligation or asm.attack_surface_asset for organisation_id = 1).
2. Authenticate as any READ role and call GET /api/v1/compliance/obligations (or /api/v1/asm/assets, /api/v1/outsourcing/arrangements, /api/v1/data-officer/dsr).
3. Observe that the response contains every row for the org with no page metadata, no 'size'/'page' query params honoured, and response size + latency grow linearly with row count. Compare with GET /api/v1/risk/risks which returns a paged envelope (content/totalElements/...) and caps at 20 by default.

Resolution

Standardise every collection-root list endpoint on Spring Data pagination, mirroring RiskController: accept @PageableDefault(size = 20) Pageable and return Page<T>; add a paged repository overload (Page<T> findByOrganisationId...(orgId, Pageable)). Keep a small number of intentionally-unbounded helper endpoints (e.g. SCM /vendors/all 'for dropdowns') but (a) rename them explicitly, (b) hard-cap them server-side (e.g. PageRequest.of(0, 500)), and (c) document the cap. Also add a global maximum page size (see PERF-PG-003) so the Page<> endpoints cannot be abused via ?size=. Prioritise the highest-cardinality registers first: ASM assets/findings, data-officer (DSR/consents/breaches/catalog), obligations, outsourcing arrangements, audit findings, BCM BIA, policy documents.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// ObligationController.java
@GetMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('COMPLIANCE_OFFICER','RISK_MANAGER','AUDITOR','CISO','PLATFORM_ADMIN','BCM_MANAGER')")
public List<ObligationResponse> list() {
    return service.list();
}

// ObligationService.java
public List<ObligationResponse> list() {
    return repo.findByOrganisationIdAndIsDeletedFalseOrderByNextDueDateAsc(org())
        .stream().map(ObligationService::toResponse).toList();
}

// ObligationRepository.java
List<Obligation> findByOrganisationIdAndIsDeletedFalseOrderByNextDueDateAsc(Long organisationId);
▲ After (fixed)
// ObligationController.java
@GetMapping
@PreAuthorize("hasAnyRole('COMPLIANCE_OFFICER','RISK_MANAGER','AUDITOR','CISO','PLATFORM_ADMIN','BCM_MANAGER')")
public Page<ObligationResponse> list(
        @PageableDefault(size = 20, sort = "nextDueDate") Pageable pageable) {
    return service.list(pageable);
}

// ObligationService.java
public Page<ObligationResponse> list(Pageable pageable) {
    return repo.findByOrganisationIdAndIsDeletedFalse(org(), pageable)
        .map(ObligationService::toResponse);
}

// ObligationRepository.java
Page<Obligation> findByOrganisationIdAndIsDeletedFalse(Long organisationId, Pageable pageable);

MediumPERF-FE-003@tanstack/react-virtual is a dependency but used by only 1 of 73 tables; 72 pages render every row via an un-virtualized, un-paginated DataTable
PerformanceRuntime rendering / virtualization▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/components/ui/DataTable.tsx:40-94 Effort L Risk Medium runtime risk that scales with data volume: the shared DataTable maps the full row array to DOM nodes with no windowing, slicing or pagination. On registers seeded with hundreds of rows (seed_real_data.py loads ~450 rows across 23 tables; production registers grow unbounded) this produces large DOM trees, slow first render, slow re-render on filter/sort, and high memory. The capability to fix it (react-virtual) is already installed but applied to only one screen.
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/components/ui/DataTable.tsx:53
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/components/ui/data-table/DataTableV2.tsx:1-1
tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json:16

Description

package.json declares `@tanstack/react-virtual: ^3.13.24` (line 16). A grep for its usage finds it imported in exactly one file: components/ui/data-table/DataTableV2.tsx. DataTableV2 (the virtualized table) is referenced by only 1 page. The non-virtualized components/ui/DataTable.tsx is imported by 72 pages, and its render body does `{rows.map(row => ... )}` (line 53) — it materialises one <tr> per row with no windowing, no `rows.slice(...)`, no pagination and no use of react-virtual (the file imports nothing from @tanstack/react-virtual). So the virtualization library that was added to the dependency tree is effectively shelf-ware: the overwhelming majority of GRC registers (risk register, vendor list, controls, obligations, vulnerabilities, complaints, etc.) render every row.

Root cause

Two table components diverged: a newer virtualized DataTableV2 (using react-virtual) and the original DataTable (full-map render). Migration stalled at one page, so 72 pages still use the un-virtualized component while the virtualization dependency sits mostly unused.

Evidence / proof
`grep -rln react-virtual src` → only components/ui/data-table/DataTableV2.tsx. `grep -rln DataTableV2 src/pages` → 1 page. `grep -rln "import.*DataTable[^V]" src/pages` → 72 pages. DataTable.tsx is 95 lines; render at line 53 is `{rows.map(row => { ... return (<tr key={row.id}> ... </tr>); })}` with no slice/window/pagination. Big pages confirmed using the un-virtualized table: CyberPage, CompliancePage, ScmPage, RiskRegisterPage all reference plain `DataTable` (not DataTableV2).

Real-world impact

On large registers the table inflates the DOM node count linearly with row count (Lighthouse dom-size is already flagged on the dashboard-class pages). Render and every subsequent filter/sort/search re-render walk the entire dataset, increasing TBT and interaction latency. Memory grows with row count. The cost is hidden today because seed data is modest, but production GRC registers (audit findings, vulnerabilities, vendors) routinely reach thousands of rows.

Reproduction

1) `grep -rln 'react-virtual' tss-grc-ui-v2/src` → single hit (DataTableV2). 2) `grep -rln 'DataTableV2' tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages | wc -l` → 1; `grep -rln "import.*DataTable[^V]" tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages | wc -l` → 72. 3) Open any large register, seed a few thousand rows, observe DOM node count = row count and sluggish sort/filter.

Resolution

Either (a) migrate the high-volume registers to the existing DataTableV2 so react-virtual actually windows the rows, or (b) if a full migration is out of scope, add row virtualization (or at minimum client-side pagination / a row cap) directly to the shared DataTable so all 72 consumers benefit. If neither table will use react-virtual broadly, remove the dependency to stop shipping it. Pick virtualization for the registers known to grow large (risk, vulnerabilities, vendors, findings, obligations).

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// components/ui/DataTable.tsx:52-92 — renders ALL rows
<tbody>
  {rows.map(row => {
    // ... one <tr> per row, no windowing
    return (<tr key={row.id}> ... </tr>);
  })}
</tbody>
▲ After (fixed)
// Route large registers through the already-virtualized DataTableV2,
// or window the shared component with the installed react-virtual:
import { useVirtualizer } from '@tanstack/react-virtual';
// const rowVirtualizer = useVirtualizer({ count: rows.length, getScrollElement: () => parentRef.current, estimateSize: () => 44, overscan: 12 });
// render only rowVirtualizer.getVirtualItems(), positioned by translateY.
