MediumPERF-FE-004vite.config.ts has no manualChunks / vendor-splitting; React, react-router, recharts and app code land in a single monolithic entry chunk
PerformanceBuild / chunking strategy▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/vite.config.ts:43-46 Effort S Risk Medium impact on caching and first load: without explicit vendor chunking, Rollup merges stable third-party code (react, react-dom, react-router-dom) with frequently-changing app code into the entry chunk. Every app deploy busts the hash on the whole chunk, so returning users re-download React + router even when only app code changed. Also enlarges the single critical chunk. No security impact.
tss-grc-ui-v2/vite.config.ts:43-46
tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json:13-24

Description

The build block in vite.config.ts is `build: { sourcemap: true, target: 'es2022' }` (lines 43-46) — there is no `rollupOptions.output.manualChunks` and no chunk-size configuration. `grep -n 'manualChunks|rollupOptions|chunkSizeWarning' vite.config.ts` returns nothing. With Vite/Rollup defaults the route-level React.lazy() splits do create per-route chunks (good), but the shared vendor libraries that every route depends on — react, react-dom, react-router-dom — are pulled into the common/entry chunk together with App.tsx and the eager pages. react-router-dom alone is 209,984 B (Lighthouse, dev), and its unused-javascript wasted estimate on /login is 168,141 B. There is no separation of long-lived vendor code from volatile app code, which is the standard caching optimisation.

Root cause

Default Rollup chunking with no manualChunks strategy. The team relied solely on route-level lazy() and never configured vendor splitting, so cross-route shared deps collapse into the entry chunk and share its content hash with app code.

Evidence / proof
vite.config.ts:43-46 `build: { sourcemap: true, target: 'es2022' }` — no manualChunks. `grep -n manualChunks vite.config.ts` = no match. Dependencies that would benefit from a stable vendor chunk (package.json:13-24): react, react-dom, react-router-dom, recharts, lucide-react, @tanstack/react-table, @stomp/stompjs, sockjs-client. Lighthouse: react-router-dom.js 209,984 B transferred, 168,141 B unused on /login.

Real-world impact

Poor long-term caching: any app-code change invalidates the entry chunk that also carries react/react-dom/react-router, forcing repeat downloads of unchanged vendor code for returning users. Larger single critical chunk also slows first parse. (Note: the build sets `sourcemap: true` — appropriate for an internal/staging build, but confirm sourcemaps are disabled or access-controlled for any public production deploy.)

Reproduction

1) `npm run build` and inspect dist/assets — confirm react/react-router are co-located with app entry code rather than in a dedicated vendor chunk. 2) Make a one-line change in any page, rebuild, and observe the entry/vendor chunk hash changes even though React did not.

Resolution

Add a manualChunks strategy to split stable vendor libraries into their own long-cached chunk(s). At minimum separate react/react-dom/react-router-dom; optionally give recharts and lucide-react their own chunks since they are large and load on distinct routes. This keeps vendor hashes stable across app deploys and shrinks the critical entry chunk.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
build: {
  sourcemap: true,
  target: 'es2022',
},
▲ After (fixed)
build: {
  sourcemap: true,
  target: 'es2022',
  rollupOptions: {
    output: {
      manualChunks: {
        'react-vendor': ['react', 'react-dom', 'react-router-dom'],
        'charts': ['recharts'],
        'icons': ['lucide-react'],
        'realtime': ['@stomp/stompjs', 'sockjs-client'],
      },
    },
  },
},
References: https://rollupjs.org/configuration-options/#output-manualchunks · https://vitejs.dev/guide/build.html#chunking-strategy
MediumPERF-FE-005Layout-direction flip after hydration (index.html dir=ltr vs i18n default ar/RTL) is a structural CLS source; Lighthouse CLS = 0.344
PerformanceLayout stability (CLS)▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/index.html:2 Effort S Risk Medium UX/score impact: Lighthouse reports cumulative-layout-shift 0.344 (score 0.32 — failing; good is <0.1). The HTML ships with dir="ltr" but the app defaults to Arabic RTL and flips documentElement.dir in a post-mount effect, so the entire layout mirrors after first paint — a guaranteed, full-page layout shift on the default (Arabic) first load. Affects perceived stability and the Lighthouse score directly.
tss-grc-ui-v2/index.html:2
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/lib/i18n.tsx:27-40

Description

index.html declares `<html lang="en" dir="ltr">` (line 2). The i18n provider defaults the language to Arabic ('ar', RTL) unless localStorage explicitly holds 'en' (i18n.tsx: initial state returns 'ar' for first-time visitors), and only sets `document.documentElement.dir = dir` inside a useEffect that runs AFTER the first render/paint (i18n.tsx:27-31). So on the default first visit the page paints LTR, React mounts, then the effect flips the document to RTL — mirroring the whole layout and producing a large layout shift. CLS is measured at 0.344, well into the failing range. This is on top of any web-font / late-CSS shift; the dir flip alone is a structural full-page reflow.

Root cause

The static HTML's dir/lang attributes are hard-coded to en/ltr and do not match the app's runtime default (ar/rtl). The correct direction is only applied imperatively after mount, so the first paint is always in the wrong direction for the default-language user.

Evidence / proof
index.html:2 `<html lang="en" dir="ltr">`. i18n.tsx initial state: `const stored = localStorage.getItem(LANG_KEY); return stored === 'en' ? 'en' : 'ar';` (defaults to Arabic). i18n.tsx:27-31 effect: `document.documentElement.lang = lang; document.documentElement.dir = dir;` runs in useEffect (post-paint). Lighthouse cumulative-layout-shift numericValue = 0.34425702372849826, score 0.32.

Real-world impact

Every default (Arabic) first load mirrors the entire UI after first paint — a jarring shift and a failing CLS contribution. Returning English users who toggled also pay a one-frame flip. Directly depresses the Lighthouse Performance and stability scores.

Reproduction

1) Clear localStorage, open the app — page paints LTR then snaps to RTL. 2) Lighthouse /login report: cumulative-layout-shift = 0.344 (failing). 3) Compare index.html dir="ltr" against i18n.tsx default 'ar'.

Resolution

Set the document direction/lang before first paint so the first frame matches the resolved language. Cheapest fix: a tiny inline script in index.html <head> that reads localStorage('grc.lang') (defaulting to 'ar') and sets document.documentElement.lang/dir synchronously before the module bundle loads. Then change index.html's static default to dir="rtl" lang="ar" to match the app default. This eliminates the post-hydration flip entirely.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
<!-- index.html -->
<html lang="en" dir="ltr">
  <head>
    <!-- ... no direction bootstrap ... -->
▲ After (fixed)
<!-- index.html -->
<html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
  <head>
    <script>
      (function () {
        var l = localStorage.getItem('grc.lang');
        var lang = l === 'en' ? 'en' : 'ar';
        document.documentElement.lang = lang;
        document.documentElement.dir = lang === 'ar' ? 'rtl' : 'ltr';
      })();
    </script>
References: https://web.dev/articles/cls · https://web.dev/articles/optimize-cls
MediumPERF-IO-003In-thread Thread.sleep retry/backoff inside transactional integration calls extends DB-connection hold time to as much as ~75s-2min
PerformanceBlocking retry/backoff inside transaction (connection-hold amplification)▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/splunk/client/LiveSplunkClient.java:69-107 Effort M Risk Medium — the retry loops in the LIVE clients block the calling (request or scheduler) thread with Thread.sleep between attempts. Because the call originates inside an open transaction (PERF-IO-001/002), the backoff sleeps are added on top of the remote latency to the connection-hold time, multiplying the pool-exhaustion window. Bounded but large worst case; depends on a failing remote system.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/splunk/client/LiveSplunkClient.java:49
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/splunk/client/LiveSplunkClient.java:94-101
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/crowdstrike/client/LiveCrowdStrikeClient.java:54
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/crowdstrike/client/LiveCrowdStrikeClient.java:187-194
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/servicenow/client/LiveServiceNowClient.java:194-216

Description

Every LIVE client retries 5xx/connection failures with an in-thread exponential backoff that calls Thread.sleep on the calling thread. Splunk and CrowdStrike cap the per-attempt backoff at BACKOFF_CAP_MS = 30_000L (LiveSplunkClient.java:49, LiveCrowdStrikeClient.java:54) over up to 3 attempts. ServiceNow's withRetry (LiveServiceNowClient.java:194-216) sleeps starting at 250ms, doubling, capped at 5000ms, with max-retries=3 (so up to 4 attempts) and a read timeout of 30s per attempt (ServiceNowProperties timeout-seconds=30, application.yml:183). Because these clients are called from inside @Transactional service methods, the entire sleep+timeout budget is added to the DB-connection-hold time. ServiceNow worst case approaches 4 x 30s read timeout + backoffs ~= 2 minutes; Splunk/CrowdStrike approach 3 x 5s timeout + ~30s+ backoff ~= 45-75s.

Root cause

Retry/backoff is implemented synchronously on the calling thread (Thread.sleep) AND the call is made while a transaction (and therefore a pooled connection) is open. The two together convert transient remote failures into prolonged connection occupancy.

Evidence / proof
LiveSplunkClient.java:99 'sleep(delayMs);' line 100 'delayMs = (long) Math.min(BACKOFF_CAP_MS, ...)' with BACKOFF_CAP_MS=30_000 (line 49) and maxAttempts from props (default retry max-attempts=3). LiveCrowdStrikeClient.java:192 'sleep(delayMs);' line 193 cap 30_000 (line 54). LiveServiceNowClient.java:207 'Thread.sleep(backoffMs);' line 212 'backoffMs = Math.min(backoffMs * 2, 5000);' with attempts = maxRetries+1 (line 195) and read timeout 30s (ServiceNowIntegrationConfig.java:61 setReadTimeout(props.getTimeoutSeconds())). All invoked from @Transactional service methods (see PERF-IO-001).

Real-world impact

A degraded third party (intermittent 503s, slow responses) turns each push into a connection held for tens of seconds to ~2 minutes. With only 20 (base) / 10 (dev) connections, even a handful of concurrent retrying pushes meaningfully shrinks the pool's effective capacity, and the leak-detection-threshold of 60s (application.yml:26) will start emitting false 'connection leak' warnings on the longest ServiceNow retry chains — masking real leaks in operational logs.

Reproduction

1) Point ServiceNow LIVE at an endpoint returning HTTP 503 on every attempt. 2) Call POST /test-push. 3) Observe the request thread (and its borrowed connection) blocked for ~ (4 x 30s) + (0.25+0.5+1.0s) ~= 121s before failing. 4) Repeat 20x concurrently and watch GrcHikariPool exhaust and unrelated DB calls time out at 30s.

Resolution

First and primarily, remove the remote call from the transaction (PERF-IO-001) so retry sleeps no longer occupy a connection. Additionally, prefer non-blocking retry (Resilience4j / Spring Retry with a separate scheduler, or async + outbox) over Thread.sleep, and lower the ServiceNow read timeout from 30s toward the 5s the other adapters use unless a specific SLA requires longer. Cap total retry budget (sum of timeouts + backoffs) well under the 60s leak-detection threshold and the 30s connection-timeout to avoid cascading symptoms.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// ServiceNowProperties: timeout-seconds: 30 (application.yml:183), max-retries: 3
// withRetry: Thread.sleep(backoffMs) between up to 4 attempts, each with a 30s read timeout,
// all executed while a @Transactional DB connection is held.
▲ After (fixed)
// 1) Move client.createIncident(...) outside @Transactional (see PERF-IO-001).
// 2) Reduce read timeout: grc.integrations.servicenow.timeout-seconds: 5
// 3) Replace in-thread Thread.sleep retry with Resilience4j @Retry on a dedicated
//    scheduler, OR push asynchronously (@Async / outbox) so no request thread blocks.
References: https://resilience4j.readme.io/docs/retry · https://github.com/brettwooldridge/HikariCP/wiki/Bad-Behavior:-Handling-Database-Down · https://docs.spring.io/spring-retry/docs/current/reference/html/
MediumPERF-IO-004OAuth token refresh performs a synchronized blocking HTTP fetch while a transaction holds a DB connection, serialising all callers
PerformanceSynchronized blocking I/O on hot path inside transaction▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/servicenow/oauth/ServiceNowOAuthTokenManager.java:53-94 Effort S Risk Medium — token refresh (every ~1h, or on any 401) runs a blocking HTTP POST under a single object monitor (synchronized) and is reached from inside the @Transactional push path via the auth-header callback. During refresh, one thread blocks on the remote token endpoint while holding both its DB connection and the lock; every other caller needing a token blocks on that lock, so a slow token endpoint stalls multiple integration requests at once.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/servicenow/oauth/ServiceNowOAuthTokenManager.java:53-94
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/integrations/servicenow/client/LiveServiceNowClient.java:137-147

Description

ServiceNowOAuthTokenManager.getAccessToken() (line 53) and refresh() (line 61) are both 'synchronized' on the manager instance. refresh() performs a blocking restClient.post() to the token URL (lines 76-81). getAccessToken() is invoked from LiveServiceNowClient.authHeader() (lines 137-147), which runs while building every outbound request — i.e. inside the @Transactional push()/update() flow. When the cached token is within the 60s expiry skew (line 33 EXPIRY_SKEW) or after a 401, the next caller triggers a blocking remote fetch while holding the monitor; all other threads calling getAccessToken() queue behind that lock. Combined with PERF-IO-001, the refreshing thread also holds its pooled DB connection for the duration of the token fetch.

Root cause

A coarse-grained 'synchronized' guards the entire refresh including the blocking network call, rather than only the cached-slot read/write, so the remote latency is held under the lock. The refresh is reached transitively from within an open transaction, compounding the connection-hold problem.

Evidence / proof
ServiceNowOAuthTokenManager.java:53 'public synchronized String getAccessToken()'; line 61 'public synchronized String refresh()'; lines 76-81 blocking 'restClient.post()....body(Map.class)' inside the synchronized method. Reached via LiveServiceNowClient.java:139-140 'case OAUTH2_CLIENT_CREDENTIALS -> h.setBearerAuth(tokenManager.getAccessToken());' inside authHeader(), called from createIncident()/getIncident()/updateIncident() which run under ServiceNowOutboundService @Transactional methods. CrowdStrike has the analogous CrowdStrikeOAuthTokenManager used by LiveCrowdStrikeClient.authHeader() (LiveCrowdStrikeClient.java:234-239).

Real-world impact

On token expiry (hourly) or a Falcon/ServiceNow secret rotation (401 path), the first integration push pays the full token-endpoint latency under the lock and under an open transaction; concurrent integration requests block on the lock and cannot proceed, amplifying connection-hold and tail latency precisely during credential refresh windows. A slow or flaky token endpoint can briefly serialise the whole integration subsystem.

Reproduction

1) ServiceNow LIVE with OAUTH2_CLIENT_CREDENTIALS; point token-url at an endpoint that delays the token response by 10s. 2) Let the cached token reach the 60s expiry skew. 3) Fire several concurrent /test-push calls. 4) Observe exactly one thread doing the token fetch (10s) while the others block on the monitor, all within their transactions/connections; measure the resulting 10s tail on every concurrent push.

Resolution

Narrow the lock so the blocking HTTP fetch happens outside the monitor (double-checked refresh, or single-flight via AtomicReference + a separate guarded fetch), and ensure token acquisition does not occur inside an open DB transaction (fixed transitively by PERF-IO-001 moving the whole client call out of @Transactional). Optionally refresh tokens proactively on a background scheduler before expiry so the request path never pays refresh latency.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
public synchronized String getAccessToken() {
    if (cachedToken != null && Instant.now().isBefore(cachedExpiry.minus(EXPIRY_SKEW))) return cachedToken;
    return refresh(); // blocking restClient.post() executed while holding the monitor
}
▲ After (fixed)
public String getAccessToken() {
    String t = cachedToken;
    if (t != null && Instant.now().isBefore(cachedExpiry.minus(EXPIRY_SKEW))) return t; // fast path, no lock
    return refreshSingleFlight();
}
private String refreshSingleFlight() {
    // single-flight: only one thread fetches; others await the result without
    // serialising the network call under a coarse 'synchronized' on the hot read path.
}
References: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-checked_locking · https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/essential/concurrency/syncrgb.html
MediumPERF-IX-002Early core-module migrations (compliance, incident, tprm) create tables with zero secondary indexes — inconsistent indexing discipline left foundational registers unindexed
✎ AdjustedPerformanceDatabase Indexing / Schema Standards▾
Adversarial verification: adjusted (severity High→Medium) — Verified: V3__compliance_module.sql (3 tables), V4__incident_module.sql (1 table) and V7__tprm_module.sql (2 tables) contain 0 CREATE INDEX statements while V8__evidence_module.sql has 8; compliance.findings declares FK_findings_assessment on assessment_id (V3:103-104) with no backing index; no later migration backfills indexes onto these exact tables. The inconsistency is real. But these are low-cardinality GRC registers (controls/assessments/findings/vendors) with a clustered PK, where table scans remain acceptable at realistic data volumes, and dev uses Python-bootstrapped DBs. A genuine schema-discipline gap with modest real-world impact — Medium, not High.
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V3__compliance_module.sql:1-112 Effort M Risk High: these are the original, most-used GRC registers (controls, assessments, findings, vendors, incidents). They were created first, are referenced by the most screens, and received no indexes at all — neither for tenant scoping nor for their FK joins. The defect is structural (a whole file with 0 indexes), not a one-off omission.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V3__compliance_module.sql:1-112
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V4__incident_module.sql:1-60
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V7__tprm_module.sql:18-90

Description

Indexing discipline in the migration chain is inconsistent: later migrations (V8 evidence: 8 indexes, V11 intake: 5 indexes, and most post-V90 modules) add nonclustered indexes, but the earliest module migrations create their tables with none. V3__compliance_module.sql creates compliance.controls, compliance.assessments and compliance.findings (3 tables, all with organisation_id + status) and contains 0 CREATE INDEX statements. V4__incident_module.sql (1 table) and V7__tprm_module.sql (tprm.vendors + tprm.vendor_assessments) likewise contain 0 indexes. These are not obscure tables — they are the foundational Compliance, Incident and Third-Party registers that nearly every dashboard, report and cross-module link reads.

Root cause

No enforced 'every CREATE TABLE ships with its indexes' rule. The team added indexes ad hoc as performance problems surfaced in later sprints, but never went back to backfill the Sprint-1/Sprint-2 core tables. The dedicated index files under db/sqlserver/indexes/ (which DO contain IX_assessments_org_framework, IX_findings_assessment_status, etc.) were authored separately and never wired into the applied migration chain (see PERF-IX-006).

Evidence / proof
grep -c 'CREATE.*INDEX' per file: V3__compliance_module.sql=0 (3 tables), V4__incident_module.sql=0 (1 table), V7__tprm_module.sql=0 (2 tables) — versus V8__evidence_module.sql=8 (7 tables), V11__intake_records.sql=5 (2 tables). compliance.findings even declares an FK on assessment_id (V3 lines 103-104) with no backing index. tprm.vendors (V7 lines 18-43): organisation_id NOT NULL, status NVARCHAR(50) with CHECK, only PK_vendors clustered on id.

Real-world impact

The most heavily-trafficked registers in the product are the slowest to read at scale. Compliance assessment lists, audit-finding inboxes, and the third-party vendor register all scan. The unindexed FK on compliance.findings.assessment_id forces a scan whenever findings are loaded for an assessment (a per-assessment drill-down) and whenever the parent assessment row is updated/deleted (FK integrity check scans the child).

Reproduction

1) `grep -c -iE 'CREATE.*INDEX' V3__compliance_module.sql` returns 0. 2) Apply V3 to a SQL Server DB and run `SELECT name, type_desc FROM sys.indexes WHERE object_id = OBJECT_ID('compliance.findings');` — only the clustered PK is returned. 3) `SELECT * FROM compliance.findings WHERE assessment_id = 42;` produces a Clustered Index Scan in the actual plan.

Resolution

Backfill index migrations for the V3/V4/V7 core tables (folding the already-authored definitions from db/sqlserver/indexes/02-module-indexes.sql) and institute a review rule that any migration adding a CREATE TABLE must also add (a) a leading-organisation_id index and (b) an index on every FK column.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
-- V3__compliance_module.sql (findings) — no index on the FK column
CREATE TABLE compliance.findings (
    id BIGINT IDENTITY(1,1) NOT NULL,
    organisation_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
    assessment_id BIGINT NULL,
    status NVARCHAR(50) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'OPEN',
    ...
    CONSTRAINT FK_findings_assessment FOREIGN KEY (assessment_id)
        REFERENCES compliance.assessments(id)
);
-- 0 CREATE INDEX in this file
▲ After (fixed)
-- Add at the end of the migration (or a new backfill migration)
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_findings_org_status
    ON compliance.findings (organisation_id, status, severity)
    WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_findings_assessment
    ON compliance.findings (assessment_id)
    WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_controls_org_status
    ON compliance.controls (organisation_id, status) WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_vendors_org_status
    ON tprm.vendors (organisation_id, status) WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO

Description

Of the tables that carry a workflow_status column, several have no index on workflow_status or status: cyber.cyber_action_plans, cyber.cyber_incidents, cyber.vuln_exceptions, cyber.vulnerabilities. These tables are filtered by status in the service layer (workflow state machines) and via repository finders. The cyber.* tables are created by setup_cyber_db.py with only an IDENTITY clustered PK and no secondary indexes at all (the script contains 0 CREATE INDEX), so a query like 'open vulnerabilities for org N' scans the whole table and filters status as a residual predicate. Even the migration-defined cyber.incidents (V1 line 781) only adds IX_cyber_inc_nist on nist_phase, not on (organisation_id, status).

Root cause

Status/workflow_status filtering was implemented in the service layer and repositories but the corresponding columns were never indexed. The dev bootstrap scripts for cyber and bcm (setup_cyber_db.py, setup_bcm_db.py) create tables with no indexes (grep CREATE INDEX = 0 in both), so status-driven queries have no seek path.

Evidence / proof
Parser: 5 tables carry workflow_status; 4 have no index on workflow_status/status (cyber.cyber_action_plans, cyber.cyber_incidents, cyber.vuln_exceptions, cyber.vulnerabilities). setup_cyber_db.py creates 10 cyber tables each with `organisation_id BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1` and `id INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY`, with grep -c 'CREATE INDEX' = 0. Repository pattern counts: findByOrganisationIdAndStatus=30, findByOrganisationIdAndStatusOrderByCreatedAtDesc=25, findByOrganisationIdAndStatusOrderByIdDesc=9.

Real-world impact

Status-filtered dashboards and worklists on cyber tables (open vulnerabilities, in-progress incidents, pending action plans) scan the full table per tenant. Because these tables also lack an org index, the cost is the union of both problems; remediating with a composite (organisation_id, status) index resolves both at once.

Reproduction

1) Run setup_cyber_db.py and `SELECT name FROM sys.indexes WHERE object_id=OBJECT_ID('cyber.vulnerabilities');` — only the PK. 2) `SELECT * FROM cyber.vulnerabilities WHERE organisation_id=1 AND status='OPEN';` shows a scan. 3) Confirm 0 status indexes: `SELECT i.name FROM sys.indexes i JOIN sys.index_columns ic ON i.object_id=ic.object_id JOIN sys.columns c ON ic.object_id=c.object_id AND ic.column_id=c.column_id WHERE c.name IN ('status','workflow_status') AND i.object_id=OBJECT_ID('cyber.vulnerabilities');`

Resolution

Add composite indexes leading with organisation_id and including status/workflow_status for the affected cyber tables, mirroring the design already present in db/sqlserver/indexes/02-module-indexes.sql (IX_vulnerabilities_org_status etc.). Apply via Flyway and update setup_cyber_db.py so the dev DB matches.

    workflow_status NVARCHAR(...)
);
-- no CREATE INDEX in the whole script
▲ After (fixed)

    WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO

MediumPERF-IX-005Foreign-key columns are not indexed — SQL Server does not auto-index FKs, so child-table joins and parent delete/update integrity checks scan
PerformanceDatabase Indexing / Foreign Keys▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V3__compliance_module.sql:103-105 Effort M Risk Medium: SQL Server creates no index for a FOREIGN KEY constraint. ~23 distinct FK column names across the schema are never used as a leading index key, so the standard 'children of parent X' drill-down and the FK integrity check on parent modify both scan the child table. Approximate (name-based) detection keeps this Medium.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V3__compliance_module.sql:103-105
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V7__tprm_module.sql:53-63

Description

Across the applied migrations there are 92 FOREIGN KEY declarations on 55 distinct FK column names. Of those, 23 FK column names are never used as the leading key of any index anywhere in the schema — including assessment_id, asset_id, engagement_id, playbook_id, subprocessor_id, parent_processor_id, parent_audit_id, step_id, snapshot_id, primary_vendor_id, reporting_year_id and others. Because SQL Server does not auto-create an index to back a FOREIGN KEY constraint, every join from parent to child on these columns (and every cascade/integrity check when the parent is modified) performs a scan of the child table. compliance.findings.assessment_id (FK_findings_assessment, V3 lines 103-105) and tprm.vendor_assessments.vendor_id (V7) are concrete examples.

Root cause

FK constraints were declared for referential integrity but the matching index on the FK column was not created. This is a well-known SQL Server gap: PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE auto-create indexes, but FOREIGN KEY does not.

Evidence / proof
Parser: 92 FK declarations, 55 distinct FK columns, 23 of those never appear as a leading index key. compliance.findings: `CONSTRAINT FK_findings_assessment FOREIGN KEY (assessment_id) REFERENCES compliance.assessments(id)` (V3:103-105) with no index on assessment_id. Note detection is name-based (a FK column may be indexed under a synonymous name), so treat the 23 as an upper bound and verify per table.

Real-world impact

Parent->child drill-downs (e.g. all findings for an assessment, all assessments for a vendor, all steps for a playbook) scan the child. Deleting or soft-deleting a parent row triggers a child scan per FK integrity check, slowing writes on busy registers.

Reproduction

1) `SELECT fk.name, c.name col FROM sys.foreign_key_columns fkc JOIN sys.foreign_keys fk ON fkc.constraint_object_id=fk.object_id JOIN sys.columns c ON fkc.parent_object_id=c.object_id AND fkc.parent_column_id=c.column_id;` to list FK columns. 2) For each, `SELECT 1 FROM sys.index_columns ic JOIN sys.columns c2 ON ic.object_id=c2.object_id AND ic.column_id=c2.column_id WHERE ic.key_ordinal=1 AND c2.name=@fkcol AND ic.object_id=@parent;` — empty means unindexed. 3) `SELECT * FROM compliance.findings WHERE assessment_id=1;` shows a scan.

Resolution

Create a nonclustered index on each FK column (leading with organisation_id where the child is tenant-scoped, otherwise leading with the FK column). Add to the schema-standard checklist alongside the org-index rule from PERF-IX-001.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
CONSTRAINT FK_findings_assessment FOREIGN KEY (assessment_id)
    REFERENCES compliance.assessments(id)
-- no index on assessment_id
▲ After (fixed)
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_findings_assessment
    ON compliance.findings (assessment_id) WHERE is_deleted = 0;
GO
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_vendor_assessments_vendor
    ON tprm.vendor_assessments (vendor_id);
GO
References: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/tables/create-foreign-key-relationships#indexes · https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/sql-server-index-design-guide
MediumPERF-IX-006Curated index files (db/sqlserver/indexes/*.sql) are orphaned — never wired into the Flyway chain or the dev Python bootstrap, so ~40 designed indexes never get created
PerformanceDatabase Indexing / Migration Wiring▾
Location tss-grc-backend/db/sqlserver/indexes/01-shared-indexes.sql:1-209 Effort M Risk Medium: the project already CONTAINS well-designed organisation_id/status/FK indexes for iam.users, risk.risks, cyber.assets, compliance.assessments, etc. in db/sqlserver/indexes/01-shared-indexes.sql and 02-module-indexes.sql — but neither file is on the Flyway classpath nor invoked by any setup_*.py, so they are dead. This is the root cause behind several other findings and an easy, high-leverage fix.
tss-grc-backend/db/sqlserver/indexes/01-shared-indexes.sql:1-209
tss-grc-backend/db/sqlserver/indexes/02-module-indexes.sql:1-161
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application-prod.yml:28
tss-grc-backend/db/sqlserver/migrations/README.md:1-60

Description

The repository contains two hand-authored index files: 01-shared-indexes.sql (~25 indexes: organizations, business_units, iam.users, user_roles, controls, workflow_instances, attachments, notifications, audit_logs, licenses) and 02-module-indexes.sql (~15 indexes: risk.risks, risk_assessments, cyber.assets, vulnerabilities, incidents, bcm.*, privacy.*, compliance.*, reporting.*). These define exactly the organisation_id/status/FK composite indexes the other findings call for. However: (a) prod Flyway is configured with `locations: classpath:db/migration/sqlserver` (application-prod.yml:28) — i.e. only the V*.sql files under src/main/resources, NOT tss-grc-backend/db/sqlserver/indexes/; (b) the dev DB is bootstrapped by setup_*.py + seed_real_data.py, none of which reference these files; (c) the only mention of them anywhere in the repo is SESSION_SUMMARY.md. The migrations/README.md even describes a legacy layout (V1.0.13__create_shared_indexes.sql / V1.0.14__create_module_indexes.sql) that does not exist in the actual V1..V224 chain. Net effect: these ~40 designed indexes are never created in any environment.

Root cause

Index DDL was authored as standalone scripts under a parallel db/sqlserver/ tree that was superseded by the consolidated src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V*.sql chain. The migration toward the V* layout never folded the index files in, and the README documenting the intended wiring went stale.

Evidence / proof
application-prod.yml:28 `locations: classpath:db/migration/sqlserver` (resolves under src/main/resources only; the indexes/ files live under tss-grc-backend/db/sqlserver/ and are not on the classpath). `grep -ril '01-shared-indexes|02-module-indexes|sqlserver/indexes'` across *.py/*.md/*.bat/*.ps1/*.sql returns only SESSION_SUMMARY.md. application-dev.yml: flyway.enabled=false and ddl-auto=none, so neither Flyway nor Hibernate creates them in dev; application.yml base uses ddl-auto=validate (Hibernate creates nothing). The 01-shared-indexes.sql file itself contains the missing IX_users_org / IX_users_active_login (lines 40-55) and IX_controls_org_active (lines 86-90) referenced by PERF-IX-003 and PERF-IX-001.

Real-world impact

The team believes the platform is indexed (the files exist and look complete) while production runs with only the inline V* indexes, leaving the gaps quantified in PERF-IX-001..005. This false sense of coverage is itself a risk: a perf regression in prod has no quick lever because the prepared indexes are not deployable as-is.

Reproduction

1) Inspect application-prod.yml:28 — Flyway location does not include db/sqlserver/indexes/. 2) `grep -ril 'sqlserver/indexes'` over the repo returns only SESSION_SUMMARY.md. 3) After a clean Flyway migrate of V1..V224 into a fresh DB, `SELECT name FROM sys.indexes WHERE name LIKE 'IX_users_%';` returns nothing (IX_users_org was never applied).

Resolution

Convert 01-shared-indexes.sql and 02-module-indexes.sql into a properly versioned Flyway migration under src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/ (e.g. V225__shared_and_module_indexes.sql) so they apply in prod, and update the dev bootstrap to run them (or run the same SQL from a setup_indexes.py). Reconcile the index set against PERF-IX-001's gap list before applying. Delete or clearly deprecate the stale migrations/README.md layout.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
# application-prod.yml
flyway:
  locations: classpath:db/migration/sqlserver   # excludes db/sqlserver/indexes/*.sql

# db/sqlserver/indexes/01-shared-indexes.sql, 02-module-indexes.sql
#   -> referenced nowhere except SESSION_SUMMARY.md (orphaned)
▲ After (fixed)
# Move/convert the curated index DDL into the applied chain:
#   src/main/resources/db/migration/sqlserver/V225__shared_and_module_indexes.sql
# containing the contents of 01-shared-indexes.sql + 02-module-indexes.sql
# (wrapped in IF NOT EXISTS guards), then for dev add a setup_indexes.py that
# executes the same SQL after the setup_*_db.py bootstrap.

tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/controlmap/service/ControlMapService.java:49-53
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/controlmap/service/ControlMapService.java:113-127
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/controlmap/service/ControlMapService.java:166-181

Description

getMappings (49-53) maps each ControlLink via resolve(scId, satisfaction). resolve (166-181) calls subControlRepository.findById, then controlRepository.findById(sc.getControlId()), then frameworkRepository.findById(ctrl.getFrameworkId()) - three per-row lookups. getEvidenceReadiness (113-127) repeats the identical three-findById chain inside its per-link loop. The aggregate rollups in getEvidenceReadiness (95-109) are correctly written as GROUP BY queries, but the sub-control/control/framework metadata resolution is per-row.

Root cause

Per-row FK chasing for reference data (the framework/control/sub-control catalog is shared, static, and small) instead of batch-loading the distinct ids or caching the catalog. The sub-control -> control -> framework chain is fixed reference data ideal for a one-time load or Caffeine cache.

Evidence / proof
ControlMapService.java:168 `EvidenceSubControl sc = subControlRepository.findById(scId).orElse(null);`
:173 `EvidenceControl ctrl = controlRepository.findById(sc.getControlId()).orElse(null);`
:176 `EvidenceFramework fw = frameworkRepository.findById(ctrl.getFrameworkId()).orElse(null);`
The same triple appears at lines 115/121/124 inside getEvidenceReadiness's per-link loop. Query count for N mapped sub-controls = 1 (links) + 3N.

Real-world impact

Moderate latency on the control-map and evidence-readiness panels; unnecessary DB chatter for data that never changes within a request and is identical across tenants. Scales linearly with the number of sub-controls mapped to an entity.

Reproduction

1. Map an entity to several sub-controls via setMappings. 2. Enable SQL logging. 3. Call getMappings(entityType, entityId) (and getEvidenceReadiness). 4. Observe three findById SELECTs per returned mapping row.

Resolution

Batch-resolve: collect the distinct subControlIds from the links, load them with findAllById, collect their controlIds and load with findAllById, collect frameworkIds and load with findAllById, then resolve from in-memory maps. Alternatively, since framework/control/sub-control are a static shared catalog, cache the lookup maps with the existing Caffeine cache (@Cacheable) and resolve from cache.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
public List<ControlLinkResponse> getMappings(String entityType, Long entityId) {
    return repo.findByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityId(orgId, entityType, entityId)
        .stream().map(l -> resolve(l.getSubControlId(), l.getSatisfaction())).toList();
}

private ControlLinkResponse resolve(Long scId, String satisfaction) {
    EvidenceSubControl sc = subControlRepository.findById(scId).orElse(null);
    EvidenceControl ctrl = controlRepository.findById(sc.getControlId()).orElse(null);
    EvidenceFramework fw = frameworkRepository.findById(ctrl.getFrameworkId()).orElse(null);
    ...
}
▲ After (fixed)
public List<ControlLinkResponse> getMappings(String entityType, Long entityId) {
    List<ControlLink> links = repo.findByOrganisationIdAndEntityTypeAndEntityId(orgId, entityType, entityId);
    Set<Long> scIds = links.stream().map(ControlLink::getSubControlId).collect(toSet());
    Map<Long, EvidenceSubControl> scs = subControlRepository.findAllById(scIds).stream().collect(toMap(EvidenceSubControl::getId, s -> s));
    Set<Long> ctrlIds = scs.values().stream().map(EvidenceSubControl::getControlId).collect(toSet());
    Map<Long, EvidenceControl> ctrls = controlRepository.findAllById(ctrlIds).stream().collect(toMap(EvidenceControl::getId, c -> c));
    Set<Long> fwIds = ctrls.values().stream().map(EvidenceControl::getFrameworkId).collect(toSet());
    Map<Long, EvidenceFramework> fws = frameworkRepository.findAllById(fwIds).stream().collect(toMap(EvidenceFramework::getId, f -> f));
    return links.stream().map(l -> resolveFromMaps(l, scs, ctrls, fws)).toList(); // zero per-row queries
}
References: https://vladmihalcea.com/n-plus-1-query-problem/ · CLAUDE.md — Caching: Caffeine L1 (suited to static reference catalogs) · https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/integration/cache/annotations.html
MediumPERF-NQ-007TreatmentPlan @OneToMany actions is EAGER, causing per-plan child query on list views (and a count that loads all children)
PerformanceEAGER Fetch / N+1 Query▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk_lc/entity/TreatmentPlan.java:77-79 Effort M Risk Medium: TreatmentPlan.actions is an EAGER @OneToMany. listForOrg() / listForRisk() load the plans for a tenant and Hibernate eagerly issues a separate actions SELECT per plan (TreatmentPlanDto.from reads e.getActions()). For P plans that is 1 + P queries. Additionally generateExternalId() calls .size() on the full plan list purely to count, materialising every plan and its actions just to derive the next sequence number.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk_lc/entity/TreatmentPlan.java:77-79
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk_lc/service/TreatmentPlanService.java:94-99
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk_lc/service/TreatmentPlanService.java:101-106
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk_lc/service/TreatmentPlanService.java:197-201
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk_lc/dto/TreatmentPlanDto.java:43

Description

TreatmentPlan.actions is annotated @OneToMany(..., fetch = FetchType.EAGER) (TreatmentPlan.java:77). TreatmentPlanService.listForOrg() (94-99) and listForRisk() (101-106) load all plans for the tenant/risk and map each via TreatmentPlanDto.from, which dereferences e.getActions() (TreatmentPlanDto.java:43). Because the collection is EAGER and the finder returns a list (not a fetch-join), Hibernate issues one actions SELECT per plan. Separately, generateExternalId() (197-201) does repo.findByOrganisationIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(orgId).size() - loading every plan (and, due to EAGER, every plan's actions) merely to compute count+1 for the next external id.

Root cause

EAGER child collection on a list-rendered entity, plus a count derived by materialising and sizing a full entity list instead of a COUNT query. EAGER ToMany cannot be batch-fetched for a list/page result, so it degrades to per-row child loads.

Evidence / proof
TreatmentPlan.java:77 `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "plan", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true, fetch = FetchType.EAGER)` -> `List<TreatmentAction> actions`.
TreatmentPlanDto.java:43 `.actions(e.getActions() == null ? List.of() : e.getActions().stream().map(TreatmentActionDto::from)...)` - touches the collection for every plan.
TreatmentPlanService.java:199 `long count = repo.findByOrganisationIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(orgId).size();` - full materialisation to count.

Real-world impact

Treatment-plan list endpoints scale at 1 + P queries with EAGER children; the external-id generator loads the entire plan+action graph on every create. Moderate latency and DB load that grows with the number of treatment plans per tenant. The EAGER collection also blocks adopting projection-based list reads later.

Reproduction

1. Seed several treatment plans, each with multiple treatment actions. 2. Enable SQL logging. 3. Call listForOrg(): observe one treatment_actions SELECT per plan in addition to the plans query. 4. Call create(): observe generateExternalId loading all plans (and their actions) to compute .size().

Resolution

Change actions to FetchType.LAZY. For list views that need actions, add a JOIN FETCH / @EntityGraph finder so the collection is fetched in one query; for list views that do not need actions, the DTO simply omits them. Replace generateExternalId's list().size() with a repository count query (e.g. countByOrganisationId) - the repository already exposes countByOrganisationIdAndStatus, so add countByOrganisationId.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// TreatmentPlan.java
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "plan", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true, fetch = FetchType.EAGER)
@Where(clause = "is_deleted = 0")
private List<TreatmentAction> actions = new ArrayList<>();

// TreatmentPlanService.java
private String generateExternalId(Long orgId) {
    long count = repo.findByOrganisationIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(orgId).size();
    return String.format("TP-%d-%03d", LocalDateTime.now().getYear(), count + 1);
}
▲ After (fixed)
// TreatmentPlan.java
@OneToMany(mappedBy = "plan", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true, fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
@Where(clause = "is_deleted = 0")
private List<TreatmentAction> actions = new ArrayList<>();

// TreatmentPlanRepository.java
@Query("SELECT DISTINCT p FROM TreatmentPlan p LEFT JOIN FETCH p.actions WHERE p.organisationId = :orgId ORDER BY p.createdAt DESC")
List<TreatmentPlan> findWithActionsByOrg(@Param("orgId") Long orgId);
long countByOrganisationId(Long organisationId);

// TreatmentPlanService.java
private String generateExternalId(Long orgId) {
    long count = repo.countByOrganisationId(orgId); // COUNT query, no materialisation
    return String.format("TP-%d-%03d", LocalDateTime.now().getYear(), count + 1);
}
References: https://vladmihalcea.com/eager-fetching-is-a-code-smell/ · https://docs.spring.io/spring-data/jpa/reference/jpa/entity-graph.html · https://thorben-janssen.com/association-mappings-multiple-eager-fetchtype-list/
MediumPERF-PG-002TPRM /assessments loads ALL vendors via Pageable.unpaged() then runs an unbounded IN-clause over every vendor id
PerformanceUnbounded result set / N+IN query▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/service/TprmService.java:83-92 Effort M Risk Medium: the endpoint is reachable by any TPRM:READ user and degrades super-linearly with vendor count (full vendor scan + a single IN-list with one parameter per vendor). Lower blast radius than PERF-PG-001 because vendor counts are typically smaller than asset/finding registers, but the explicit use of Pageable.unpaged() defeats the very pagination the module otherwise offers.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/service/TprmService.java:83-92
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/controller/TprmController.java:64-68
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/tprm/repository/VendorAssessmentRepository.java:10-13

Description

GET /api/v1/tprm/assessments (no vendorId param) calls TprmService.listAssessments(null). The implementation first fetches EVERY vendor for the tenant using vendorRepo.findByOrganisationId(orgId, Pageable.unpaged()) — explicitly disabling pagination — maps them to a List<Long> of ids, then calls assessmentRepo.findByVendorIdIn(vendorIds), which has no Pageable and emits a SQL IN (?, ?, ... ) with one bind parameter per vendor. The result List<VendorAssessment> contains every assessment for the org. So a single request does a full vendor table scan plus a full assessment fetch, with the IN-list growing with vendor count. SQL Server has a practical/parser ceiling on IN-list and parameter counts (and a 2100-parameter limit), so beyond a few thousand vendors this can also fail outright rather than merely being slow.

Root cause

The list endpoint returns the full register but the data model has no direct organisation_id on VendorAssessment, so the author worked around it by materialising all vendor ids client-side (in the service) and using findByVendorIdIn. Pageable.unpaged() was used to grab the whole vendor set, which is the anti-pattern.

Evidence / proof
TprmService.listAssessments (lines 83-92):
  public List<VendorAssessment> listAssessments(Long vendorId) {
      if (vendorId != null) { ... return assessmentRepo.findByVendorId(vendorId, Pageable.unpaged()).getContent(); }
      List<Long> vendorIds = vendorRepo.findByOrganisationId(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(), Pageable.unpaged())
          .map(Vendor::getId).getContent();
      return assessmentRepo.findByVendorIdIn(vendorIds);
  }
VendorAssessmentRepository (lines 10-13): no paged finder for the org-wide list:
  Page<VendorAssessment> findByVendorId(Long vendorId, Pageable pageable);
  List<VendorAssessment> findByVendorIdIn(List<Long> vendorIds);   // unbounded
Controller (lines 64-68): public List<VendorAssessment> listAssessments(@RequestParam(required = false) Long vendorId)

Real-world impact

Two unbounded fetches per request plus a parameterised IN-clause that scales with vendor count. On large tenants this is both slow (two full result sets into the heap) and potentially failing (SQL Server parameter/IN-list ceiling), turning a routine register read into an error or a long-running query that holds a DB connection.

Reproduction

1. Seed many vendors and assessments for organisation_id = 1.
2. Call GET /api/v1/tprm/assessments (omit vendorId).
3. Enable Hibernate SQL logging and observe (a) SELECT of all vendors, (b) a single SELECT ... WHERE vendor_id IN (?, ?, ...) with one bind var per vendor, and the full assessment list returned with no page envelope. Scale vendors past a few thousand to hit the IN/parameter ceiling.

Resolution

Add organisation_id (or a join) to VendorAssessment and a paged org-scoped finder: Page<VendorAssessment> findByOrganisationId(Long orgId, Pageable pageable). Change the controller to return Page<VendorAssessment> with @PageableDefault and the service to delegate directly to the paged finder, eliminating both the Pageable.unpaged() vendor scan and the IN-list. For the vendorId-scoped branch, accept a Pageable and return a Page instead of .getContent().

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// TprmController.java
@GetMapping("/assessments")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('TPRM', 'READ')")
public List<VendorAssessment> listAssessments(@RequestParam(required = false) Long vendorId) {
    return tprmService.listAssessments(vendorId);
}

// TprmService.java
public List<VendorAssessment> listAssessments(Long vendorId) {
    if (vendorId != null) { getVendor(vendorId); return assessmentRepo.findByVendorId(vendorId, Pageable.unpaged()).getContent(); }
    List<Long> vendorIds = vendorRepo.findByOrganisationId(TenantContext.getCurrentTenant(), Pageable.unpaged())
        .map(Vendor::getId).getContent();
    return assessmentRepo.findByVendorIdIn(vendorIds);
}
▲ After (fixed)
// TprmController.java
@GetMapping("/assessments")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('TPRM', 'READ')")
public Page<VendorAssessment> listAssessments(@RequestParam(required = false) Long vendorId,
                                              @PageableDefault(size = 20) Pageable pageable) {
    return tprmService.listAssessments(vendorId, pageable);
}

// TprmService.java
public Page<VendorAssessment> listAssessments(Long vendorId, Pageable pageable) {
    Long orgId = TenantContext.getCurrentTenant();
    if (vendorId != null) { getVendor(vendorId); return assessmentRepo.findByVendorId(vendorId, pageable); }
    return assessmentRepo.findByOrganisationId(orgId, pageable); // requires org_id column + finder
}
References: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/odbc/reference/develop-app/use-table-valued-parameters-odbc · https://docs.spring.io/spring-data/jpa/reference/repositories/query-methods-details.html#repositories.special-parameters · SQL Server limit of 2100 parameters per statement
MediumPERF-PG-003No global maximum page size — paginated Page<> endpoints accept arbitrary ?size= and can be coerced to return all rows
PerformanceUnbounded result set / missing page-size cap▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application.yml:1-1 Effort S Risk Medium: turns the otherwise-correct Page<> endpoints (risk, incident, compliance, evidence, users, vendors, cyber, etc.) back into unbounded queries on demand. Any authenticated reader can request ?size=2147483647 and force a full-table fetch, so the pagination defence is bypassable.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/risk/controller/RiskController.java:30-35
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/iam/controller/UserController.java:26-35
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/platform/auditlog/controller/AuditLogController.java:32-41

Description

The project relies on @PageableDefault(size = 20) for the DEFAULT page size, but there is no configured maximum. A scan for spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size / PageableHandlerMethodArgumentResolver.setMaxPageSize / maxPageSize across src/main returned no matches, so Spring's resolver uses its built-in default behaviour where the client-supplied ?size= overrides the default with no server-side ceiling. Consequently every 'correctly paginated' endpoint — e.g. GET /api/v1/risk/risks?size=1000000, GET /api/v1/admin/users?size=1000000, GET /api/v1/incidents?size=1000000 — will attempt to fetch and serialise that many rows in one page, re-introducing exactly the unbounded-result-set problem the Page<> envelope was meant to prevent. AuditLogController even hand-rolls page/size as plain @RequestParam(defaultValue = "100") int size with no clamp, so the same applies there.

Root cause

Spring Data web pagination ships without a max page size unless one is configured; the platform never set spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size (nor clamped hand-rolled size params), so the per-endpoint @PageableDefault only constrains the default, not the maximum a caller may request.

Evidence / proof
grep -rniE 'max-page-size|maxPageSize|setMaxPageSize|PageableHandlerMethodArgumentResolver|spring.data.web' src/main  ->  (no matches)
RiskController.java:32  @PageableDefault(size = 20, sort = "createdAt") Pageable pageable   // default only; no max
AuditLogController.java:38-39  @RequestParam(defaultValue="0") int page, @RequestParam(defaultValue="100") int size  // unclamped
Result: ?size=<arbitrary> is honoured on all Page<> endpoints, defeating pagination.

Real-world impact

The pagination control protecting ~122 endpoints is bypassable by a query parameter. A single authenticated user can issue ?size=2_000_000_000 against the largest register and force a full-table fetch + serialisation, reproducing the heap pressure / latency / OOM risk of PERF-PG-001 even on the modules that were done correctly. It also undermines any fix for PERF-PG-001 unless the cap is added at the same time.

Reproduction

1. Authenticate as any READ user. 2. Call GET /api/v1/risk/risks?size=1000000 (or /api/v1/admin/users?size=1000000, /api/v1/audit-log?size=1000000). 3. Observe the server attempts to return up to that many rows in one page (no clamp); response size and DB fetch scale with the requested size rather than being capped.

Resolution

Set a global maximum page size via configuration (spring.data.web.pageable.max-page-size: 100) so the resolver clamps any oversized ?size=. For hand-rolled size params (AuditLogController, CyberController pageOf, etc.), clamp explicitly with Math.min(size, MAX). Optionally also set spring.data.web.pageable.default-page-size to centralise the default. Combine with PERF-PG-001 so that both the missing pagination and the missing cap are closed together.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
# application.yml — no pagination limits configured
spring:
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false
# (no spring.data.web.pageable.* keys present anywhere)
▲ After (fixed)
# application.yml
spring:
  data:
    web:
      pageable:
        default-page-size: 20
        max-page-size: 100   # resolver clamps any client-supplied ?size= to <=100
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false

// AuditLogController.java (hand-rolled size) — clamp explicitly
int safeSize = Math.min(Math.max(size, 1), 100);
return service.list(actionType, sourceModule, severity, page, safeSize);

LowPERF-IO-005Hikari pool sizing (base=20 / dev=10) is undersized for blocking-integration workloads and dev overrides drop leak-detection visibility
PerformanceConnection-pool sizing / configuration▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application.yml:19-26 Effort S Risk Low — sizing itself is reasonable for pure DB work against SQL Server Express, but given the blocking-I/O-under-transaction patterns (PERF-IO-001..004) the effective pool capacity is much lower than the nominal 20/10. The k6 breakpoint run did not reach an error threshold in the captured log (no failed iterations through ~67 VUs / ~325 iters/s on a read-only endpoint that does not touch the integration paths), so this is a forward-looking sizing/observability concern rather than an observed outage.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application.yml:19-26
tss-grc-backend/src/main/resources/application-dev.yml:27-29

Description

The base Hikari pool is maximum-pool-size=20 with minimum-idle=5, connection-timeout=30000, leak-detection-threshold=60000 (application.yml:21-26). The dev profile overrides ONLY minimum-idle (2) and maximum-pool-size (10) (application-dev.yml:27-29), inheriting the base connection-timeout and leak-detection-threshold. Two observations: (1) Sizing of 20 is fine for CPU-bound DB work on SQL Server Express (Express has no hard low connection cap; the real Express limits are ~1.4 GB buffer pool / 4 cores / 10 GB data), but it is small once connections are routinely tied up for seconds-to-minutes by the blocking integration paths — the formula connections = ((core_count x 2) + effective_spindle_count) assumes connections are released quickly, which the integration code violates. (2) The leak-detection-threshold=60000 is below the worst-case integration connection-hold computed in PERF-IO-003 (~121s for ServiceNow), so once those slow paths run they will emit spurious leak warnings, eroding trust in the leak detector. The k6 load.js exercises only GET /api/v1/risk/risks (load.js readRisks), which never touches the integration adapters, so the load test does not characterise the at-risk path.

Root cause

Pool size and connection-timeout were tuned for fast DB-only requests; the integration adapters' blocking-under-transaction behaviour was not accounted for, so nominal pool capacity overstates real capacity. The leak-detection threshold is not aligned with the (unintended) long connection holds the integration code can produce.

Evidence / proof
application.yml:22 'maximum-pool-size: 20'; :24 'connection-timeout: 30000'; :26 'leak-detection-threshold: 60000'. application-dev.yml:29 'maximum-pool-size: 10' (overrides only size + minimum-idle; inherits the rest). k6 load.js: readRisks() hits GET /api/v1/risk/risks only; k6.log shows the breakpoint scenario climbing to ~67 VUs / ~325.75 iters/s with '0 interrupted iterations' and no captured error spike (the log ends mid-breakpoint at ~93%; no final handleSummary block / k6-summary.json was produced).

Real-world impact

Under any real integration load the platform behaves as if it had far fewer than 20 connections, making pool exhaustion (PERF-IO-001/002) reachable at modest concurrency. The mismatch between leak-detection-threshold (60s) and integration connection-hold (up to ~121s) will generate misleading leak warnings. The current load test gives false confidence because it does not exercise the integration code paths.

Reproduction

1) Compare application.yml:19-26 vs application-dev.yml:27-29 — confirm dev inherits connection-timeout/leak-detection from base. 2) Note k6 load.js exercises only a read endpoint. 3) Combine with the PERF-IO-001 reproduction to show exhaustion at < 20 concurrent integration pushes despite a nominal pool of 20.

Resolution

Primary fix is PERF-IO-001..004 (stop holding connections across remote I/O). Independently: (a) make the integration HTTP work run on a bounded, separate executor/outbox so it cannot consume the primary DB pool at all; (b) once remote calls are out of transactions, keep maximum-pool-size=20 for base but add a dedicated, smaller bounded thread pool for outbound integration work; (c) raise leak-detection-threshold above the realistic worst-case hold OR (preferably) reduce the worst-case hold below 60s so the existing threshold stays meaningful; (d) extend the k6 suite with a scenario that drives the integration endpoints (test-push / poll) to characterise the actually-at-risk path.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
# application.yml
hikari:
  maximum-pool-size: 20
  connection-timeout: 30000
  leak-detection-threshold: 60000
# application-dev.yml (overrides only size + idle)
hikari:
  minimum-idle: 2
  maximum-pool-size: 10
▲ After (fixed)
# Keep DB pool for fast DB work; run integration HTTP off-pool (async/outbox).
# After PERF-IO-001..004, integration calls no longer borrow DB connections, so
# 20 (base) / 10 (dev) is adequate. Ensure leak-detection-threshold stays above the
# realistic max DB-only transaction time (now << 60s) so it flags only true leaks.
# Add a k6 scenario that exercises /api/v1/integrations/*/test-push to load-test the
# real at-risk path (current load.js hits only GET /api/v1/risk/risks).

LowPERF-NQ-006BcmDependencyGraphService re-queries BIA per plan despite already holding all BIAs in memory
PerformanceN+1 Query / Redundant Fetch▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/cycle/service/BcmDependencyGraphService.java:61-142 Effort S Risk Low: build() loads all BIAs up front (paged at 1000), then in the BCP/DRP plan loop calls bias.findByIdAndOrganisationId per plan to perform RTO-mismatch detection. That is one extra query per plan for data already resident in memory. Bounded by plan count (paged at 1000) and only on the dependency-graph endpoint, so impact is limited, but it is a clear avoidable N+1.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/cycle/service/BcmDependencyGraphService.java:71-73
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/cycle/service/BcmDependencyGraphService.java:106-138
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/cycle/service/BcmDependencyGraphService.java:127

Description

build() first loads all BIAs for the tenant into biaRows (lines 71-73). It then loops over BCP/DRP plans (line 106) and, for each plan with a sourceBiaId and rtoHours, calls bias.findByIdAndOrganisationId(p.getSourceBiaId(), org) (line 127) to compare the plan's RTO against the source BIA's RTO. Since every BIA was already loaded at line 71, this is a redundant per-plan query - the BIA could be looked up from a Map<Long, BcmBiaAssessment> built from biaRows.

Root cause

The already-materialised BIA list is not indexed into a map for reuse; the RTO-mismatch check re-fetches the parent BIA from the repository inside the plan loop.

Evidence / proof
Line 71-73 `List<BcmBiaAssessment> biaRows = bias.findByOrganisationIdOrderByIdDesc(org, PageRequest.of(0, 1000)).getContent();`
Line 127 `bias.findByIdAndOrganisationId(p.getSourceBiaId(), org).ifPresent(b -> { ... });` inside `for (BcpPlan p : plans...)`.
Query count adds one BIA SELECT per plan that has a sourceBiaId, all redundant because biaRows already contains them.

Real-world impact

One redundant DB round trip per BCP/DRP plan on the dependency-graph build. Minor latency and DB load; the feature is called out as a common first-demo screen, so the waste is visible under demo conditions but bounded.

Reproduction

1. Seed BIAs and BCP/DRP plans with sourceBiaId set and rtoHours populated. 2. Enable SQL logging. 3. Call BcmDependencyGraphService.build() (the /bcm-dependency graph endpoint). 4. Observe one BIA SELECT per plan in addition to the initial bulk BIA query.

Resolution

Build a Map<Long, BcmBiaAssessment> from biaRows once, and resolve the source BIA from that map inside the plan loop instead of calling bias.findByIdAndOrganisationId. This removes the per-plan query entirely and reuses data already in the persistence context.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
List<BcmBiaAssessment> biaRows = bias.findByOrganisationIdOrderByIdDesc(org, PageRequest.of(0, 1000)).getContent();
...
for (BcpPlan p : plans.findByOrganisationIdOrderByIdDesc(org, PageRequest.of(0,1000)).getContent()) {
    ...
    if (p.getSourceBiaId() != null && p.getRtoHours() != null) {
        bias.findByIdAndOrganisationId(p.getSourceBiaId(), org).ifPresent(b -> { // per-plan query
            if (b.getRtoHours() != null && p.getRtoHours() > b.getRtoHours()) { ... }
        });
    }
}
▲ After (fixed)
List<BcmBiaAssessment> biaRows = bias.findByOrganisationIdOrderByIdDesc(org, PageRequest.of(0, 1000)).getContent();
Map<Long, BcmBiaAssessment> biaById = biaRows.stream().collect(Collectors.toMap(BcmBiaAssessment::getId, b -> b));
...
for (BcpPlan p : plans.findByOrganisationIdOrderByIdDesc(org, PageRequest.of(0,1000)).getContent()) {
    ...
    if (p.getSourceBiaId() != null && p.getRtoHours() != null) {
        BcmBiaAssessment b = biaById.get(p.getSourceBiaId()); // in-memory, no query
        if (b != null && b.getRtoHours() != null && p.getRtoHours() > b.getRtoHours()) { ... }
    }
}
References: https://vladmihalcea.com/n-plus-1-query-problem/ · https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/util/stream/Collectors.html#toMap-java.util.function.Function-java.util.function.Function-
LowPERF-PG-004Cyber & SCM expose explicit '/all' register dumps (assets, controls, vendors) that bypass the module's own pagination
PerformanceUnbounded result set / intentional full-dump endpoint without cap▾
Location tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/controller/CyberController.java:79-83 Effort M Risk Low: these endpoints are deliberately unpaged for UI dropdowns, but they carry no server-side row cap, so they grow unbounded with the asset/control/vendor inventory. Lower severity because they are typically backing select boxes (smaller cardinality and used less often than the main register), but they still allow a full-table fetch on demand.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/controller/CyberController.java:79-83
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/controller/CyberController.java:329-333
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/controller/CyberController.java:55-59
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/service/CyberService.java:154-156
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/service/CyberService.java:179-181
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/service/CyberService.java:494-496
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/scm/controller/ScmController.java:42-45

Description

Several modules pair a properly-paginated register endpoint with an explicit '/all' (or root) variant that returns the entire org-scoped set, for populating UI dropdowns. CyberController exposes GET /api/v1/cyber/controls (Page<CyberControl>) alongside GET /api/v1/cyber/controls/all (List<CyberControl>), and GET /api/v1/cyber/assets (Page) alongside GET /api/v1/cyber/assets/all (List), plus GET /api/v1/cyber/frameworks (List). Each '/all' calls cyberService.getAllControls/getAllAssets/getFrameworks which delegate to controlRepo/assetRepo/frameworkRepo.findAllByOrganisationId(orgId) — repository finders that return List with no Pageable. ScmController.allVendors() is documented '/vendors/all — List all vendors (no pagination — for dropdowns)'. The asset inventory in particular (regulator-grade asset register) can grow very large, so a dropdown that fetches every asset is unbounded.

Root cause

Intentional convenience endpoints for select-box population that were never given an upper bound. The repository exposes both findByOrganisationId(orgId, Pageable) and an unbounded findAllByOrganisationId(orgId); the '/all' endpoints deliberately call the unbounded one.

Evidence / proof
CyberController.java:79-83  @GetMapping("/controls/all") public ResponseEntity<List<CyberControl>> getAllControls() { return ok(cyberService.getAllControls(orgId())); }
CyberController.java:329-333 @GetMapping("/assets/all")   public ResponseEntity<List<CyberAsset>> getAllAssets()  { return ok(cyberService.getAllAssets(orgId())); }
CyberService.java:179-181 getAllControls -> controlRepo.findAllByOrganisationId(orgId)
CyberService.java:494-496 getAllAssets   -> assetRepo.findAllByOrganisationId(orgId)
CyberAssetRepository: List<CyberAsset> findAllByOrganisationId(Long orgId)  // no Pageable (paged variant findByOrganisationId(orgId, Pageable) also exists)
ScmController.java:42-45 @GetMapping("/vendors/all") @Operation(summary="List all vendors (no pagination — for dropdowns)") public List<VendorDtos.Response> allVendors() { return service.allVendors(); }

Real-world impact

On large tenants a dropdown population request pulls the entire asset/control/vendor inventory into memory and over the wire. For the cyber asset register (which the platform markets as regulator-grade and can hold thousands of assets) this is a meaningful per-request cost and another path to the PERF-PG-001 heap-pressure problem, even though the main register endpoint is paginated.

Reproduction

1. Seed many cyber assets for organisation_id = 1. 2. Call GET /api/v1/cyber/assets/all. 3. Observe the full asset set is returned with no page envelope and no size cap, regardless of how many rows exist (contrast GET /api/v1/cyber/assets which caps at 20).

Resolution

Cap the '/all' endpoints server-side. Prefer returning a lightweight projection (id + label only) for dropdowns and hard-limit the row count (e.g. PageRequest.of(0, 500)); if a register legitimately exceeds the cap, the UI should switch to a server-side type-ahead search endpoint instead of a full dump. At minimum add an explicit limit so the query can never fetch the entire table.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// CyberController.java
@GetMapping("/assets/all")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('CYBER', 'READ')")
public ResponseEntity<List<CyberAsset>> getAllAssets() {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(cyberService.getAllAssets(orgId()));
}

// CyberService.java
public List<CyberAsset> getAllAssets(Long orgId) {
    return assetRepo.findAllByOrganisationId(orgId);   // unbounded
}
▲ After (fixed)
// CyberController.java — lightweight, capped picker for dropdowns
@GetMapping("/assets/picker")
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission('CYBER', 'READ')")
public ResponseEntity<List<AssetOption>> assetPicker(
        @RequestParam(required = false) String q) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok(cyberService.assetPicker(orgId(), q)); // id+name only, capped
}

// CyberService.java
private static final int PICKER_CAP = 500;
public List<AssetOption> assetPicker(Long orgId, String q) {
    var page = PageRequest.of(0, PICKER_CAP, Sort.by("name"));
    return assetRepo.findOptionsByOrganisationId(orgId, q, page) // projection query, capped
            .stream().toList();
}
References: https://docs.spring.io/spring-data/jpa/reference/repositories/projections.html · https://docs.spring.io/spring-data/jpa/reference/repositories/query-methods-details.html#repositories.limit-query-result · OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption
InfoPERF-FE-006Lighthouse /login (Performance 38) was captured against the Vite DEV server (unbundled, unminified) — FCP 37s / LCP 72s / unminified-JS 7.5 MB are dev-mode artefacts, not production metrics
PerformanceMeasurement validity / methodology▾
Location audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json:1-1 Effort S Risk Informational: this finding does not describe a code defect but warns that the headline numbers (Performance 38, FCP 37.4s, LCP 72.3s, unminified-javascript est. savings 7,521 KiB) come from a development build and overstate the production penalty. Acting on the raw dev numbers without a production-build re-measure would mis-prioritise the audit. The structural findings (PERF-FE-001..005) remain valid regardless.
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json:1-1
tss-grc-ui-v2/vite.config.ts:20-27

Description

The Lighthouse report's network-requests and total-byte-weight items are all served from http://localhost:5173 — the Vite dev server (vite.config.ts server.port 5173) — including raw unbundled modules like /src/App.tsx, /src/translations/ar.ts, /@vite/client, /@react-refresh and /node_modules/.vite/deps/*. In dev mode Vite serves unminified, unbundled ES modules with HMR injected, so: (a) unminified-javascript reports 'Est savings of 7,521 KiB' (essentially the whole app, because dev code is never minified) and (b) FCP 37.4s / LCP 72.3s reflect waterfall module fetching + on-the-fly transform, not a production bundle. These specific numbers will improve dramatically against `vite build` output. Notably, the dev-only metrics that do NOT depend on minification — total-blocking-time (40 ms), bootup-time (0.17s), main-thread work (1.2s) — already pass, and CLS (0.344) is a real code issue independent of build mode.

Root cause

Lighthouse was pointed at the dev server (npm run dev / port 5173) rather than a production preview (npm run build && npm run preview). Dev servers intentionally trade size/latency for fast HMR.

Evidence / proof
All Lighthouse resource URLs are localhost:5173 with dev-only paths: /@vite/client (137,996 B), /@react-refresh (117,841 B), /node_modules/.vite/deps/lucide-react.js?v=8de9a796 (1,157,309 B), /src/App.tsx (463,783 B raw TSX), /src/translations/ar.ts (1,076,314 B raw TS). unminified-javascript displayValue 'Est savings of 7,521 KiB' — characteristic of an unminified dev build. FCP/LCP numericValue 37,409 ms / 72,262 ms.

Real-world impact

Risk of mis-prioritisation: the catastrophic-looking FCP/LCP and 'unminified JS' savings are largely eliminated by a production build alone, whereas the genuine structural wins are PERF-FE-001 (eager heavy pages), PERF-FE-002 (dual dictionaries), PERF-FE-004 (no vendor chunking) and PERF-FE-005 (CLS). Those persist in production.

Reproduction

Inspect audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json network-requests: every URL is localhost:5173 with /@vite, /@react-refresh, /node_modules/.vite/deps and raw /src/*.ts(x) paths — the signature of `vite` (dev), not `vite preview` (prod).

Resolution

Re-run Lighthouse against a production preview: `npm run build && npm run preview` (or serve dist/ behind a static host with gzip/brotli), then capture /login again. Use that report as the audit baseline for FCP/LCP/byte-weight, and keep the dev report only as evidence for the structural findings. Then re-confirm PERF-FE-001/002/004 against the real bundle/chunk graph.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
# Measured against dev server:
npm run dev   # http://localhost:5173 — unbundled, unminified, HMR
▲ After (fixed)
# Measure against production build:
npm run build && npm run preview   # serves dist/ minified + chunked
# then run Lighthouse on the preview URL /login
References: https://vitejs.dev/guide/build.html · https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/overview

Phase 4 — Functional (Unit + Integration)

5 findings — 3 High · 1 Medium · 1 Low
HighFUNC-001Frontend (tss-grc-ui-v2) ships with zero executable automated tests and no test runner wired into the build
✓ VerifiedFunctionalTest Coverage / Quality Assurance▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Verified: package.json scripts = dev/build/preview/typecheck only (no "test"), devDependencies carry no vitest/jest/@testing-library/playwright, and no vitest.config/jest.config exists. The only two test files (src/__tests__/threeLines.test.ts, mobileCrisis.test.ts) both import node:test and are unrunnable by the project toolchain — fed only through tsc --noEmit. The production UI ships zero executable automated tests wired into the build; CI gates the frontend on type-checking alone. High is correct for the active production UI.
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json:1-40 Effort M Risk High business risk (not a CVSS-scored vuln). The entire React/TypeScript SPA — auth flow, tenant-scoped data tables, RTL bilingual rendering, 200+ pages across 17 modules — has no executed regression net. Any refactor or dependency bump can silently break the only interface end users touch; defects reach production undetected because the sole automated check is type-checking, which proves nothing about runtime behaviour.
tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json (scripts: dev/build/preview/typecheck only — no "test" script)
tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json (devDependencies: no vitest, jest, @testing-library/* or playwright)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/__tests__/threeLines.test.ts
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/__tests__/mobileCrisis.test.ts

Description

The active frontend (tss-grc-ui-v2) is the production UI, yet it has no test runner installed and no executable test suite. package.json defines only four scripts — dev, build, preview, typecheck — and the devDependencies list (@types/*, @vitejs/plugin-react, typescript, vite) contains no test framework (no vitest, jest, @testing-library/react, or playwright). Two files exist under src/__tests__ (threeLines.test.ts, mobileCrisis.test.ts) but they import from Node's built-in node:test/node:assert and, per their own header comments, were written because 'The tss-grc-ui-v2 project has no test framework installed yet'. They are never executed by any npm script and are only fed through tsc --noEmit. So while two test FILES are present, the count of tests actually RUN in CI/build is zero. The only automated frontend signal captured in the audit is `tsc --noEmit` (audit/raw/tsc.log) which reported 0 errors — type correctness, not behavioural correctness — and a 6-case Playwright smoke suite that lives OUTSIDE the repo in audit/artifacts/e2e (it covers login happy/sad path and screenshots only, not module CRUD, validation, tenant scoping, or workflow transitions).

Root cause

No testing dependency or `test` npm script was ever added to tss-grc-ui-v2; the v1 static UI (tss-grc-ui) likewise has none. Component, hook, and integration testing was deferred ('once a runner is added', per the test-file comments) and never picked up. CI therefore gates the frontend on type-checking alone.

Evidence / proof
audit/raw/tsc.log: `tss-grc-ui-v2@0.1.0 typecheck` / `tsc --noEmit` (clean, 0 errors). package.json scripts block contains no "test" entry; devDependencies = [@types/node, @types/react, @types/react-dom, @types/sockjs-client, @vitejs/plugin-react, typescript, vite] — no test framework. `find tss-grc-ui-v2/src -iname '*.test.*' -o -iname '*.spec.*'` => 2 files, both using node:test and unrunnable by the project toolchain. No vitest.config.* / jest.config.* present. Backend, by contrast, runs 1858 JUnit tests (audit/raw/mvn-test.log, 174 surefire reports, 0 failures/0 errors/0 skipped).

Real-world impact

Regressions in authentication, multi-tenant data display, bilingual/RTL layout, form validation, and workflow UI ship undetected. There is no guard against breaking changes during dependency upgrades (e.g. React/Vite/Bootstrap bumps) or refactors. Frontend defects are caught only by manual QA or in production. Given the platform is bilingual + multi-tenant, subtle locale/tenant bugs are exactly the class of error unit/component tests catch cheaply and humans miss.

Reproduction

1) `cd tss-grc-ui-v2 && cat package.json` — observe no `test` script and no test framework in devDependencies. 2) `npm test` — fails / no-op (no script). 3) `cat src/__tests__/threeLines.test.ts` — header states there is no test framework; it imports node:test. 4) Confirm the only CI signal is `npm run typecheck` (tsc --noEmit), which passed with 0 errors but executes 0 assertions.

Resolution

Adopt Vitest + @testing-library/react + jsdom (Vite-native, minimal config). Add a `test` script and a `coverage` gate. Convert the two existing node:test files to Vitest. Prioritise: (1) auth/session helpers and the API client (token handling, 401 refresh), (2) the i18n/RTL switch, (3) per-module list/detail pages with mocked API responses, (4) form validation. Add Playwright as a committed e2e dependency (the audit's external 6-case suite proves the app is automatable) and expand beyond login to module CRUD and tenant-switch flows. Target an initial 40% line coverage gate, rising per sprint.
