HighFUNC-002Backend branch coverage is 26.0% and 762 of 1324 classes (57.6%) have 0% coverage — decision logic is largely unexercised
✓ VerifiedFunctionalTest Coverage / Quality Assurance▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Recomputed directly from jacoco.csv (1324 class rows): BRANCH 26.0% (5308 covered / 15079 missed), COMPLEXITY 22.3% (4203/14636), INSTRUCTION 37.1%, LINE 38.5%, METHOD 31.9% — every cited figure matches. 762/1324 classes (57.6%) have 0 instruction coverage. The named vulnerable classes are confirmed at 0%: AuthController, EvidenceMatrixService, DataOfficerService, OtAssetService. Decision logic is largely unexercised. High is correct.
Location tss-grc-backend/target/site/jacoco/jacoco.csv:1-1324 Effort L Risk High quality risk. 1858 passing tests give false confidence: only 26% of branches and 22.3% of cyclomatic complexity are exercised, and over half of all classes are never touched at runtime by any test. Conditional logic — exactly where defects and security checks live — is the least-covered dimension. Untested error paths, validation branches, and authorization decisions can regress without any test turning red.
tss-grc-backend/target/site/jacoco/jacoco.csv (aggregate)
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/auth/AuthController.java (0% — login/refresh logic)
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/evidence/service/EvidenceMatrixService.java (0% — also PERF-NQ-003 Critical)
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/data_officer/service/DataOfficerService.java (0% — 1000+ line god-service, QUAL-ESG-001)

Description

JaCoCo (computed from tss-grc-backend/target/site/jacoco/jacoco.csv over 1324 classes) reports: LINE 38.5% (17,324 covered / 27,728 missed), INSTRUCTION 37.1% (93,819 / 159,128), BRANCH 26.0% (5,308 / 15,079), METHOD 31.9% (2,656 / 5,667), and COMPLEXITY (cyclomatic) just 22.3% (4,203 / 14,636). Branch and complexity are the weakest, which is the worst dimension to be weak in: branches are the if/else, switch, ternary, and exception decisions where logic errors hide. Aggregating per-class, 762 of 1324 classes (57.6%) have ZERO instruction coverage — no test ever loads them. Notably, several classes carrying confirmed Critical/High findings sit at 0%: AuthController (SEC-AUTH-001), EvidenceMatrixService (Critical PERF-NQ-003 + High QUAL-IE-001), DataOfficerService (QUAL-ESG-001), OtAssetService (Critical SEC-CYB-002). The 1858-test count is real and all pass, but it is concentrated in service happy-paths; whole layers (controllers, integration glue, error handling) are dark.

Root cause

Tests are predominantly Mockito unit tests on service classes covering nominal flows. Controllers, exception handlers, validation branches, and many newer modules were never given tests. There is no enforced coverage gate (no JaCoCo `check` rule failing the build below a threshold), so coverage drifted down as modules were added faster than tests.

Evidence / proof
jacoco.csv aggregate: BRANCH covered=5308 missed=15079 => 26.0%; COMPLEXITY covered=4203 missed=14636 => 22.3%; INSTRUCTION 37.1%; LINE 38.5%; METHOD 31.9%. Per-class scan: 762/1324 classes at 0% instruction coverage. Vulnerable-class coverage sample — AuthController 0%/0%/0% (instr/branch/line), EvidenceMatrixService 0%/0%/0%, DataOfficerService 0%/0%/0%, OtAssetService 0%/0%/0%, BcmService 25%/43%/31%, CyberService 44%/55%/45%, EvidenceItemService 60%/36%/61%. Test totals from surefire: 1858 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skipped across 174 classes (audit/raw/mvn-test.log).

Real-world impact

High-complexity, low-coverage classes are the most likely to harbour latent bugs and to regress silently. Because branch coverage is 26%, most conditional paths — including authorization checks, tenant-scope guards, status-transition guards, and error handling — are never asserted. A change that flips a condition (e.g. removes a tenant predicate, as in several confirmed IDOR findings) will not fail any test. Refactoring the 0%-covered god-services (DataOfficerService 1000+ lines, OutsourcingService) is effectively unguarded.

Reproduction

1) Open tss-grc-backend/target/site/jacoco/jacoco.csv and sum BRANCH_COVERED / (BRANCH_COVERED+BRANCH_MISSED) => 0.260. 2) Count rows where INSTRUCTION_COVERED=0 and INSTRUCTION_MISSED>0 => 762. 3) Filter those rows by CLASS ending 'Controller' => 201 fully-uncovered controllers. 4) Grep AuthController / EvidenceMatrixService rows => 0 across all metrics.

Resolution

Introduce a JaCoCo coverage gate in pom.xml that fails the build below a floor and ratchets up over time (e.g. start at line 38% / branch 26% — current levels — then +2% per sprint). Prioritise the 0%-coverage classes that carry findings or high complexity: write branch-focused tests for AuthController (login success/lockout/refresh-rotation), EvidenceMatrixService (matrix build + N+1 path), and the god-services. Track branch coverage specifically, not just line, in CI reporting.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
<!-- tss-grc-backend/pom.xml — jacoco plugin used for report only, no gate -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
  <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions>
    <execution><goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals></execution>
    <execution><id>report</id><phase>test</phase><goals><goal>report</goal></goals></execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
▲ After (fixed)
<!-- tss-grc-backend/pom.xml — add a ratcheting coverage gate -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
  <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions>
    <execution><goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals></execution>
    <execution><id>report</id><phase>test</phase><goals><goal>report</goal></goals></execution>
    <execution>
      <id>coverage-gate</id><phase>verify</phase><goals><goal>check</goal></goals>
      <configuration><rules>
        <rule>
          <element>BUNDLE</element>
          <limits>
            <limit><counter>LINE</counter><value>COVEREDRATIO</value><minimum>0.38</minimum></limit>
            <limit><counter>BRANCH</counter><value>COVEREDRATIO</value><minimum>0.26</minimum></limit>
          </limits>
        </rule>
      </rules></configuration>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>

// Example: cover AuthController login branches (0% -> exercised). Uses MockMvc with security.
@SpringBootTest @AutoConfigureMockMvc
class AuthControllerIT {
  @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
  @Test void login_success_returns_token() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/api/auth/login").contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
        .content("{\"username\":\"admin\",\"password\":\"Admin@12345\"}"))
       .andExpect(status().isOk())
       .andExpect(jsonPath("$.accessToken").exists());
  }
  @Test void login_bad_credentials_returns_401() throws Exception {

HighFUNC-003Confirmed Critical/High security findings have no test asserting the vulnerable path — 5 of 6 Critical findings sit on classes at 0% coverage or with tests that miss the exploit
✓ VerifiedFunctionalTest Coverage / Security Regression Testing▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Verified end-to-end. OtAssetService, IntakeController and ApprovalChainController have 0 *Test.java files (and 0% JaCoCo). CustomSqlRunner.java (module/ccm/runner) has 0 references to organisation/tenant/TenantContext, so no test could assert tenant-scoped SELECT. BcmService.java:221-232 updateBia and 235-237 deleteBia call biaRepo.findById(id)/deleteById(id) with no tenant predicate (unlike the tenant-scoped listExercises), while BcmServiceTest has getPlan_other_tenant_throws / invokePlan_other_tenant_throws but ZERO bia tests (only the @Mock field references 'bia'). The exploit-path test gap is real. Minor nit: the narrative says '6 Critical findings' but crit_high.json actually holds 8 Critical / 57 High; the count is slightly off but the substantive claim is fully supported. High.
Location audit/crit_high.json:1-55 Effort M Risk High. The test suite gives no protection against the platform's most serious confirmed defects. Of the 6 Critical security findings in audit/crit_high.json, 3 sit on classes with NO test file at all and the other 3 have a *Test.java that exercises only nominal paths, never the cross-tenant/SQLi/mass-assignment exploit. There is therefore no regression net: a future fix could be reverted and every test would still pass. This is the gap that lets IDOR/BFLA findings persist undetected.
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/socops/service/OtAssetService.java (SEC-CYB-002 Critical — NO test, 0% coverage)
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/intake/controller/IntakeController.java (SEC-FIN-001 Critical — NO test, 0% coverage)
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/workflow/approval_chains/controller/ApprovalChainController.java (SEC-IAM-001 Critical — NO test, 0% coverage)
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/ccm/runner/CustomSqlRunner.java (SEC-INT-001 Critical — test exists but only checks DML rejection, not cross-tenant SELECT)
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/service/CyberService.java (SEC-CYB-001 Critical — test exists, no cross-tenant assertion)
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/bcm/service/BcmService.java (SEC-BCM-001 High — test covers plan tenant-scope but NOT the vulnerable BIA path)

Description

Cross-referencing every Critical/High Java finding in audit/crit_high.json against the 174 backend test classes shows the suite does not exercise the vulnerable code paths. Of 6 Critical findings: SEC-CYB-002 (OtAssetService mass-assignment), SEC-FIN-001 (IntakeController unauthenticated PII leak), and SEC-IAM-001 (ApprovalChainController approval forgery) have NO corresponding *Test.java and their classes are at 0% JaCoCo coverage. SEC-INT-001 (CustomSqlRunner cross-tenant SQL exfiltration) has CustomSqlRunnerTest, but reading it shows 8 tests that only verify INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/chained-statement REJECTION and threshold logic — none asserts that a legitimate SELECT (e.g. `SELECT * FROM iam.users`) is constrained to the caller's tenant; indeed the source has no organisation/tenant predicate at all. SEC-CYB-001 (CyberService IDOR) has CyberServiceTest (14 tests) that stub repos with the caller's own ORG_ID and never simulate an attacker requesting another org's id. The clearest example is SEC-BCM-001: BcmServiceTest DOES contain tenant-isolation tests (getPlan_other_tenant_throws_EntityNotFound, invokePlan_other_tenant_throws) for the BcmPlan path — proving the team knows the pattern — yet the High finding is on the BIA path (updateBia/deleteBia at BcmService.java:221-236 call biaRepo.findById(id)/deleteById(id) with NO tenant scope), and there is no test for createBia/updateBia/deleteBia or any cross-tenant BIA assertion. The defensive test pattern exists but was simply never applied to the vulnerable method.

Root cause

Security-negative test cases (attacker requests another tenant's id; SQLi payload; mass-assignment of a foreign id) were not written. Tests assert what the code does on the happy path, not what it must refuse. Controllers carrying authorization findings have no MockMvc/security-context tests, so missing @PreAuthorize annotations are invisible to the suite.

Evidence / proof
Automated cross-reference (audit/crit_high.json x src/test): Critical findings missing any *Test.java => OtAssetService, IntakeController, ApprovalChainController (all 0% JaCoCo). BcmService.java:221-232 updateBia / 235-237 deleteBia call `biaRepo.findById(id)` and `biaRepo.deleteById(id)` with no TenantContext predicate; BcmServiceTest method list contains getPlan_other_tenant_throws_EntityNotFound and invokePlan_other_tenant_throws_EntityNotFound but ZERO methods referencing bia/createBia/updateBia/deleteBia (grep 'bia' => only the @Mock field). CustomSqlRunnerTest (115 lines, 8 tests): insertIsRejected/updateIsRejected/deleteIsRejected/chainedSelectIsRejected/threshold tests only — no cross-tenant SELECT test; CustomSqlRunner.java has 0 matches for 'organisation|tenant|TenantContext'. CyberServiceTest: all repo stubs use ORG_ID (the caller's own org); no OTHER_ORG/forbidden/cross-tenant case.

Real-world impact

The most severe confirmed defects (cross-tenant data theft, unauthenticated PII exposure, approval forgery, SQL-driven exfiltration) are completely unguarded by automated tests. When these are remediated, nothing prevents a later change from re-introducing them. Conversely, until remediated, the green test suite actively masks their existence and gives auditors/management false assurance.

Reproduction

1) `python` cross-reference: for each finding in audit/crit_high.json, derive ClassNameTest.java and check existence in src/test => OtAssetService/IntakeController/ApprovalChainController have none. 2) Read BcmServiceTest.java — confirm tenant tests exist only for plan, none for BIA; read BcmService.java:221-237 — confirm biaRepo.findById/deleteById are unscoped. 3) Read CustomSqlRunnerTest.java — confirm only DML-rejection tests; read CustomSqlRunner.java — confirm no tenant predicate. 4) Read CyberServiceTest.java — confirm all stubs use the caller's ORG_ID with no foreign-org case.

Resolution

Add a security-negative test for every Critical/High finding, co-located with the fix, asserting the exploit is now refused. Pattern: arrange a record owned by OTHER_ORG, set TenantContext to ORG_ID, assert EntityNotFound/AccessDenied. For controllers, use @SpringBootTest + MockMvc + @WithMockUser to assert 403 for unauthorized roles and isolation across tenants. Mirror the existing BcmServiceTest plan-tenant pattern onto the BIA path. For CustomSqlRunner, assert a SELECT against a foreign tenant's rows is blocked (after adding a tenant guard / read-only constrained datasource). Make these tests part of the regression gate so the findings cannot silently return.

void updateBia_other_tenant_throws_EntityNotFound() {
    BiaRecord foreign = new BiaRecord();
    foreign.setId(ID);
    foreign.setProcessId(PROC_ID_OTHER_ORG);              // process belongs to OTHER_ORG
    when(biaRepo.findById(ID)).thenReturn(Optional.of(foreign));
    when(processRepo.findById(PROC_ID_OTHER_ORG))
        .thenReturn(Optional.of(process(OTHER_ORG)));     // tenant check resolves to foreign org
    TenantContext.setCurrentTenant(ORG_ID);
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.updateBia(ID, foreign))
        .isInstanceOf(EntityNotFoundException.class);     // must NOT leak / mutate foreign BIA
    verify(biaRepo, never()).save(any());
}

    when(processRepo.findById(PROC_ID_OTHER_ORG)).thenReturn(Optional.of(process(OTHER_ORG)));

MediumFUNC-004Authorization is untested end-to-end: 201 of 231 controllers (87%) have 0% coverage and only 4 tests use MockMvc — BFLA findings are invisible to the suite
FunctionalTest Coverage / Authorization Testing▾
Location tss-grc-backend/target/site/jacoco/jacoco.csv:1-1324 Effort L Risk Medium-to-High. The eleven 'Broken Function Level Authorization' findings in audit/crit_high.json (controllers gated only by isAuthenticated() or missing @PreAuthorize entirely) cannot be caught by the current suite because controller tests instantiate the controller with @InjectMocks and call methods directly, bypassing Spring Security. Only 4 of 174 test classes wire MockMvc/SpringBootTest, and none target the vulnerable controllers. Authorization correctness is therefore asserted nowhere.
tss-grc-backend/src/test/java/com/tss/grc/module/compliance/obligation/controller/ObligationControllerTest.java (representative @InjectMocks style — bypasses security)
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/policy/controller/PolicyController.java (SEC-CMP-003, 0% coverage)
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/attachment/controller/AttachmentController.java (SEC-EVD-001, 0% coverage)
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/cyber/controller/CloudServiceController.java (SEC-CYB-003, 0% coverage)
tss-grc-backend/src/main/java/com/tss/grc/module/sust/ghg/controller/GhgEmissionRecordController.java (SEC-ESG-001, 0% coverage)

Description

The platform exposes 2175 endpoints across 231 controllers, but only 28 controllers (12%) have a *ControllerTest, and JaCoCo shows 201 of those 231 controllers (87%) at 0% coverage. More importantly, the EXISTING controller tests do not test authorization: the representative pattern (e.g. ObligationControllerTest) uses `@Mock` for the service and `@InjectMocks` for the controller, then calls controller methods as plain Java — Spring Security, the @PreAuthorize layer, and the JWT/tenant filter are never in the loop. Only 4 of 174 test classes reference MockMvc/SpringBootTest/WebMvcTest/@AutoConfigureMockMvc (CoiControllerTest and the three integration-webhook controller tests), and 19 reference @WithMockUser. Crucially, NONE of those security-aware tests cover the eleven BFLA findings (PolicyController, ControlMapController, CloudServiceController, GhgEmissionRecordController, AttachmentController, ConsentRecordController, NdiAssessmentCycleController/NdiAuditController, LicensingController, AutomationRuleController, SupplierResilienceController). Because authorization is enforced by annotations resolved at the Spring proxy/filter layer — not in the method body — a missing or wrong @PreAuthorize is structurally invisible to @InjectMocks-style tests. The suite can be fully green while every BFLA hole is open.

Root cause

Controller tests were written as plain unit tests (service mocked, controller called directly) rather than as MockMvc slice/integration tests that route through Spring Security. No convention exists for asserting @PreAuthorize / role gates / tenant isolation at the HTTP boundary. The bulk of controllers have no test at all.

Evidence / proof
jacoco.csv: 231 classes ending 'Controller'; 201 at 0% instruction coverage. `find -name '*ControllerTest.java'` => 28. `grep -rlE 'WebMvcTest|MockMvc|SpringBootTest|@AutoConfigureMockMvc' src/test` => 4 files (CoiControllerTest, CrowdStrikeControllerTest, ServiceNowControllerTest, TenableControllerTest). `grep -rlE 'WithMockUser' src/test` => 19. ObligationControllerTest header: `@Mock private ObligationService service; @InjectMocks private ObligationController controller;` (no MockMvc, no security). Endpoint total 2175 across 231 controllers per audit facts.

Real-world impact

The platform's authorization model is unverified at runtime. Adding, removing, or mis-scoping a @PreAuthorize on any of 2175 endpoints produces no test failure. This is the direct cause of the BFLA findings going undetected in development. For a multi-tenant GRC product where tenant isolation and least-privilege are core selling points, having zero HTTP-level authorization tests is a material assurance gap.

Reproduction

1) `find tss-grc-backend/src/test -name '*ControllerTest.java' | wc -l` => 28; `find tss-grc-backend/src/main -name '*Controller.java' | wc -l` => 231. 2) `grep -rlE 'MockMvc|SpringBootTest|WebMvcTest' tss-grc-backend/src/test | wc -l` => 4. 3) Open ObligationControllerTest.java — confirm @InjectMocks direct-call style, no security. 4) jacoco.csv => 201/231 controllers at 0%.

Resolution

Establish a MockMvc-based authorization test convention. For each controller, add a security slice test asserting: (a) anonymous => 401, (b) authenticated-but-wrong-role => 403, (c) correct role => 2xx, (d) cross-tenant id => 404/403. Start with the controllers carrying BFLA findings, then expand. Consider an automated guard test that scans all @RequestMapping handler methods and fails if any write/delete endpoint lacks a @PreAuthorize (reflection-based meta-test) to prevent regressions across all 2175 endpoints cheaply.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// ObligationControllerTest.java — representative: bypasses Spring Security entirely
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class ObligationControllerTest {
    @Mock private ObligationService service;
    @InjectMocks private ObligationController controller;   // called directly, no @PreAuthorize, no filter
    // ... tests invoke controller.method(...) as plain Java
}
▲ After (fixed)
// PolicyControllerSecurityIT.java — MockMvc routes through Spring Security so @PreAuthorize is enforced
@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
class PolicyControllerSecurityIT {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

    @Test void anonymous_publish_is_401() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(post("/api/policies/1/publish")).andExpect(status().isUnauthorized());
    }

    @Test @WithMockUser(authorities = "AUDITOR")
    void wrong_role_publish_is_403() throws Exception {           // currently PASSES the hole (no role gate) -> test FAILS -> hole exposed
        mvc.perform(post("/api/policies/1/publish")).andExpect(status().isForbidden());
    }

    @Test @WithMockUser(authorities = "COMPLIANCE_MANAGER")
    void correct_role_publish_is_2xx() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(post("/api/policies/1/publish")).andExpect(status().is2xxSuccessful());
    }
}

// AuthorizationGuardMetaTest.java — reflection guard across ALL 2175 endpoints (cheap regression net)
class AuthorizationGuardMetaTest {
    @Test void every_mutating_endpoint_has_PreAuthorize() {
        var scanner = new ClassPathScanningCandidateComponentProvider(false);
        scanner.addIncludeFilter(new AnnotationTypeFilter(RestController.class));
        List<String> offenders = new ArrayList<>();
        for (var bd : scanner.findCandidateComponents("com.tss.grc.module")) {
            Class<?> c = Class.forName(bd.getBeanClassName());
            for (Method m : c.getDeclaredMethods()) {
                boolean mutating = m.isAnnotationPresent(PostMapping.class)
                    || m.isAnnotationPresent(PutMapping.class)
                    || m.isAnnotationPresent(DeleteMapping.class)
                    || m.isAnnotationPresent(PatchMapping.class);
                if (mutating && !m.isAnnotationPresent(PreAuthorize.class))
                    offenders.add(c.getSimpleName() + "#" + m.getName());
            }
        }
        assertThat(offenders).as("mutating endpoints missing @PreAuthorize").isEmpty();
    }
}

Description

A Playwright run captured in audit/raw/playwright.log executed 6 tests, all passing (1.1m): E2E login success -> /risk, login failure -> error shown, demo-skip bypass navigates without auth, session persists across reload, plus an a11y+screenshots pass across key pages and a responsive mobile-screenshots pass. This suite lives in audit/artifacts/e2e (an audit-time scaffold), not in tss-grc-ui-v2, so it is not part of the project's committed build and would not run in the team's CI. Functionally it is a thin smoke test: it proves the app boots, login works, and pages render for screenshotting — it asserts nothing about creating a risk, advancing a workflow (e.g. the 9-step cyber incident state machine), submitting a BIA, switching tenants, or rendering Arabic/RTL data correctly. Combined with FUNC-001 (no committed frontend unit tests) and FUNC-004 (no HTTP authorization tests), there is no automated check that the integrated system behaves correctly for any real user task beyond logging in.

Root cause

E2E testing was set up only as an audit artifact, not adopted into the repo. No page-object structure, no per-module scenarios, and the suite is not wired to any npm script in tss-grc-ui-v2. The 'demo-skip bypass navigates without auth' case being a passing test also hints at an intentional auth-bypass affordance that itself warrants review.

Evidence / proof
audit/raw/playwright.log: 'Running 6 tests using 1 worker ... 6 passed (1.1m)'; test titles = login success->/risk, login failure, demo-skip bypass navigates without auth, session persists across reload, a11y + screenshots across key pages, responsive mobile screenshots. Suite location: audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts (single spec file) with its own package.json/playwright.config.ts under audit/artifacts/e2e — outside tss-grc-ui-v2. tss-grc-ui-v2 has no playwright dependency or e2e script.

Real-world impact

Integration regressions — broken API contracts between the SPA and the 2175 endpoints, workflow transition bugs, tenant-scope leaks visible only through the UI, RTL/locale data defects — are not caught automatically. Manual QA is the only safety net for full user journeys. The e2e harness exists but delivers near-zero functional assurance beyond authentication.

Reproduction

1) `cat audit/raw/playwright.log` — observe 6 tests, all smoke/login/screenshot. 2) `ls audit/artifacts/e2e/tests` => single audit.spec.ts; confirm it lives outside tss-grc-ui-v2. 3) `grep -i playwright tss-grc-ui-v2/package.json` => no match (not a committed dependency).

Resolution

Promote the Playwright harness into tss-grc-ui-v2 (add @playwright/test devDependency and an `e2e` script). Build a small page-object layer and add critical-journey specs per module: create+list a risk, run an evidence review four-eyes flow, advance a cyber incident through its state machine, switch tenants and assert data isolation in the UI, and toggle EN/AR asserting RTL + Arabic field rendering. Run e2e against a seeded DB (seed_real_data.py) in CI nightly. Separately, security-review the 'demo-skip bypass' that navigates without auth — ensure it is dev-only and cannot reach production.

Phase 5 — End-to-End & Workflow

8 findings — 4 Medium · 1 Low · 3 Info
MediumE2E-003Access token (full JWT with roles) stored in JS-readable sessionStorage — confirmed by E2E artifact
E2ESession Management / Token Storage (CWE-522, CWE-1004 analog)▾
Location audit/artifacts/e2e/results/session-keys.txt:1 Effort M Risk CVSS ~5.4 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:L/A:N) — a single XSS or malicious dependency can read the bearer token and impersonate the user for the token lifetime
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/session-keys.txt:1
audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts:41-42

Description

The login-success test reads the access token directly from sessionStorage via page.evaluate(sessionStorage.getItem('grc.accessToken') || sessionStorage.getItem('accessToken') || keys.join(',')) and writes it to session-keys.txt. The artifact contains a complete, decodable JWT. The header is {"alg":"HS384"}; the payload carries sub:1, usr:admin, org:1, a full roles array (incl. ROLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN, CYBER_WRITE/DELETE, SCM_WRITE/DELETE, EVIDENCE_WRITE/DELETE), enabled_modules, iat and exp. Because the token lives in sessionStorage it is readable by any JavaScript running in the page (XSS, malicious npm dependency, browser extension). This matches CLAUDE.md's documented design ('access token ... stored in sessionStorage') and is corroborated dynamically here. Refresh is in an HttpOnly cookie (good), but the access token itself is exposed.

Root cause

Architectural choice to keep the bearer access token in Web Storage (sessionStorage) so api.js can attach Authorization: Bearer headers. Web Storage has no HttpOnly equivalent, so any script in the origin can exfiltrate it.

Evidence / proof
session-keys.txt holds a raw JWT 'eyJhbGciOiJIUzM4NCJ9.<payload>.<sig>'. Decoded header: {"alg":"HS384"}. Decoded payload includes: roles=[CYBER_READ,SCM_READ,SCM_DELETE,EVIDENCE_WRITE,SCM_WRITE,EVIDENCE_DELETE,CYBER_DELETE,EVIDENCE_READ,ROLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN,CYBER_WRITE], org=1, exp=1781793757. The test wrote a token value (not just key names), proving getItem returned the JWT from sessionStorage.

Real-world impact

Any XSS, compromised third-party script, or malicious browser extension on the app origin can read the full bearer token and replay it against :8084 as the authenticated user (here, a platform admin) until exp. The token also leaks the role/module entitlement model to the client. Severity capped at Medium because exploitation still requires script execution in the origin (no independent XSS confirmed by this artifact).

Reproduction

1) Log in as admin on :5173. 2) Open DevTools console and run sessionStorage.getItem('grc.accessToken'). 3) Observe the full JWT is returned and base64url-decodes to the claims above. Equivalent to audit.spec.ts:41-42 / session-keys.txt.

Resolution

Prefer keeping the access token in memory (a module-scoped variable, never persisted) and relying on the existing HttpOnly refresh cookie + silent refresh to survive reloads, instead of persisting the access token to sessionStorage. If Web Storage must be used, add a strict Content-Security-Policy to shrink the XSS surface, keep access-token TTL short (prod is already 15m), and bind tokens where feasible. Treat session-keys.txt as a secret artifact and exclude it from any shared/committed report bundle.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// auth.js (current behavior, as exercised by the E2E test)
sessionStorage.setItem('grc.accessToken', resp.accessToken);
// ...later
const token = sessionStorage.getItem('grc.accessToken');
▲ After (fixed)
// Keep the access token only in memory; rehydrate via the HttpOnly refresh cookie on load.
let _accessToken = null;
export function setAccessToken(t) { _accessToken = t; }      // never persisted
export function getAccessToken() { return _accessToken; }
export async function bootstrapSession() {
  // on page load / reload, exchange the HttpOnly refresh cookie for a new access token
  const r = await fetch('/api/auth/refresh', { method: 'POST', credentials: 'include' });
  if (r.ok) setAccessToken((await r.json()).accessToken);
}

MediumE2E-005No E2E coverage for CRUD or multi-step workflow journeys (create -> approve -> archive)
E2ETest Coverage Gap — Business Workflows / State Machines▾
Location audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts:71-111 Effort L Risk N/A (coverage gap) — the documented module state machines have zero end-to-end verification despite being the platform's core value
audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts:10-20
audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts:71-111

Description

The only interaction with the module pages (/risk, /compliance, /cyber, /privacy, /tprm, /bcm, etc.) is page.goto + screenshot + axe scan. There is NO journey that creates a record, transitions it through its documented workflow_status state machine (e.g. cyber incident DETECTION -> ... -> LESSONS_LEARNED, or a risk/compliance create -> submit -> approve -> archive), and verifies the resulting state and persistence. The workflows are the heart of a GRC product; state-transition guards live in the service layer (per CLAUDE.md) and are exactly the logic most likely to regress, yet nothing exercises them through the UI + API together.

Root cause

The E2E suite was built as a login + visual/a11y smoke harness. Authoring data-mutating, multi-step workflow journeys (and the fixtures/teardown they need) was out of scope for this pass.

Evidence / proof
audit.spec.ts iterates AUTH_PAGES (lines 10-20) only to goto+screenshot+axe (lines 86-97); the loop body contains no .fill on a record form, no submit of a create, and no assertion on workflow_status or row presence. playwright.log shows the AUTH_PAGES work folded into one test: 'a11y + screenshots across key pages (47.1s)'.

Real-world impact

A broken state transition (e.g. an incident that can be archived while skipping approval, or a risk that loses its workflow_status on save) would not be caught. For an auditable compliance platform, undetected workflow-integrity regressions are high-business-impact.

Reproduction

Inspect the AUTH_PAGES loop in audit.spec.ts: it never mutates data. No create/approve/archive assertion exists anywhere in the spec.

Resolution

Add at least one full lifecycle journey per high-value module (start with risk and cyber-incident). Drive the real UI: create a record, advance it through each allowed transition, and assert both the rendered state and the persisted state (via an API read). Use a dedicated throwaway tenant/fixture and clean up in afterEach.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
for (const p of AUTH_PAGES) {
  await page.goto(p.path); await settle(page);
  await page.screenshot({ path: `${OUT}/shots/${p.name}.png`, fullPage: true });
  const r = await new AxeBuilder({ page }).withTags(WCAG).analyze();
}
▲ After (fixed)
test('E2E: risk lifecycle create -> submit -> approve -> archive', async ({ page }) => {
  await doLogin(page);
  await page.goto('/risk');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /new risk|add risk/i }).click();
  await page.fill('#title', 'E2E lifecycle risk');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: /save|create/i }).click();
  const row = page.getByRole('row', { name: /E2E lifecycle risk/ });
  await expect(row).toBeVisible();
  await row.getByRole('button', { name: /submit/i }).click();
  await expect(row).toContainText(/UNDER_REVIEW|SUBMITTED/i);
  await row.getByRole('button', { name: /approve/i }).click();
  await expect(row).toContainText(/APPROVED/i);
  await row.getByRole('button', { name: /archive/i }).click();
  await expect(row).toContainText(/ARCHIVED/i);
  // verify persisted state via API, not just the DOM
  const api = await page.request.get('/api/risk?q=E2E lifecycle risk');
  expect((await api.json()).content?.[0]?.workflowStatus).toBe('ARCHIVED');
});
MediumE2E-006No negative / permission-denied E2E (403 / hidden-action) journeys
E2ETest Coverage Gap — Authorization (broken-access-control regressions)▾
Location audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts:24-30 Effort M Risk N/A (coverage gap) — method-level @PreAuthorize and UI gating are unverified end-to-end; a privilege-escalation regression would ship silently
audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts:24-30
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/session-keys.txt:1

Description

Every journey authenticates as admin (PLATFORM_ADMIN with a broad roles array — confirmed in the decoded JWT in session-keys.txt) and only exercises allowed actions. There is no test that logs in as a lower-privileged seeded role (riskmanager / Risk@12345, auditor / Audit@12345) and asserts that a forbidden action is blocked: that the API returns 403 for an action the role lacks (e.g. an AUDITOR attempting CYBER:WRITE) and that the corresponding UI control is hidden/disabled. The backend relies on @PreAuthorize(hasPermission('MODULE','ACTION')) via ModulePermissionEvaluator (per CLAUDE.md); none of that authorization surface is exercised end-to-end.

Root cause

doLogin() is hard-coded to the admin superuser (audit.spec.ts:24-30), so the suite can only ever observe the permit path. No per-role fixtures exist.

Evidence / proof
audit.spec.ts:24-30 doLogin always fills 'admin'/'Admin@12345'. session-keys.txt decodes to roles including ROLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN + CYBER_WRITE/DELETE + SCM_WRITE/DELETE + EVIDENCE_WRITE/DELETE — the most-privileged principal, so no denial is ever observable. No 'expect(...).toBe(403)' or 'toBeHidden' on a gated control appears in the spec.

Real-world impact

A broken-access-control regression (a missing @PreAuthorize, an over-broad role grant, or a UI control that should be hidden but is not) would pass CI undetected. Broken access control is OWASP A01 and directly relevant to a multi-tenant GRC tool.

Reproduction

Review doLogin (audit.spec.ts:24-30) — only admin is used. No lower-privilege login or 403 assertion exists.

Resolution

Add per-role login helpers and at least one negative journey per sensitive action: log in as auditor (read-only), assert a write control is absent/disabled in the UI, and assert the corresponding API call returns 403. Repeat for riskmanager attempting an admin-only action.

}
▲ After (fixed)
async function loginAs(page: Page, user: string, pass: string) {
  await page.goto('/login');
  await page.fill('#username', user);
  await page.fill('#password', pass);
  await page.locator('form.login-form button[type="submit"]').click();

}

  const res = await page.request.post('/api/cyber/incidents', { data: { title: 'should-fail' } });
  expect(res.status()).toBe(403);                                                    // enforced in API
});
MediumE2E-007No cross-tenant isolation E2E (multi-tenant data-leak regressions unverified)
E2ETest Coverage Gap — Multi-Tenancy / Tenant Isolation (CWE-639 analog)▾
Location audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts:24-30 Effort M Risk N/A (coverage gap) — the per-query organisation_id filter (the core tenancy control) has no end-to-end verification
audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts:24-30
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/session-keys.txt:1

Description

The decoded session JWT carries org:1, meaning every journey runs entirely inside tenant org_id=1 (TSS GRC). CLAUDE.md documents that there is NO global Hibernate tenant filter — every repository query must hand-filter by organisation_id, making this an error-prone, per-query control. The seed data sets up three tenants (org_id 1, 2, 3: TSS GRC, Aramco Trading, STC Bank). Nothing in the suite logs in under two different tenants and asserts that tenant A cannot read tenant B's records (neither via the UI nor by directly requesting another tenant's resource id from tenant A's session). Tenant isolation is therefore completely unverified end-to-end.

Root cause

Single-tenant test fixture (admin in org 1 only) and no second-tenant credential, so a cross-tenant read can never be attempted, let alone asserted to fail.

Evidence / proof
session-keys.txt JWT payload: 'org':'1'. CLAUDE.md: 'Every repository query must filter by organisation_id ... There is no global Hibernate filter for this; it is the developer's responsibility per query.' seed_real_data.py documents tenants org_id 1/2/3. The spec has no second-tenant login and no cross-tenant fetch assertion.

Real-world impact

A single repository method that forgets its findBy...OrganisationId filter would leak another tenant's GRC data (risks, incidents, evidence). For a multi-tenant compliance platform this is among the highest-impact failure modes, and it is invisible to the current suite.

Reproduction

Inspect the suite — only org_id=1 (admin) is ever authenticated. No tenant-B principal or cross-tenant resource fetch exists.

Resolution

Seed a user in a second tenant (org_id=2). Add an E2E that: as tenant A, creates/locates a record and notes its id; as tenant B, attempts to GET that id and asserts 403/404 (not 200 with the row); and asserts tenant B's list views never contain tenant A's records. This must be re-run whenever a repository finder changes.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// every test runs as admin in org_id=1 only; no second tenant is ever authenticated
▲ After (fixed)
test('E2E: tenant B cannot read tenant A record (org isolation)', async ({ browser }) => {
  const a = await browser.newContext(); const pa = await a.newPage();
  await loginAs(pa, 'admin', 'Admin@12345');            // org_id=1
  const created = await pa.request.post('/api/risk', { data: { title: 'tenantA-secret' } });
  const id = (await created.json()).id;

  const b = await browser.newContext(); const pb = await b.newPage();
  await loginAs(pb, 'tenantb_admin', 'TenantB@12345');  // org_id=2 (seed required)
  const leak = await pb.request.get(`/api/risk/${id}`);
  expect([403, 404]).toContain(leak.status());          // must NOT be 200 with the row
  const list = await pb.request.get('/api/risk');
  expect(JSON.stringify(await list.json())).not.toContain('tenantA-secret');
  await a.close(); await b.close();
});

LowE2E-004No E2E coverage for logout / session termination
E2ETest Coverage Gap — Session Lifecycle▾
Location audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts:38-111 Effort S Risk N/A (coverage gap) — the entire logout / session-invalidation path is unverified by any automated journey
audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts:38-111
audit/raw/playwright.log

Description

The suite covers login success, login failure, route-guard bypass attempt, session-on-reload, a11y and responsive screenshots, but there is NO test that logs out and verifies the session is actually terminated: that the access token is cleared from sessionStorage, that the HttpOnly refresh cookie is invalidated server-side, and that subsequently navigating back to a protected route (or hitting Back) bounces to /login. Given that the access token is held in sessionStorage (see E2E-003) and refresh in an HttpOnly cookie, logout correctness is security-relevant and currently unverified end-to-end.

Root cause

Suite was scoped to login + a11y/screenshot smoke tests; the destructive/lifecycle half of the auth flow (logout, refresh-token revocation, back-button after logout) was never authored.

Evidence / proof
playwright.log lists exactly 6 tests (login success, login failure, demo-skip, reload, a11y, responsive) — none reference logout. Grep of audit.spec.ts shows no 'logout', 'signout', or refresh-revocation step; the spec ends at line 121.

Real-world impact

A regression that fails to clear the sessionStorage token, fails to revoke the refresh cookie, or lets the Back button restore an authenticated view after logout would ship undetected. For a multi-tenant GRC platform this is a real session-fixation / shared-device risk.

Reproduction

Review audit.spec.ts — no logout test exists. Manually: log in, log out, press Back / re-navigate to /risk; today nothing asserts you are bounced to /login.

Resolution

Add an E2E that logs in, triggers logout, then asserts: (a) sessionStorage no longer holds the access token, (b) the refresh cookie is cleared/rejected (a subsequent /api/auth/refresh returns 401), and (c) navigating to /risk lands on /login.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// no logout test exists in audit.spec.ts
▲ After (fixed)
test('E2E: logout clears token, revokes refresh, blocks back-nav', async ({ page, context }) => {
  await doLogin(page);
  await page.locator('[data-testid="logout"], #logout, button:has-text("Logout")').first().click();
  await page.waitForURL(/\/login/);
  const tok = await page.evaluate(() => sessionStorage.getItem('grc.accessToken'));
  expect(tok).toBeNull();                                 // access token cleared
  const refresh = await page.request.post('/api/auth/refresh');
  expect(refresh.status()).toBe(401);                     // refresh cookie revoked server-side
  await page.goto('/risk');
  await page.waitForURL(/\/login/);                        // cannot return to protected route
});
InfoE2E-001Route guard enforces authentication: unauthenticated deep-link bounces to /login (verified)
E2EAccess Control / Authentication (positive control)▾
Location audit/artifacts/e2e/results/demo-bypass-url.txt:1 Effort S Risk N/A (positive finding) — confirms the SPA refuses to render a protected route without a session and preserves the intended destination via ?next=
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/demo-bypass-url.txt:1
audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts:54-61
audit/raw/playwright.log

Description

The Playwright test named 'E2E: demo-skip bypass navigates without auth' clicks the first type=button (the ghost 'continue as demo / skip login' control) on the login form and records the resulting URL. The test name expects an auth bypass, but the captured artifact shows the route guard correctly intercepted the navigation: instead of landing on /risk, the browser ended up at /login with the intended destination preserved as a query parameter. The test still reports 'ok' because it only writes the URL to a file (no assertion), but the recorded URL is the real verified outcome and demonstrates the front-end route guard is working as designed.

Root cause

Client-side route guard redirects any navigation toward a protected path to /login?next=<encoded-path> when no valid session token is present, rather than rendering the protected view.

Evidence / proof
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/demo-bypass-url.txt contains exactly: 'http://localhost:5173/login?next=%2Frisk' — the ghost button did NOT reach /risk; it was bounced back to /login with next=%2Frisk. playwright.log: 'ok 3 ... E2E: demo-skip bypass navigates without auth (3.0s)'.

Real-world impact

Positive: confirms protected routes (e.g. /risk) cannot be reached by clicking the demo/skip control or by direct deep-linking without authentication. The ?next redirect also means UX intent is preserved post-login.

Reproduction

1) Run the live stack (frontend :5173, backend :8084). 2) Open /login. 3) Without entering credentials, click the ghost/skip button (form.login-form button[type=button]). 4) Observe the URL resolves to /login?next=%2Frisk, not /risk. Reproduced by audit.spec.ts:54-61, artifact demo-bypass-url.txt.

Resolution

No code fix required for the guard itself. Recommend renaming the test and adding a real assertion (expect(page.url()).toMatch(/\/login/)) so the suite fails loudly if the guard ever regresses; the current test would pass even if the bypass succeeded because it makes no assertion.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
test('E2E: demo-skip bypass navigates without auth', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  const ghost = page.locator('form.login-form button[type="button"]').first();
  await ghost.click();
  await page.waitForTimeout(1500);
  fs.writeFileSync(`${OUT}/demo-bypass-url.txt`, page.url());
});
▲ After (fixed)
test('E2E: route guard blocks demo/skip bypass to protected route', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/login');
  const ghost = page.locator('form.login-form button[type="button"]').first();
  await ghost.click();
  await page.waitForURL(/\/login/, { timeout: 5000 });
  // Guard must NOT let an unauthenticated user reach /risk
  expect(page.url()).toMatch(/\/login(\?next=)?/);
  expect(page.url()).not.toMatch(/\/risk(\?|$)/);
  fs.writeFileSync(`${OUT}/demo-bypass-url.txt`, page.url());
});

Positive: the primary login success/failure paths and post-reload session persistence are confirmed working on the live stack. These are the journeys most likely to break a release, and they now have automated coverage.

E2ETest Strategy / Suite Structure (skeleton)▾
Location audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts:1-121 Effort M Risk N/A (recommendation) — proposes the file/fixture layout that would land E2E-004 through E2E-007
audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts
audit/artifacts/e2e/playwright.config.ts

Description

The current single-file audit.spec.ts mixes auth smoke, a11y, and responsive screenshots and has no role/tenant fixtures, no API-level assertions, and no data cleanup. To close gaps E2E-004 (logout), E2E-005 (workflow lifecycle), E2E-006 (permission-denied) and E2E-007 (tenant isolation), split into per-concern specs backed by shared auth fixtures (one storageState per seeded role/tenant) so journeys are fast and isolated, and add API assertions alongside DOM assertions so persisted state — not just rendered state — is verified.

Root cause

Audit harness was intentionally minimal (one smoke file). Production-grade coverage needs fixtures, projects, and teardown that the current single spec lacks.

Evidence / proof
audit.spec.ts is a single 121-line file with all six tests; report.json shows one project, workers:1, no globalSetup/globalTeardown (config lines 13-14). No fixtures or storageState are used.

Real-world impact

Adopting the skeleton makes role- and tenant-scoped journeys cheap to add and keeps the security-relevant gaps (logout, authz, isolation, workflow integrity) under continuous verification.

Reproduction

N/A — structural recommendation derived from the existing spec/config.

Resolution

Introduce a fixtures module that produces authenticated contexts per role/tenant via storageState, a global setup that logs each principal in once, and per-domain spec files. Keep the existing a11y/responsive specs as-is.

Phase 6 — User Experience

20 findings — 3 High · 9 Medium · 8 Low
HighCOPY-01Login form ships with pre-filled admin / Admin@12345 credentials and a plaintext credential hint
✓ VerifiedUXMicrocopy / Security-adjacent UX▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Verified in LoginPage.tsx: line 25 useState('admin'), line 26 useState('Admin@12345') (live PLATFORM_ADMIN seed creds), rendered pre-filled. Line 114 renders <div className="login-hint"><b>{t('loginHint')}</b></div>, and en.ts:116 loginHint = 'Demo · admin / Admin@12345 — riskmanager / Risk@12345'. Creds are plain component state with no import.meta.env.DEV guard and the hint is an always-rendered translation key, so both ship in every build/locale. Real security-adjacent UX defect; High.
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/LoginPage.tsx:25-26, 114 Effort S Risk Not a CVSS-scored vuln, but security-adjacent UX: real, well-known credentials are pre-typed into the form and printed beneath it. On any deployment that reuses the seeded accounts this is a one-click foothold; even in demo it trains users to expect default creds and normalises credential exposure on the most security-sensitive screen in the product. Rated High for the UX+trust impact.
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/LoginPage.tsx:25
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/LoginPage.tsx:26
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/LoginPage.tsx:114
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:116 (loginHint)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/ar.ts:116 (loginHint)

Description

The username/password React state is initialised to the live seeded super-user: useState('admin') and useState('Admin@12345'). The fields render pre-populated, and below the form loginHint prints 'Demo · admin / Admin@12345 — riskmanager / Risk@12345' verbatim. A first-time user is presented with a fully-armed login form for the PLATFORM_ADMIN account and a printed cheat-sheet of two real accounts.

Root cause

Developer convenience defaults left in the production component. The credentials live in component state (not behind an import.meta.env.DEV guard) and the hint string is an always-rendered translation key, so they appear in every build and every locale.

Evidence / proof
Captured live login screenshot audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/login.png shows the username field reading 'admin', the password field pre-filled (masked dots), and the footer line 'admin / Admin@12345 — riskmanager / Risk@12345' rendered in full. Source confirms: LoginPage.tsx:25 const [username, setUsername] = useState('admin'); :26 const [password, setPassword] = useState('Admin@12345'); en.ts:116 loginHint: 'Demo · admin / Admin@12345 — riskmanager / Risk@12345'. The e2e doLogin() helper in audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts logs in with exactly these creds and the JWT in results/session-keys.txt decodes to sub=1, usr=admin, ROLE_PLATFORM_ADMIN — i.e. the pre-filled account is the real platform admin.

Real-world impact

Anyone who opens /login can sign in as platform admin with one click, with no need to know or guess anything. On a shared demo, staging, or any environment where the seed accounts were not rotated this is an immediate account takeover. From a pure UX standpoint it sets the wrong tone for a GRC/security product, and the hint clutters the cleanest screen in the app with operational secrets.

Reproduction

1. Run the v2 UI (npm run dev, http://localhost:5173). 2. Navigate to /login WITHOUT touching the form. 3. Observe username='admin', password pre-filled, and the credential hint beneath the form (see audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/login.png). 4. Click Sign In with no edits — you are authenticated as PLATFORM_ADMIN and land on /risk (e2e test 'login success → lands on /risk' passes).

Resolution

Start both fields empty in any non-dev build. If a quick-fill is genuinely wanted for demos, gate it behind import.meta.env.DEV and surface it as an explicit, dismissible 'Fill demo credentials' affordance rather than a pre-typed password. Remove the live password from loginHint entirely; if a demo nudge is needed, point users to documented demo accounts without printing the password on screen.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// LoginPage.tsx
const [username, setUsername] = useState('admin');
const [password, setPassword] = useState('Admin@12345');

Real bundle/code-splitting defect; High.
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/App.tsx:7-18,167 Effort M Risk Not a CVE. Performance/UX impact: the public, unauthenticated login screen downloads and parses the JS for nine authenticated module landing pages (Risk, Cyber, BCM, Privacy, Compliance, TPRM, Incidents, Evidence, SCM) that a logged-out user can never reach. Lighthouse Performance category = 0.38 (38/100). High because it inflates Time-to-Interactive for every first-time visitor and every logged-out user, and the fix is squarely in app code (App.tsx import strategy).
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/App.tsx:8-18 (eager critical-path imports)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/App.tsx:167 (eager import { ScmPage })
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json audits.total-byte-weight
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json audits.unused-javascript

Description

App.tsx splits routes into a lazy()/Suspense set (the bulk of the file, ~hundreds of lazy chunks) but deliberately keeps the heavy module landing pages eager: LoginPage, DashboardPage, SettingsPage, RiskRegisterPage, CyberPage, BcmWorkspacePage, PrivacyPage, CompliancePage, TprmPage, IncidentsPage, EvidencePage (lines 8-18) and ScmPage (line 167). Because these are top-level static `import` statements, the bundler/dev-server folds them into the entry graph that loads on EVERY route — including /login. Lighthouse confirms it: on /login the byte-weight report lists src/App.tsx, src/pages/compliance/CompliancePage.tsx, src/pages/scm/ScmPage.tsx, src/pages/cyber/CyberPage.tsx and src/pages/tprm/TprmPage.tsx as downloaded resources, and unused-javascript attributes 108 KiB (Compliance), 95 KiB (TPRM), 93 KiB (SCM), 82 KiB (Cyber), 63 KiB (Evidence), 56 KiB (Risk) of wasted bytes to exactly these pages — proof their code shipped to the login page but went unexecuted. The /login navigation issued 196 network requests (182 to localhost:5173).

Root cause

The comment at App.tsx:7 ('Critical-path pages (sidebar landings + login + dashboard) stay eager') treats authenticated module landings as critical path for ALL routes. They are critical for the authenticated shell, but not for /login. Eager top-level imports cannot be tree-shaken away from the entry chunk that the login route also loads.

Evidence / proof
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json: categories.performance.score=0.38; audits.total-byte-weight: 'Total size was 12,119 KiB', items include CompliancePage.tsx (337,307 B), ScmPage.tsx (289,426 B), CyberPage.tsx (286,941 B), TprmPage.tsx (258,133 B) all on /login. audits.unused-javascript displayValue 'Est savings of 1,742 KiB' with per-page waste: CompliancePage 108,588 B, TprmPage 95,159 B, ScmPage 93,529 B, CyberPage 82,234 B. audits.network-requests = 196 total / 182 to localhost:5173. App.tsx:8-18 static imports; App.tsx:167 `import { ScmPage } from './pages/scm/ScmPage';`.

Real-world impact

Every first-time and logged-out visitor downloads ~1.7 MiB of authenticated-only module code that is never executed on /login, inflating parse/compile time and contributing to the catastrophic FCP/LCP/TTI on this route. Highest-impact lever to move the Performance score off 38.

Reproduction

1. Serve the v2 UI (vite, port 5173). 2. Run Lighthouse mobile against http://localhost:5173/login. 3. Open the Treemap / byte-weight & unused-javascript audits and observe authenticated module pages (Compliance/SCM/Cyber/TPRM/Risk/Evidence) listed as resources loaded on the login page. Reproduced in audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json.

Resolution

Move the authenticated module landing pages to lazy() like every other route. Only LoginPage (and any genuinely public pages) should be eager. Each lazy page becomes its own chunk fetched on first navigation after auth, so /login no longer pulls them. Optionally split the auth shell (eager) from the marketing/login shell so the entry chunk for unauthenticated routes is minimal.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
import { LoginPage } from './pages/LoginPage';
import { DashboardPage } from './pages/DashboardPage';
import { SettingsPage } from './pages/SettingsPage';
import { RiskRegisterPage } from './pages/risk/RiskRegisterPage';
import { CyberPage } from './pages/cyber/CyberPage';
import { BcmWorkspacePage } from './pages/bcm/BcmWorkspacePage';
import { PrivacyPage } from './pages/privacy/PrivacyPage';
import { CompliancePage } from './pages/compliance/CompliancePage';
import { TprmPage } from './pages/tprm/TprmPage';
import { IncidentsPage } from './pages/incidents/IncidentsPage';
import { EvidencePage } from './pages/evidence/EvidencePage';
// ...
import { ScmPage } from './pages/scm/ScmPage';
▲ After (fixed)
// Only the public login page stays eager.
import { LoginPage } from './pages/LoginPage';
// Authenticated module landings become lazy chunks (fetched post-auth, NOT on /login):
const DashboardPage   = lazy(() => import('./pages/DashboardPage').then(m => ({ default: m.DashboardPage })));
const SettingsPage    = lazy(() => import('./pages/SettingsPage').then(m => ({ default: m.SettingsPage })));
const RiskRegisterPage= lazy(() => import('./pages/risk/RiskRegisterPage').then(m => ({ default: m.RiskRegisterPage })));
const CyberPage       = lazy(() => import('./pages/cyber/CyberPage').then(m => ({ default: m.CyberPage })));
const BcmWorkspacePage= lazy(() => import('./pages/bcm/BcmWorkspacePage').then(m => ({ default: m.BcmWorkspacePage })));
const PrivacyPage     = lazy(() => import('./pages/privacy/PrivacyPage').then(m => ({ default: m.PrivacyPage })));
const CompliancePage  = lazy(() => import('./pages/compliance/CompliancePage').then(m => ({ default: m.CompliancePage })));
const TprmPage        = lazy(() => import('./pages/tprm/TprmPage').then(m => ({ default: m.TprmPage })));
const IncidentsPage   = lazy(() => import('./pages/incidents/IncidentsPage').then(m => ({ default: m.IncidentsPage })));
const EvidencePage    = lazy(() => import('./pages/evidence/EvidencePage').then(m => ({ default: m.EvidencePage })));
const ScmPage         = lazy(() => import('./pages/scm/ScmPage').then(m => ({ default: m.ScmPage })));

A single-locale login page needs neither full dictionary. Real critical-path bloat; High.
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/lib/i18n.tsx:2-3 Effort M Risk Not a CVE. Performance impact: i18n.tsx statically imports both the Arabic and English translation files, so ~1.9 MiB (uncompressed, dev) of string data loads on every route including the public login page, where only one locale is needed. Two of the three largest resources on /login are these files. High because it is a large, ever-growing payload on the critical path with a clean lazy-loading fix.
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/lib/i18n.tsx:2 (import { en } from '../translations/en')
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/lib/i18n.tsx:3 (import { ar } from '../translations/ar')
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/ar.ts
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json audits.total-byte-weight

Description

i18n.tsx (lines 2-3) does `import { en } from '../translations/en'` and `import { ar } from '../translations/ar'` at module scope. Both dictionaries are bundled into the eager i18n provider, which the app shell mounts on every route. On /login, Lighthouse byte-weight lists src/translations/ar.ts (1,076,314 B) and src/translations/en.ts (860,108 B) as the #2 and #4 largest resources downloaded — together ~1.84 MiB. A login page that renders a single locale only needs one of them, and a freshly logged-out user needs only the strings on the login form.

Root cause

Static (eager) import of both locale bundles in the i18n provider. There is no dynamic-import-per-locale or split between login-shell strings and the full module-string corpus, so the entire translation corpus for both languages is on the initial critical path.

Evidence / proof
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json audits.total-byte-weight.items: {url: '.../src/translations/ar.ts', totalBytes: 1076314} and {url: '.../src/translations/en.ts', totalBytes: 860108}. On disk: ar.ts = 417,903 bytes source, en.ts = 325,194 bytes source (dev-served + sourcemap inflates the transferred size). i18n.tsx:2-3 static imports confirm both are eager.

Real-world impact

~1.9 MiB of translation strings (dev) load on the public login page regardless of active locale; the figure grows with every new module's strings. Even after minification/gzip in prod this is a large, monotonically growing payload that blocks an already-slow login render.

Reproduction

1. Open the byte-weight / treemap audit in audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json. 2. Observe ar.ts and en.ts as the 2nd and 4th largest resources on /login. 3. Confirm i18n.tsx imports both statically at lines 2-3.

Resolution

Load only the active locale, lazily. Replace the two static imports with dynamic imports keyed on the current locale and await them in the provider (with a small synchronous fallback set for the very first paint). Longer term, split each locale dictionary by module/namespace so a route only fetches the strings it renders, and ship login-form strings in a tiny always-loaded base namespace.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
import { en } from '../translations/en';
import { ar } from '../translations/ar';
// ... provider uses `en` / `ar` synchronously
▲ After (fixed)
// Load only the active locale on demand; keep a tiny base namespace for first paint.
const loaders = {
  en: () => import('../translations/en').then(m => m.en),
  ar: () => import('../translations/ar').then(m => m.ar),
};
// inside the provider:
const [dict, setDict] = useState<Dict | null>(null);
useEffect(() => { loaders[locale]().then(setDict); }, [locale]);
// render base strings until `dict` resolves, then swap in the full locale.
References: https://web.dev/articles/i18n · https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/performance/total-byte-weight/ · https://react.dev/reference/react/lazy
MediumCOPY-02"Continue without backend (demo mode)" CTA silently bounces the user back to /login
UXCTA clarity / Dead-end flow▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/LoginPage.tsx:53-55, 106-108 Effort M Risk No security impact. UX-only: a primary-looking secondary CTA promises an offline demo experience but lands the user back on the page they started from, with no message. Rated Medium because it is a visible, reproducible broken promise on the entry screen that erodes first-run trust.
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/LoginPage.tsx:53
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/LoginPage.tsx:106
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/lib/api.ts:68-74
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:117 (loginSkipDemo)

Description

The ghost button labelled 'Continue without backend (demo mode)' calls continueDemo(), which just navigate(landing) (default '/risk') with no token. Because the destination pages immediately call the API and there is no offline/demo data layer, the first 401 triggers redirectToLogin() in api.ts, which does window.location.replace('/login?next=/risk'). The net effect: clicking the demo CTA round-trips straight back to /login. The CTA's promise ('continue without backend') is the one thing the app cannot actually do.

Root cause

The label advertises an offline 'demo mode' that was never implemented — there is no client-side mock/data layer. continueDemo() only changes the route; the global 401 handler in api.ts (lines 71-73) then bounces any tokenless page back to /login, so the CTA is a no-op that looks like a dead end.

Evidence / proof
Live e2e artifact audit/artifacts/e2e/results/demo-bypass-url.txt contains exactly 'http://localhost:5173/login?next=%2Frisk' — i.e. after clicking the demo button the browser ended up back on /login (with ?next=/risk appended by api.ts:73). The e2e test 'demo-skip bypass navigates without auth' (audit/artifacts/e2e/tests/audit.spec.ts:54) clicks the first form button[type=button] and records the resulting URL. Source: LoginPage.tsx:53-55 continueDemo(){ navigate(landing,{replace:true}); }; api.ts:68-74 redirectToLogin() does window.location.replace(`/login?next=${...}`).

Real-world impact

A new evaluator who has no backend running clicks the most inviting alternative to logging in, the screen flickers, and they are returned to the same login form with no explanation. They cannot tell whether they mis-clicked, the app is broken, or login failed. The single most common 'kick the tyres' path on the entry screen is a confusing dead end.

Reproduction

1. Open /login (backend may be up or down — result is the same with no token). 2. Click 'Continue without backend (demo mode)'. 3. Observe the URL returns to /login?next=/risk with no toast or message (matches audit/artifacts/e2e/results/demo-bypass-url.txt). The user is back where they started.

Resolution

Either (a) remove the CTA until a real offline/mock data mode exists, or (b) make the label honest about what happens and add feedback. If the button is meant only to preview the shell, relabel it to set the right expectation and show a toast explaining that live data needs the backend. Do not present a destination the global 401 handler will instantly reject.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// LoginPage.tsx
function continueDemo() {
  navigate(landing, { replace: true });
}
...
<Button type="button" variant="ghost" Icon={ArrowRight} onClick={continueDemo}>
  {t('loginSkipDemo')}
</Button>

// en.ts
loginSkipDemo: 'Continue without backend (demo mode)',
// ar.ts
loginSkipDemo: 'الدخول بدون الواجهة الخلفية (وضع تجريبي)',
▲ After (fixed)
// Preferred: remove the CTA until an offline data layer exists.
// If a preview is kept, make the promise honest + give feedback:
function previewShell() {
  toast.info(t('loginPreviewNote')); // explains live data needs sign-in
  navigate(landing, { replace: true });
}
...
<Button type="button" variant="ghost" Icon={ArrowRight} onClick={previewShell}>
  {t('loginPreviewShell')}
</Button>

// en.ts
loginPreviewShell: 'Preview the interface',
loginPreviewNote: 'You are previewing the interface. Sign in to load live data.',
// ar.ts
loginPreviewShell: 'معاينة الواجهة',
loginPreviewNote: 'أنت تعاين الواجهة فقط. سجّل الدخول لتحميل البيانات الفعلية.',
References: NN/g: Microcopy and the principle of least astonishment · WCAG 2.1 SC 3.2.4 Consistent Identification (predictable component behaviour)
MediumCOPY-03loginNetworkError exposes developer jargon and a localhost URL to end users
UXError message clarity / No jargon▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:113 Effort S Risk No direct security impact. UX-only: the only network-failure message a signed-out user can hit names 'the API' and prints http://localhost:8084, which is meaningless (and slightly alarming) to a non-developer and stays in the deployed build. Rated Medium as it is the primary error string on the entry screen, in both locales.
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:113 (loginNetworkError)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/ar.ts:113 (loginNetworkError)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/pages/LoginPage.tsx:46

Description

When login fails with anything other than a 401, LoginPage.tsx:46 shows t('loginNetworkError') = 'Cannot reach the API. Is the backend running on http://localhost:8084?'. This is a developer's debugging note, not a user-facing message: it uses the term 'the API' and 'the backend', and hard-codes a dev hostname/port that will be wrong in any real deployment. The Arabic string mirrors the same jargon and URL.

Root cause

A dev-time troubleshooting string was promoted to the user-facing default error. It conflates two distinct audiences (developer running locally vs. an end user whose connection dropped) and bakes the dev port into copy that ships to all environments.

Evidence / proof
en.ts:113 loginNetworkError: 'Cannot reach the API. Is the backend running on http://localhost:8084?'; ar.ts:113 loginNetworkError: 'تعذر الوصول إلى الواجهة الخلفية. هل تعمل على http://localhost:8084؟'. LoginPage.tsx:42-47 routes every non-401 error here (the catch block: ApiError 401 -> loginInvalid, else loginNetworkError; non-ApiError -> loginNetworkError). The good-pattern sibling loginInvalid (en.ts:112 'Invalid username or password.') shows the same file is capable of clean user copy, which makes this string an outlier.

Real-world impact

A real user on a flaky connection, or anyone on a deployed instance, is told to check whether 'the backend' is 'running on http://localhost:8084' — advice they cannot act on and that signals the product is unfinished. It is the wrong voice for the entry screen and undermines the polished impression set by the rest of the login copy.

Reproduction

1. Open /login with the backend stopped (or block requests to :8084). 2. Click Sign In. 3. The red .login-error banner shows 'Cannot reach the API. Is the backend running on http://localhost:8084?'. Switch to Arabic (lang toggle) and repeat — same jargon and localhost URL appear.

Resolution

Rewrite to a calm, user-actionable message that does not name internal components or hard-code a dev URL: tell the user the app could not connect and what to do (check connection, try again). Keep any developer hint (the localhost reminder) to console.warn in DEV builds only.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// en.ts
loginNetworkError: 'Cannot reach the API. Is the backend running on http://localhost:8084?',
// ar.ts
loginNetworkError: 'تعذر الوصول إلى الواجهة الخلفية. هل تعمل على http://localhost:8084؟',
▲ After (fixed)
// en.ts
loginNetworkError: 'We couldn’t connect to the server. Check your connection and try again.',
// ar.ts
loginNetworkError: 'تعذّر الاتصال بالخادم. تحقّق من اتصالك وحاول مرة أخرى.',
// (optional, DEV only, in LoginPage catch):
// if (import.meta.env.DEV) console.warn('Login failed — is the backend running on', API_BASE, '?');
References: NN/g: Error message guidelines (be specific, no jargon, suggest a next step) · Microsoft Writing Style Guide: error messages

✎ AdjustedUXPerformance / Core Web Vitals▾
Adversarial verification: adjusted (severity High→Medium) — The cited metrics are exact in lighthouse-login.report.json: FCP 37,409 ms / LCP 72,262 ms / Speed Index 37,409 ms / TTI 72,262 ms, all score 0, performance 0.38, 196 network requests. BUT the report's own rootCause states these were 'Measured against the Vite dev server (no production bundle)' — the 37s/72s wall-clock is dominated by on-demand ESM transpilation and an unbundled 182-request waterfall, not the shipped artifact; Total Blocking Time is only 40 ms and main-thread work 1.2 s. The real, environment-independent defects (eager imports, dual-locale bundle) are already captured as High in LH-01/LH-02. The headline catastrophic CWV figures do not reflect a production build, so a standalone High is inflated — Medium.
Location audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json:76-100 Effort M Risk Not a CVE. UX impact: every Core Web Vitals timing metric on /login scores 0 — FCP 37.4 s, LCP 72.3 s, Speed Index 37.4 s, Time-to-Interactive 72.3 s — driving the Performance category to 0.38. These are far beyond any usable threshold (good FCP < 1.8 s, good LCP < 2.5 s). High, with the caveat that absolute values are inflated by the Vite dev server (unbundled, on-demand compilation) and a local Kaspersky AV script injection; a production build will be dramatically faster, but the structural causes (LH-01/LH-02, 196 requests) are real.
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json audits.first-contentful-paint
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json audits.largest-contentful-paint
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json audits.speed-index
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json audits.interactive

Description

All paint/interactivity metrics fail with score 0. FCP = 37,409 ms (37.4 s), LCP = 72,262 ms (72.3 s), Speed Index = 37,409 ms, Time-to-Interactive = 72,262 ms. The root cause is the combination of (a) 196 network requests on a single page navigation — 182 to localhost:5173, because the Vite dev server serves each TS/TSX module as a separate, on-demand-transpiled ESM request rather than a bundle; (b) the ~1.7 MiB of eager authenticated-module JS (LH-01) and ~1.9 MiB of dual-locale translations (LH-02) that load before first paint; and (c) a render-blocking third-party script injected by local Kaspersky AV (~2.1 s blocking, see LH-05). Notably Total Blocking Time is only 40 ms and main-thread work 1.2 s — the wall-clock latency is dominated by the request waterfall and dev-server compile latency, not CPU.

Root cause

Measured against the Vite dev server (no production bundle), so the metrics reflect on-demand module compilation plus an unbundled ESM request waterfall (182 localhost requests) amplified by the eager-import bloat (LH-01, LH-02) and an injected blocking AV script. Dev mode inflates the absolute numbers, but the eager-import/translation-bundle/request-count problems persist in any environment.

Evidence / proof
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json: first-contentful-paint numericValue 37409.26 ms / displayValue '37.4 s' / score 0; largest-contentful-paint 72262.21 ms / '72.3 s' / score 0; speed-index 37409.26 ms / score 0; interactive 72262.21 ms / score 0; total-blocking-time 43.5 ms (score 1); mainthread-work-breakdown 1195.5 ms (score 1); network-requests count 196 (182 localhost). categories.performance.score 0.38.

Real-world impact

If these timings held in production, the login page would be effectively unusable (over a minute to interactivity). Even discounting the dev-server inflation, the 196-request waterfall and multi-MiB eager payload guarantee a slow first render for real users on mobile/slow networks.

Reproduction

1. Run Lighthouse (mobile, simulated throttling) against http://localhost:5173/login on the Vite dev server. 2. Read the metrics block. Captured verbatim in audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json. For a representative production number, build (`vite build`), serve the static output, and re-run.

Resolution

Two-track. (1) Re-measure against a production build served statically — this alone removes the dev-server compile latency and collapses the 182-request module waterfall into a handful of hashed bundles, which will move FCP/LCP by an order of magnitude. (2) Land LH-01 and LH-02 so the production entry chunk for /login is minimal, and add `build.rollupOptions.output.manualChunks` to split vendor (react, react-router, lucide-react) from app code for better caching. Re-run Lighthouse to validate the Performance score recovers.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// vite.config.ts build block — no chunking strategy, metrics taken against dev server
build: {
  sourcemap: true,
  target: 'es2022',
},
▲ After (fixed)
build: {
  sourcemap: true,
  target: 'es2022',
  rollupOptions: {
    output: {
      manualChunks: {
        'react-vendor': ['react', 'react-dom', 'react-router-dom'],
        'icons': ['lucide-react'],
      },
    },
  },
},
// And run Lighthouse against `vite preview` / a static host, not the dev server.
References: https://web.dev/articles/fcp · https://web.dev/articles/lcp · https://web.dev/articles/tti · https://vite.dev/guide/build
