audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json: cumulative-layout-shift numericValue 0.34425702372849826 / displayValue '0.344' / score 0.32; layout-shifts displayValue '6 layout shifts found' / score 0; cls-culprits-insight score 0.

Real-world impact

Form fields and buttons move under the user during the multi-second load, risking accidental focus loss or mis-clicks on the credential fields and submit button; degrades the professional feel of the first screen users see.

Reproduction

1. Lighthouse /login run, open the CLS and 'Avoid large layout shifts' audits in audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json. 2. Observe CLS 0.344 and 6 shift events.

Resolution

Reserve space for late-arriving content: give the login card/brand fixed dimensions or a min-height; preload the brand/logo image and set explicit width/height; show a skeleton matching final layout while translations resolve; ensure web fonts use `font-display: optional/swap` with size-adjust metrics to avoid reflow. Once LH-02 ships a base login-string namespace synchronously, the locale-swap shift disappears.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
/* Login card renders with intrinsic height; localized labels swap in after first paint, causing reflow */
<div className="login-card"> ... </div>
▲ After (fixed)
/* Reserve space so async strings/fonts/logo don't reflow the form */
<div className="login-card" style={{ minHeight: 480 }}> ... </div>
/* and on the logo: <img src=... width={160} height={48} /> */
References: https://web.dev/articles/cls · https://web.dev/articles/optimize-cls · https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/performance/layout-shifts/
MediumUX-001Topbar page title is crushed to 2–3 glyphs because the search box holds a fixed 320px width
UXLayout consistency / Information hierarchy▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/shell.css:166-211 Effort S Risk Medium user impact: the single strongest wayfinding cue (the page title) is illegible on every module page at the captured 1366px viewport, harming orientation; no data loss or security impact.
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/risk-register.png (top-right title reads "إد..." / "...RM")
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/bcm.png ("الا..." / "...MA")
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/compliance.png ("الا..." / "...MA")
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/settings.png ("الإ..." / "تعدي...")
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/shell.css:182 (.topbar-title ellipsis)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/shell.css:200 (.search-box width:320px)

Description

On the inner module pages the topbar title block is squeezed to almost nothing — the captured screenshots show the page title rendered as only "إد...", "الا..." or "الإ..." with the eyebrow truncated to "...RM"/"...MA"/"تعدي...". The topbar lays out a fixed-width search box (320px), a context-pack selector, an environment pill, and five icon buttons, all in a flex-shrink:0 right group, while the title block (the only flex-shrinkable child) absorbs all the remaining-space deficit and collapses to ~30px. The title therefore conveys no information at this viewport.

Root cause

.topbar (shell.css:166) is a single flex row with overflow:hidden. .topbar-right (line 191) and .search-box (line 200, width:320px) are flex-shrink:0 / fixed-width, so the only element that can give up width is the title block (line 180 min-width:0). With ~8 right-side controls plus a 320px search field, on a 1366px-wide canvas minus the 280px sidebar there is no room left for the title, and its text-overflow:ellipsis (line 182) clips it to 2–3 characters.

Evidence / proof
shell.css:200 `.search-box { ... width: 320px; }`; shell.css:182 `.topbar-title { ... white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; }`. Captured renders: risk-register.png shows the heading "إدارة المخاطر المؤسسية" reduced to "إد..." and the eyebrow to "...RM"; the same crush appears in bcm.png, compliance.png and settings.png.

Real-world impact

Users cannot read which screen they are on from the topbar on any module page at common laptop widths. The page H1 inside the body still shows the full title, so the topbar title is pure redundant chrome that now actively misleads (it looks broken). The truncated eyebrow ("...RM", "...MA") looks like a rendering bug to auditors evaluating the product.

Reproduction

Run the v2 UI (localhost:5173), log in as admin/Admin@12345, open any module (Risk Register / BCM / Compliance / Settings) in a ~1366px-wide window. The topbar title and eyebrow appear clipped to a few characters. Reproduced in the captured shots risk-register.png, bcm.png, compliance.png, settings.png.

Resolution

Make the search box shrinkable and give the title priority: set `.search-box { width: clamp(160px, 22vw, 320px); min-width: 0; }` and collapse it to an icon-only button below ~1100px. Alternatively, since the page body already renders the full H1, drop the duplicate topbar title on inner pages (keep it only on the dashboard) and reallocate that width to the search box. Ensure the title block keeps `flex: 1 1 auto; min-width: 0;` so it wins remaining space over the controls.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
.search-box {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 8px;
  background: var(--surface-2);
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  border-radius: var(--r-md);
  padding: 7px 11px;
  width: 320px;
  transition: all var(--dur-fast);
}
▲ After (fixed)
.search-box {
  display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 8px;
  background: var(--surface-2);
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  border-radius: var(--r-md);
  padding: 7px 11px;
  /* Shrink with the viewport so the title block keeps its width. */
  width: clamp(160px, 22vw, 320px);
  min-width: 0;
  flex-shrink: 1;
  transition: all var(--dur-fast);
}
@media (max-width: 1100px) {
  /* Collapse to an icon trigger; the title and eyebrow stay readable. */
  .search-box { width: var(--touch-lg); }
  .search-box input, .search-box kbd { display: none; }
}
References: WCAG 2.4.2 Page Titled · WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow
MediumUX-002Risk Register KPI tiles show a number and a stray arrow but no visible metric label
UXInformation hierarchy / CTA clarity▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/components.css:248-347 Effort S Risk Medium user impact: the four headline risk metrics (19 / 4 / 2 / 51) are ambiguous because their labels are visually subordinated and one tile shows an arrow affordance with no apparent destination, slowing comprehension of the register's top-line numbers.
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/risk-register.png (four tiles: 19 مفتوحة, 4 مُعالجة, 2 المخاطر الحرجة, 51 إجمالي المخاطر)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/components.css:329 (.kpi-value)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/components.css:285 (.kpi-clickable arrow)

Description

The Risk Register KPI strip renders large numbers (19, 4, 2, 51) with a leading arrow icon in each tile's corner and a small grey label beneath the number. In the captured shot the arrow reads as a clickable CTA but its target is unclear, and the label sits below the giant number in --ink-3 grey at a much smaller size, so the eye lands on a bare number first ("19", "4") with the meaning ("Open", "Critical risks") demoted. Two of the four tiles have no icon-color/tone differentiation that ties the number to its severity, so "2 critical" does not read as more urgent than "19 open".

Root cause

The .kpi tile pushes the value to the bottom (`.kpi-value { margin-top: auto; }`, components.css:334) and the label is the smaller .kpi-label in --ink-3. The .kpi-clickable arrow (components.css:285-290) is shown on every tile but the affordance reads as decorative when the destination is the same register the user is already on, and tone classes (.kpi-tone-danger etc., lines 344-347) are only applied to some tiles, so the critical count is not visually escalated.

Evidence / proof
components.css:329-339 `.kpi-value { font: 800 var(--num-clamp)/1 ...; margin-top: auto; }`; components.css:285-290 define the per-tile `.kpi-arrow` hover affordance. risk-register.png shows the 4 tiles where the number dominates and the arabic label (مفتوحة / مُعالجة / المخاطر الحرجة / إجمالي المخاطر) is the smaller secondary line, and each tile carries a directional arrow.

Real-world impact

A first-time auditor reading the Risk Register cannot immediately tell what "19" and "4" count without reading the small grey caption; the arrow implies an action that may navigate nowhere new, eroding trust in the affordance. The most important number (critical risks) is not visually prioritised over the routine counts.

Reproduction

Open the Risk Register page (risk-register.png). Observe the four KPI tiles: each shows a bold number, a corner arrow, and a small grey label. Hover a tile to see the arrow shift (components.css:287) even when the navigation target is ambiguous.

Resolution

Lift the label to the top of the tile in --ink-2 (eyebrow style) and keep the number as the value, so the reading order is label → number, not number → caption. Only render the .kpi-arrow on tiles that genuinely navigate (and give them a tooltip/aria-label naming the destination, e.g. "View 2 critical risks"); make the rest non-clickable. Apply .kpi-tone-danger to the critical-risks tile so the number reads red.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
.kpi-value {
  font: 800 var(--num-clamp)/1 var(--font-sans);
  color: var(--ink-1);
  letter-spacing: var(--tracking-num);
  font-feature-settings: 'tnum' 1, 'lnum' 1;
  margin-top: auto;
  min-width: 0;
  white-space: nowrap;
  overflow: hidden;
  text-overflow: ellipsis;
}
▲ After (fixed)
/* Promote the label above the number so tiles read label -> value. */
.kpi-label {
  order: -1;
  font: 700 var(--text-2xs)/1.3 var(--font-sans);
  color: var(--ink-2);
  letter-spacing: var(--tracking-wide);
  text-transform: uppercase;
  margin-bottom: 4px;
}
.kpi-value {
  font: 800 var(--num-clamp)/1 var(--font-sans);
  color: var(--ink-1);
  letter-spacing: var(--tracking-num);
  font-feature-settings: 'tnum' 1, 'lnum' 1;
  margin-top: 2px;
  min-width: 0;
  white-space: nowrap;
  overflow: hidden;
  text-overflow: ellipsis;
}
/* Arrow only on tiles that actually navigate; others lose the cursor cue. */
.kpi:not(.kpi-clickable) .kpi-arrow { display: none; }
References: WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships · WCAG 2.4.6 Headings and Labels
MediumUX-003Login error/feedback states are not visible; the only guidance is a literal credentials hint baked into the page
UXForm feedback states▾
Location audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/login.png:n/a Effort M Risk Medium user impact: the sign-in form gives no inline validation or error affordance in the captured state and instead displays raw demo credentials (admin/Admin@12345, riskmanager/Risk@12345) on the production-styled login page, which is both a UX and a credential-exposure concern.
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/login.png (footer block "تجريبي · admin / Admin@12345 · riskmanager / Risk@12345")

Description

The login screen pre-fills the username "admin" and a masked password, shows required-field asterisks, and a footer panel that prints two live demo credential pairs verbatim. There is no visible inline error region, no field-level validation styling, and no indication of how an invalid login is communicated. The credential hint is presented as ordinary page furniture, so a real deployment that forgets to strip it would leak working logins, and a user who mistypes has no feedback contract to rely on.

Root cause

A dev/demo affordance (printed credentials) is rendered unconditionally on the login page, and the form appears to rely on browser-native validation rather than a styled inline error/aria-live region for failed authentication.

Evidence / proof
login.png renders a footer card reading "تجريبي · admin / Admin@12345 · riskmanager / Risk@12345" directly beneath the sign-in button, plus a "الدخول بدون الواجهة الخلفية (وضع تجريبي)" link. The username field is pre-populated with "admin". No error/validation element is visible in the captured state.

Real-world impact

New users have no learnable feedback model for failed sign-in (was the password wrong? the account locked?). The printed credentials normalise insecure behaviour and would be a finding on their own in a banking-sector deployment; they also clutter the otherwise clean hero layout.

Reproduction

Open login.html / the v2 login route. The credentials hint and "offline demo" link render below the submit button (login.png). Submitting bad credentials should surface a styled, screen-reader-announced error — verify whether one exists; none is present in the captured state.

Resolution

Gate the demo-credentials block and the offline-mode link behind import.meta.env.DEV (or a feature flag) so they never ship to staging/prod. Add a persistent inline error region with role="alert"/aria-live="assertive" above the form that renders auth failures (wrong credentials, lockout, network) in --danger styling, and add aria-invalid + a field-level message on the offending input.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
{/* login form footer */}
<div className="login-demo-hint">
  تجريبي · admin / Admin@12345 · riskmanager / Risk@12345
</div>
<a href="#" className="login-offline">الدخول بدون الواجهة الخلفية (وضع تجريبي)</a>
▲ After (fixed)
{/* Auth error region — always present for SR users, populated on failure */}
{authError && (
  <div className="form-error" role="alert" aria-live="assertive">
    {authError}
  </div>
)}
{/* Demo affordances only in dev builds */}
{import.meta.env.DEV && (
  <>
    <div className="login-demo-hint">
      تجريبي · admin / Admin@12345 · riskmanager / Risk@12345
    </div>
    <a href="#" className="login-offline">الدخول بدون الواجهة الخلفية (وضع تجريبي)</a>
  </>
)}
References: WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification · WCAG 3.3.3 Error Suggestion · WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages
MediumUX-004Mobile Risk Register page title wraps to one word per line, consuming most of the first screen
UXResponsive behaviour▾
Location audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/mobile/risk-register.png:257-262 Effort M Risk Medium user impact: on a phone viewport the page header (eyebrow + title + 3-line subtitle) stacks vertically and the title breaks one Arabic word per line, pushing all actionable content below the fold and wasting the most valuable mobile real estate.
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/mobile/risk-register.png (title "سجل المخاطر" wraps; subtitle stacks ~9 lines)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/shell.css:255-262 (.page / .page-title / .page-sub)

Description

On the captured ~390px phone shot, the Risk Register header occupies roughly the top half of the screen: the eyebrow, title and subtitle compete with the floating "مباشر" live pill and the action buttons (تصفية / العروض) which overlap the eyebrow. The Arabic title and the long ISO 31000 / COSO ERM subtitle wrap aggressively (the subtitle breaks to ~9 short lines), so a user must scroll past a wall of descriptive text before reaching the records list or any KPI.

Root cause

.page-header (shell.css:257) keeps display:flex with justify-content:space-between and the actions on the same row even on small screens; there is no mobile rule to stack header + actions or to clamp/hide the descriptive .page-sub (line 262 caps max-width:600px but does not shorten it). breakpoints.css contains table/KPI/form mobile rules but nothing for .page-header density.

Evidence / proof
mobile/risk-register.png shows "سجل المخاطر" wrapped across two lines and the subtitle "دورة حياة المخاطر التشغيلية وفق ISO 31000 9 COSO ERM" broken into ~9 stacked tokens, with the تصفية/العروض buttons overlapping the eyebrow at the top. shell.css:257 `.page-header { display:flex; ... justify-content:space-between; }` has no max-width:767px override.

Real-world impact

First-screen mobile content is descriptive boilerplate rather than the risk records. The overlap between the floating live pill and the action buttons looks broken. Field users (the audience for mobile) have to scroll before they can act.

Reproduction

Open the Risk Register on a ~390px viewport (mobile/risk-register.png). The header consumes the top portion of the screen; the subtitle wraps to many lines and the action buttons overlap the eyebrow.

Resolution

Add a mobile rule that stacks the header (flex-direction:column), moves actions to their own row, clamps the title to two lines and hides or collapses the long .page-sub behind a tap-to-expand on small screens, so the records list rises toward the fold.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
.page-header { display: flex; align-items: flex-start; justify-content: space-between; margin-bottom: 22px; gap: 16px; }
.page-sub { font-size: 13px; color: var(--ink-3); margin: 6px 0 0; max-width: 600px; line-height: var(--leading-normal); }
▲ After (fixed)
.page-header { display: flex; align-items: flex-start; justify-content: space-between; margin-bottom: 22px; gap: 16px; }
.page-sub { font-size: 13px; color: var(--ink-3); margin: 6px 0 0; max-width: 600px; line-height: var(--leading-normal); }

@media (max-width: 639px) {
  .page-header { flex-direction: column; gap: 12px; margin-bottom: 16px; }
  .page-actions { width: 100%; justify-content: flex-start; flex-wrap: wrap; }
  /* Collapse the descriptive subtitle on phones; keep it for SR/desktop. */
  .page-sub {
    display: -webkit-box; -webkit-line-clamp: 2; -webkit-box-orient: vertical;
    overflow: hidden;
  }
}
References: WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow · WCAG 2.4.2 Page Titled
MediumUX-005Mobile dashboard renders the gauge above its own title, leaving the headline number labelled by overlapping clipped text
UXResponsive behaviour / Information hierarchy▾
Location audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/mobile/dashboard.png:270-281 Effort M Risk Medium user impact: the dashboard's primary score widget is unreadable on mobile — the radial gauge overlaps the greeting and the score caption, so the headline governance number (50/100) sits on top of clipped Arabic text rather than a clear label.
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/mobile/dashboard.png (gauge overlaps "مساء الخير، أيمن" and "مؤشر الحوكمة الشامل")
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/shell.css:270-281 (.dash-grid collapses but inner card not reflowed)

Description

On the phone shot the top hero card places the radial score gauge (value "50 /100") so that it overlaps the greeting "مساء الخير، أيمن" and the date row, and the gauge arc visibly crosses over the Arabic caption text — the digits and the label collide. The export buttons (PDF / PPTX / تصدير) stack vertically above the card and take a full screen-height before the actual KPIs (19 residual risks etc.) appear. The trend pill "-4% · 30 يوم" floats mid-card without a clear anchor.

Root cause

.dash-grid collapses to one column under 1100px (shell.css:279-281), but the hero score card's internal layout (gauge + greeting + caption) is an absolutely/overlap-positioned composition tuned for the wide two-column desktop card and is not re-flowed for a single narrow column, so the SVG gauge and the text stack into the same box.

Evidence / proof
mobile/dashboard.png shows the gauge ring drawn across "مساء الخير، أيمن" and "مؤشر الحوكمة الشامل", with "50" and "100/" partially overlapping the caption; the export controls (ملف المجلس · PDF, ملف المجلس · PPTX, تصدير) are stacked full-width above it. shell.css:270 `.dash-grid { grid-template-columns: 1.4fr 1fr; }` → :279 collapses to 1fr but the card internals are unchanged.

Real-world impact

The single most important dashboard number (the overall governance score) is illegible on mobile because text and graphic overlap. The export buttons monopolise the first screen, so a mobile user opening the dashboard sees controls and a broken gauge before any actual metric.

Reproduction

Open the dashboard on a ~390px viewport (mobile/dashboard.png). The hero score gauge overlaps the greeting and the "مؤشر الحوكمة الشامل" caption; export buttons stack full-width above the card.

Resolution

Give the hero score card a mobile layout: stack greeting → gauge → caption vertically with explicit gaps (no overlap), shrink the gauge to fit one column, and move the export buttons into a single collapsed "تصدير" menu on small screens instead of three stacked full-width buttons. Reserve the first mobile screen for the score + top KPIs, not export chrome.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
.dash-grid    { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1.4fr 1fr; gap: 16px; margin-bottom: 20px; }
@media (max-width: 1100px) {
  .dash-grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
}
▲ After (fixed)
.dash-grid    { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1.4fr 1fr; gap: 16px; margin-bottom: 20px; }
@media (max-width: 1100px) {
  .dash-grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
}
/* Phone: stack the hero score card so the gauge and text never overlap. */
@media (max-width: 639px) {
  .dash-hero-card { display: flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: center; gap: 8px; text-align: center; }
  .dash-hero-card .score-gauge { position: static; width: 160px; height: 160px; }
  /* Collapse the three export buttons into one menu trigger on mobile. */
  .dash-export-row { display: none; }
  .dash-export-menu { display: inline-flex; }
}
References: WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow · WCAG 1.4.4 Resize Text
LowCOPY-04Generic, non-actionable load-failure messages across modules ("Failed to load X" with no recovery path)
UXError message clarity / Actionability▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:455, 1656, 1681, 1734, 4977, 5049, 5141, 5220, 5322, 5374, 5403, 5459, 5489, 5556, 5603, 5649, 5692, 5734 Effort M Risk No security impact. UX-only: a repeated family of ~18 terse load errors tells users what broke but never what to do next (retry, contact admin), leaving a dead state on data-fetch failure. Low severity given they are recoverable on reload, but the pattern is system-wide.
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:455 (riskLoadError)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:1656 (annexLoadFailed)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:5220 (comLoadFailed)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:5556 (f4pLoadFailed)

Description

There is a large, consistent family of fetch-failure strings of the form 'Failed to load <thing>' / 'Could not load <thing>.' — riskLoadError 'Could not load risks.', annexLoadFailed 'Failed to load annex data', comLoadFailed 'Failed to load committees', f4pLoadFailed 'Failed to load fourth-party register', and ~14 more. None offers a recovery action (no 'try again', no 'reload', no 'contact your administrator'). When a list fails to load the user is left on a terse red line with no obvious next step.

Root cause

Error copy was authored as a status label ('what failed') rather than as guidance ('what failed + what to do'). Each module added its own *LoadFailed key by copy-pasting the same terse template, so the missing call-to-action propagated to ~18 keys.

Evidence / proof
grep over en.ts: 18 keys match '/LoadFailed:/' plus riskLoadError (en.ts:455 'Could not load risks.'). Representative values: annexLoadFailed 'Failed to load annex data' (1656), comLoadFailed 'Failed to load committees' (5220), f4pLoadFailed 'Failed to load fourth-party register' (5556), srtLoadFailed 'Failed to load resilience tests' (5734). Contrast with the project's own strong empty-state copy that DOES give a next step, e.g. riskEmptySub 'Click "New Risk" to register the first one.' (en.ts:187) — proving the convention exists but was not applied to load errors.

Real-world impact

On any transient fetch failure the user sees a dead-end message and must guess that reloading might help. For a GRC tool where users may be screening alerts or controls under time pressure, the lack of a retry affordance/instruction adds friction and support tickets. Multiplied across ~18 registers it is a consistent quality gap.

Reproduction

1. Sign in. 2. Open a register whose API is briefly unavailable (e.g. throttle/kill the relevant endpoint) — Risk, Committees, Fourth-party, etc. 3. Observe the failure text is e.g. 'Failed to load committees' / 'Could not load risks.' with no retry button or guidance on what to do next.

Resolution

Add a recovery clause to the load-failure copy and pair it with a Retry affordance in the shared error component. Standardise on one template ('We couldn’t load <thing>. Try again, or contact your administrator if it persists.') and reuse it across the *LoadFailed keys.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// en.ts (representative)
riskLoadError: 'Could not load risks.',
annexLoadFailed: 'Failed to load annex data',
comLoadFailed:   'Failed to load committees',
f4pLoadFailed:   'Failed to load fourth-party register',
▲ After (fixed)
// en.ts — state the failure AND the next step (and render a Retry button)
riskLoadError: 'We couldn’t load your risks. Try again, or contact your administrator if it persists.',
annexLoadFailed: 'We couldn’t load the annex data. Try again, or contact your administrator if it persists.',
comLoadFailed:   'We couldn’t load committees. Try again, or contact your administrator if it persists.',
f4pLoadFailed:   'We couldn’t load the fourth-party register. Try again, or contact your administrator if it persists.',
// ar.ts (mirror, e.g. comLoadFailed):
// 'تعذّر تحميل اللجان. حاول مرة أخرى، أو تواصل مع مسؤول النظام إذا استمرت المشكلة.'
References: NN/g: Error message guidelines (offer a constructive next step) · WCAG 2.1 SC 3.3.1 Error Identification
LowCOPY-05Inconsistent error voice across modules — "Failed to load" vs "Could not load" vs "Could not save"
UXVoice & tone consistency▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:100, 198, 455, 485, 877, 1656 Effort M Risk No security impact. UX-only consistency defect: the same class of failure is phrased three different ways across modules, weakening the impression of a single, coherent product voice. Low severity, system-wide.
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:100 (orgSwitchFailed)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:198 (exportFailed)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:455 (riskLoadError)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:485 (toastRiskFailed)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:877 (sigSignFailedToast)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts:1656 (annexLoadFailed)

Description

Failure copy mixes verb choice, capitalisation and punctuation between otherwise-identical situations. Across en.ts there are 20 strings beginning 'Failed to …' but only 7 beginning 'Could not …'; some end with a full stop ('Could not load risks.'), most do not ('Failed to load committees', 'Export failed'); some are noun-first labels ('Export failed') while others are sentence-style. The result is three competing voices for the same kind of event.

Root cause

No shared copy convention for failure messages; each module/author picked their own phrasing and punctuation, and there is no lint/style guide enforcing one error template, so divergence accumulated as modules were added.

Evidence / proof
grep counts over en.ts: 20 strings start with 'Failed to', 7 start with 'Could not'. Concrete clashes: riskLoadError 'Could not load risks.' (455, period) vs annexLoadFailed 'Failed to load annex data' (1656, no period); toastRiskFailed 'Could not save the risk' (485) vs sigSignFailedToast 'Could not record the signature' (877) vs exportFailed 'Export failed' (198, noun-first). Same product, three styles.

Real-world impact

Inconsistent failure voice makes the UI feel assembled by many hands and reduces perceived quality and trust — especially noticeable in a bilingual enterprise GRC tool where copy is part of the compliance/professionalism signal. It also complicates Arabic translation review since there is no single target phrasing to mirror.

Reproduction

Static review: open tss-grc-ui-v2/src/translations/en.ts and compare lines 100, 198, 455, 485, 877, 1656 — note 'Failed to load …' (no period), 'Could not load …' (period), and 'Export failed' (noun-first) all coexist for the same class of failure.

Resolution

Adopt one failure template and apply it everywhere: choose a single verb ('We couldn’t …' / 'Could not …'), consistent sentence case, and consistent terminal punctuation; document it in the UI style guide and sweep the existing keys. Keep EN and AR phrasing aligned to the chosen template.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// en.ts — three voices for the same event
orgSwitchFailed: 'Could not switch organisation',
exportFailed:    'Export failed',
riskLoadError:   'Could not load risks.',
toastRiskFailed: 'Could not save the risk',
annexLoadFailed: 'Failed to load annex data',
▲ After (fixed)
// en.ts — one template: "We couldn’t <verb> <thing>."
orgSwitchFailed: 'We couldn’t switch organisations. Try again.',
exportFailed:    'We couldn’t export the file. Try again.',
riskLoadError:   'We couldn’t load your risks. Try again.',
toastRiskFailed: 'We couldn’t save the risk. Try again.',
annexLoadFailed: 'We couldn’t load the annex data. Try again.',
// ar.ts mirrors the same single template: 'تعذّر … . حاول مرة أخرى.'
References: NN/g: Maintain consistency and standards (Nielsen heuristic #4) · Microsoft / Apple HIG writing style: consistent error phrasing
LowLH-05Insecure (HTTP) requests and render-blocking script from local Kaspersky AV injection on the login page
UXBest Practices / Security posture (environmental)▾
Location audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json:20-67 Effort S Risk Not a CVE in the app. Best-Practices impact: is-on-https scores 0 ('6 insecure requests found') and the render-blocking-insight attributes ~2.1 s of blocking to an injected http:// script. All six insecure requests are to gc.kis.v2.scr.kaspersky-labs.com — a local Kaspersky antivirus extension man-in-the-middling the page, NOT app-served content. Low because it is an artifact of the test machine's AV, not the application; however it documents that the app is served over plain HTTP in this environment, which is a real prod-readiness concern.
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json audits.is-on-https
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json audits.render-blocking-insight

Description

The is-on-https audit lists 6 insecure (http://) requests, all to gc.kis.v2.scr.kaspersky-labs.com (Kaspersky's local web-shield injects scripts into pages). The render-blocking-insight audit (Est savings 1,050 ms) and unused-javascript both implicate the same injected main.js (~201 KB, 2,104 ms blocking). These are introduced by the auditor's machine, not the application bundle. Separately, the app itself is served over http://localhost:5173 in dev with no HTTPS, which is acceptable for local dev but must be HTTPS in staging/prod (CLAUDE.md notes prod uses SSL/PKCS12).

Root cause

Local Kaspersky antivirus browser integration injects its own HTTP scripts and beacons into every page it scans; Lighthouse counts them against the page. The underlying app is plain HTTP in the dev profile.

Evidence / proof
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json is-on-https: score 0, displayValue '6 insecure requests found', all items url host = gc.kis.v2.scr.kaspersky-labs.com. render-blocking-insight: displayValue 'Est savings of 1,050 ms', top item url = http://gc.kis.v2.scr.kaspersky-labs.com/.../main.js, wastedMs 2104, totalBytes 201599. network-requests: 6 of 196 are kaspersky.

Real-world impact

On the audited machine the AV script blocks rendering for ~2.1 s and triggers the HTTPS failure, distorting the Best-Practices score (0.77) and the timing metrics. It does not affect end users who lack this AV, but it inflates the audit and masks the app's true numbers. The real, app-attributable point is that the app must be served over HTTPS outside dev.

Reproduction

1. Inspect is-on-https and render-blocking-insight in audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json; note every insecure/blocking third-party URL is kaspersky-labs.com. 2. Re-run Lighthouse on a machine without Kaspersky web-shield, or in an incognito profile with extensions disabled, and these 6 requests + the blocking script disappear.

Resolution

Re-run the audit on a clean profile (no AV script injection, extensions disabled) to get representative Best-Practices/timing numbers. Confirm prod is served strictly over HTTPS (the prod profile already mandates SSL/PKCS12 per CLAUDE.md) and add a strict Content-Security-Policy + HSTS so injected http scripts are blocked in production. No change to the login page code is required for the AV artifact itself.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
# Audited on a workstation with Kaspersky web-shield active; app served over http://localhost:5173 (dev).
▲ After (fixed)
# Re-audit with `--chrome-flags="--disable-extensions"` on a clean profile;
# enforce HTTPS + HSTS + CSP in staging/prod (prod profile already uses PKCS12 SSL).
References: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/pwa/is-on-https/ · https://web.dev/articles/render-blocking-resources · https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Strict-Transport-Security
LowLH-06Console error on /login: favicon.ico returns 404 (errors-in-console audit fails)
UXBest Practices▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/index.html:1-22 Effort S Risk Not a CVE. Best-Practices impact: the errors-in-console audit scores 0 because the browser logs a failed request — GET /favicon.ico returns 404 (Not Found). Low: cosmetic and a noisy console entry, but it contributes to the Best-Practices score (0.77) and signals a missing static asset / favicon link.
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json audits.errors-in-console
tss-grc-ui-v2/index.html (no <link rel="icon"> declared)

Description

errors-in-console fails (score 0) with a single logged error: 'Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 404 (Not Found)' for http://localhost:5173/favicon.ico. index.html declares no <link rel="icon"> and there is no favicon.ico at the web root / public dir (public/ contains brand/ and sw.js but no favicon.ico), so the browser's default /favicon.ico probe 404s and logs an error.

Root cause

No favicon is provided at the default location and index.html does not declare an icon link, so the browser's implicit /favicon.ico request 404s. A brand/ directory exists under public/ but is not wired to a favicon link.

Evidence / proof
audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json errors-in-console: score 0, items[0] = {source: 'network', description: 'Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 404 (Not Found)', sourceLocation.url: 'http://localhost:5173/favicon.ico'}. tss-grc-ui-v2/index.html head contains <title>, charset, viewport, theme-color but no icon link. public/ listing: brand/, sw.js (no favicon.ico).

Real-world impact

Every page load logs a 404 error in the console (noise that hides real errors during debugging) and the tab shows no favicon. Counts against the Best-Practices category score.

Reproduction

1. Open audit/raw/lighthouse-login.report.json errors-in-console — note the /favicon.ico 404. 2. Load http://localhost:5173/login in a browser and check DevTools Console / Network for the 404 on favicon.ico.

Resolution

Add a favicon asset (e.g. public/favicon.ico or an SVG from the existing public/brand/ set) and declare it in index.html with <link rel="icon">. This removes the 404 and the console error.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
    <title>TSS GRC Platform</title>
    <!-- no icon link; browser probes /favicon.ico -> 404 -->
▲ After (fixed)
    <title>TSS GRC Platform</title>
    <link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/brand/logo.svg" />
    <!-- or place a real /public/favicon.ico -->
References: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/lighthouse/best-practices/errors-in-console/ · https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Favicon

Lighthouse SEO category is 0.82, with meta-description (and the environmental robots-txt audit, which reports 27 errors but is not under app control on localhost) as the contributors.

LowUX-006Workflow "start" stage rail and action chip rows are dense undifferentiated chains with no clear primary next step
UXCTA clarity / Information hierarchy▾
Location audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/risk-register.png:n/a Effort M Risk Low user impact: the lifecycle stage rail and the row of quick-action chips present 5–7 equally weighted pills with numeric badges, so a user cannot tell which step is the recommended next action; comprehension is slowed but no task is blocked.
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/risk-register.png ("ابدأ معالجاً" rail: 5 chevron pills; lower chip row with red !-badges)
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/bcm.png ("ابدأ معالجاً" rail: 6 pills)
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/compliance.png (chip row with 6 chips, several red "!" badges)

Description

Each module page shows an "ابدأ معالجاً" (start processing) rail of chevron-linked pills (e.g. تحديد وتقييم المخاطر 5 خ, خطة معالجة المخاطر 4 خ, قبول المخاطر 3 خ, إقرار دوري بالمخاطر 1 خ) and, below the KPIs, a second wrapping row of action chips with small red "!" count badges (e.g. "خطة معالجة المخاطر 4 !", "تصعيد تجاوز شهية المخاطر 1"). All pills share the same size, weight and border, so nothing signals which is the primary or most urgent next action; the red "!" badges indicate attention items but are visually identical in shape to the neutral count badges, and the chevrons imply sequence on a row that wraps.

Root cause

The stage rail and the quick-action chip row use a single uniform chip style with a trailing count; there is no primary/secondary hierarchy and no visual escalation tying the red "!" attention badges apart from neutral counters beyond color. With 5–7 items wrapping, the chevron "flow" metaphor breaks.

Evidence / proof
risk-register.png renders the rail "ابدأ معالجاً" with 5 chevron pills of equal weight, and a lower chip row where "خطة معالجة المخاطر" carries a red "4 !" and "الاستجابة لتجاوز عتبات المؤشرات" carries "3 !". compliance.png shows the same pattern with 6 chips, several bearing red "!" badges. bcm.png shows a 6-pill rail.

Real-world impact

A user landing on a module cannot quickly identify the single recommended next action or distinguish overdue/attention items from routine ones at a glance; this dilutes the value of the otherwise informative attention badges and adds cognitive load on every module entry.

Reproduction

Open Risk Register / BCM / Compliance (respective shots). Observe the "ابدأ معالجاً" rail of equal-weight chevron pills and the lower wrapping chip row mixing red "!" attention badges with neutral counters in the same shape.

Resolution

Promote one chip as the primary next action (filled --primary, larger), demote the rest to secondary outline chips, and give the red "!" attention badges a distinct shape/icon (e.g. a triangle warning glyph) plus an aria-label like "4 items need attention" so they are not confused with neutral counts. Cap the rail to the active stage plus next, with a "+N" overflow, rather than rendering all stages as equal pills.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
.wf-filter-chip {
  /* uniform chip — same weight for primary and secondary actions */
  font-size: var(--chip-font);
  padding: var(--chip-pad);
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  border-radius: var(--chip-radius);
}
▲ After (fixed)
.wf-filter-chip {
  font-size: var(--chip-font);
  padding: var(--chip-pad);
  border: 1px solid var(--border);
  border-radius: var(--chip-radius);
}
/* One recommended next action stands out. */
.wf-filter-chip--primary {
  background: var(--primary);
  color: var(--on-primary);
  border-color: var(--primary);
  font-weight: 700;
}
/* Attention badge gets its own shape + accessible name, not just red. */
.wf-chip-attention {
  background: var(--danger-bg); color: var(--danger-fg);
  border-radius: var(--r-xs); /* square-ish vs round neutral counter */
}
.wf-chip-attention::before { content: '\26A0'; margin-inline-end: 3px; }
References: WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color · WCAG 2.4.6 Headings and Labels
LowUX-007Settings customizer applies theme/color changes immediately with no preview boundary or confirmation copy
UXForm feedback states / CTA wording▾
Location audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/settings.png:n/a Effort M Risk Low user impact: the workspace customizer auto-applies and auto-saves every change to the device with only a one-line note and a single "restore defaults" escape, risking accidental, non-obvious changes (e.g. an unreadable color) with no undo of the last action.
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/settings.png (subtitle "التغييرات تُطبّق فورًا وتُحفظ على هذا الجهاز"; only control: استعادة الافتراضيات)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/tokens.css:234-250 (--ui-scale / live theme application)

Description

The "تخصيص مساحة العمل" page states that changes apply instantly and are saved to this device, and offers presets, a quick-colors row, font-size tiles, and sidebar/header sliders. The only safety control is "استعادة الافتراضيات" (restore defaults), which is an all-or-nothing reset. There is no per-change undo, no explicit Save/Cancel boundary, and no warning when a user picks a custom page-background/identity color that could reduce text contrast (the color swatches show raw hex like #F2EEE6 / #FAF8F4 with no contrast feedback).

Root cause

The customizer writes directly to CSS variables/localStorage on every interaction (tokens.css exposes --ui-scale and per-token overrides applied via inline style.setProperty per the comment at lines 234-257), so there is no staged/preview state to commit or discard, and no validation that a chosen color preserves legible contrast against ink tokens.

Evidence / proof
settings.png subtitle: "تعديل الألوان وحجم الخط والشريط الجانبي والتخطيط. التغييرات تُطبّق فورًا وتُحفظ على هذا الجهاز." with "استعادة الافتراضيات" as the sole non-content control. tokens.css:234-257 documents the live-applied --ui-scale and the per-token user overrides that "win because inline style.setProperty wins over stylesheet rules."

Real-world impact

A user can pick a near-white identity/background color and make text unreadable with no inline warning and no way to undo just that one change short of resetting everything. The lack of a Save/Cancel model also makes the customizer feel risky to explore on a shared/work device.

Reproduction

Open Settings → تخصيص مساحة العمل (settings.png). Change a quick color or background swatch; the whole UI re-themes immediately with no confirmation and no single-step undo, only a global restore-defaults.

Resolution

Add an inline contrast check on the page-background / identity color pickers that warns when the chosen color fails AA against --ink-1 (e.g. a small "تباين منخفض" badge), and add a lightweight per-change Undo (toast with "تراجع") alongside the existing restore-defaults so users can revert the last action without losing all customisation. Clarify the persistence copy to name where it is saved (this browser/device).

▼ Before (vulnerable)
// color picker change handler
onChange={(hex) => setToken('--bg', hex)} // applies + persists immediately
▲ After (fixed)
// color picker change handler with contrast guard + undoable apply
onChange={(hex) => {
  const ratio = contrastRatio(hex, getToken('--ink-1'));
  setContrastWarning(ratio < 4.5); // surface "\u062a\u0628\u0627\u064a\u0646 \u0645\u0646\u062e\u0641\u0636" badge
  const prev = getToken('--bg');
  setToken('--bg', hex);
  toast.undoable('\u062a\u0645 \u062a\u063a\u064a\u064a\u0631 \u0627\u0644\u0644\u0648\u0646', () => setToken('--bg', prev));
}}
References: WCAG 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) · WCAG 3.3.4 Error Prevention · WCAG 3.2.2 On Input
LowUX-008Recent-records list and KPI strip have no visible empty/zero-state treatment distinct from low real values
UXEmpty / loading / error states▾
Location audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/bcm.png:972-985 Effort S Risk Low user impact: BCM shows a "0 بنود غير ممتثلة" tile and other modules can render zero counts that read identically to a still-loading or no-data state, creating brief ambiguity about whether data is absent or genuinely zero.
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/shots/bcm.png (tile "0 بنود غير ممتثلة"; readiness index 31.7/100)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/components.css:972-985 (.placeholder / .empty-inline)

Description

BCM renders a KPI tile with value "0" (بنود غير ممتثلة / non-compliant items). A zero in a KPI tile is visually indistinguishable from a tile that failed to load or has no underlying data — the same big-number layout is used. The codebase has both a full .placeholder empty state and a calibrated .empty-inline mini empty state (components.css:972-985), but KPI tiles render a literal 0 rather than choosing an explicit "no data" vs "genuinely zero" treatment, so a 0 could equally mean "clean" (good) or "not yet measured" (unknown).

Root cause

KPI tiles render the numeric value unconditionally; there is no branch that swaps a missing/uninitialised metric for the existing .empty-inline-compact treatment (components.css:985 is explicitly scoped "even denser for sidebars / KPI cells" but is not wired into the KPI render path here).

Evidence / proof
bcm.png shows the tile "0" with label "بنود غير ممتثلة" next to "2 أزمات نشطة", "5 فجوات مفتوحة", "1 تحليلات BIA معتمدة", and a readiness index of 31.7/100. components.css:972-985 defines `.empty-inline` and `.empty-inline-compact` ("even denser for sidebars / KPI cells") that exist for exactly this case but are not applied to the zero tiles.

Real-world impact

Users cannot tell at a glance whether "0 non-compliant items" means the program is clean or the metric has never been computed, which matters for a compliance audience where "zero findings" and "not assessed" have very different meanings.

Reproduction

Open BCM (bcm.png). Note the "0" KPI tile; compare to the readiness index which is computed (31.7/100). There is no visual cue distinguishing a true zero from an unmeasured metric.

Resolution

When a metric is genuinely zero, render the number with a subtle confirming cue (e.g. a small "✓ لا توجد" tone or success tint) and when a metric is unavailable/uninitialised render the existing .empty-inline-compact "—" treatment with a tooltip ("لم يُحتسب بعد"), so zero-good and no-data are unambiguous.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
<div className="kpi">
  <div className="kpi-value">{value}</div>
  <div className="kpi-label">{label}</div>
</div>
▲ After (fixed)
<div className={`kpi ${value === 0 ? 'kpi-tone-success' : ''}`}>
  {value == null
    ? <div className="empty-inline-compact" title="\u0644\u0645 \u064a\u064f\u062d\u062a\u0633\u0628 \u0628\u0639\u062f">\u2014</div>
    : <div className="kpi-value">{value}</div>}
  <div className="kpi-label">{label}</div>
</div>
References: WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships · WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color

Phase 7 — Accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA)

7 findings — 3 High · 3 Medium · 1 Info
HighA11Y-001Sidebar muted text (--sb-text-3) fails WCAG 1.4.3 contrast on every authenticated page (2.4:1)
✓ VerifiedAccessibilityColor Contrast▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Verified: tokens.css:116 --sb-text-3 = #4A5C58 on tokens.css:112 --sb-bg = #0B1F22. Recomputed WCAG ratio = 2.40:1 (matches the finding), far below the 4.5:1 AA floor for the 9-10px sidebar captions/group labels. axe dashboard.json confirms nodes with fg #4a5c58 / bg #0b1f22 / contrastRatio 2.4, and the sidebar shell renders on every authenticated page. Sibling token --sb-text-2 (#7E928F) measures 5.19:1, confirming the wrong tier was assigned. Genuine WCAG 1.4.3 failure (serious); High.
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/tokens.css:116 Effort S Risk Not a CVSS-scored vulnerability. Risk rationale: this single token drives 3 of the 68 color-contrast instances on ALL 9 authenticated pages (the sidebar version sub-line plus two collapsible group labels), so it is the most pervasive defect. WCAG 2.1 Level AA conformance (1.4.3) is a contractual/regulatory requirement for Saudi public-sector and banking GRC procurement; a 2.4:1 ratio is barely over half the 4.5:1 floor and renders the version banner and risk/administration group headers effectively unreadable for low-vision users. High because it is global, repeated, and a named AA failure, but not Critical because it affects secondary/navigational chrome rather than primary task content.
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/tokens.css:116 (--sb-text-3: #4A5C58)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/shell.css:36 (.sb-sub uses var(--sb-text-3))
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/shell.css:40 (.sb-section)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/shell.css:101 (collapsible group label)
DOM selectors: .sb-sub, button[aria-controls="sb-group-risk"] > span, button[aria-controls="sb-group-administration"] > span

Description

The dark sidebar uses the design token --sb-text-3 (#4A5C58) for its muted captions: the version/locale sub-line (“الإصدار ٢٫٠ · الرياض”) and the collapsible navigation group headers (إدارة المخاطر / الإدارة). On the sidebar background --sb-bg (#0B1F22) this yields a measured contrast ratio of 2.4:1, well below the WCAG 2.1 AA minimum of 4.5:1 for normal-size text. Because the sidebar is part of the global app shell injected on every route, axe flags these same 3 nodes on all 9 authenticated pages (login has no shell, hence 0 violations).

Root cause

Token --sb-text-3 was chosen for visual subtlety against the very dark petrol sidebar without verifying contrast. At #4A5C58 on #0B1F22 it only reaches 2.4:1. The sibling token --sb-text-2 (#7E928F) already measures 5.19:1 on the same background and passes AA — the wrong (darker) tier of the two muted greys was assigned to these labels.

Evidence / proof
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/axe/dashboard.json nodes[0..2]: fgColor #4a5c58, bgColor #0b1f22, contrastRatio 2.4, expectedContrastRatio 4.5:1 (font 10px normal for .sb-sub; 9px bold for the two group labels). Identical 3-node block appears in every per-page file (risk-register, dashboard, compliance, cyber, privacy, tprm, bcm, settings, knowledge-base). Recomputed locally with the WCAG relative-luminance formula: #4A5C58 on #0B1F22 = 2.40:1; proposed #9DB0AB = 7.49:1.

Real-world impact

Low-vision users, users on low-quality/glare-affected displays, and users in bright ambient light cannot reliably read the product version, environment/region indicator, or the navigation group headers that organise the entire left-hand menu. This degrades wayfinding across the whole product and is a hard AA failure on every page.

Reproduction

1. Run the live app (http://localhost:5173, backend :8084) and log in as admin/Admin@12345. 2. Open any authenticated route (e.g. /dashboard). 3. Run axe-core (the captured Playwright harness) → color-contrast violation with fgColor #4a5c58 / bgColor #0b1f22 / ratio 2.4 on .sb-sub and the two sb-group button spans. Artifact: audit/artifacts/e2e/results/axe/dashboard.json.

Resolution

Promote the sidebar muted captions to a contrast-checked tone. Re-define --sb-text-3 to a value that clears 4.5:1 on --sb-bg (#0B1F22). #9DB0AB (7.49:1) or #93A8A3 (6.79:1) both pass with comfortable margin while staying in the same desaturated teal-grey family. Apply the same change in the [data-theme="dark"] block (tokens.css:349) where --sb-text-3 is also #4A5C58 on an even darker #060F11 sidebar. After the change, re-run axe to confirm the 3 sidebar nodes drop on all 9 pages.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
/* tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/tokens.css:116 */
--sb-text-3:    #4A5C58;   /* 2.4:1 on --sb-bg #0B1F22 — FAILS WCAG AA */
▲ After (fixed)

--sb-text-3:    #9DB0AB;   /* 7.49:1 on --sb-bg #0B1F22 — passes WCAG AA */

Recomputed ratio = 2.71:1 (matches), below 4.5:1 AA. axe settings.json shows 3 .scale-seg-label nodes with fg #8c9690 / bg #f5f1e9 / contrastRatio 2.7. --ink-4 is a token-level token reused for .text-dim and secondary captions, so not a one-off; adjacent --ink-3 (#5C6A65) reaches 5.03:1. Genuine WCAG 1.4.3 failure; High.
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/tokens.css:28 Effort M Risk Not CVSS-scored. Risk rationale: --ink-4 (#8C9690) is referenced by dozens of component and page rules (text-dim, scale-seg-label, placeholders, empty-state captions, audit/capa/ethics/changes page labels) so although axe only caught it on /settings (3 of the 6 instances), the token is a latent AA failure anywhere it lands on a light surface. The team already documented and partially fixed this exact token for form placeholders (components.css:91, switched placeholders to --ink-3), which both proves the root cause and shows the fix is safe; remaining unconverted usages still fail. High due to breadth of usage on primary content labels.
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/tokens.css:28 (--ink-4: #8C9690)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/components.css:1935 (.scale-seg-label color: var(--ink-4))
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/components.css:1648 (.text-dim)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/components.css:2045, 1959
DOM selectors on /settings: .scale-seg-btn:nth-child(1)/(3)/(4) > .scale-seg-label (font-size labels صغير / كبير / كبير جدًا)

Description

The font-size segmented control on the Settings (تخصيص مساحة العمل) page renders its option labels (.scale-seg-label) in --ink-4 (#8C9690) over the segmented-control track surface --surface-2 (#F5F1E9). Measured contrast is 2.7:1 against the 4.5:1 AA floor. axe flagged 3 such labels on /settings. The same token is used for .text-dim and many secondary captions across components and page stylesheets, so this is a token-level defect, not a one-off.

Root cause

--ink-4 (#8C9690) is the lightest 'still-text' ink in the ramp and was used for de-emphasised labels, but at #8C9690 it only reaches 2.71:1 on --surface-2 (#F5F1E9) and 2.88:1 on --surface (documented in components.css:91). The adjacent ramp tier --ink-3 (#5C6A65) reaches 5.03:1 on --surface-2 / 5.34:1 on --surface and passes AA — the same correction the team already applied to input placeholders (components.css:100, 136).

Evidence / proof
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/axe/settings.json nodes[3..5]: fgColor #8c9690, bgColor #f5f1e9, contrastRatio 2.7, font 9.5px bold, expectedContrastRatio 4.5:1, target .scale-seg-btn ... > .scale-seg-label. Source comment components.css:91 already records “placeholder var(--ink-4) on var(--surface) = 2.88:1 → FAILS AA (4.5)”. Recomputed: #8C9690/#F5F1E9 = 2.71:1; #5C6A65/#F5F1E9 = 5.03:1.

Real-world impact

Secondary labels, de-emphasised captions, empty-state text and the font-size picker labels are unreadable for low-vision users on light surfaces. Because --ink-4 is used widely, the real-world AA failure surface is larger than the 3 instances axe happened to catch on /settings.

Reproduction

1. Log in (admin/Admin@12345), open /settings. 2. Run axe → color-contrast on .scale-seg-label spans, fgColor #8c9690 / bgColor #f5f1e9 / ratio 2.7. Artifact: audit/artifacts/e2e/results/axe/settings.json.

Resolution

Two-part fix. (a) For the specific failing control, change .scale-seg-label color from var(--ink-4) to var(--ink-3) (components.css:1935) — mirrors the documented placeholder fix. (b) Strategically, audit all var(--ink-4) text usages and migrate any that sit on light surfaces (--surface / --surface-2 / --surface-3) to var(--ink-3); reserve --ink-4 for non-text decoration (icons, borders, scrollbar thumb) where 1.4.3 does not apply. Optionally bump the --ink-4 token itself toward #6E7A75 (>=4.5:1 on --surface-2) if it must remain a text colour. Re-run axe on /settings to confirm.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
/* tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/components.css:1931 */
.scale-seg-label {
  ...
  color: var(--ink-4);   /* #8C9690 on --surface-2 = 2.71:1 — FAILS AA */
}
▲ After (fixed)
/* tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/components.css:1931 */
.scale-seg-label {
  ...
  color: var(--ink-3);   /* #5C6A65 on --surface-2 = 5.03:1 — passes AA */
}
/* General rule: text in var(--ink-4) on any light --surface* must become
   var(--ink-3); keep --ink-4 for icons/borders only. */
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) · EN 301 549 9.1.4.3

✓ VerifiedAccessibilityColor Contrast▾
Adversarial verification: confirmed — Verified: tokens.css:98 --risk-vhigh = #D87560; the .score-pill pairs it with hard-coded white text. Recomputed white-on-#D87560 = 3.17:1 (matches the cited 3.16, rounding), below the 4.5:1 AA floor for 11px bold (not large-text exempt). axe risk-register.json confirms 28 total color-contrast nodes of which 25 are fg #ffffff / bg #d87560 / contrastRatio 3.16 — the dominant source of the page's violations. Dark ink #15201D on the same fill would reach 5.28:1. Genuine WCAG 1.4.3 failure; High.
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/tokens.css:98 Effort M Risk Not CVSS-scored. Risk rationale: this is the single largest contributor — 25 of the 28 risk-register instances and 25 of the 68 total. The failing element is the residual/inherent risk SCORE PILL, primary decision-grade content in a risk-management tool. A user relying on these numerals to triage ‘very high’ risks is exactly the high-stakes path; an unreadable score in a GRC register is materially worse than chrome text, hence High.
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/tokens.css:98 (--risk-vhigh: #D87560)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/components.css:790 (.score-pill)
DOM: span.score-pill style="background: var(--risk-vhigh); color: rgb(255,255,255)" (values 12/15 etc.) on /risk

Description

On the Risk Register (/risk) the residual/inherent score pills render white (#FFFFFF) numerals on the --risk-vhigh fill (#D87560). Measured contrast is 3.16:1, below the 4.5:1 AA floor for normal text (the pill text is 11px bold, which is NOT 'large text' — large-text exemption requires >=18.66px bold / 24px). axe reported 25 identical instances on /risk, making this the dominant source of the page's 28 violations.

Root cause

The --risk-vhigh heatmap tone (#D87560) is a mid-light terracotta tuned to look correct as a heatmap CELL fill, but it is too light to carry white text at small sizes: white-on-#D87560 = 3.16:1. The .score-pill component pairs that same fill with hard-coded white text, inheriting the failure. The heatmap-cell variant correctly uses dark text, but the pill does not.

Evidence / proof
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/axe/risk-register.json: 25 nodes with fgColor #ffffff, bgColor #d87560, contrastRatio 3.16, font 11px bold, expectedContrastRatio 4.5:1; html ‘<span class="score-pill" style="background: var(--risk-vhigh); color: rgb(255,255,255)">12</span>’. axe-summary.json shows risk-register color-contrast(28). Recomputed: #FFFFFF/#D87560 = 3.17:1; white on a darkened #B5453A = 5.42:1; dark ink #15201D on #D87560 = 5.28:1.

Real-world impact

Numeric risk scores — the most decision-critical content in the register — are below AA contrast for 25 cells. Low-vision risk managers may misread or fail to read scores, undermining the core triage function of the module.

Reproduction

1. Log in, open /risk. 2. Run axe → 25 color-contrast violations, fgColor #ffffff / bgColor #d87560 / ratio 3.16 on span.score-pill. Artifact: audit/artifacts/e2e/results/axe/risk-register.json.

Resolution

Two viable fixes; prefer (a) to preserve the heatmap hue. (a) Switch .score-pill on the very-high tone to dark ink (color: var(--ink-1) #15201D) instead of white → 5.28:1; gate via a modifier class so only the light tones (med/high/vhigh) get dark ink while crit/danger keep white. (b) Introduce a dedicated, darker pill-fill token --risk-vhigh-strong (e.g. #B5453A, white text = 5.42:1) used only for .score-pill, leaving --risk-vhigh unchanged for heatmap cells. Do NOT simply darken --risk-vhigh globally without re-checking heatmap-cell dark-text contrast. Re-run axe on /risk.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
/* tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/components.css:790 */
.score-pill {
  ... /* background: var(--risk-vhigh) #D87560; color: #fff inline */
}
/* white (#fff) on #D87560 = 3.16:1 — FAILS AA */
▲ After (fixed)
/* Option A — dark ink on light risk tones (keep heatmap hue) */
.score-pill.score-pill--light { color: var(--ink-1); }  /* #15201D on #D87560 = 5.28:1 */
/* apply --light modifier for med/high/vhigh fills; keep white for crit */

/* Option B — dedicated darker pill token (tokens.css) */
--risk-vhigh-strong: #B5453A;  /* white text = 5.42:1, used by .score-pill only */
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) · EN 301 549 9.1.4.3

AccessibilityColor Contrast▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/tokens.css:58,74 Effort S Risk Not CVSS-scored. Risk rationale: borderline failures (3.0–3.9:1) on KPI/progress numerals across dashboard, compliance, cyber, privacy, bcm. They are small in count (1–2 per page) and partly transition-render artifacts, but they are still flagged AA failures on data-bearing figures. Medium: real but marginal, and one variant (the 48px BCM number at 2.58:1) only needs the 3:1 large-text threshold which a token swap clears.
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/tokens.css:58 (--accent-700: #876019)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/tokens.css:74 (--warning: #C8932A)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/components.css:348,399,2133 (kpi/stat-tile/accent value uses var(--accent-700))
DOM: progress-label spans color:var(--accent-700) on /dashboard,/compliance,/cyber,/privacy; bcm score number color:var(--warning,#c47e00) at 48px

Description

Two related accent/amber colours produce small under-contrast figures on the cream surface --surface (#FAF8F4). (1) Progress-percentage and KPI numerals coloured var(--accent-700): axe sampled fgColor #a07622 (the value mid-CSS-transition) at 3.87:1 on dashboard, compliance, cyber, privacy. (2) The BCM readiness hero number (48px/700) coloured var(--warning) #C8932A measured 2.58:1; because it is large text the applicable threshold is 3:1, which it still fails.

Root cause

TWO contributing causes. (i) The global CSS transition rule (tokens.css:368, `html * { transition: color 180ms }`) means axe occasionally samples an INTERMEDIATE colour while text animates — the static --accent-700 (#876019) actually measures 5.33:1 on #FAF8F4 and PASSES, but the captured rendered value #a07622 was a transition frame at 3.87:1. (ii) Independently, --warning (#C8932A) is genuinely too light for text on cream (2.58:1) and was used directly for the 48px BCM figure instead of the readable --warning-fg (#876019, 5.33:1).

Evidence / proof
dashboard.json / compliance.json: fgColor #a07622, bgColor #faf8f4, contrastRatio 3.87, 12px bold, target .progress-label span (color: var(--accent-700)). bcm.json node[3]: fgColor #c8932a, bgColor #faf8f4, contrastRatio 2.58, 48px bold, expectedContrastRatio 3:1, html color:var(--warning,#c47e00). Recomputed: static --accent-700 #876019/#FAF8F4 = 5.33:1 (passes); --warning #C8932A/#FAF8F4 = 2.58:1 (fails 3:1); --warning-fg #876019 = 5.33:1 (passes 3:1).

Real-world impact

KPI and progress percentages, and the BCM readiness score, render at sub-AA contrast at least transiently, and the BCM large number persistently. Low-vision users may misread compliance/readiness figures. Lower-impact than A11Y-001..003 because counts are small and one cause is a transient animation frame.

Reproduction

1. Log in, open /bcm → axe color-contrast on the 48px readiness number, fgColor #c8932a / ratio 2.58 (artifact bcm.json). 2. Open /dashboard or /compliance → color-contrast on .progress-label spans, rendered fgColor #a07622 / ratio 3.87 (artifacts dashboard.json, compliance.json).

Resolution

(a) For data figures, never use --warning/--accent-500 as a TEXT colour on light surfaces; use --warning-fg / --accent-700 (the dedicated readable foreground tones). Change the BCM hero number from color: var(--warning) to color: var(--warning-fg) (#876019, 5.33:1, clears the 3:1 large-text bar with margin). (b) To stop axe sampling transition frames AND to remove the marginal accent-700 failures, exclude `color` from the global transition on text, or shorten it: the audit color should be the settled value. Consider tightening --accent-700 to #73520F (6.73:1) for extra headroom so even a transition frame stays safe. Re-run axe on /bcm and /dashboard.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
/* BCM readiness number (inline) */
<div style="font-size:48px; font-weight:700; color: var(--warning, #c47e00)">31.7</div>
/* #C8932A on #FAF8F4 = 2.58:1 — FAILS 3:1 large-text */
▲ After (fixed)
/* use the readable foreground tone */
<div style="font-size:48px; font-weight:700; color: var(--warning-fg)">31.7</div>
/* #876019 on #FAF8F4 = 5.33:1 — passes */
/* optional, tokens.css:58 → --accent-700: #73520F; (6.73:1) for KPI headroom */
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA) · WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (Level AA)
MediumA11Y-005Heatmap score numerals fail contrast on medium/high risk cells (3.0–3.4:1)
AccessibilityColor Contrast▾
Location tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/components.css:82,83 Effort S Risk Not CVSS-scored. Risk rationale: the 5×5 risk heatmap on /dashboard renders cell scores (10/15/16) in a tinted dark amber/terracotta that drops to 3.0–3.4:1 on the --risk-med / --risk-high fills. These are data-bearing numerals but redundant with cell position/colour, and the count is small (5 of dashboard's 10). Medium.
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/tokens.css:96 (--risk-med: #F0D58A), 97 (--risk-high: #E8A878)
DOM: td.heatmap-cell[style*=var(--risk-med|--risk-high)] > .heatmap-score on /dashboard

Description

The dashboard 5×5 risk heatmap renders the numeric score inside each cell (.heatmap-score). On the --risk-med fill (#F0D58A) the auto-derived dark text (#78714e) measures 3.41:1, and on --risk-high (#E8A878) the dark text (#745d46) measures 3.03:1 — both below the 4.5:1 AA floor for the 12px bold numerals. axe reported 5 such cells on /dashboard.

Root cause

The heatmap-score text colour is a muted brown tuned to sit softly on the tint, but it does not reach AA against the lighter med/high fills. The fills themselves are correct heatmap tones; the score text simply needs a darker, higher-contrast ink rather than a hue-matched muted brown.

Evidence / proof
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/axe/dashboard.json nodes for td[title="L2 × I5 = 10"] etc.: fgColor #78714e / bgColor #f0d58a / 3.41:1, and fgColor #745d46 / bgColor #e8a878 / 3.03:1, 12px bold, expectedContrastRatio 4.5:1. Recomputed with a high-contrast ink --ink-2 #2E3A36: on #F0D58A = 8.22:1, on #E8A878 = 5.81:1 (both pass AA).

Real-world impact

The numeric scores overlaid on medium/high heatmap cells are below AA contrast. The information is partially redundant (cell colour + position convey severity), so impact is moderate, but the explicit numerals are still hard to read for low-vision users.

Reproduction

1. Log in, open /dashboard. 2. Run axe → color-contrast on td.heatmap-cell > .heatmap-score for the med/high cells (fgColor #78714e/#745d46). Artifact: audit/artifacts/e2e/results/axe/dashboard.json.

Resolution

Set the .heatmap-score text colour to a fixed high-contrast dark ink (var(--ink-2) #2E3A36 or --ink-1) for the light tones (vlow/low/med/high) rather than a hue-matched brown. --ink-2 on #F0D58A = 8.22:1 and on #E8A878 = 5.81:1, both pass AA, and the same ink reads cleanly across all light heatmap fills. For the dark vhigh/crit fills keep white/light text. Re-run axe on /dashboard.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
/* .heatmap-score derives a muted-brown ink per tone */
.heatmap-score { color: <hue-matched brown e.g. #78714e / #745d46>; }
/* on --risk-med #F0D58A = 3.41:1, on --risk-high #E8A878 = 3.03:1 — FAIL AA */
▲ After (fixed)
/* fixed dark ink on light heatmap tones */
.heatmap-cell.tone-med  .heatmap-score,
.heatmap-cell.tone-high .heatmap-score { color: var(--ink-2); } /* #2E3A36 → 8.22:1 / 5.81:1 */
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA)
MediumA11Y-006Manual-only WCAG criteria not covered by automated axe scan — keyboard, focus, landmarks, motion (require manual verification)
AccessibilityManual Verification Required▾
Location audit/artifacts/e2e/results/axe-summary.json:1 Effort L Risk Not CVSS-scored. Risk rationale: automated tools detect only ~30–40% of WCAG issues. The captured axe run covers parseable rules (contrast, names, roles, landmarks-as-coded) but CANNOT assert keyboard operability, visible focus, logical focus order, meaningful sequence, or motion preferences — all AA/A criteria that must be verified by a human. Flagging as Medium because these are unverified, not confirmed failures; they represent audit coverage gaps that block a clean AA sign-off.
Whole authenticated app shell (tss-grc-ui-v2): sidebar nav, collapsible groups (button[aria-controls="sb-group-*"]), modals/dialogs, data tables (.score-pill rows on /risk), segmented controls (.scale-seg-btn on /settings)
tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/motion.css and tokens.css:367 (prefers-reduced-motion handling)

Description

axe-core verified that /login has 0 violations and that all 9 authenticated pages fail ONLY color-contrast (68 instances). However, axe cannot evaluate interaction- and structure-level success criteria. The following AA/A criteria are NOT covered by the captured artifacts and require manual testing before an AA conformance claim can be made: (a) 2.1.1 Keyboard — every control (sidebar toggles, modals, tables, segmented font-size control) operable without a mouse and no traps (2.1.2); (b) 2.4.7 Focus Visible — a clearly visible focus indicator on every focusable element; the design defines --focus-ring tokens (tokens.css:217) but their actual application must be verified per component; (c) 2.4.3 Focus Order — tab order matches the visual/RTL reading order (critical for an Arabic-primary RTL UI); (d) 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence and 1.3.1 Info & Relationships — DOM order and landmark/heading structure (the app injects a global shell into #app-shell; <aside class="sb"> exists but presence of <nav>/<main>/<header> landmarks and a logical heading hierarchy must be confirmed); (e) 2.3.1/2.3.3 motion — the global `html * { transition }` and any animations must honour prefers-reduced-motion.

Root cause

Automated scanning has inherent coverage limits; the dynamic test harness ran axe (rule-based) and Lighthouse (which gave /login a11y = 100, also automated-only). No keyboard-walk, screen-reader pass, or reduced-motion check was captured. This is a methodology coverage gap, not a code defect — but it means AA conformance is currently unproven for the interaction/structure criteria.

Evidence / proof
audit/artifacts/e2e/results/axe-summary.json shows every authenticated page has exactly 1 violation = color-contrast and login = 0; rules arrays contain ONLY 'color-contrast(n)'. No axe rule output exists for focus-order, keyboard, or motion (axe does not test these). Lighthouse a11y score for /login = 100 is likewise automated-only and does not assert keyboard/SR behaviour. The shell DOM (relatedNodes html '<aside class="sb">') confirms a sidebar exists but the artifacts do not capture landmark/role coverage for <main>/<nav>/<header>.

Real-world impact

Without manual verification, the platform cannot claim WCAG 2.1 AA conformance even after the contrast fixes land. Keyboard-only and screen-reader users (a regulated requirement for Saudi government/banking procurement) may be blocked by issues invisible to axe — e.g. an unreachable modal, a missing focus ring, an RTL tab-order mismatch, or non-throttled motion.

Reproduction

Manual protocol (to be executed against http://localhost:5173, admin/Admin@12345): 1) Keyboard walk every page using only Tab/Shift+Tab/Enter/Space/Esc/arrows — confirm all controls reachable, no traps, sidebar group buttons (aria-controls) expand/collapse via keyboard. 2) Observe a visible focus indicator on each focusable element (verify --focus-ring renders). 3) Confirm tab order follows RTL visual order. 4) Run a screen reader (NVDA + Windows / VoiceOver) and verify landmarks (nav/main/header), heading order, and that aria-controls/aria-pressed states are announced. 5) Enable OS 'reduce motion' and confirm transitions/animations are suppressed.

Resolution

Commission a manual WCAG 2.1 AA pass covering SC 2.1.1, 2.1.2, 2.4.3, 2.4.7, 1.3.1, 1.3.2, 2.3.1, 2.3.3 and screen-reader smoke tests with NVDA + VoiceOver. Ensure the app shell wraps content in semantic landmarks (<nav> for .sb, <main> for content, <header> for the top bar), that --focus-ring is applied to all interactive elements (not just inputs), and that a `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block neutralises the global transition (tokens.css:367 already guards the mode-switch transition behind prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference — verify ALL motion is similarly guarded). Track each criterion in the pass/fail matrix in A11Y-007.

▼ Before (vulnerable)
/* Coverage gap — not a single source line. Verify, e.g., that the
   global transition is fully gated for reduced-motion users. */
/* tokens.css:367 already does this for theme-switch: */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference) { html, html * { transition: ... } }
▲ After (fixed)
/* Confirm motion.css and component animations honour reduce-motion too: */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after { animation-duration: .01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important; transition-duration: .01ms !important; }
}
/* + ensure shell renders <nav>/<main>/<header> landmarks and --focus-ring on all controls. */
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 2.1.1 Keyboard (A) · WCAG 2.1 SC 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap (A) · WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.3 Focus Order (A) · WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.7 Focus Visible (AA) · WCAG 2.1 SC 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (A) · WCAG 2.1 SC 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence (A) · WCAG 2.1 SC 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below (A) · WCAG 2.1 SC 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions (AAA)

Manual SR confirmation still advised. | | 1.3.1 Info & Relationships | A | NOT TESTED (manual) | Landmark/heading structure not asserted by artifacts — A11Y-006. | | 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence | A | NOT TESTED (manual) | RTL DOM/reading-order — A11Y-006. | | 2.1.1 Keyboard / 2.1.2 No Trap | A | NOT TESTED (manual) | A11Y-006. | | 2.4.3 Focus Order | A | NOT TESTED (manual) | A11Y-006. | | 2.4.7 Focus Visible | AA | NOT TESTED (manual) | --focus-ring tokens defined (tokens.css:217); per-component application unverified — A11Y-006. | | 2.3.1 Three Flashes / 2.3.3 Animation | A/AAA | NOT TESTED (manual) | Global transition present; reduce-motion coverage to confirm — A11Y-006. | NET: The only AUTOMATED-detectable AA failure is 1.4.3, and it is fully traced to design tokens with exact before/after values (A11Y-001..005). All remaining AA/A criteria are unverified pending the manual pass (A11Y-006). /login already passes the automated scan (0 violations, Lighthouse a11y = 100).

Root cause

All 68 automated failures share ONE category (color-contrast / SC 1.4.3) and reduce to FIVE design tokens defined in tss-grc-ui-v2/src/styles/tokens.css. Fixing those tokens (per A11Y-001..005) clears the entire automated AA gap; the manual criteria (A11Y-006) are a separate coverage workstream.

Evidence / proof
axe-summary.json: login violations=0; risk-register color-contrast(28), dashboard(10), compliance(6), settings(6), cyber(4), privacy(4), bcm(4), tprm(3), knowledge-base(3) = 68 total, every byImpact = {serious:1}, every rules entry = color-contrast only. Per-page files confirm the distinct fg/bg pairs: #4a5c58/#0b1f22 (2.4), #8c9690/#f5f1e9 (2.7), #ffffff/#d87560 (3.16), #a07622/#faf8f4 (3.87), #c8932a/#faf8f4 (2.58), #78714e/#f0d58a (3.41), #745d46/#e8a878 (3.03). Lighthouse a11y /login = 100 (automated).

Real-world impact

Gives auditors and the dev team a single criterion-level scoreboard: one AA rule fails automatically (fixable via 5 token edits), several criteria remain unproven and need a manual pass before an AA conformance statement is defensible for Saudi public-sector / banking procurement.

Reproduction

Re-run the captured Playwright + axe-core harness against all 10 routes and Lighthouse against /login; compare against audit/artifacts/e2e/results/axe-summary.json. After applying A11Y-001..005, expect color-contrast(n) to drop to 0 on all pages; then execute the A11Y-006 manual protocol to close the remaining criteria.

Resolution

1) Land token fixes A11Y-001..005 (effort S–M each) and re-run axe to confirm 1.4.3 reaches 0 violations on all 9 pages. 2) Execute the A11Y-006 manual protocol (keyboard, focus, landmarks, SR, motion) and record each criterion as Pass/Fail in this matrix. 3) Only after both are green may an AA conformance claim (e.g. a VPAT/ACR) be issued. Keep /login as the regression baseline (0 violations).

▲ After (fixed)

  2.1.1, 2.4.3, 2.4.7, 1.3.1, 1.3.2, 2.3.x = verified PASS via manual protocol
